question_en:
A company runs a Python script on an employee’s laptop to transform and update data that is stored in an Amazon RDS database. The company wants to migrate the transformation workload to the AWS Cloud. The solution must run the Python script every 30 minutes. Each run of the script takes approximately 20 seconds to update the data in the RDS database.



Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Launch an Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance to run the Python script. Configure the EC2 instance to access the RDS database. Configure a cron job to invoke the Python script.
options.B: Launch an Amazon EC2 Spot Instance to run the Python script. Configure the EC2 instance to access the RDS database. Configure a cron job to invoke the Python script.
options.C: Configure an AWS Lambda function to access the RDS database. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to invoke the Lambda function.
options.D: Configure an AWS Lambda function to access the RDS database. Configure the Lambda function with provisioned concurrency. Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API to invoke the Lambda function.

explanation.full_text: AWS Lambda with Amazon EventBridge Scheduler is the most cost-effective solution because the workload is short, periodic, and does not require a continuously running server. The Python script runs every 30 minutes and takes only about 20 seconds, so paying for EC2 capacity that remains mostly idle would waste money. Lambda charges based on requests and execution duration, which fits this intermittent workload well. EventBridge Scheduler can invoke the Lambda function on a recurring schedule. Provisioned concurrency is unnecessary because this is not a latency-sensitive user-facing workload. API Gateway is also unnecessary because the script does not need an HTTP endpoint. Spot Instances reduce EC2 cost but still add instance management and interruption risk.
explanation.why_correct: Lambda with EventBridge Scheduler is serverless and charges only for actual execution time (20 seconds every 30 minutes = 48 executions/day). This eliminates idle time costs completely. EventBridge Scheduler natively supports cron expressions for recurring invocations without additional infrastructure.

why_wrong.A: EC2 On-Demand runs 24/7 but the script only executes 20 seconds every 30 minutes. You'd pay for 99% idle time, making this extremely cost-inefficient for such short, periodic tasks.
why_wrong.B: Spot Instances can be interrupted with 2-minute warning, which could break mid-execution. Managing interruptions adds operational complexity. Still pays for idle time between script runs.
why_wrong.D: Provisioned concurrency keeps Lambda warm continuously, which adds unnecessary hourly charges. API Gateway is redundant since EventBridge can invoke Lambda directly on schedule.

explanation.exam_tips: For periodic, short-duration tasks (<15 minutes), always prefer Lambda + EventBridge over EC2. Key phrase: 'runs every X minutes' + 'takes only Y seconds' = serverless pattern.
memorize: Lambda charges per 1ms of execution, not for idle time
EventBridge Scheduler supports cron/rate expressions natively
Provisioned concurrency is for latency-sensitive applications, not scheduled jobs
EC2 charges hourly regardless of actual CPU usage

question_en:
A company runs multiple workloads in separate AWS environments. The company wants to optimize its AWS costs but must maintain the same level of performance for the environments. The company ' s production environment requires resources to be highly available. The other environments do not require highly available resources. Each environment has the same set of networking components, including the following: • 1 VPC • 1 Application Load Balancer • 4 subnets distributed across 2 Availability Zones (2 public subnets and 2 private subnets)



• 2 NAT gateways (1 in each public subnet) • 1 internet gateway Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Do not change the production environment workload. For each non-production workload, remove one NAT gateway and update the route tables for private subnets to target the remaining NAT gateway for the destination 0.0.0.0/0.
options.B: Reduce the number of Availability Zones that all workloads in all environments use.
options.C: Replace every NAT gateway with a t4g.large NAT instance. Update the route tables for each private subnet to target the NAT instance that is in the same Availability Zone for the destination 0.0.0.0/0.
options.D: In each environment, create one transit gateway and remove one NAT gateway. Configure routing on the transit gateway to forward traffic for the destination 0.0.0.0/0 to the remaining NAT gateway. Update private subnet route tables to target the transit gateway for the destination 0.0.0.0/0.

explanation.full_text: Maintaining two NAT gateways for production ensures high availability. Reducing to one NAT gateway in non-production environments lowers cost while maintaining necessary connectivity. This approach is recommended by AWS for cost optimization in non-critical environments. Reference Extract: " For environments that do not require high availability, you can reduce costs by using a single NAT gateway and updating route tables accordingly. " Source: AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Official Study Guide, Cost Optimization and NAT Gateway section.
explanation.why_correct: NAT Gateways cost ~$0.045/hour each ($32/month). Production keeps 2 for HA across AZs. Non-production environments don't need HA, so removing 1 NAT Gateway saves $32/month per environment. Route table updates ensure private subnets still reach internet via remaining gateway.

why_wrong.B: Reducing Availability Zones breaks the production HA requirement. You need at least 2 AZs for fault tolerance. This would violate the constraint that production 'requires resources to be highly available'.
why_wrong.C: NAT instances (t4g.large) require management, patching, and monitoring. They also become single points of failure and don't auto-scale. More operational overhead than managed NAT Gateways without significant cost savings.
why_wrong.D: Transit Gateway costs $0.05/hour ($36/month) plus $0.02/GB data processed. Adding TGW to save one NAT Gateway ($32/month) increases cost and complexity. TGW is for multi-VPC architectures, not single-VPC optimization.

explanation.exam_tips: NAT Gateway HA pattern: deploy one per AZ for production. For dev/test, single NAT Gateway in one AZ is acceptable trade-off. Watch for 'non-production' or 'test' keywords—they signal HA is not required.
memorize: NAT Gateway charges: $0.045/hour + $0.045/GB processed
HA pattern = 1 NAT Gateway per AZ
Non-prod optimization = reduce to 1 NAT Gateway total
Transit Gateway is for interconnecting multiple VPCs, not cost optimization within one VPC

question_en: A company ' s expense tracking application gives users the ability to upload images of receipts. The application analyzes the receipts to extract information and stores the raw images in Amazon S3. The application is written in Java and runs on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The compute costs and storage costs have increased with the popularity of the application. Which solution will provide the MOST cost savings without affecting application performance?

options.A: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for the maximum number of necessary EC2 instances. Store the uploaded files in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).
options.B: Decrease the minimum number of EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group. Use On-Demand Instances for peak scaling. Store the uploaded files in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).
options.C: Decrease the maximum number of EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group. Set up S3 Lifecycle policies to archive the raw images to lower-cost storage tiers after 30 days.
options.D: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for the minimum number of necessary EC2 instances. Use OnDemand Instances for peak scaling. Set up S3 Lifecycle policies to archive the raw images to lowercost storage tiers after 30 days.

explanation.full_text: The question asks for the most cost savings while not affecting application performance, and it explicitly calls out both compute costs and storage costs increasing. The best answer is the option that optimizes both cost drivers without reducing capacity needed for peak performance. Option D accomplishes this by combining two well-established cost optimization mechanisms: a Compute Savings Plan for baseline compute usage and S3 Lifecycle policies for lower-cost storage of older receipt images.
explanation.why_correct: This optimizes BOTH cost drivers: compute (Savings Plan for baseline) and storage (Lifecycle policies). Savings Plans offer up to 72% discount on baseline capacity while On-Demand handles unpredictable spikes. S3 Lifecycle moves old receipts to cheaper tiers after 30 days when access frequency naturally drops.

why_wrong.A: EFS costs ~$0.30/GB vs S3 Standard $0.023/GB—13x more expensive for object storage. Savings Plan for maximum capacity wastes money on unused commitment during low-traffic periods.
why_wrong.B: Decreasing minimum instances risks slower scale-out during traffic spikes, harming performance. EFS is still wrong storage choice (expensive + unnecessary for objects).
why_wrong.C: Decreasing MAXIMUM instances directly violates 'without affecting performance'—caps peak capacity during high load, causing throttling or outages during popularity surges.

explanation.exam_tips: When question mentions BOTH compute AND storage costs: look for solution addressing both. 'Baseline + burst' pattern: commitment pricing for minimum, On-Demand for peaks. S3 Lifecycle is default for aging object data.
memorize: Compute Savings Plans offer up to 72% savings vs On-Demand
Apply Savings Plans to minimum steady-state capacity only
S3 Standard → S3 Standard-IA after 30 days saves ~45% on storage
Never reduce max Auto Scaling capacity if performance must be maintained
EFS costs 13x more than S3 for object storage patterns

question_en: A company needs to create an AWS Lambda function that will run in a VPC in the company ' s primary AWS account. The Lambda function needs to access files that the company stores in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. The EFS file system is located in a secondary AWS account. As the company adds files to the file system, the solution must scale to meet the demand. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create a new EFS file system in the primary account. Use AWS DataSync to copy the contents of the original EFS file system to the new EFS file system.
options.B: Create a VPC peering connection between the VPCs that are in the primary account and the secondary account.
options.C: Create a second Lambda function in the secondary account that has a mount that is configured for the file system. Use the primary account ' s Lambda function to invoke the secondary account ' s Lambda function.
options.D: Move the contents of the file system to a Lambda layer. Configure the Lambda layer ' s permissions to allow the company ' s secondary account to use the Lambda layer.

explanation.full_text: Amazon EFS is a regional, elastic file system that scales to petabytes and can be accessed from thousands of compute instances concurrently. You can mount EFS across VPCs and across AWS accounts by providing network connectivity (e.g., VPC peering) to the EFS mount targets and allowing NFS (TCP 2049) in the mount target security group, optionally using EFS access points and a file system policy for cross-account access control.
explanation.why_correct: VPC peering enables cross-account EFS access with NO hourly charge and minimal operational overhead. EFS automatically scales as files are added. Just update security groups to allow NFS (port 2049) and optionally use EFS file system policies for access control.

why_wrong.A: Duplicates ALL data using DataSync, incurring sync costs ($0.0125/GB), double storage costs, and sync lag. Violates single source of truth principle.
why_wrong.C: Adds extra Lambda invocation costs and latency (cross-account invoke + file read). Primary Lambda still can't directly access filesystem—defeats purpose of shared EFS.
why_wrong.D: Lambda layers have 50MB compressed/250MB uncompressed limits and are IMMUTABLE. Cannot handle dynamic, growing file sets. Layers are for code dependencies, not data storage.

explanation.exam_tips: Cross-account EFS access = VPC peering + security group rule (NFS port 2049) + optional file system policy. VPC peering is free for data transfer within same region. Lambda layers are NEVER for data—only for code/libraries.
memorize: VPC peering has NO hourly charge (only data transfer costs)
EFS mount requires NFS protocol on TCP port 2049
Lambda layers: 50MB compressed / 250MB uncompressed limit
Lambda layers are immutable—not for dynamic data
Cross-account EFS: peering + security groups + optional IAM policy

question_en: A company deploys a stateful application on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in multiple Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application workload is predictable, and the company has not received any CPU usage alerts. The company expects to run the application for at least 1 year. The company expects CPU usage to increase by 50% during an upcoming 2-week holiday period. The company wants to optimize costs for the application for both the holiday period and normal operations. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Continue to use On-Demand Instances to handle the existing workload. Purchase additional OnDemand Instances to handle the capacity requirement for the upcoming holiday period.
options.B: Purchase a 12-month EC2 Instance Savings Plan to handle the existing workload. Use On-Demand Instances to handle the additional capacity requirement for the upcoming holiday period.
options.C: Purchase a 12-month Compute Savings Plan to handle the existing workload. Use Spot Instances to handle the additional capacity requirement for the upcoming holiday period.
options.D: Purchase a 12-month Compute Savings Plan to handle both the existing workload and the additional capacity requirement for the upcoming holiday period.

explanation.full_text: The correct answer is B because the company has a predictable baseline workload that will run for at least 1 year, plus a temporary 2-week increase in demand during a holiday period. The most cost-effective approach is to use a long-term discount option for the steady-state workload and a flexible pricing model for the short-term burst capacity.
explanation.why_correct: EC2 Instance Savings Plan provides up to 72% savings on committed baseline capacity for 1 year. For the 2-week holiday spike (50% increase), On-Demand avoids overcommitting. This matches AWS best practice: commitment for steady-state, flexible pricing for temporary bursts.

why_wrong.A: Misses ALL savings on baseline workload by staying 100% On-Demand. Could save up to 72% on predictable capacity that runs all year.
why_wrong.C: Application is STATEFUL—Spot interruptions would lose session state and user data. Spot Instances require fault-tolerant, stateless workloads. Wrong pricing model for stateful apps.
why_wrong.D: Overcommits for 12 months including holiday spike capacity. After 2-week peak, pays for unused commitment for 50 weeks. Wastes money on capacity used only 4% of commitment period.

explanation.exam_tips: Savings Plan decision tree: predictable 1+ year workload = Savings Plan for baseline. Temporary spikes = On-Demand. STATEFUL application = never use Spot (interruptions lose state). Don't commit long-term to short-term capacity needs.
memorize: EC2 Instance Savings Plans: up to 72% discount for 1 or 3 year commitment
Stateful applications cannot tolerate Spot interruptions
Never buy long-term commitment for short-term capacity spikes
Holiday/seasonal traffic: On-Demand for temporary increase only
Compute Savings Plan = more flexible but slightly lower discount than EC2 Instance SP

question_en: A company wants to store a large amount of data as objects for analytics and long-term archiving. Resources from outside AWS need to access the data. The external resources need to access the data with unpredictable frequency. However, the external resource must have immediate access when necessary. The company needs a cost-optimized solution that provides high durability and data security. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Apply S3 Lifecycle policies to transition older data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.B: Store the data in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
options.C: Store the data in Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Use expedited retrieval to provide immediate access when necessary.
options.D: Store the data in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Infrequent Access (IA). Use lifecycle policies to archive older files.

explanation.full_text: Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for data with unknown or changing access patterns. It automatically moves data between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on usage. This tier offers immediate access to all objects, regardless of which tier they are stored in, while optimizing storage costs.
explanation.why_correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically optimizes costs for UNPREDICTABLE access patterns by moving objects between tiers based on usage. Provides IMMEDIATE access (millisecond retrieval) from all tiers. No retrieval fees, no operational overhead. Perfect for 'unpredictable frequency' + 'immediate access' requirement.

why_wrong.A: Glacier Deep Archive requires 12+ hours for standard retrieval. Does NOT provide immediate access. Would need to predict which objects need fast access—contradicts 'unpredictable' pattern.
why_wrong.C: Glacier Flexible Retrieval: expedited = 1-5 minutes + $0.03/GB retrieval cost. Not truly immediate. Retrieval fees add up with unpredictable access. Designed for archival, not active use.
why_wrong.D: EFS IA is for file system access, not object storage. More expensive than S3. External resources would need VPN/Direct Connect for access—complex and costly.

explanation.exam_tips: Key phrase: 'unpredictable frequency' + 'immediate access' = S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Glacier classes = NOT immediate (minutes to hours retrieval). Intelligent-Tiering has NO retrieval fees and NO operational overhead.
memorize: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatic cost optimization for unknown access patterns
Glacier Flexible Retrieval: 1-5 min (expedited), 3-5 hrs (standard), 5-12 hrs (bulk)
Glacier Deep Archive: 12-48 hours retrieval time
S3 Intelligent-Tiering has NO retrieval fees
Immediate access = S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, or S3 Standard-IA only

question_en: A company uses Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) to run workloads that belong to service teams. Each service team uses an owner tag to specify the ECS containers that the team owns. The company wants to generate an AWS Cost Explorer report that shows how much each service team spends on ECS containers on a monthly basis. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Create a custom report in Cost Explorer. Apply a filter for Amazon ECS.
options.B: Create a custom report in Cost Explorer. Apply a filter for the owner resource tag.
options.C: Set up AWS Compute Optimizer. Review the rightsizing recommendations.
options.D: Activate the owner tag as a cost allocation tag. Group the Cost Explorer report by linked account.
options.E: Activate the owner tag as a cost allocation tag. Group the Cost Explorer report by the owner cost allocation tag.

explanation.full_text: To allocate costs based on team ownership, AWS recommends tagging resources using cost allocation tags. Activating the 'owner' tag as a cost allocation tag allows AWS Cost Explorer to categorize and group spending. Additionally, filtering for Amazon ECS services enables the visibility into service-specific usage.
explanation.why_correct: A: Filters Cost Explorer to show ONLY ECS costs (excludes other services). E: Activates 'owner' tag as cost allocation tag + groups by it = shows per-team breakdown. Together: ECS costs split by owning team. Most operationally efficient—native Cost Explorer features, no custom code.

why_wrong.B: Filtering by owner tag WITHOUT activating it as cost allocation tag won't work—tags must be activated first in Billing console to appear in Cost Explorer.
why_wrong.C: Compute Optimizer provides rightsizing recommendations, NOT cost allocation reports. Wrong tool for team spending visibility.
why_wrong.D: Grouping by 'linked account' shows costs per AWS account, NOT per team. Multiple teams can share one account, so this doesn't answer 'how much each service team spends'.

explanation.exam_tips: Cost allocation workflow: (1) Tag resources (2) Activate tags in Billing console as cost allocation tags (3) Wait 24 hrs (4) Use Cost Explorer with filters + grouping. Multi-select questions: look for 2-step processes. 'Linked account' ≠ team ownership.
memorize: Tags must be activated as cost allocation tags before appearing in Cost Explorer
Cost allocation tags take up to 24 hours to appear in reports
Compute Optimizer = rightsizing, NOT cost allocation
Filter = narrow scope (e.g., only ECS), Group by = categorize costs
User-defined tags vs AWS-generated tags—both can be cost allocation tags

question_en: A company has a development account that contains Amazon EC2 instances. The company uses the EC2 instances for testing. A recent audit of the development account showed that some developers occasionally forget to stop instances after the tests are finished, which incurs extra costs. The company wants to optimize costs for the development account. The company wants to use AWS Budgets to implement a budget for the account. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Define an alert in AWS Budgets for when the budget threshold reaches 100% of forecasted costs. Configure AWS Budgets to send an Amazon SNS notification to an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to stop the EC2 instances when the function receives a notification.
options.B: Define an alert in AWS Budgets for when the budget threshold reaches 100% of forecasted costs. Implement an action in the alert to automatically stop the EC2 instances.
options.C: Define an alert in AWS Budgets for when the budget threshold reaches 100% of the budgeted amount. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule. Implement an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instances based on the scheduled rule.
options.D: Define an alert in AWS Budgets for when the budget threshold reaches 100% of the budgeted amount. Implement an action in the alert to automatically stop the EC2 instances.

explanation.full_text: Option B is the best answer because AWS Budgets can take automated actions, and forecast-based thresholds let the company intervene before actual spending fully lands. AWS documentation explains that AWS Budgets actions can target EC2 instances, and forecast-based budget alerts are specifically intended to warn when projected spend is expected to exceed the threshold during the period.
explanation.why_correct: AWS Budgets Actions can automatically stop/terminate EC2 instances—native feature, no custom code. FORECASTED costs (100% of forecast) triggers BEFORE actual overspend occurs—proactive cost control. Simpler and faster than SNS + Lambda chain.

why_wrong.A: Works but adds unnecessary operational complexity: SNS topic + Lambda function + IAM permissions. AWS Budgets Actions already have EC2 stop capability built-in—no need for custom Lambda.
why_wrong.C: EventBridge scheduled rule ignores budget state—runs on schedule regardless of spending. Would stop instances at fixed times, not when budget exceeded. Wrong trigger type.
why_wrong.D: Triggers at 100% of ACTUAL budgeted amount = reactive (spending already occurred). Forecasted costs (option B) = proactive (stops instances when trending toward overage).

explanation.exam_tips: AWS Budgets Actions can: stop EC2, stop RDS, apply SCPs, apply IAM policies. Forecasted vs Actual: forecasted = proactive (before overspend), actual = reactive (after overspend). Prefer native AWS features over SNS + Lambda patterns when available.
memorize: AWS Budgets Actions: stop EC2/RDS, apply SCPs, apply IAM policies
Forecasted cost alert = proactive (based on usage trends)
Actual cost alert = reactive (after spending occurred)
Budget Actions are free—only pay for underlying AWS service actions
Scheduled rules (EventBridge) don't respond to budget state

question_en: A company runs a fleet of Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances to support a document processing application that has variable usage patterns. The company wants to optimize compute costs for the application. The company needs a solution that can tolerate occasional disruptions to document processing jobs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Replace the EC2 instances with an Amazon EKS cluster that uses AWS Fargate Spot capacity.
options.B: Use the EC2 Spot Instance placement score feature to identify which instance type to use. Deploy the application on Spot Instances.
options.C: Create a single EC2 Auto Scaling group. Set a mixed configuration of EC2 On-Demand Instances and EC2 Spot Instances.
options.D: Continue to use EC2 On-Demand Instances. Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances.

explanation.full_text: A mixed Auto Scaling group with both On-Demand and Spot Instances is the best answer because AWS documents that mixed instances groups let you launch and automatically scale a fleet of On-Demand and Spot Instances in a single Auto Scaling group to optimize cost while maintaining scale and performance.
explanation.why_correct: Mixed Auto Scaling group balances cost (Spot = up to 90% discount) with reliability (On-Demand base capacity). Can tolerate 'occasional disruptions' per requirements. Single ASG simplifies management. AWS handles Spot interruptions gracefully with automatic replacement.

why_wrong.A: Moving entire architecture to EKS + Fargate Spot is major re-architecture. High migration effort. Fargate Spot still has interruptions—doesn't reduce disruption risk vs mixed EC2. More expensive than EC2 Spot (Fargate overhead).
why_wrong.B: 100% Spot means ALL instances can be interrupted simultaneously during capacity constraints. No guaranteed baseline capacity. 'Spot Instance placement score' helps select instances, but doesn't prevent interruptions.
why_wrong.D: Reserved Instances require 1-3 year commitment. Question says 'variable usage patterns'—RI is for predictable workloads. Won't optimize costs for variable usage as effectively as Spot.

explanation.exam_tips: Variable usage + can tolerate disruptions = mixed On-Demand/Spot ASG. Spot savings: up to 90% but with 2-min interruption notice. Don't go 100% Spot unless workload is fully fault-tolerant. Reserved Instances = predictable usage, not variable.
memorize: Spot Instances: up to 90% discount vs On-Demand
Spot interruption: 2-minute warning via EC2 instance metadata
Mixed ASG: define On-Demand base + Spot percentage above base
Reserved Instances: 1 or 3 year commitment for predictable workloads
Spot placement score: 1-10 rating for interruption likelihood

question_en: An ecommerce company runs a PostgreSQL database on an Amazon EC2 instance. The database stores data in Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. The daily peak input/output transactions per second (IOPS) do not exceed 15,000 IOPS. The company wants to migrate the database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and to provision disk IOPS performance that is independent of disk storage capacity. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volumes. Provision a 5 TiB volume.
options.B: Configure Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1) EBS volumes. Provision 15,000 IOPS.
options.C: Configure General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS volumes. Provision 15,000 IOPS.
options.D: Configure magnetic EBS volumes to achieve maximum IOPS.

explanation.full_text: EBS gp3 volumes allow you to independently configure IOPS and throughput, up to 16,000 IOPS, regardless of the volume size, and at a lower cost compared to io1/io2 provisioned IOPS volumes. This meets the requirement for cost-effective, predictable IOPS performance for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.
explanation.why_correct: gp3 decouples IOPS from storage capacity—provision exactly 15,000 IOPS regardless of volume size. Cheaper than io1 (~20% cost reduction). Baseline 3,000 IOPS free, then $0.005/provisioned IOPS/month. Meets 'independent of capacity' requirement directly.

why_wrong.A: gp2 IOPS tied to volume size: 3 IOPS/GB. For 15,000 IOPS need 5,000GB (5TiB). Wastes storage capacity if actual data is smaller. More expensive than gp3 for same IOPS.
why_wrong.B: io1 supports 15,000 IOPS but costs ~50% more than gp3 for same performance. io1/io2 designed for >16,000 IOPS or sub-millisecond latency needs—overkill here.
why_wrong.D: Magnetic volumes (HDD) max out at ~500 IOPS. Cannot achieve 15,000 IOPS. Legacy storage type—AWS doesn't recommend for new workloads.

explanation.exam_tips: gp3 vs gp2: gp3 = IOPS independent of size, cheaper. gp2 = 3 IOPS/GB coupling. io1/io2 = for >16K IOPS or single-digit ms latency needs. Key phrase: 'IOPS independent of capacity' = gp3. Magnetic volumes max 500 IOPS.
memorize: gp3: 3,000 IOPS baseline (free), up to 16,000 IOPS configurable
gp3: $0.08/GB/month + $0.005/IOPS/month above 3,000 IOPS
gp2: 3 IOPS per GB (min 100 IOPS, max 16,000 IOPS)
io1/io2: up to 64,000 IOPS (256,000 for io2 Block Express)
Magnetic volumes: legacy, max 500 IOPS

question_en: A company needs a durable storage solution for telemetry data. The company wants to encrypt the data by using keys that the company manages. The storage solution must rotate the encryption keys every 90 days. The company will access the telemetry data infrequently during the first 30 days. The storage solution must expire the data after 360 days. Which solutions will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Store the telemetry data in an Amazon S3 bucket by using the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Configure an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days and expire the objects after 360 days.
options.B: Create an AWS KMS customer managed key with customer-provided key material. Update the AWS KMS key policy to grant the selected storage service permission to use the key.
options.C: Store the telemetry data in an Amazon S3 bucket by using the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Configure an S3 Lifecycle rule to expire objects that are older than 360 days.
options.D: Use Amazon EFS General Purpose performance mode to store the telemetry data. Use Amazon EventBridge to schedule an AWS Lambda function to scan the file system and delete files that are older than 360 days.
options.E: Store a company-defined encryption key in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the secret to rotate every 90 days. Grant AWS Secrets Manager permission to access the storage service.

explanation.full_text: S3 Standard-IA is appropriate for durable data that is accessed infrequently but still requires immediate retrieval during its initial 30-day period. After 30 days, an S3 Lifecycle rule can transition the objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, which lowers long-term storage costs. A second lifecycle action can permanently expire the objects after 360 days.
explanation.why_correct: A: S3 Standard-IA (infrequent access first 30 days) → Glacier Flexible (long-term archive) → Expire at 360 days = optimized storage progression. B: KMS customer managed key with imported key material = company controls keys. Manual 90-day rotation via re-import meets rotation requirement.

why_wrong.C: S3 Intelligent-Tiering costs more than S3 Standard-IA for data with KNOWN infrequent access pattern (first 30 days). Intelligent-Tiering is for UNKNOWN patterns. Wastes monitoring fees ($0.0025/1000 objects).
why_wrong.D: EFS + Lambda deletion: operational complexity (schedule Lambda, handle failures), costs more than S3 Lifecycle (automatic, free). EFS storage more expensive than S3 ($0.30/GB vs $0.023/GB).
why_wrong.E: Secrets Manager is for credentials/secrets (database passwords, API keys), NOT for S3 encryption keys. S3 uses KMS keys, not secrets. Wrong service for encryption key management.

explanation.exam_tips: Multi-select pattern: look for complementary pieces (storage strategy + encryption strategy). KMS imported key material = manual rotation (re-import new material). AWS managed keys auto-rotate yearly. S3 Standard-IA minimum 30-day charge—matches access pattern perfectly.
memorize: S3 Standard-IA: $0.0125/GB, 30-day minimum charge, millisecond access
S3 Glacier Flexible: $0.0036/GB, 90-day minimum, 1-5 min retrieval
KMS customer managed key with imported material = manual rotation
AWS Secrets Manager: for credentials, NOT encryption keys
S3 Lifecycle transitions: free operation, automated

question_en: A company runs an application on Microsoft SQL Server databases in an on-premises data center. The company wants to migrate to AWS and optimize costs for its infrastructure on AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Migrate the databases to Amazon EC2 instances that use SQL Server Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) provided by AWS.
options.B: Migrate to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL by using Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL.
options.C: Migrate the databases to a PostgreSQL database that runs on Amazon EC2 instances.
options.D: Migrate the databases to Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server.

explanation.full_text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with Babelfish allows SQL Server applications to run directly on Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal code changes. Babelfish adds a SQL Server-compatible endpoint, significantly lowering costs compared to running licensed SQL Server instances on RDS or EC2.
explanation.why_correct: Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL understands T-SQL and SQL Server wire protocol—minimal application changes needed. Eliminates SQL Server licensing costs (can be 3-10x DB compute cost). Aurora = fully managed, automatic scaling, 3-5x faster than PostgreSQL. Maximum cost optimization.

why_wrong.A: EC2 with SQL Server AMIs: still pay Microsoft licensing (included in AMI price or BYOL). Requires instance management (patching, backups, HA setup). More expensive and operational overhead than managed services.
why_wrong.C: PostgreSQL on EC2: requires application rewrites (T-SQL → PostgreSQL SQL), manual schema conversion, code changes. High migration risk and effort. Self-managed = operational burden.
why_wrong.D: RDS for SQL Server: eliminates management but still includes Microsoft licensing costs in pricing. 3-10x more expensive than Aurora PostgreSQL for equivalent capacity.

explanation.exam_tips: SQL Server cost optimization = Babelfish (eliminates licensing). Babelfish supports T-SQL, stored procedures, and SQL Server drivers—minimal app changes. Key phrase: 'migrate' + 'optimize costs' from SQL Server = Babelfish. RDS for SQL Server = easier but not cost-optimized.
memorize: Babelfish: SQL Server compatibility layer on Aurora PostgreSQL
SQL Server licensing can cost 3-10x the compute infrastructure
Babelfish supports T-SQL, triggers, stored procedures, replication protocol
Aurora PostgreSQL: 3-5x performance vs standard PostgreSQL
RDS for SQL Server includes licensing in pricing

question_en: An online food delivery company wants to optimize its storage costs. The company has been collecting operational data for the last 10 years in a data lake that was built on Amazon S3 by using a Standard storage class. The company does not keep data that is older than 7 years. A solutions architect frequently uses data from the past 6 months for reporting and runs queries on data from the last 2 years about once a month. Data that is more than 2 years old is rarely accessed and is only used for audit purposes. Which combination of solutions will optimize the company ' s storage costs? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration rule to transition data that is older than 6 months to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Create another S3 Lifecycle configuration rule to transition data that is older than 2 years to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.
options.B: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration rule to transition data that is older than 6 months to the S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) storage class. Create another S3 Lifecycle configuration rule to transition data that is older than 2 years to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class.
options.C: Use the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class to store data instead of the S3 Standard storage class.
options.D: Create an S3 Lifecycle expiration rule to delete data that is older than 7 years.
options.E: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration rule to transition data that is older than 7 years to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.

explanation.full_text: To optimize costs for long-term data storage, AWS recommends using S3 Lifecycle policies to automate transitions across storage classes and ultimately expire old data. S3 Standard-IA is suited for data that is accessed less frequently but requires millisecond retrieval times. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost option, designed for data accessed once or twice a year.
explanation.why_correct: A: S3 Standard-IA for 6mo-2yr data (monthly queries) → Glacier Deep Archive for 2yr+ audit data = optimal cost progression. D: Expires data at 7 years per retention policy, preventing unnecessary storage costs. Together: full lifecycle from active → archival → deletion.

why_wrong.B: S3 One Zone-IA lacks multi-AZ redundancy—risky for 12-year compliance data. Glacier Flexible costs more than Deep Archive for rarely-accessed audit data ($0.0036/GB vs $0.00099/GB).
why_wrong.C: Intelligent-Tiering adds $0.0025/1000 objects monitoring fee for KNOWN infrequent access pattern. Wastes money when access pattern is already defined (frequent first 6mo, monthly 6mo-2yr, rare 2yr+).
why_wrong.E: Transitioning to Glacier at 7 years defeats purpose—data expires at 7 years. Would store in most expensive archival tier right before deletion. Should archive earlier to maximize savings.

explanation.exam_tips: Multi-select lifecycle questions: need BOTH storage strategy (transitions) AND data management (expiration). S3 Standard-IA minimum = 30 days. Glacier Deep Archive = cheapest but 12-48hr retrieval. Match storage class to access frequency: frequent=Standard, monthly=Standard-IA, annual=Glacier.
memorize: S3 Standard-IA: $0.0125/GB, 30-day minimum, millisecond access
S3 Glacier Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB, 180-day minimum, 12-48hr retrieval
S3 Glacier Flexible: $0.0036/GB, 90-day minimum, 1-5min expedited
Lifecycle expiration = delete, transition = move to cheaper tier
Intelligent-Tiering: for UNKNOWN patterns, charges monitoring fee

question_en: An analytics application runs on multiple Amazon EC2 Linux instances that use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard storage. The files vary in size and access frequency. The company accesses the files infrequently after 30 days. However, users sometimes request older files to generate reports. The company wants to reduce storage costs for files that are accessed infrequently. The company also wants throughput to adjust based on the size of the file system. The company wants to use the TransitionToIA Amazon EFS lifecycle policy to transition files to Infrequent Access (IA) storage after 30 days. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: storage after 30 days. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options.B: Specify the provisioned throughput mode only.
options.C: Configure files to transition back to Standard storage when a user accesses the files again. Specify the bursting throughput mode.
options.D: Specify the bursting throughput mode only.

explanation.full_text: Amazon EFS allows automatic transitions to Infrequent Access (IA) and back to Standard when accessed again using the lifecycle policy. By specifying the bursting throughput mode, throughput scales automatically with file system size.
explanation.why_correct: TransitionToIA after 30 days saves costs (IA = $0.025/GB vs Standard $0.30/GB). Transition BACK to Standard on access ensures performance for active files. Bursting throughput scales with file system size automatically—no manual provisioning. Perfect for variable file sizes.

why_wrong.A: Option text corrupted/incomplete in source data.
why_wrong.B: Provisioned throughput requires manually setting throughput level independent of storage—adds cost and operational overhead. Question wants throughput to 'adjust based on file system size' = bursting mode.
why_wrong.D: Missing the transition BACK to Standard on access. Files would stay in IA even when accessed for reports, causing higher latency (milliseconds vs microseconds) for active usage.

explanation.exam_tips: EFS lifecycle: files automatically move TO IA after N days of no access, and automatically BACK to Standard when accessed again. Bursting throughput = scales with storage size (baseline 50MB/s per TB). Provisioned = fixed throughput regardless of size. 'Variable' workloads = bursting.
memorize: EFS Standard: $0.30/GB/month, microsecond latencies
EFS IA: $0.025/GB/month (92% savings), millisecond latencies
Bursting throughput: 50MB/s baseline per TB stored, bursts to 100MB/s
Provisioned throughput: pay separately for fixed throughput level
Lifecycle policy: 7, 14, 30, 60, 90 days options for transition to IA

question_en: A company runs an online order management system on AWS. The company stores order and inventory data for the previous 5 years in an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. The company deletes inventory data after 5 years. The company wants to optimize costs to archive data. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Create an AWS Glue crawler to export data to Amazon S3. Create an AWS Lambda function to compress the data.
options.B: Use the SELECT INTO OUTFILE S3 query on the Aurora database to export the data to Amazon S3. Configure S3 Lifecycle rules on the S3 bucket.
options.C: Create an AWS Glue DataBrew job to migrate data from Aurora to Amazon S3. Configure S3 Lifecycle rules on the S3 bucket.
options.D: Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to replicate data from Aurora to Amazon S3. Use the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class.

explanation.full_text: Amazon Aurora MySQL supports the SELECT INTO OUTFILE S3 SQL syntax to export query results directly to Amazon S3. This is an efficient and low-overhead method for archiving data. Once data is in S3, Lifecycle rules can be configured to automatically transition older data to lower-cost storage classes or delete it after a defined period.
explanation.why_correct: SELECT INTO OUTFILE S3 is native Aurora MySQL feature—no additional services needed. Exports directly from database to S3 in parallel. S3 Lifecycle automates cost optimization (Standard → Standard-IA → Glacier → expiration). Minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: AWS Glue crawler discovers schemas for analytics—overkill for simple export. Lambda for compression adds complexity. Glue crawler + Lambda = extra services and costs vs built-in Aurora export.
why_wrong.C: DataBrew is for data preparation/transformation (cleaning, normalization). Not needed for simple archival export. Adds unnecessary service and complexity.
why_wrong.D: AWS SCT (Schema Conversion Tool) is for heterogeneous migrations (e.g., Oracle → PostgreSQL schema conversion). Not for routine data archival. DMS would continuously replicate—wasting resources for 5-year-old data.

explanation.exam_tips: Aurora to S3 export: use SELECT INTO OUTFILE S3 (native, simple). Glue/DataBrew = for complex ETL. DMS/SCT = for migrations, not archival. Always prefer native service features over multi-service orchestration when available.
memorize: SELECT INTO OUTFILE S3: Aurora MySQL/PostgreSQL native export feature
AWS Glue crawler: discovers schema for data catalog
AWS DataBrew: visual data preparation tool
AWS SCT: converts database schemas between engines
DMS: continuous database replication, not for one-time archival

question_en: A solutions architect is creating a data processing job that runs once daily and can take up to 2 hours to complete. If the job is interrupted, it has to restart from the beginning. How should the solutions architect address this issue in the MOST cost-effective manner?

options.A: Create a script that runs locally on an Amazon EC2 Reserved Instance that is triggered by a cron job.
options.B: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
options.C: Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Fargate task triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.
options.D: Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task running on Amazon EC2 triggered by an Amazon EventBridge scheduled event.

explanation.full_text: AWS Fargate with Amazon ECS is a serverless, fully managed compute engine for containers. Fargate eliminates the need to provision or manage servers, and is ideal for periodic, long-running batch jobs. You only pay for the resources consumed during job execution, making it cost-effective for jobs that run infrequently.
explanation.why_correct: Fargate supports up to 2 hours easily (no 15-min limit like Lambda). Serverless—no EC2 management. Pay-per-use pricing (per-second, 1-min minimum). EventBridge schedules daily execution. If interrupted, container restarts from beginning (requirement stated).

why_wrong.A: Reserved Instances require 1-3 year commitment for workload running once daily for 2 hours. Wastes 22 hours/day of paid capacity. RI optimizes for 24/7 workloads, not scheduled batch jobs.
why_wrong.B: Lambda maximum execution time = 15 minutes. Job takes up to 2 hours. Lambda would timeout and fail. Wrong compute service for long-running tasks.
why_wrong.D: ECS on EC2 requires provisioning, patching, and managing EC2 instances. Higher operational overhead than Fargate. Still pay for EC2 instance hours even when job not running (22hrs/day waste).

explanation.exam_tips: Job duration decision tree: <15min=Lambda, 15min-hours=Fargate, always-on=EC2. Scheduled batch jobs=serverless (Lambda/Fargate) to avoid idle costs. 'Restart from beginning if interrupted'=acceptable for both Fargate and EC2, but Fargate is cheaper for infrequent jobs.
memorize: Lambda max execution: 15 minutes
Fargate: serverless containers, pay per vCPU-second and GB-second
Fargate minimum billing: 1 minute per task
Reserved Instances: 1 or 3 year commitment, for predictable 24/7 workloads
EventBridge Scheduler: free for first 14M invocations/month

question_en: A company wants a flexible compute solution that includes Amazon EC2 instances and AWS Fargate. The company does not want to commit to multi-year contracts. Which purchasing option will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Purchase a 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the All Upfront option.
options.B: Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan with the No Upfront option.
options.C: Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan with the Partial Upfront option.
options.D: Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan with the All Upfront option.

explanation.full_text: To optimize costs for both Amazon EC2 and AWS Fargate, the best option is a Compute Savings Plan because it offers flexibility across instance families, Regions, and compute options including EC2, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda. Since the company does not want to commit to multi-year contracts or large upfront payments, the 1-year No Upfront Compute Savings Plan provides the greatest flexibility.
explanation.why_correct: Compute Savings Plan covers BOTH EC2 and Fargate (requirement: 'flexible compute solution'). 1-year = no multi-year commitment (requirement). No Upfront = no large upfront payment, maximum flexibility. Still saves up to 66% vs On-Demand.

why_wrong.A: EC2 Instance Savings Plan applies ONLY to EC2, not Fargate. Violates 'flexible compute solution including...Fargate' requirement. All Upfront locks capital when company prefers flexibility.
why_wrong.C: Partial Upfront requires some upfront payment—reduces flexibility vs No Upfront. Savings difference between Partial and No Upfront is minimal (~1-2%) but Partial reduces cash flow flexibility.
why_wrong.D: All Upfront requires 100% payment upfront—least flexible. Maximum savings (~5% more than No Upfront) doesn't outweigh flexibility loss when company explicitly wants flexibility.

explanation.exam_tips: Savings Plan types: EC2 Instance (EC2 only, most savings), Compute (EC2+Fargate+Lambda, flexible). Upfront options: All (max savings), Partial (middle), No (max flexibility). 'Flexible' + 'no commitment' + Fargate = Compute Savings Plan + No Upfront.
memorize: EC2 Instance Savings Plan: up to 72% savings, applies only to EC2
Compute Savings Plan: up to 66% savings, applies to EC2+Fargate+Lambda
No Upfront: ~66% savings, pay monthly, maximum flexibility
Partial Upfront: ~67% savings, 50% upfront + monthly
All Upfront: ~68-72% savings, 100% upfront, least flexibility

question_en: A company runs an ecommerce application on premises on Microsoft SQL Server. The company is planning to migrate the application to the AWS Cloud. The application code contains complex T-SQL queries and stored procedures. The company wants to minimize database server maintenance and operating costs after the migration is completed. The company also wants to minimize the need to rewrite code as part of the migration effort. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. Turn on Babelfish.
options.B: Migrate the database to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum for query processing.
options.C: Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for SQL Server. Turn on Kerberos authentication.
options.D: Migrate the database to an Amazon EMR cluster that includes multiple primary nodes.

explanation.full_text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible with Babelfish is designed for SQL Server migrations: it helps applications written for SQL Server to run with reduced code changes by providing compatibility for commonly used SQL Server semantics, including T-SQL constructs, procedural logic, and SQL Server-style connectivity patterns.
explanation.why_correct: Babelfish understands T-SQL syntax, stored procedures, and SQL Server wire protocol—MINIMAL code changes (meets 'minimize rewrite' requirement). Aurora = fully managed, reduces maintenance/operating costs vs self-managed. Eliminates SQL Server licensing costs (3-10x savings).

why_wrong.B: S3 + Redshift Spectrum = data warehouse/analytics, NOT operational ecommerce database. Cannot run stored procedures. Wrong workload type (OLAP vs OLTP).
why_wrong.C: RDS for SQL Server = same Microsoft licensing costs (built into pricing). Doesn't 'minimize operating costs' as effectively as moving off SQL Server. Managed service helps but licensing dominates cost.
why_wrong.D: EMR = big data processing (Hadoop, Spark), NOT relational database. Cannot run SQL Server stored procedures. Wrong tool for ecommerce transactional workload.

explanation.exam_tips: SQL Server cost optimization = Babelfish (eliminates licensing). RDS for SQL Server = easier management but same licensing costs. Babelfish supports most T-SQL, triggers, stored procs. Key phrase: 'T-SQL queries and stored procedures' + 'minimize costs' = Babelfish.
memorize: Babelfish: SQL Server compatibility layer on Aurora PostgreSQL
SQL Server licensing: can be 3-10x the compute infrastructure cost
Babelfish supports: T-SQL, stored procedures, triggers, TDS protocol
RDS for SQL Server: includes licensing in per-hour pricing
Aurora PostgreSQL: 3-5x throughput vs standard PostgreSQL

question_en: A company runs a Java-based job on an Amazon EC2 instance. The job runs every hour and takes 10 seconds to run. The job runs on a scheduled interval and consumes 1 GB of memory. The CPU utilization of the instance is low except for short surges during which the job uses the maximum CPU available. The company wants to optimize the costs to run the job.

options.A: Use AWS App2Container (A2C) to containerize the job. Run the job as an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task on AWS Fargate with 0.5 virtual CPU (vCPU) and 1 GB of memory.
options.B: Copy the code into an AWS Lambda function that has 1 GB of memory. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to run the code each hour.
options.C: Use AWS App2Container (A2C) to containerize the job. Install the container in the existing Amazon Machine Image (AMI). Ensure that the schedule stops the container when the task finishes.
options.D: Configure the existing schedule to stop the EC2 instance at the completion of the job and restart the EC2 instance when the next job starts.

explanation.full_text: AWS Lambda is event driven and scales automatically with the number of requests, charging per request and compute duration in milliseconds. For a 10-second, once-per-hour job, Lambda eliminates instance idle time, providing the lowest cost and no servers to manage.
explanation.why_correct: Lambda charges: 48 executions/day × 10 sec × $0.0000166667/GB-sec = ~$0.02/day. EventBridge Scheduler = free. No idle time costs. 1GB memory provides proportional CPU for 10-sec burst. Fully managed, no infrastructure.

why_wrong.A: Fargate: 1-minute minimum billing. For 10-sec job = billed 1 min/hour = ~$0.04/day (2x Lambda cost). Still better than EC2 but more expensive than Lambda for <1min jobs.
why_wrong.C: Keeping container in AMI + managing stop/start adds operational complexity. Still need EC2 instance running part-time or orchestration. Not cost-optimized vs serverless.
why_wrong.D: Stop/start EC2 adds ~2-3 minutes boot time per start. For hourly 10-sec job, spend more time booting than working. Complex orchestration. Still pay for stopped EBS volumes. Lambda is simpler and cheaper.

explanation.exam_tips: Job duration + frequency decision tree: <15min + periodic = Lambda first. Fargate: 1-min minimum billing. EC2: charges full hour (or second with minimum 60-sec). For 10-sec hourly job, Lambda is ~50x cheaper than EC2. Key: 'runs once daily/hourly' + 'seconds of runtime' = Lambda.
memorize: Lambda pricing: $0.20 per 1M requests + $0.0000166667 per GB-second
Lambda max execution: 15 minutes
Fargate minimum billing: 1 minute
EC2: charges per second, 60-second minimum (On-Demand)
EventBridge Scheduler: free for first 14M invocations/month

question_en: A company is developing software that uses a PostgreSQL database schema. The company needs to configure development environments and test environments for its developers. Each developer at the company uses their own development environment, which includes a PostgreSQL database. On average, each development environment is used for an 8-hour workday. The test environments will be used for load testing that can take up to 2 hours each day. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure development environments and test environments with their own Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 PostgreSQL database.
options.B: For each development environment, configure an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Single-AZ DB instance. For the test environment, configure a single Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance.
options.C: Configure development environments and test environments with their own Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster.
options.D: Configure an Amazon Aurora global database. Allow developers to connect to the database with their own credentials.

explanation.full_text: Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 provides cost-effective, on-demand, and auto-scaling database capacity. You pay only for actual usage, making it ideal for development and test environments that are not used continuously. It supports PostgreSQL and is suitable for variable and short-duration workloads.
explanation.why_correct: Aurora Serverless v2 scales from 0.5 ACU to 128 ACU automatically. Charges per ACU-second (like Lambda for databases). Dev environments used 8hrs/day = pay for 8hrs only. Test environments used 2hrs/day = pay for 2hrs only. Huge savings vs always-on instances.

why_wrong.B: RDS Single/Multi-AZ instances run 24/7 and charge full time even when idle. Dev envs idle 16hrs/day, test envs idle 22hrs/day. Paying for ~70-90% unused capacity. Multi-AZ adds cost for test env that doesn't need HA.
why_wrong.C: Aurora provisioned clusters charge for minimum 1 instance 24/7. Multiple developers = multiple clusters = multiple always-on charges. Much more expensive than serverless for intermittent usage.
why_wrong.D: Aurora Global Database = multi-region replication for disaster recovery. Massive overkill for dev/test. Charges for instances in multiple regions + replication. 10-20x more expensive than needed.

explanation.exam_tips: Dev/test + intermittent usage + 'cost-effective' = Aurora Serverless v2. Scales to zero when inactive (v2 scales to 0.5 ACU minimum, v1 scales to zero). Provisioned RDS/Aurora = for 24/7 production workloads. Key phrase: 'used for X hours per day' = serverless.
memorize: Aurora Serverless v2: $0.12 per ACU-hour (1 ACU ≈ 2GB RAM)
Aurora Serverless v2: scales 0.5-128 ACU, sub-second scaling
RDS instances: charge 24/7 regardless of usage
Aurora provisioned: minimum 1 instance (0.5 vCPU, 1GB RAM) running always
Use serverless for: dev/test, intermittent, variable, unpredictable workloads

question_en: A company is planning to deploy a managed MySQL database solution for its non-production applications. The company plans to run the system for several years on AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance. Purchase a Reserved Instance.
options.B: Create an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance. Use the instance on an on-demand basis.
options.C: Create an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster with writer and reader nodes. Use the cluster on an ondemand basis.
options.D: Create an Amazon EC2 instance. Manually install and configure MySQL Server on the instance.

explanation.full_text: Amazon RDS for MySQL Reserved Instances provide significant savings over on-demand pricing when you plan to run the database for long periods. This is the most cost-effective option for non-production, long-running managed MySQL workloads.
explanation.why_correct: RDS Reserved Instances: up to 69% savings vs On-Demand for 1-year commitment. 'Several years on AWS' = long-term predictable usage = perfect for RI. Fully managed (automated backups, patching, monitoring). Non-production = Single-AZ RI is sufficient (cheaper than Multi-AZ).

why_wrong.B: On-Demand charges full price with no commitment. For 'several years' usage, missing 60-70% savings opportunity. On-Demand is for variable/unpredictable workloads, not multi-year commitments.
why_wrong.C: Aurora with multiple nodes costs more than RDS MySQL for same workload. Question says 'MySQL database'—Aurora is overengineered if simple MySQL meets needs. On-demand adds more cost vs RI.
why_wrong.D: Self-managed MySQL on EC2: requires patching, backups, HA setup, monitoring. High operational overhead. Managed RDS includes all this. License cost same (MySQL is open source). RDS is simpler and similarly priced.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Several years' + 'managed' + specific engine (MySQL) = RDS Reserved Instance. Aurora = when need 5x throughput or multi-region. Self-managed EC2 = only when need OS-level control or unsupported MySQL version. Non-production = Single-AZ RI is fine.
memorize: RDS Reserved Instances: up to 69% savings, 1 or 3 year terms
RDS pricing: Single-AZ cheaper than Multi-AZ (~50% less)
Aurora: 3-5x throughput vs MySQL, automatic scaling, multi-region replication
RDS managed: automated backups, patching, monitoring included
MySQL is open source—no licensing costs on EC2 or RDS

question_en: A data science team needs storage for nightly log processing. The size and number of logs is unknown, and the logs persist for only 24 hours. What is the MOST cost-effective solution?

options.A: Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
options.B: Amazon S3 Standard
options.C: Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering
options.D: Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)

explanation.full_text: Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for unknown or unpredictable access patterns, automatically moving objects to the most cost-effective tier without performance impact. It is ideal when you do not know object size or access frequency. Data persists only 24 hours.
explanation.why_correct: Unknown size + unknown logs count + 24-hour lifecycle = unpredictable pattern. Intelligent-Tiering optimizes automatically without manual configuration. No retrieval fees. Frequent tier = immediate access for processing. After 24hrs, logs deleted—no long-term storage charges.

why_wrong.A: Glacier Deep Archive: 12-48 hour retrieval time. Cannot process logs 'nightly' with 12+ hour delay. Wrong storage class for active processing workloads.
why_wrong.B: S3 Standard works but costs more than Intelligent-Tiering if logs accessed infrequently. Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves to infrequent tier if not accessed within 30 days (though logs deleted at 24hrs here, principle applies).
why_wrong.D: S3 One Zone-IA: 30-day minimum storage charge. Logs persist only 24 hours = pay for 30 days anyway, wasting 29 days of charges. Also has $0.01/GB retrieval fee for active processing.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Unknown size/count/pattern' = Intelligent-Tiering. Short-lived data (<30 days) + frequent access = S3 Standard also acceptable. Never use IA storage classes for <30-day data (minimum storage charges). Glacier = NOT for active processing (retrieval delays).
memorize: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: $0.0025/1000 objects monitoring fee
S3 Standard-IA minimum: 30 days storage duration
S3 One Zone-IA: 30-day minimum + single AZ (99.5% vs 99.99% availability)
Glacier Deep Archive: 180-day minimum, 12-48hr retrieval
Intelligent-Tiering: no retrieval fees, automatic optimization

question_en: A company hosts a website on multiple Amazon EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group. Users are reporting slow responses during peak times between 6 PM and 11 PM every weekend. A solutions architect must implement a solution to improve performance during these peak times. What is the MOST operationally efficient solution that meets these requirements?

options.A: Create a scheduled Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function to increase the desired capacity before peak times.
options.B: Configure a scheduled scaling action with a recurrence option to change the desired capacity before and after peak times.
options.C: Create a target tracking scaling policy to add more instances when memory utilization is above 70%.
options.D: Configure the cooldown period for the Auto Scaling group to modify desired capacity before and after peak times.

explanation.full_text: This workload has a predictable recurring traffic pattern, so the most operationally efficient solution is scheduled scaling in Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling. AWS documentation states that scheduled actions let you change desired capacity at specific times or on recurring schedules.
explanation.why_correct: Scheduled scaling with recurrence handles PREDICTABLE patterns (every weekend 6-11pm). Auto Scaling executes action at specified time—no custom code needed. One-time configuration, runs automatically forever. Most operationally efficient.

why_wrong.A: EventBridge + Lambda to modify capacity works but adds operational overhead: Lambda code to maintain, IAM permissions, EventBridge rule management. Scheduled scaling is native ASG feature—simpler.
why_wrong.C: Target tracking = REACTIVE scaling (responds to metric breach). Question describes PREDICTABLE pattern—should scale PROACTIVELY before peak starts. Reactive scaling causes performance degradation during scale-up delay.
why_wrong.D: Cooldown period controls minimum time between scaling activities—doesn't trigger scaling. Completely wrong concept. Cooldown prevents thrashing, doesn't initiate capacity changes.

explanation.exam_tips: Predictable patterns = scheduled scaling. Unpredictable patterns = dynamic scaling (target tracking/step/simple). Scheduled scaling types: one-time (specific date/time) or recurring (cron expression). Cooldown = anti-thrashing delay, NOT a trigger.
memorize: Scheduled scaling: for predictable time-based patterns
Target tracking: maintains metric at target value (e.g., 70% CPU)
Step scaling: scales in steps based on CloudWatch alarm severity
Simple scaling: adds/removes fixed capacity on alarm
Default cooldown: 300 seconds (5 minutes)

question_en: A company uses Amazon EC2 instances spread across two Availability Zones to provide large and small maps to customers. The large maps do not change. The company updates the small maps by adding small metadata files each day. Customers download the large maps once but download the smaller maps frequently. Several Amazon EBS volumes containing replicated data are spread between the Availability Zones. Which solutions will store the map data MOST cost-effectively? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Deploy an Amazon EFS file system. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances. Move the map and metadata files to the file system. Apply a lifecycle policy to move files older than 30 days to the EFS Infrequent Access storage class.
options.B: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the application to read data files from the S3 bucket. Apply an S3 Lifecycle rule to move files older than 30 days to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access storage class.
options.C: Create an Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system. Move the map and metadata files to the file system. Configure the file system to use the Intelligent-Tiering storage class.
options.D: Create a shared EBS volume. Connect the EC2 instances to the shared volume. Move the map and metadata files to the new volume. Detach and delete the original EBS volumes.
options.E: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses the SCRATCH_2 deployment type. Move the map and metadata files to the file system.

explanation.full_text: Amazon EFS provides a regional, shared file system that EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones can access concurrently. An EFS lifecycle policy can move files that have not been accessed recently to the lower-cost EFS Infrequent Access storage class. Amazon S3 is another cost-effective solution for immutable map objects.
explanation.why_correct: A: EFS eliminates duplicated EBS volumes—single shared filesystem across AZs. Lifecycle moves old large maps to IA (92% savings). B: S3 for immutable objects = cheapest storage. App reads directly from S3. Lifecycle moves old maps to Standard-IA. Both solutions remove EBS duplication.

why_wrong.C: FSx for OpenZFS: expensive ($0.20-1.30/GB/month) vs EFS ($0.30/GB Standard, $0.025/GB IA). No built-in Intelligent-Tiering—claim in option is incorrect. Overengineered for static map storage.
why_wrong.D: EBS cannot be shared across AZs natively. EBS Multi-Attach supports limited scenarios (specific instance types, same AZ only). Cannot eliminate cross-AZ duplication with EBS.
why_wrong.E: FSx for Lustre SCRATCH_2: temporary high-performance storage for HPC. Data can be lost. 'SCRATCH' = non-persistent. Wrong for production map storage requiring fault tolerance.

explanation.exam_tips: Multi-AZ file sharing = EFS or S3 (with app changes). EBS = single-AZ only (Multi-Attach is limited special case). FSx Lustre SCRATCH = temporary HPC storage, not for persistent data. Static/immutable content = S3 is cheapest.
memorize: EFS: shared NFS filesystem across AZs, $0.30/GB Standard, $0.025/GB IA
EBS: block storage, single-AZ, $0.08-0.125/GB depending on type
FSx for Lustre PERSISTENT vs SCRATCH: SCRATCH = faster, cheaper, temporary
FSx for OpenZFS: $0.20-1.30/GB depending on throughput tier
S3 Standard: $0.023/GB, S3 Standard-IA: $0.0125/GB

question_en: A finance company uses scheduled scripts to store and visualize stock market data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company deletes records after a month to optimize costs. However, the company needs a costoptimized solution to generate reports and visualizations based on historical data. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use an integration between DynamoDB and Amazon Redshift to load records directly into Amazon Redshift. Use the built-in Amazon Redshift query engine to generate reports and visualizations.
options.B: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose to stream DynamoDB records to an Amazon S3 bucket. Load the data into Amazon Redshift. Use the built-in Amazon Redshift query editor to query the data to generate reports and visualizations.
options.C: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose to stream DynamoDB records to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to generate reports and visualizations.
options.D: Use AWS DMS to continuously copy DynamoDB records into an Amazon RDS database for long-term storage. Use Amazon QuickSight to generate reports and visualizations.

explanation.full_text: A cost-optimized pattern is to stream DynamoDB changes to Amazon S3 and then query and visualize from the data lake. DynamoDB changes can be captured in near real time and delivered to Amazon S3 by using Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose. Athena is serverless and queries data directly in S3.
explanation.why_correct: Kinesis Data Streams captures DynamoDB changes via DynamoDB Streams. Firehose delivers to S3 (batched, compressed). Athena queries S3 directly—no cluster to maintain. QuickSight visualizes Athena queries. Serverless end-to-end, lowest cost for historical analytics.

why_wrong.A: DynamoDB doesn't have native direct integration to Redshift requiring continuous loading. Would need custom ETL. Redshift requires cluster management and costs ~$180/month minimum (dc2.large). Expensive for sporadic reporting.
why_wrong.B: Works but Redshift cluster adds unnecessary cost for historical reporting. Kinesis→S3→Athena is serverless and cheaper than maintaining Redshift cluster. Redshift better for complex OLAP, overkill here.
why_wrong.D: DMS continuously replicates DynamoDB to RDS—wastes money replicating operational data for reports. RDS runs 24/7 even when reports not generated. S3 data lake pattern is more cost-effective.

explanation.exam_tips: DynamoDB historical analytics = DynamoDB Streams → Kinesis → Firehose → S3 → Athena. Redshift = for complex OLAP with large datasets, not simple historical reports. Athena = serverless SQL on S3, pay per query. Data lake pattern cheaper than maintaining database cluster.
memorize: DynamoDB Streams: captures item-level changes, 24-hour retention
Kinesis Data Firehose: batches, compresses, delivers to S3/Redshift/others
Athena: $5 per TB scanned, serverless
Redshift: minimum ~$180/month (dc2.large node)
QuickSight: $9/user/month (readers), $24/user/month (authors)

question_en: A company hosts an application on AWS and has generated approximately 2.5 TB of data over 12 years. The data is stored on Amazon EBS volumes. The company wants a cost-effective backup solution for long-term storage and must be able to retrieve the data within minutes for audits. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create EBS snapshots.
options.B: Use Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.C: Use Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
options.D: Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).

explanation.full_text: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is designed for infrequently accessed data that must still be retrievable quickly. It provides substantially lower storage cost than EBS snapshots or EFS while supporting expedited retrievals, which can return data within minutes when required for audits.
explanation.why_correct: Glacier Flexible Retrieval: $0.0036/GB storage (vs EBS snapshots $0.05/GB). Expedited retrieval = 1-5 minutes (meets 'within minutes' requirement). Standard retrieval = 3-5 hours, Bulk = 5-12 hours. Expedited costs $0.03/GB but used rarely for audits.

why_wrong.A: EBS snapshots stored in S3 backend but charged at $0.05/GB—much more expensive than Glacier for 12-year 2.5TB dataset (~$1,500/year vs ~$100/year). Snapshots better for active backup/restore, not long-term archival.
why_wrong.B: Glacier Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB (cheapest) but 12-48 hour retrieval. Does NOT meet 'within minutes' requirement. Designed for data accessed once or twice per year with flexible retrieval times.
why_wrong.D: EFS: $0.30/GB Standard or $0.025/GB IA. For 2.5TB = $750/month Standard or $62.50/month IA. Much more expensive than Glacier Flexible ($0.0036/GB = $9/month). EFS is for active file systems, not archival.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Long-term + low cost + retrieval in minutes' = Glacier Flexible Retrieval with expedited. Deep Archive = cheapest but hours retrieval. S3 Standard-IA = millisecond retrieval but more expensive. Map storage cost vs retrieval time requirements carefully.
memorize: Glacier Flexible: $0.0036/GB, expedited=1-5min ($0.03/GB + $0.01/request)
Glacier Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB, standard=12hrs, bulk=48hrs
EBS snapshots: $0.05/GB, incremental, instant restore
S3 Standard-IA: $0.0125/GB, millisecond retrieval, 30-day minimum
EFS IA: $0.025/GB, millisecond access, 90-day minimum recommended

question_en: A solutions architect needs to build a log storage solution for a client. The client has an application that produces user activity logs that track user API calls to the application. The application typically produces 50 GB of logs each day. The client needs a storage solution that makes the logs available for occasional querying and analytics.

options.A: Store user activity logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to perform queries and analytics.
options.B: Store user activity logs in an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster. Use OpenSearch Dashboards to perform queries and analytics.
options.C: Store user activity logs in an Amazon RDS instance. Use an Open Database Connectivity (ODBC) connector to perform queries and analytics.
options.D: Store user activity logs in an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to perform queries and analytics.

explanation.full_text: For infrequent or ad hoc querying of log data, Amazon S3 + Amazon Athena provides the most cost-effective, serverless, and scalable analytics solution. Athena is an interactive query service that makes it easy to analyze data in Amazon S3 using standard SQL. Athena is serverless, so there is no infrastructure to manage.
explanation.why_correct: S3 Standard: $0.023/GB × 50GB/day × 30 days = $34.50/month storage. Athena: $5/TB scanned, pay only for queries run. 'Occasional querying' = low query costs. Serverless—no cluster management. Scales automatically for any data volume.

why_wrong.B: OpenSearch: requires cluster (min 3 nodes × $0.10/hr = $216/month). Better for real-time search and frequent low-latency queries. Overkill and expensive for 'occasional querying and analytics'.
why_wrong.C: RDS: designed for OLTP, not log analytics. Poor performance for large log queries. 50GB/day = 1.5TB/month quickly exceeds reasonable RDS size. Expensive and wrong tool for log analytics.
why_wrong.D: CloudWatch Logs: $0.50/GB ingestion + $0.03/GB storage beyond 5GB. 50GB/day = $25/day ingestion = $750/month. Plus storage costs. 10-20x more expensive than S3. CW Logs designed for operational monitoring, not long-term analytics.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Occasional querying' + 'log analytics' = S3 + Athena. OpenSearch = for real-time search, high-frequency queries. CloudWatch Logs = for operational monitoring, expensive for long-term storage. Athena = serverless SQL on S3, pay per query.
memorize: Athena: $5 per TB of data scanned
S3 Standard: $0.023/GB/month
CloudWatch Logs: $0.50/GB ingestion, $0.03/GB storage (>5GB)
OpenSearch: minimum 3-node cluster, ~$0.10/hr per node
Partitioning S3 data reduces Athena scanning costs

question_en: A company wants to migrate from an on-premises data center to AWS. The data center hosts a storage server that stores data in an NFS-based file system. The storage server stores 200 GB of data. The company needs to migrate the data without interruption to existing services. Multiple resources in AWS must be able to access the data by using the NFS protocol. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system.
options.B: B. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system.
options.C: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to receive the data.
options.D: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows file system.
options.E: Install an AWS DataSync agent in the on-premises data center. Use a DataSync task between the onpremises file system and the AWS file system.

explanation.full_text: Amazon EFS is a fully managed, elastic, shared file system that provides NFSv4 access across many EC2 instances and AZs, ideal for lift-and-shift of Linux NFS workloads. AWS DataSync automates moving data between on-premises NFS servers and Amazon EFS, performing incremental, parallel transfers with encryption and integrity checks.
explanation.why_correct: B: EFS = managed NFS, multi-resource access, scales automatically. E: DataSync migrates NFS→EFS with minimal disruption (incremental sync + cutover). Together: NFS compatibility maintained, multiple AWS resources access via NFS, cost-effective for 200GB.

why_wrong.A: FSx for Lustre: high-performance filesystem for HPC, ML, media processing. Overkill for 200GB NFS share. More expensive than EFS. Integrates with S3, not designed as general NFS replacement.
why_wrong.C: S3 is object storage—not directly mountable as NFS by multiple EC2 instances. Would require gateway or application changes to use. Violates 'multiple resources must access via NFS protocol'.
why_wrong.D: FSx for Windows: provides SMB/CIFS protocol for Windows, NOT NFS. Source is Linux NFS server. Protocol mismatch.

explanation.exam_tips: NFS migration = EFS + DataSync. FSx for Lustre = HPC workloads. FSx for Windows = SMB/CIFS. S3 = object storage (not NFS). Multi-resource file access on AWS = EFS. DataSync handles cutover with minimal disruption via incremental sync.
memorize: EFS: NFSv4, Linux workloads, multi-AZ, $0.30/GB Standard
FSx for Lustre: POSIX + S3 integration, HPC/ML, sub-ms latency
FSx for Windows: SMB/CIFS, Active Directory integration, Windows workloads
DataSync: on-prem to AWS migration, 10x faster than open-source tools
S3 is object storage—use S3 File Gateway for NFS interface

question_en: A company uses AWS to run its workloads. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage its accounts. The company needs to identify which departments are responsible for specific costs. New accounts are constantly created in the Organizations account structure. The Organizations continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) framework already adds the populated department tag to the AWS resources.
