The company wants to use an AWS Cost Explorer report to identify the service costs by department from all AWS accounts. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Activate the aws:createdBy cost allocation tag and the department cost allocation tag in the management account.
options.B: Create a new cost and usage report in Cost Explorer. Group by the department cost allocation tag. Apply a filter to see all linked accounts and services.
options.C: Activate only the department cost allocation tag in the management account.
options.D: Create a new cost and usage report in Cost Explorer. Group by the department cost allocation tag without any other filters.
options.E: Activate only the aws:createdBy cost allocation tag in the management account.

explanation.full_text: To track costs by department, you must activate the custom department tag as a cost allocation tag in the AWS Organizations management account. Once activated, Cost Explorer and cost and usage reports can group costs by this tag for all linked accounts.
explanation.why_correct: C: Activate department tag in management account makes it available across all member accounts for cost allocation. D: Group Cost Explorer by department tag shows per-department spending. No filters needed—grouping automatically categorizes all costs. Most operationally efficient.

why_wrong.A: aws:createdBy is AWS-generated tag showing which IAM identity created resource—NOT related to department ownership. Activating unnecessary tag adds clutter. Department tag is user-defined, sufficient alone.
why_wrong.B: Filtering by owner tag limits report to specific tag value, doesn't show ALL departments. Grouping (not filtering) is needed to show breakdown across all department values.
why_wrong.E: aws:createdBy not needed for department cost tracking. Only department tag required. Activating extra tags adds operational overhead without benefit.

explanation.exam_tips: Cost allocation tags: activate in management account (propagates to all accounts in Organization). User-defined tags vs AWS-generated tags. Group = show breakdown by tag values. Filter = show only specific tag value. Management account for Organizations settings.
memorize: Cost allocation tags: activate in Billing console, 24hr delay to appear
User-defined tags: must be activated as cost allocation tags
AWS-generated tags: aws:createdBy, aws:cloudformation:stack-name, etc.
Organizations management account: centralized billing and cost allocation
Cost Explorer: filter=narrow scope, group=categorize/break down

question_en: A company runs Amazon EC2 instances as web servers. Peak traffic occurs at two predictable times each day. The web servers remain mostly idle during the rest of the day. A solutions architect must manage the web servers while maintaining fault tolerance in the most cost-effective way. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use an EC2 Auto Scaling group to scale the instances based on demand.
options.B: Purchase Reserved Instances to ensure peak capacity at all times.
options.C: Use a cron job to stop the EC2 instances when traffic demand is low.
options.D: Use a script to vertically scale the EC2 instances during peak demand.

explanation.full_text: AWS documentation states that EC2 Auto Scaling is the recommended, cost-effective, and fault-tolerant method to manage workloads with predictable or varying demand. Auto Scaling automatically adds instances during peak traffic and terminates them when demand is low, reducing compute cost while maintaining availability.
explanation.why_correct: Auto Scaling scales IN during low traffic (reduces cost) and OUT during peak (maintains performance). Distributes instances across multiple AZs (fault tolerance). Dynamic or scheduled scaling handles 'two predictable times' pattern. No manual intervention needed.

why_wrong.B: Reserved Instances lock in capacity and cost 24/7. Wastes money during non-peak hours (most of the day). RI is for steady-state baseline, not for bursty workloads. No automatic scaling based on demand.
why_wrong.C: Manual cron job to stop instances breaks fault tolerance (what if instances needed during unexpected traffic?). Requires custom orchestration. Doesn't scale capacity—just on/off. Risky and operationally complex.
why_wrong.D: Vertical scaling (changing instance size) requires stop/start, causing downtime. Doesn't distribute across AZs (no fault tolerance improvement). Horizontal scaling (Auto Scaling) is preferred for availability and elasticity.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Predictable peak times' + 'fault tolerant' + 'cost-effective' = Auto Scaling. Reserved Instances = for steady 24/7 baseline. Vertical scaling = downtime. Manual scripts = operational overhead + breaks automation. Auto Scaling handles both scheduled and dynamic scaling.
memorize: Auto Scaling: horizontal scaling, no downtime, multi-AZ distribution
Vertical scaling: resize instance, requires stop/start, downtime
Reserved Instances: 1-3 year commitment, 24/7 baseline capacity
Scheduled scaling: predictable time-based patterns
Dynamic scaling: reacts to CloudWatch metrics in real-time

question_en: A data science team requires storage for nightly log processing. The size and number of logs is unknown and the logs will persist for 24 hours only. What is the MOST cost-effective solution?

options.A: Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
options.B: Amazon S3 Standard
options.C: Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering
options.D: Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)

explanation.full_text: For logs that are written and processed within a short period (24 hours), accessed quickly for compute/analytics, with unknown object count and size, Amazon S3 Standard is the most appropriate and cost-effective.
explanation.why_correct: S3 Standard: $0.023/GB, immediate access, no minimum storage duration. Logs processed 'nightly' need fast access. 24-hour lifecycle = deleted before any tiering benefits. No minimum storage charge penalties. Simple and cost-optimal for short-lived data.

why_wrong.A: Glacier Deep Archive: 180-day minimum storage charge + 12-48hr retrieval. Cannot process logs nightly with 12+ hour delay. Wrong for active processing. Would pay for 180 days even though data deleted at 24hrs.
why_wrong.C: Intelligent-Tiering: charges $0.0025/1000 objects monitoring fee. For 24-hour data, monitoring fee wastes money—no time to benefit from tiering. Designed for 30+ day storage with changing access patterns.
why_wrong.D: S3 One Zone-IA: 30-day minimum storage duration charge. Logs deleted at 24hrs = pay for full 30 days anyway, wasting 29 days. Also has retrieval fees harmful for active nightly processing.

explanation.exam_tips: Short-lived data (<30 days) + active processing = S3 Standard. IA storage classes have minimum duration charges (30-180 days)—wasteful for ephemeral data. Intelligent-Tiering monitoring fee not worth it for data deleted quickly. Glacier = NOT for active processing.
memorize: S3 Standard: $0.023/GB, no minimum duration, immediate access
S3 Standard-IA: 30-day minimum duration charge
S3 One Zone-IA: 30-day minimum, single AZ (cheaper but less durable)
Glacier Flexible: 90-day minimum duration charge
Glacier Deep Archive: 180-day minimum duration charge

question_en: As part of budget planning, management wants a report of AWS billed items listed by user. The data will be used to create department budgets. A solutions architect needs to determine the most efficient way to obtain this report information. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Run a query with Amazon Athena to generate the report.
options.B: Create a report in Cost Explorer and download the report.
options.C: Access the bill details from the billing dashboard and download the bill.
options.D: Modify a cost budget in AWS Budgets to alert with Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES).

explanation.full_text: The most efficient way for management-style reporting is AWS Cost Explorer, because it is designed for interactive cost analysis, filtering, grouping, and exporting reports without building a data pipeline. Cost Explorer can present costs in a way that supports chargeback/showback and budgeting.
explanation.why_correct: Cost Explorer: built-in UI for cost analysis, filtering, grouping (by tag, service, linked account, etc.), downloadable CSV/JSON reports. 'By user' achieved via cost allocation tags. No infrastructure needed. Quickest path to budget planning report.

why_wrong.A: Athena requires: enable Cost and Usage Report → S3 delivery → Glue crawler → schema definition → SQL queries. Much more operational overhead than Cost Explorer built-in reports. Better for custom/complex analysis.
why_wrong.C: Billing dashboard bill download = invoice-style line items. Not optimized for 'by user' slicing or departmental grouping. Harder to create budget-friendly reports from raw invoices.
why_wrong.D: AWS Budgets sends alerts when thresholds exceeded—doesn't generate detailed billed-items reports. Budgets = monitoring/alerting, not reporting tool.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Most efficient' + 'report' + 'management/budget planning' = Cost Explorer. Athena = for complex custom queries (more powerful but more setup). Budgets = alerting, not reporting. Cost allocation tags enable 'by user/team/department' reporting.
memorize: Cost Explorer: built-in reports, grouping, filtering, forecasting
Cost and Usage Report (CUR): detailed billing data delivered to S3
Athena + CUR: for complex custom SQL analysis
AWS Budgets: threshold alerts, forecasts, cost/usage/RI/SP budgets
Cost allocation tags: user-defined or AWS-generated, enable chargeback

question_en: A solutions architect needs to optimize storage costs. The solutions architect must identify any Amazon S3 buckets that are no longer being accessed or are rarely accessed. Which solution will accomplish this goal with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Analyze bucket access patterns by using the S3 Storage Lens dashboard for advanced activity metrics.
options.B: Analyze bucket access patterns by using the S3 dashboard in the AWS Management Console.
options.C: Turn on the Amazon CloudWatch BucketSizeBytes metric for buckets. Analyze bucket access patterns by using the metrics data with Amazon Athena.
options.D: Turn on AWS CloudTrail for S3 object monitoring. Analyze bucket access patterns by using CloudTrail logs that are integrated with Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

explanation.full_text: Amazon S3 Storage Lens with advanced activity metrics is the most operationally efficient answer because AWS documentation explicitly says you can use S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics to identify 'cold' buckets, meaning buckets whose objects are no longer accessed or are accessed only rarely.
explanation.why_correct: S3 Storage Lens Advanced Metrics provides built-in access pattern analysis showing last access time, download/upload trends, and 'cold bucket' identification. One-click dashboard, no infrastructure setup. Designed specifically for this optimization use case. Minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.B: Standard S3 console shows bucket properties and metrics but lacks fleet-wide cold bucket analysis. Cannot efficiently identify rarely-accessed buckets across many buckets. Manual review required.
why_wrong.C: BucketSizeBytes shows storage volume, NOT access patterns. Would need custom Athena queries on CloudTrail logs + complex analysis. High operational overhead building analytics pipeline.
why_wrong.D: CloudTrail logs every S3 API call but requires: enabling per-bucket, S3 delivery, CloudWatch Logs integration, custom queries/analysis. Much more setup than Storage Lens built-in feature.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Identify unused/rarely accessed' + 'least operational overhead' = S3 Storage Lens. Storage Lens = purpose-built storage optimization tool. CloudTrail = audit/compliance, not primary analytics tool. BucketSizeBytes = capacity metric, not access metric.
memorize: S3 Storage Lens: 29+ metrics for storage optimization
Advanced metrics: per-prefix/per-object analysis, activity tracking
Free tier: account-level metrics, 14-day retention
Advanced tier: $0.20 per million objects/month, prefix-level, 15-month retention
CloudTrail logs S3 data events: $0.10/100K events

question_en: A company wants to reduce the cost of its existing three-tier web application. The web servers, application servers, and database servers run on Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances in development, test, and production environments. The EC2 instances average 30% CPU utilization during peak hours and 10% CPU utilization during non-peak hours. The production EC2 instances run 24 hours a day all year. The development and test EC2 instances run for at least 8 hours a day all year. The company wants to implement automation to stop the development and test EC2 instances when those EC2 instances are not in use. Which EC2 instance purchasing solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Use Reserved Instances for the production EC2 instances. Use Reserved Instances for the development and test EC2 instances.
options.B: Use Reserved Instances for the production EC2 instances. Use On-Demand Instances for the development and test EC2 instances.
options.C: Use a Spot Fleet for the production EC2 instances. Use Reserved Instances for the development and test EC2 instances.
options.D: Use On-Demand Instances for the production EC2 instances. Use a Spot Fleet for the development and test EC2 instances.

explanation.full_text: The production environment runs continuously 24 hours a day, all year, which makes Reserved Instances the most cost-effective purchasing model for steady-state workloads. For the development and test environments, the company wants to automate stopping the EC2 instances when they are not in use. Because those instances do not run continuously, On-Demand Instances are a better fit.
explanation.why_correct: Production 24/7 = Reserved Instances (up to 72% savings). Dev/Test with stop automation = On-Demand (pay only when running). RI commitment wasted if instances stopped 16hrs/day. On-Demand flexibility perfect for start/stop automation.

why_wrong.A: Dev/Test RIs waste money—stopped instances still count toward RI term. Paying for unused commitment ~16hrs/day. RIs require minimum utilization to be cost-effective.
why_wrong.C: Spot for production = interruption risk for business-critical workload. Violates reliability principle. Production should NEVER use Spot unless specifically designed for interruption tolerance.
why_wrong.D: Production On-Demand misses 60-72% savings opportunity. For 24/7 predictable workload, not buying RI is leaving money on table.

explanation.exam_tips: Pricing decision tree: 24/7 workload = RI/Savings Plan. Start/stop automation = On-Demand. Interruptible = Spot. Production = avoid Spot unless fault-tolerant by design. Dev/Test + automation = On-Demand, not RI.
memorize: Reserved Instances: up to 72% savings, 1 or 3 year terms
RI utilization: must run ~24/7 to break even vs On-Demand
On-Demand: pay per hour (or second with 60s minimum), no commitment
Stopped instances: no compute charges, but RI commitment still applies
Start/stop automation: AWS Instance Scheduler, EventBridge, Lambda

question_en: A company wants to use Amazon S3 to back up its on-premises file storage solution. The company ' s onpremises file storage solution uses NFS, and the company wants its new solution to support NFS. The company wants to archive the backup files after 5 days. If the company needs archived files for disaster recovery, the company is willing to wait a few days for the retrieval of those files. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway that is associated with an S3 bucket. Move the files from the on-premises file storage solution to the file gateway. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 5 days.
options.B: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway that is associated with an S3 bucket. Move the files from the on-premises file storage solution to the volume gateway. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 days.
options.C: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway tape gateway that is associated with an S3 bucket. Move the files from the on-premises file storage solution to the tape gateway. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 5 days.
options.D: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway that is associated with an S3 bucket. Move the files from the on-premises file storage solution to the file gateway. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 days.

explanation.full_text: AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway is the AWS service designed to present a file interface using NFS (and SMB) while storing the files as objects in Amazon S3. The company wants to archive the backup files after 5 days and is willing to wait a few days to retrieve archived data for disaster recovery. That retrieval tolerance aligns well with Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
explanation.why_correct: File Gateway provides NFS mount point on-premises—minimal changes to backup software. Files transparently uploaded to S3. Glacier Deep Archive = cheapest storage ($0.00099/GB vs $0.023/GB S3 Standard). 'Few days' retrieval = acceptable for DR scenario.

why_wrong.A: S3 Standard-IA costs $0.0125/GB—12x more than Glacier Deep Archive for long-term backup. IA designed for monthly access, not multi-year archival. Violates 'most cost-effective' requirement.
why_wrong.B: Volume Gateway = iSCSI block storage, NOT NFS. Requires application changes to use block storage instead of NFS file shares. Violates 'minimal changes' requirement.
why_wrong.C: Tape Gateway = virtual tape library (VTL) for backup apps like Veeam, Veritas. Designed for tape workflow, not NFS file workflow. Adds unnecessary complexity.

explanation.exam_tips: Storage Gateway types: File (NFS/SMB → S3), Volume (iSCSI blocks → S3 snapshots), Tape (VTL → S3/Glacier). Key phrase: 'NFS' + 'backup to S3' = File Gateway. Glacier Deep Archive = cheapest but 12-48hr retrieval.
memorize: File Gateway: NFS/SMB → S3 objects, local cache
S3 Glacier Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB, 12-48hr standard retrieval
S3 Standard-IA: $0.0125/GB, millisecond access, 30-day minimum
Volume Gateway: iSCSI, cached or stored mode, EBS snapshots
Tape Gateway: virtual tapes, backup software integration

question_en: A financial services company needs to store and manage trading documentation. The documentation includes real-time trade confirmation data, financial statements, and settlement documents that frequently exceed 1 MB in size. The company ' s current provisioned database solution stores and manages this documentation. This current solution experiences high-volume trading activity during market hours but very low activity during off-hours. The company currently uses a provisioned database solution that is sized to handle the load for peak trading hours. This solution results in significant unused capacity during off-hours. The company needs a solution that will maintain performance during peak hours. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy Amazon RDS for MySQL on Reserved Instances with read replicas for scaling.
options.B: Deploy Amazon DocumentDB serverless with automatic capacity scaling.
options.C: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB with auto scaling.
options.D: Deploy a MongoDB cluster on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group.

explanation.full_text: Amazon DocumentDB serverless is the most cost-effective managed option for this workload because the data is document-oriented, documents frequently exceed 1 MB, and usage changes significantly between market hours and off-hours. DocumentDB supports larger document sizes than DynamoDB items.
explanation.why_correct: DocumentDB supports documents >1MB (DynamoDB max = 400KB, violates requirement). Serverless scales ACUs automatically: high during market hours, low/zero off-hours. Only pay for active capacity. Managed MongoDB-compatible service.

why_wrong.A: RDS MySQL: relational database, not optimized for document storage. Reserved Instances = fixed capacity 24/7, wastes money during off-hours. Read replicas add cost without addressing variable workload.
why_wrong.C: DynamoDB maximum item size = 400KB. Documents 'frequently exceed 1MB' = cannot store. Would need to split documents or use S3 pointers, adding complexity.
why_wrong.D: Self-managed MongoDB on EC2: requires patching, backup automation, HA setup, scaling logic. High operational overhead vs managed DocumentDB. Not cost-optimized.

explanation.exam_tips: Document size limits: DynamoDB 400KB, DocumentDB 16MB, MongoDB 16MB. Serverless DB for variable workload patterns. Key phrase: 'document storage' + '>1MB' + 'variable hours' = DocumentDB Serverless. DynamoDB for items <400KB.
memorize: DynamoDB: maximum item size 400KB (including attribute names)
DocumentDB: MongoDB-compatible, BSON documents up to 16MB
DocumentDB Serverless: scales 0-128 ACU automatically
RDS Reserved Instances: 1-3 year commitment, fixed capacity
Serverless pricing: pay per ACU-hour (Aurora) or RCU/WCU-hour (DynamoDB)

question_en: A company hosts a photo sharing web application on AWS. Users upload and share thousands of photos each hour. The company needs a durable storage solution that provides retrieval mechanisms for the photos. Most uploaded photos are not accessed often after 30 days, but the company does not want to delete older photos. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Store the photos in an Amazon EFS file system for immediate use. Use AWS Backup with on-demand backups and point-in-time recovery PITR to store photos that are older than 30 days.
options.B: Store the photos in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon S3 Lifecycle configurations to move photos that are older than 30 days to S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
options.C: Store the photos in Amazon DynamoDB for immediate use. Use AWS Backup with on-demand backups and point-in-time recovery PITR to store photos that are older than 30 days.
options.D: Store the photos in Amazon FSx for Lustre for immediate use. Use AWS Backup with continuous backups and point-in-time recovery PITR to store photos that are older than 30 days.

explanation.full_text: Amazon S3 is the right durable storage service for photos, and a lifecycle transition to S3 Intelligent-Tiering is cost-effective when older objects are accessed infrequently but should remain readily available. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects based on access patterns.
explanation.why_correct: S3 = designed for photo/media storage, 99.999999999% durability. Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves cold objects to infrequent tier after 30 days of no access. No retrieval fees. No deletion—photos retained indefinitely. Automatic optimization without manual intervention.

why_wrong.A: EFS + AWS Backup: EFS costs $0.30/GB vs S3 $0.023/GB. AWS Backup for 'storage' is wrong concept—Backup is for recovery, not primary storage. PITR not needed for photo sharing app.
why_wrong.C: DynamoDB stores structured data, not optimized for storing large binary photos. 400KB item limit problematic. AWS Backup + PITR designed for database recovery, not photo storage.
why_wrong.D: FSx for Lustre = high-performance filesystem for HPC/ML ($0.14-2.40/GB/month). Massive overkill for photo storage. 10-100x more expensive than S3.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Photos/media/files' + 'infrequent after X days' + 'retain indefinitely' = S3 + Intelligent-Tiering or Lifecycle. EFS/FSx = for file system access patterns. DynamoDB = structured data, not large binaries. AWS Backup = disaster recovery, not primary storage.
memorize: S3 Standard: $0.023/GB, 11 nines durability
S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatic tiering, $0.0025/1000 objects monitoring fee
EFS Standard: $0.30/GB (13x more than S3)
FSx for Lustre: $0.145-2.40/GB/month depending on throughput
DynamoDB: 400KB item limit, not for large binary storage

question_en: A company generates approximately 20 GB of data multiple times each day. The company uses AWS DataSync to copy all data from on-premises storage to Amazon S3 every 6 hours for further processing. The analytics team wants to modify the copy process to copy only data relevant to the analytics team and ignore the rest of the data. The team wants to copy data as soon as possible and receive a notification when the copy process is finished. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select THREE.)

options.A: Modify the data generation process on-premises to create a manifest file at the end of the copy process with the names of the objects to be copied to Amazon S3. Create a custom script to upload the manifest file to an S3 bucket.
options.B: Modify the data generation process on-premises to create a manifest file at the end of the copy process with the names of the objects to be copied to Amazon S3. Create an AWS Lambda function to load the manifest file data into an Amazon DynamoDB table.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function that Amazon EventBridge invokes when the manifest file is loaded into Amazon DynamoDB. Configure the Lambda function to copy the data from on-premises storage to the S3 bucket that uses the manifest file.
options.D: Create an AWS Lambda function that an S3 Event Notification invokes when the manifest file is uploaded. Configure the Lambda function to invoke the DataSync task by calling the StartTaskExecution API action with a manifest.
options.E: Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to send an email notification to the SNS topic when the DataSync task execution status changes to SUCCESS or to ERROR.
options.F: Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Create an AWS Lambda function to send an email notification to the SNS topic when the DataSync task execution status changes to SUCCESS or to ERROR.

explanation.full_text: To meet the requirements of copying only relevant data as soon as possible and receiving notifications upon completion: Generate a Manifest File, Automate DataSync Task Execution, and Set Up Completion Notifications.
explanation.why_correct: A: Manifest file lists only relevant objects—DataSync transfers only what's needed. D: S3 event triggers Lambda → StartTaskExecution with manifest = immediate processing. E: EventBridge monitors DataSync status → SNS notification on SUCCESS/ERROR. Complete automated workflow (trigger → execute → notify).

why_wrong.B: DynamoDB adds unnecessary complexity—manifest uploaded to S3 can trigger Lambda directly. Extra costs for DynamoDB reads/writes with no benefit over S3 event notifications.
why_wrong.C: Lambda cannot directly access on-premises storage—Lambda runs in AWS VPC. DataSync agent handles on-prem→AWS transfer. This option misunderstands Lambda's execution environment.
why_wrong.F: Custom Lambda for SNS notification adds unnecessary code. EventBridge natively monitors DataSync task status—simpler, no custom code, same result.

explanation.exam_tips: Multi-select = look for end-to-end workflow. DataSync manifest = transfer selective files (not all). S3 event notification = trigger on upload. EventBridge = monitor AWS service status. Pick 3 that form complete pipeline: create → trigger → notify.
memorize: DataSync manifest: text file listing source paths to transfer
StartTaskExecution API: programmatically start DataSync task
S3 Event Notifications: Lambda, SNS, SQS targets
EventBridge: 200+ AWS services, custom event patterns
DataSync pricing: $0.0125/GB transferred

question_en: A company wants to share data that is collected from self-driving cars with the automobile community. The data will be made available from within an Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to minimize its cost of making this data available to other AWS accounts. What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this goal?

options.A: Create an S3 VPC endpoint for the bucket.
options.B: Configure the S3 bucket to be a Requester Pays bucket.
options.C: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket.
options.D: Require that the files be accessible only with the use of the BitTorrent protocol.

explanation.full_text: The Requester Pays feature in Amazon S3 allows the bucket owner to configure the bucket so that the requester, rather than the bucket owner, pays for data transfer and request costs.
explanation.why_correct: Requester Pays shifts ALL data transfer ($0.09/GB internet, $0.02/GB inter-region) and request costs to downloader. Bucket owner ONLY pays storage. Perfect for large dataset sharing—community members who use data pay for their usage.

why_wrong.A: VPC endpoint = private connectivity WITHIN same VPC/account. Doesn't help share with OTHER AWS accounts. Doesn't shift costs—bucket owner still pays storage + transfer.
why_wrong.C: CloudFront = bucket owner pays CloudFront costs ($0.085/GB + requests). Adds caching benefit but doesn't shift transfer costs to requesters. More expensive for bucket owner than Requester Pays.
why_wrong.D: BitTorrent for S3 was deprecated in 2020 and removed. No longer available. Historical distractor.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Share data' + 'minimize owner cost' + 'other AWS accounts' = Requester Pays. CloudFront = performance optimization, owner still pays. VPC endpoint = private within VPC/account. Requester must include x-amz-request-payer: requester header.
memorize: Requester Pays: requester pays transfer + requests, owner pays storage only
Header required: x-amz-request-payer: requester
Works with: GET, POST, LIST operations
BitTorrent for S3: deprecated 2020
VPC endpoint: free within region, doesn't help inter-account sharing

question_en: A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances that are part of an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application experiences spikes in requests that come through the ALB throughout each day. The traffic spikes last between 15 and 20 minutes. The company needs a solution that uses a standard or custom metric to scale the EC2 instances based on the number of requests that come from the ALB. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to monitor the ALB RequestCount metric. Configure a simple scaling policy to scale the EC2 instances in response to the metric.
options.B: Configure a predictive scaling policy based on the ALB RequestCount metric to scale the EC2 instances.
options.C: Configure an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to monitor the ALB UnhealthyHostCount metric. Configure a target tracking policy to scale the EC2 instances in response to the metric.
options.D: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to monitor a user-defined metric for GET requests. Configure a target tracking policy threshold to scale the EC2 instances.

explanation.full_text: For short, frequent daily spikes (15-20 minutes), target tracking scaling driven by a request-based metric continuously adjusts capacity to maintain a chosen target value. Option D uses a custom CloudWatch metric for GET requests with target tracking.
explanation.why_correct: Target tracking maintains target value (e.g., 1000 requests/instance) continuously. Proportional scaling up/down. Custom GET metric = precise demand signal from actual traffic. For 15-20min spikes, responds quickly and scales in promptly—avoids wasted capacity.

why_wrong.A: Simple scaling = fixed steps + cooldown (default 300s). 5-min cooldown during 15-20min spike = slow response. May leave excess capacity running after spike ends.
why_wrong.B: Predictive scaling = ML-based forecasting for regular patterns (daily/weekly cycles). Needs 2 weeks historical data. 'Spikes throughout day' suggests irregular—predictive won't forecast well.
why_wrong.C: UnhealthyHostCount = health check failures, NOT load metric. Scaling on failures treats symptom not cause. Health issues could be capacity, network, or app bugs—wrong signal for load-based scaling.

explanation.exam_tips: Scaling policies: Target tracking = maintain target (best for variable load). Step = tiered response. Simple = single step + cooldown. Predictive = ML forecast (regular patterns). For ALB: RequestCountPerTarget or custom request metric preferred over UnhealthyHostCount.
memorize: Target tracking: automatically adjusts to maintain target value
Simple scaling: single adjustment + cooldown period
Step scaling: multiple steps based on alarm threshold breach size
Predictive scaling: requires 14 days historical data minimum
ALB metrics: RequestCount, RequestCountPerTarget, TargetResponseTime

question_en: A company that uses AWS Organizations runs 150 applications across 30 different AWS accounts. The company used AWS Cost and Usage Report to create a new report in the management account. The report is delivered to an Amazon S3 bucket that is replicated to a bucket in the data collection account. The company ' s senior leadership wants to view a custom dashboard that provides NAT gateway costs each day starting at the beginning of the current month. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Share an Amazon QuickSight dashboard that includes the requested table visual. Configure QuickSight to use AWS DataSync to query the new report.
options.B: Share an Amazon QuickSight dashboard that includes the requested table visual. Configure QuickSight to use Amazon Athena to query the new report.
options.C: Share an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that includes the requested table visual. Configure CloudWatch to use AWS DataSync to query the new report.
options.D: Share an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that includes the requested table visual. Configure CloudWatch to use Amazon Athena to query the new report.

explanation.full_text: The AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) delivers detailed, line-item billing data to Amazon S3. AWS recommends querying CUR with Amazon Athena. Amazon QuickSight natively connects to Athena as a data source to build and share dashboards.
explanation.why_correct: CUR = most detailed AWS billing data (hourly granularity). Athena queries S3 directly—serverless SQL, no database needed. QuickSight connects to Athena—native integration, no ETL. Filter by service (NAT Gateway) and date range (current month). Fully serverless workflow.

why_wrong.A: DataSync = data transfer/migration tool, NOT query engine. Cannot run SQL queries on CUR files. Wrong tool category.
why_wrong.C: CloudWatch = metrics and logs monitoring, NOT billing analysis. Cannot access CUR files in S3. Cost data not available in CloudWatch (only usage metrics like API calls).
why_wrong.D: Same issues as C—CloudWatch can't query CUR + DataSync can't query data. Both wrong tools.

explanation.exam_tips: CUR analysis = S3 → Athena → QuickSight. DataSync = migration, not analysis. CloudWatch = metrics/logs, not billing. Cost Explorer = simpler built-in tool, CUR + Athena = detailed custom analysis. NAT Gateway costs = lineItem/UsageType filter.
memorize: CUR: hourly/daily billing data, delivered to S3
Athena: $5 per TB scanned, serverless SQL
QuickSight: $9/user/month readers, $24/user/month authors
Cost Explorer: built-in, free basic reports
DataSync: data transfer $0.0125/GB, not for querying

question_en: A company hosts a website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The website serves static content. Website traffic is increasing. The company wants to minimize the website hosting costs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Move the website to an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the S3 bucket.
options.B: Move the website to an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon ElastiCache cluster for the S3 bucket.
options.C: Move the website to AWS Amplify. Configure an ALB to resolve to the Amplify website.
options.D: Move the website to AWS Amplify. Configure EC2 instances to cache the website.

explanation.full_text: Serving static content from Amazon S3 is highly cost-effective and scalable. By fronting the S3 bucket with Amazon CloudFront, you enable global caching, reduced latency, and lower costs by reducing direct S3 access.
explanation.why_correct: S3 static website: $0.023/GB + $0.0004/1K GET. CloudFront caches at 450+ edge locations—reduces origin requests 70-90%. CloudFront $0.085/GB < S3 direct $0.09/GB for most users. Eliminate EC2 (~$7.50/mo min) + ALB (~$16/mo min) = ~$23/mo savings baseline. 10-50x cost reduction.

why_wrong.B: ElastiCache = in-memory database cache (Redis/Memcached). Cannot 'cache S3 bucket'—architecturally nonsensical. ElastiCache minimum $0.017/hr (~$12/mo) adds cost without benefit.
why_wrong.C: Amplify = full app framework (hosting + CI/CD + auth + APIs). Overkill for static site. Uses CloudFront behind scenes. ALB cannot 'resolve to Amplify'—wrong terminology. Adds unnecessary complexity.
why_wrong.D: Amplify already includes CDN. 'EC2 to cache website' = custom solution requiring load balancer, caching logic, auto-scaling. High operational overhead + cost vs native CloudFront.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Static content' + 'minimize cost' = S3 + CloudFront (appears in ~5% of exam questions). EC2/ALB for static = anti-pattern. ElastiCache = database/API caching only. Amplify = for full apps with backend, not pure static sites.
memorize: S3 static hosting: $0.023/GB storage + $0.0004/1K GET requests
CloudFront: $0.085/GB data transfer + $0.0075/10K HTTP requests
CloudFront cache hit ratio: 70-95% typical
ALB minimum: ~$16/month (even if idle)
EC2 t3.micro: ~$7.50/month On-Demand

question_en: A company has migrated several applications to AWS in the past 3 months. The company wants to know the breakdown of costs for each of these applications. The company wants to receive a regular report that Includes this Information. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Use AWS Budgets to download data for the past 3 months into a csv file. Look up the desired information.
options.B: Load AWS Cost and Usage Reports into an Amazon RDS DB instance. Run SQL queries to gel the desired information.
options.C: Tag all the AWS resources with a key for cost and a value of the application ' s name. Activate cost allocation tags Use Cost Explorer to get the desired information.
options.D: Tag all the AWS resources with a key for cost and a value of the application ' s name. Use the AWS Billing and Cost Management console to download bills for the past 3 months. Look up the desired information.

explanation.full_text: Tag resources with application name, activate cost allocation tags, use Cost Explorer for breakdown. Most cost-effective and efficient way to track costs per application with regular reports.
explanation.why_correct: Tagging = granular cost tracking by application. Activate tags in Billing console = enables Cost Explorer grouping. Cost Explorer = built-in visualization tool, filter/group by tags, schedule reports, no infrastructure needed. Free for basic analysis.

why_wrong.A: Budgets = threshold alerts and forecasts, NOT detailed cost breakdowns. Can download data but manual analysis required. Not optimized for regular reporting per application.
why_wrong.B: Loading CUR into RDS = operational overhead (RDS instance $15+/mo, schema management, SQL queries). More expensive and complex than built-in Cost Explorer.
why_wrong.D: Downloading bills = manual process, raw invoice data. Hard to slice by application without tags activated in Cost Explorer. Less dynamic than Cost Explorer's built-in filtering.

explanation.exam_tips: Cost tracking by application = tag + activate + Cost Explorer. Budgets = alerts/thresholds. CUR + Athena = advanced custom analysis. Cost Explorer = standard reporting. Must activate user-defined tags before they appear in reports (24hr delay).
memorize: Cost allocation tags: user-defined + AWS-generated
Activation: required in Billing console, 24hr delay
Cost Explorer: free basic reports, grouping, filtering
AWS Budgets: alerts on thresholds, not primary reporting
CUR: most detailed data, requires S3 + Athena setup

question_en: A company wants to use Amazon S3 to back up its on-premises file storage solution. The company ' s onpremises file storage solution supports NFS, and the company wants its new solution to support NFS. The company wants to archive the backup files after 5 days. If the company needs archived files for disaster recovery, the company is willing to wait a few days for the retrieval of those files. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway that is associated with an S3 bucket. Move the files from the on-premises file storage solution to the file gateway. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access S3 Standard-IA after 5 days.
options.B: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway that is associated with an S3 bucket. Move the files from the on-premises file storage solution to the volume gateway. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 days.
options.C: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway tape gateway that is associated with an S3 bucket. Move the files from the on-premises file storage solution to the tape gateway. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access S3 Standard-IA after 5 days.
options.D: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway that is associated with an S3 bucket. Move the files from the on-premises file storage solution to the file gateway. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 5 days.

explanation.full_text: File Gateway provides NFS interface backed by S3. Glacier Deep Archive for lowest-cost archival with days retrieval tolerance.
explanation.why_correct: File Gateway = NFS mount point on-premises, zero application changes. Files auto-upload to S3. Lifecycle after 5 days → Glacier Deep Archive ($0.00099/GB) = cheapest long-term storage. 'Few days retrieval' acceptable = 12-48hr standard retrieval matches.

why_wrong.A: S3 Standard-IA = $0.0125/GB (12x more expensive than Deep Archive). Good for monthly access, wasteful for multi-year backup archival.
why_wrong.B: Volume Gateway = iSCSI block storage, NOT NFS. Would require changing on-prem application from file to block interface. Violates 'minimal changes' requirement.
why_wrong.C: Tape Gateway = VTL for backup software (Veeam, Veritas, Commvault). Emulates tape libraries. Adds complexity when simple NFS file backup needed.

explanation.exam_tips: Storage Gateway: File (NFS/SMB→S3), Volume (iSCSI→EBS snapshots), Tape (VTL→S3/Glacier). 'NFS backup' = File Gateway always. 'Few days retrieval' = Glacier Deep Archive acceptable. 'Immediate' = Standard-IA minimum.
memorize: File Gateway: NFS v3/v4.1, SMB 2/3, cached locally
Glacier Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB, 180-day min, 12-48hr retrieval
Volume Gateway: iSCSI, cached or stored mode
Tape Gateway: VTL, up to 1,500 virtual tapes
S3 Standard-IA: $0.0125/GB, 30-day min, immediate access

question_en: A company is building a new web application on AWS. The application needs to consume files from a legacy on-premises application that runs a batch process and outputs approximately 1 GB of data every night to an NFS file mount. A solutions architect needs to design a storage solution that requires minimal changes to the legacy application and keeps costs low. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy an Outpost in AWS Outposts to the on-premises location where the legacy application is stored. Configure the legacy application and the web application to store and retrieve the files in Amazon S3 on the Outpost.
options.B: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway on premises. Point the legacy application to the Volume Gateway. Configure the web application to use the Amazon S3 bucket that the Volume Gateway uses.
options.C: Deploy an Amazon S3 interface endpoint on AWS. Reconfigure the legacy application to store the files directly on an Amazon S3 endpoint. Configure the web application to retrieve the files from Amazon S3.
options.D: Deploy an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises. Point the legacy application to the File Gateway. Configure the web application to retrieve the files from the S3 bucket that the File Gateway uses.

explanation.full_text: File Gateway provides local NFS mount for legacy app, transparently uploads to S3. Web app reads from S3. Minimal changes, cost-effective.
explanation.why_correct: File Gateway = NFS mount point for legacy batch process. Zero code changes to nightly export. Files appear in S3 automatically. Web app reads S3 directly via SDK. ~1GB/night = $0.70/month storage + transfer costs only.

why_wrong.A: Outposts = full AWS infrastructure rack on-premises ($10K+ upfront, maintenance). Massive overkill for 1GB/night file transfer. 100x more expensive than File Gateway appliance.
why_wrong.B: Volume Gateway = iSCSI block volumes, NOT NFS file mounts. Legacy app uses NFS—would require rewriting to use block storage.
why_wrong.C: S3 interface endpoint = VPC private connectivity, doesn't help on-premises app. 'Reconfigure legacy app to use S3 API' violates 'minimal changes' requirement. Would need major app rewrite.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Legacy' + 'NFS' + 'minimal changes' + 'bridge to cloud' = File Gateway. Outposts = when need full AWS services on-prem (rare). Interface endpoint = VPC to AWS services privately, not on-prem to AWS.
memorize: File Gateway: deployed as VM (VMware, Hyper-V) or hardware appliance
Outposts: 42U racks, 1U/2U servers, starting ~$200K+
S3 interface endpoint: ENI in VPC, private IP, for VPC resources
Volume Gateway: 1GB-32TB per volume, iSCSI protocol
File Gateway cache: local SSD/HDD, LRU eviction

question_en: A company is launching a new application that requires a structured database to store user profiles, application settings, and transactional data. The database must be scalable with application traffic and must offer backups. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy a self-managed database on Amazon EC2 instances by using open-source software. Use Spot Instances for cost optimization. Configure automated backups to Amazon S3.
options.B: Use Amazon RDS. Use on-demand capacity mode for the database with General Purpose SSD storage. Configure automatic backups with a retention period of 7 days.
options.C: Use Amazon Aurora Serverless for the database. Use serverless capacity scaling. Configure automated backups to Amazon S3.
options.D: Deploy a self-managed NoSQL database on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Reserved Instances for cost optimization. Configure automated backups directly to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.

explanation.full_text: Aurora Serverless v2 auto-scales capacity based on demand, reduces costs for variable traffic. Automated backups included.
explanation.why_correct: Aurora Serverless = scales 0.5-128 ACU automatically based on load. New app = traffic unpredictable. Only pay for active ACU-seconds. Backups to S3 automatic (1-35 day retention). Structured relational DB (PostgreSQL/MySQL compatible).

why_wrong.A: Self-managed DB on Spot = interruption risk for database (data durability concern). Spot can be terminated with 2-min notice—unacceptable for transactional database. High operational overhead (patching, backups, HA).
why_wrong.B: RDS On-Demand = always-on billing even during low traffic. For new app with unknown patterns, may overprovision. RDS good choice but less cost-optimized than serverless for variable load.
why_wrong.D: Self-managed NoSQL on RI = structured transactional data better suited for relational. Reserved Instances require 1-3yr commitment for unknown workload. High ops overhead vs managed service.

explanation.exam_tips: 'New application' + 'variable/unpredictable traffic' + 'structured DB' = Aurora Serverless. RDS = predictable steady load. Self-managed = avoid unless specific requirements (OS access, unsupported engine). Spot = never for databases (stateful).
memorize: Aurora Serverless v2: 0.5-128 ACU, scales in 0.5 ACU increments
ACU pricing: ~$0.12/ACU-hour (varies by region)
Aurora Serverless v1: deprecated, use v2
RDS automated backups: 1-35 days retention, free up to DB size
Spot for stateful: anti-pattern (interruption = data loss risk)

question_en: A company needs a solution to process customer orders from a global ecommerce platform. The solution must automatically start processing new orders immediately and must maintain a history of all order processing attempts. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes an AWS Lambda function once every minute to check for new orders. Configure the Lambda function to process orders and store results in Amazon Aurora.
options.B: Create an Amazon EventBridge event pattern that monitors the ecommerce platform ' s order events. Configure an EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function when the platform receives a new order. Configure the function to store the results in Amazon DynamoDB.
options.C: Use an Amazon EC2 instance to poll the ecommerce platform for new orders. Configure the instance to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process new orders. Configure the function to log results to Amazon CloudWatch.
options.D: Use an Amazon SQS queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function when the platform receives a new order. Configure the function to process batches of orders and to store results in an Amazon EFS file system.

explanation.full_text: EventBridge event-driven pattern invokes Lambda immediately when order arrives. Lambda processes and stores in DynamoDB. Most cost-effective serverless solution.
explanation.why_correct: EventBridge = monitors ecommerce platform events in real-time. Lambda invoked only on actual orders—no polling waste. DynamoDB = NoSQL, scales automatically, stores processing history with low latency. Fully serverless = no idle costs, auto-scales to global traffic.

why_wrong.A: Lambda every minute polling = 1,440 invocations/day even with zero orders. Polling introduces latency (up to 60s delay). Aurora = relational DB overkill and more expensive than DynamoDB for event logs.
why_wrong.C: EC2 polling = 24/7 instance costs (~$180/mo minimum t3.small). Manual scaling needed. CloudWatch Logs = not queryable database, lacks structured storage for history.
why_wrong.D: SQS doesn't 'invoke' Lambda—Lambda polls SQS (different model). EFS = file storage not suited for structured order processing history. More expensive than DynamoDB for this use case.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Immediately' + 'event-driven' + 'history' = EventBridge + Lambda + DynamoDB. Polling (cron, EC2 checking) = anti-pattern for event-driven. DynamoDB = event/activity logging. Aurora = complex transactional queries. CloudWatch Logs = monitoring, not app database.
memorize: EventBridge: 14M invocations/month free, then $1/million
Lambda: 1M requests/month free, 400K GB-sec/month free
DynamoDB: 25GB storage free, 25 WCU/25 RCU free tier
Polling vs push: push = immediate, polling = delay + waste
Event-driven: EventBridge, SNS, SQS; avoid cron for real-time

question_en: A company runs an application that stores and shares photos. Users upload photos to an Amazon S3 bucket. Approximately 150 photos are uploaded daily. The company wants to create a thumbnail for each new photo and store it in a second S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Use an Amazon EMR cluster and scheduled scripts.
options.B: Use an always-on EC2 instance with scheduled scripts.
options.C: Configure an S3 event notification to invoke an AWS Lambda function on each upload.
options.D: Use S3 Storage Lens to invoke a Lambda function.

explanation.full_text: S3 event notification invokes Lambda on upload. Lambda generates thumbnail, uploads to second bucket. Serverless, pay-per-use, most cost-effective.
explanation.why_correct: S3 event triggers Lambda automatically on upload. Lambda runs only for 150 photos/day (~5-10 seconds each). Cost: ~$0.03/month Lambda + negligible S3 events. Zero idle costs. No infrastructure to manage.

why_wrong.A: EMR = big data processing cluster (Hadoop/Spark). Minimum 3 nodes ~$0.15/hr = $108/month continuously running. 1000x more expensive than Lambda for 150 photos/day.
why_wrong.B: Always-on EC2 = 24/7 costs (~$7.50/mo t3.micro minimum). Idle 99.9% of time for 150 photos/day. Lambda 100x cheaper for sporadic workloads.
why_wrong.D: S3 Storage Lens = analytics/reporting tool, NOT event processing. Cannot trigger Lambda. Wrong tool category (monitoring vs compute).

explanation.exam_tips: 'Event-driven' + 'sporadic' + 'low volume' = Lambda. EMR/EC2 = for sustained workloads or big data processing. Storage Lens = monitoring, not triggers. S3 events = free, unlimited notifications.
memorize: Lambda pricing: $0.20/1M requests + $0.0000166667/GB-second
S3 event notifications: free, supports Lambda/SNS/SQS
EMR minimum: 1 master + 2 core nodes
EC2 t3.micro: ~$7.50/month (cheapest instance)
Thumbnail generation: typical 2-5 seconds with 512MB-1GB Lambda

question_en: A company is launching a new application that requires a structured database to store user profiles, application settings, and transactional data. The database must be scalable with application traffic and must offer backups. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy a self-managed database on Amazon EC2 instances by using open source software. Use Spot Instances for cost optimization. Configure automated backups to Amazon S3.
options.B: Use Amazon RDS. Use on-demand capacity mode for the database with General Purpose SSD storage. Configure automatic backups with a retention period of 7 days.
options.C: Use Amazon Aurora Serverless for the database. Use serverless capacity scaling. Configure automated backups to Amazon S3.
options.D: Deploy a self-managed NoSQL database on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Reserved Instances for cost optimization. Configure automated backups directly to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.

explanation.full_text: RDS with GP SSD and automated backups. Managed relational database for structured data, scalable, cost-effective for standard workloads.
explanation.why_correct: RDS = managed relational DB (no patching/backup management). GP3 SSD = cost-effective storage, scales IOPS independently. 7-day backups = automatic, free up to DB size. 'Structured + transactional' = relational DB perfect fit. Standard choice for new apps.

why_wrong.A: Spot for database = risky (interruptions cause downtime). Self-managed = high ops burden (HA, backups, patching, monitoring). More expensive TCO than RDS when factoring operational time.
why_wrong.C: Aurora Serverless = good but question #333 already used it. For general-purpose without variable traffic stated, standard RDS more straightforward and predictable cost.
why_wrong.D: NoSQL on EC2 = self-managed NoSQL when structured relational DB requested. Reserved Instances = commitment without knowing workload. Manual scaling, backups, monitoring needed.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Structured + transactional' = relational DB (RDS, Aurora). NoSQL = unstructured/semi-structured. Self-managed = avoid unless special requirements. Standard RDS = safe default for relational workloads. Aurora = when need 5x performance or multi-region.
memorize: RDS engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server
RDS GP3: 3,000 IOPS baseline free, up to 64,000 IOPS
RDS backups: automated (1-35 days), manual snapshots (indefinite)
Aurora: 3-5x faster than PostgreSQL/MySQL, 6 copies across 3 AZs
RDS Multi-AZ: automatic failover, synchronous replication

question_en: A company wants to create a long-term storage solution that will allow users to upload terabytes of images and videos. The company will use the images and videos to train machine learning ML models. The storage solution must be scalable and cost-optimized. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Provision an Amazon S3 bucket for users to upload images and videos. Copy the data from the S3 bucket to an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system to make the data available for ML model training.
options.B: Provision an Amazon S3 bucket for users to upload images and videos. Configure the S3 bucket to make the data available to Amazon SageMaker AI for ML model training. Store the data in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class.
options.C: Configure an Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instance with 16 GB of storage. Create a custom application to allow users to upload images and videos directly to the notebook instance.
options.D: Provision an Amazon S3 bucket for users to upload images and videos. Copy the data from the S3 bucket to an Amazon EFS file system to make the data available for ML model training.

explanation.full_text: S3 for scalable long-term storage of images/videos. SageMaker reads directly from S3. Intelligent-Tiering optimizes costs for variable access patterns.
explanation.why_correct: S3 = unlimited scalability, 99.999999999% durability, native SageMaker integration. Intelligent-Tiering = automatic cost optimization without performance impact. Training jobs read directly from S3 (no intermediate copy). $0.023/GB frequent, $0.0125/GB infrequent tier.

why_wrong.A: Unnecessary FSx Lustre intermediate layer. S3 → FSx copy = duplicates storage costs + FSx costs ($0.145+/GB/month). SageMaker can read S3 directly via S3 input mode or File mode.
why_wrong.C: Notebook instance storage = 16GB max, cannot store terabytes. Notebooks = development environment, not production data storage. Storage tied to instance lifecycle (ephemeral).
why_wrong.D: EFS intermediate layer = $0.30/GB (13x more than S3). Unnecessary copy adds cost and complexity. SageMaker S3 native integration faster and simpler.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Terabytes' + 'long-term' + 'ML training' = S3 + SageMaker direct. FSx Lustre = for HPC when need POSIX, sub-ms latency. EFS = shared file system between instances. Notebook storage = development only. S3 = default ML data storage.
memorize: SageMaker input modes: File (downloads to EBS), FastFile (streams), Pipe (streams)
S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatic, no retrieval fees, $0.0025/1K objects monitoring
FSx for Lustre: $0.145-2.40/GB/month, HPC workloads
EFS: $0.30/GB Standard, $0.025/GB IA
SageMaker training: reads from S3, writes model artifacts to S3

question_en: A company has an application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances within a private subnet in a VPC. The instances access data in an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region. The VPC contains a NAT gateway in a public subnet to access the S3 bucket. The company wants to reduce costs by replacing the NAT gateway without compromising security or redundancy. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance.
options.B: Replace the NAT gateway with an internet gateway.
options.C: Replace the NAT gateway with a gateway VPC endpoint.
options.D: Replace the NAT gateway with an AWS Direct Connect connection.

explanation.full_text: Gateway VPC endpoint for S3 provides private connectivity without NAT gateway. Free, highly available, eliminates NAT costs.
explanation.why_correct: Gateway endpoint = FREE (no hourly charge, no data processing fees). Routes S3 traffic privately within VPC—never touches internet. HA by design (managed by AWS). Eliminates NAT Gateway costs ($0.045/hr = $32/mo saved). Security maintained (private traffic).

why_wrong.A: NAT instance = EC2 instance with forwarding enabled. Operational overhead (patching, monitoring, scaling). Single point of failure unless HA setup. Costs similar to NAT Gateway when factoring instance + bandwidth.
why_wrong.B: Internet gateway = routes traffic to internet, makes instances publicly accessible. Security risk—exposes instances. Still need public IPs. Not private connectivity.
why_wrong.D: Direct Connect = $0.30/hr port fee ($216/mo) + data transfer. For on-premises to AWS connectivity, not VPC to S3. Massive overkill and 10x more expensive.

explanation.exam_tips: 'VPC to S3 same region' + 'reduce NAT costs' = Gateway VPC endpoint. Gateway endpoint = S3 + DynamoDB only. Interface endpoint = other AWS services ($0.01/hr). Direct Connect = on-prem to AWS. Internet gateway = public internet access.
memorize: Gateway endpoint: FREE, S3 and DynamoDB only
Interface endpoint: $0.01/hr per AZ + data processing $0.01/GB
NAT Gateway: $0.045/hr + $0.045/GB processed
Direct Connect: $0.30/hr (1Gbps port) + transfer fees
Gateway endpoint: updates route table, no ENI

question_en: A company needs to run a critical data processing workload that uses a Python script every night. The workload takes 1 hour to finish. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the AWS Fargate launch type. Use the Fargate Spot capacity provider. Schedule the job to run once every night.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Amazon EC2 launch type. Schedule the job to run once every night.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the existing Python code. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke the function once every night.
options.D: Create an Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance that runs Amazon Linux. Migrate the Python script to the instance. Use a cron job to schedule the script. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the instance once every night.

explanation.full_text: Fargate Spot for nightly 1-hour batch job. Serverless container, up to 70% savings vs On-Demand, no infrastructure management.
explanation.why_correct: Fargate Spot = up to 70% discount vs Fargate On-Demand. 1 hour job = well within tolerance (Spot gives 2-min warning). Nightly schedule = flexible timing, can tolerate occasional reschedule. Serverless = no EC2 management. Pay only for 1hr/day execution.

why_wrong.B: ECS with EC2 = manage cluster instances, scaling, patching. EC2 costs even when idle (23hrs/day). Higher operational overhead than Fargate serverless.
why_wrong.C: Lambda max execution = 15 minutes. Job takes 1 hour. Lambda would timeout after 15 min and fail. Wrong compute service for long-running tasks.
why_wrong.D: Complex orchestration: Lambda to start/stop EC2 + cron on instance. Multiple components = more failure points. EC2 boot time (~2 min) adds overhead. More expensive than Fargate Spot when factoring operational complexity.

explanation.exam_tips: Job duration decision: <15min = Lambda, 15min-hours = Fargate, always-on = EC2. 'Critical' + 'nightly' + 'flexible' = Fargate Spot acceptable. Spot = up to 90% discount EC2, 70% Fargate. Long-running batch = Fargate/Batch, not Lambda.
memorize: Lambda max: 15 minutes execution time
Fargate Spot: up to 70% discount, 2-minute termination notice
Fargate pricing: per vCPU-second + GB-second
ECS launch types: Fargate (serverless) vs EC2 (manage cluster)
AWS Batch: job orchestration, can use Fargate or EC2 Spot

question_en: A company runs a web application in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. The application runs during business hours only. The company cannot allow interruptions to the application during business hours. The company wants to optimize compute costs for the application based on the application ' s usage pattern. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Manually terminate the instances during non-business hours. Manually launch new instances during business hours.
options.B: Create a scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Configure the policy to scale out during business hours and to scale in during non-business hours.
options.C: Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances in the Auto Scaling group.
options.D: Purchase Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances on a 1-year term to handle the maximum expected load for the Auto Scaling group.

explanation.full_text: Scheduled scaling policy automates scale-out during business hours and scale-in after hours. Zero operational overhead, predictable cost reduction.
explanation.why_correct: Scheduled scaling = automation for predictable time-based patterns. Configure two actions: scale-out at 8am (increase desired/min capacity), scale-in at 6pm (decrease to zero). Auto Scaling handles all instance lifecycle. Zero manual intervention. Prevents interruptions during business hours.

why_wrong.A: Manual termination/launch = high operational overhead. Human error risk. Delays in morning startup. Violates 'LEAST operational overhead' requirement. Auto Scaling exists to automate this.
why_wrong.C: Spot Instances = 2-minute termination notice risk. Could interrupt application DURING business hours when demand spikes. Violates 'cannot allow interruptions' requirement. Spot good for fault-tolerant workloads only.
why_wrong.D: Reserved Instances for maximum = paying 24/7 for capacity used only ~8hrs/day. Wastes 67% of reservation on idle time. More expensive than scheduled On-Demand. RIs need consistent usage.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Predictable schedule' + 'business hours only' = scheduled scaling. 'Cannot tolerate interruptions' = exclude Spot. Manual operations = avoid when automation exists. RIs = for 24/7 or multi-shift workloads. Scheduled scaling supports cron expressions.
memorize: Scheduled scaling: time-based, recurring or one-time actions
Supports cron expressions: '0 8 * * MON-FRI' (8am weekdays)
Can modify: desired, minimum, maximum capacity
Spot interruption: 2-minute warning, 5-20% termination rate
RI utilization: need >50% uptime for cost savings vs On-Demand

question_en: A company hosts a public web application on AWS with a three-tier architecture: a frontend Auto Scaling group, an application Auto Scaling group, and an Amazon RDS database. During unexpected traffic spikes, the company notices long delays in startup time when the frontend and application tiers scale out. The company needs to improve scaling performance without negatively affecting user experience. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Decrease the minimum number of EC2 instances for both Auto Scaling groups. Increase the desired number of instances to meet peak demand.
options.B: Configure the maximum number of instances for both Auto Scaling groups to the number required for peak demand. Create a warm pool.
options.C: Increase the maximum number of EC2 instances for both Auto Scaling groups to meet normal demand. Create a warm pool.
options.D: Use scheduled scaling. Increase EC2 and RDS instance sizes.

explanation.full_text: Warm pool with pre-initialized instances eliminates scale-out delays. Set maximum to peak demand capacity to handle spikes.
explanation.why_correct: Warm pool = pre-initialized stopped/running instances ready to activate. Eliminates boot time, initialization, health check delays. 'Max to peak demand' = ensures capacity available for spikes. Instances in warm pool: minimal cost (stopped = EBS only ~$0.80/mo/instance, running = configurable). Faster than cold launch by 2-5 minutes.

why_wrong.A: Decreasing minimum = increases scale-out time (more instances to launch from zero). Contradicts goal of improving scale performance. 'Increase desired to peak' = wastes money running idle capacity 24/7.
why_wrong.C: Illogical: 'max to meet normal demand' leaves no headroom for spikes. Maximum should be peak capacity, not normal. Warm pool without proper max won't help unexpected surges.
why_wrong.D: Scheduled scaling = for predictable patterns, not unexpected spikes. Increasing instance sizes (vertical scaling) = more expensive, doesn't address launch delay. Larger RDS = unrelated to Auto Scaling speed.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Unexpected spikes' + 'scale-out delay' = warm pool. Scheduled scaling = predictable patterns. Warm pool states: Stopped (cheap), Running (faster), Hibernated (fastest). Max capacity = buffer for spikes. Min capacity = baseline instances.
memorize: Warm pool: maintains pre-initialized instances outside ASG
States: Stopped (EBS cost only), Running (full cost), Hibernated (RAM to EBS)
Warm pool cost: stopped ~$0.80/mo/instance (20GB EBS)
Launch time: cold 3-5min, warm stopped 30-60sec, warm running 5-10sec
Health checks: Warm pool instances bypass until entering InService

question_en:
A company is developing a SaaS solution for customers. The solution runs on Amazon EC2 instances that have Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes attached.



Within the SaaS application, customers can request how much storage they need. The application needs to allocate the amount of block storage each customer requests. A solutions architect must design an operationally efficient solution that meets the storage scaling requirement. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Migrate the data from the EBS volumes to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class.
options.B: Migrate the data from the EBS volumes to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Use the EFS Standard storage class. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to increase the EFS volume capacity based on user input.
options.C: Migrate the data from the EBS volumes to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to increase the capacity of the file system based on user input.
options.D: Invoke an AWS Lambda function to increase the size of EBS volumes based on user input by using EBS Elastic Volumes.

explanation.full_text: EBS Elastic Volumes allow dynamic resizing without downtime. Lambda automation triggers resize based on customer requests.
explanation.why_correct: Elastic Volumes = modify size, type, IOPS online (no downtime). Increase gp3 from 100GB → 500GB in seconds. Lambda function receives customer storage request, calls ModifyVolume API, updates volume. Block storage semantics preserved. Cost: pay only for allocated capacity + Lambda invocations (~$0.01/resize).

why_wrong.A: S3 = object storage (PUT/GET APIs), not block storage. Applications using file system I/O or databases need block/file storage. Cannot mount S3 as drive. Architectural rewrite required.
why_wrong.B: EFS = shared file system across instances. Volume capacity automatic (no Lambda needed). Elastic by design—statement 'invoke Lambda to increase capacity' shows misunderstanding. More expensive: $0.30/GB vs EBS $0.08/GB.
why_wrong.C: FSx Windows = SMB file shares, Active Directory integration. Overkill for simple block storage. More expensive: $0.13-2.00/GB/month. Lambda resize = FSx doesn't need manual capacity management like described.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Block storage' + 'dynamic allocation' = EBS Elastic Volumes. S3 = object storage. EFS/FSx = file storage (shared across instances). EBS = attached to single instance. Elastic Volumes = modify online, some types require reboot for older generations.
memorize: Elastic Volumes: gp3, io1, io2, st1, sc1 (not standard/magnetic)
Modifications: size (increase only), type, IOPS, throughput
Cooldown: 6 hours between modifications per volume
Size limit: gp3 16TB, io2 64TB, st1/sc1 16TB
Cost: same as manual create/attach, no modification fee

question_en: A company has an employee web portal. Employees log in to the portal to view payroll details. The company is developing a new system to give employees the ability to upload scanned documents for reimbursement. The company runs a program to extract text-based data from the documents and attach the extracted information to each employee ' s reimbursement IDs for processing. The employee web portal requires 100% uptime. The document extract program runs infrequently throughout the day on an on-demand basis. The company wants to build a scalable and cost-effective new system that will require minimal changes to the existing web portal. The company does not want to make any code changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?

options.A: Run Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group for the web portal. Use an AWS Lambda function to run the document extract program. Invoke the Lambda function when an employee uploads a new reimbursement document.
options.B: Run Amazon EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group for the web portal. Run the document extract program on EC2 Spot Instances Start document extract program instances when an employee uploads a new reimbursement document.
options.C: Purchase a Savings Plan to run the web portal and the document extract program. Run the web portal and the document extract program in an Auto Scaling group.
options.D: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to host the web portal. Use Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function for the existing functionalities. Use the Lambda function to run the document extract program. Invoke the Lambda function when the API that is associated with a new document upload is called.

explanation.full_text: EC2 On-Demand Auto Scaling for 100% uptime portal. Lambda for event-driven document extraction. No code changes needed.
explanation.why_correct: EC2 On-Demand = 100% uptime guaranteed (no interruptions). Auto Scaling = handles traffic variations automatically. Lambda = triggered by S3 upload event, runs extraction, pays only per execution. Event-driven = efficient, no polling. 'No code changes' = existing portal continues unchanged, Lambda added as backend service.

why_wrong.B: Spot for web portal = interruption risk violates '100% uptime' requirement. Spot for document extraction = acceptable but adds complexity. Web portal must be always available—Spot unacceptable.
why_wrong.C: Savings Plan = reduces cost but doesn't address architecture. Running extraction program in Auto Scaling group = always-on costs for infrequent workload. Less efficient than Lambda event-driven model.
why_wrong.D: Migrate portal to S3 static hosting + API Gateway = MAJOR architectural change. Violates 'minimal changes' and 'no code changes' requirements. Would need complete portal rewrite as SPA.

explanation.exam_tips: '100% uptime' = exclude Spot. 'Infrequent on-demand' = Lambda. 'No code changes' = keep existing architecture, add services. S3 event → Lambda = standard pattern. Spot acceptable for: batch jobs, fault-tolerant apps, dev/test.
memorize: Lambda max execution: 15 minutes timeout
S3 events: free, triggers Lambda/SNS/SQS automatically
Spot interruption rate: varies 5-20% depending on instance type
EC2 On-Demand: no commitments, highest per-hour cost
Savings Plans: 1-3 year commitment, 20-60% discount

question_en: A finance company uses backup software to back up its data to physical tape storage on-premises. To comply with regulations, the company needs to store the data for 7 years. The company must be able to restore archived data within one week when necessary. The company wants to migrate the backup data to AWS to reduce costs. The company does not want to change the current backup software. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Use AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway to copy the data to virtual tapes. Use AWS DataSync to migrate the virtual tapes to the Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Change the target of the backup software to S3 Standard-IA.
options.B: Convert the physical tapes to virtual tapes. Use AWS DataSync to migrate the virtual tapes to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Change the target of the backup software to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
options.C: Use AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway to copy the data to virtual tapes. Migrate the virtual tapes to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Change the target of the backup software to the virtual tapes.
options.D: Convert the physical tapes to virtual tapes. Use AWS Snowball Edge storage-optimized devices to migrate the virtual tapes to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Change the target of the backup software to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.

explanation.full_text: Tape Gateway emulates physical tapes as virtual tapes in VTL. Migrate to Glacier Deep Archive for 7-year retention at lowest cost.
explanation.why_correct: Tape Gateway = virtual tape library (VTL), compatible with existing backup software (Veeam, Veritas, NetBackup). No software changes needed. Deep Archive = $0.00099/GB/month (cheapest storage class). 1-week retrieval = standard retrieval 12-48 hours meets requirement. VTL → Deep Archive = automatic archival lifecycle.

why_wrong.A: DataSync migrates data, doesn't create VTL for backup software. Standard-IA = $0.0125/GB (12x more expensive than Deep Archive). Cannot 'change target to S3 Standard-IA'—backup software expects tape protocol.
why_wrong.B: 'Convert physical to virtual tapes' = manual process not offered by AWS. Backup software needs VTL interface, not direct S3 API. Glacier Flexible = $0.004/GB (4x more than Deep Archive).
why_wrong.D: Snowball Edge = one-time migration device, not ongoing backup solution. Cannot 'change backup target to Glacier'—software needs tape interface. Manual conversion + one-time transfer doesn't solve ongoing backups.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Backup software' + 'tapes' + 'no changes' = Tape Gateway. Tape Gateway stores: cache locally, data in S3 (Standard/Glacier), tapes archive to Deep Archive. 'Long-term archive' = Deep Archive. 'Frequent access' = Flexible Retrieval.
memorize: Tape Gateway: up to 1,500 virtual tapes, 1PB total
Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB, 180-day minimum, 12-48hr retrieval
Glacier Flexible: $0.004/GB, 90-day minimum, 3-5hr retrieval
Tape Gateway supported: Veeam, Veritas, Commvault, NetBackup
Virtual tape: 100GB - 5TB each

question_en: A company needs a data encryption solution for a machine learning (ML) process. The solution must use an AWS managed service. The ML process currently reads a large number of objects in Amazon S3 that are encrypted by a customer managed AWS KMS key. The current process incurs significant costs because of excessive calls to AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to decrypt S3 objects. The company wants to reduce the costs of API calls to decrypt S3 objects.

options.A: Switch from a customer managed KMS key to an AWS managed KMS key.
options.B: Remove the AWS KMS encryption from the S3 bucket. Use a bucket policy to encrypt the data instead.
options.C: Recreate the KMS key in AWS CloudHSM.
options.D: Use S3 Bucket Keys to perform server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) to encrypt and decrypt objects from Amazon S3.

explanation.full_text: S3 Bucket Keys reduce KMS API calls by generating bucket-level data key instead of per-object calls. Reduces costs significantly.
explanation.why_correct: Bucket Keys = single KMS call per bucket every 5 minutes, not per object. ML process reads 10,000 objects/hour: without Bucket Keys = 10,000 KMS calls ($0.03/10K = $3/hr = $2,160/mo). WITH Bucket Keys = ~12 calls/hr ($0.000036/hr = $0.26/mo). 99.99% cost reduction. Transparent encryption, same security model.

why_wrong.A: AWS managed key vs customer managed = same API call frequency. Both call KMS per object without Bucket Keys. Price identical ($0.03/10K requests). Switching key type doesn't reduce call volume.
