why_wrong.B: Removing encryption = violates 'must use AWS managed service' requirement. Bucket policy cannot encrypt data—policies control access, not encryption. Security/compliance violation.
why_wrong.C: CloudHSM = $1.45/hr per HSM ($1,044/mo) + setup complexity. More expensive than current KMS + adds operational overhead. Doesn't reduce API call frequency—same issue persists.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Excessive KMS costs' + 'many S3 objects' = enable Bucket Keys. Bucket Keys compatible with: SSE-KMS only (not SSE-S3 or SSE-C). Reduces costs for: ML pipelines, ETL jobs, high-volume reads. AWS/Customer managed = same call pattern without Bucket Keys.
memorize: S3 Bucket Keys: reduces KMS requests by ~99% for SSE-KMS
KMS pricing: $0.03 per 10,000 requests (first 20K/mo free)
Without Bucket Keys: 1 KMS call per object operation
With Bucket Keys: 1 KMS call per ~bucket per 5 minutes
CloudHSM: $1.45/hr per HSM, customer manages keys

question_en: A company has a large data workload that runs for 6 hours each day. The company cannot lose any data while the process is running. A solutions architect is designing an Amazon EMR cluster configuration to support this critical data workload. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances.
options.B: Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node and core nodes on On-Demand Instances and the task nodes on Spot Instances.
options.C: Configure a transient cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance and the core nodes and task nodes on Spot Instances.
options.D: Configure a long-running cluster that runs the primary node on an On-Demand Instance, the core nodes on Spot Instances, and the task nodes on Spot Instances.

explanation.full_text: Transient EMR cluster terminates after job completes. Primary + core nodes On-Demand for data integrity, task nodes Spot for cost savings.
explanation.why_correct: Transient cluster = runs 6 hours, terminates, saves 18 hours daily idle costs. Primary node = cluster manager (YARN, metadata). Core nodes = HDFS data storage. Both On-Demand = no interruption, no data loss. Task nodes = processing only (no HDFS), Spot acceptable, up to 70% discount. 6hr/day * $3/hr * 10 nodes = $180/day vs $720/day long-running.

why_wrong.A: Long-running cluster = 24/7 charges for 6hr/day workload. Wastes 75% of hours on idle cluster. Configuration correct (primary/core On-Demand, task Spot) but cluster type wrong.
why_wrong.C: Core nodes on Spot = HDFS data at risk. Spot interruption = potential data loss. Violates 'cannot lose any data' requirement. Core nodes must be On-Demand or Reserved.
why_wrong.D: Long-running + core on Spot = double failure. Idle costs + data loss risk. Most expensive option with highest risk.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Short duration' + 'scheduled' = transient cluster. 'Long-running/always-on' = persistent cluster. Primary + core = critical (On-Demand/Reserved). Task = processing only (Spot OK). HDFS replication = 3 by default but Spot interruption still risks data.
memorize: EMR node types: Primary (1, cluster manager), Core (1+, HDFS + compute), Task (0+, compute only)
Transient: auto-terminates after job completion
Persistent: stays running between jobs
Spot interruption: 2-min warning, EMR can tolerate on task nodes
Core node Spot: not recommended, risks HDFS data loss

question_en: A company runs multiple workloads in separate AWS environments. The company wants to optimize its AWS costs but must maintain the same level of performance for the environments. The company ' s production environment requires resources to be highly available. The other environments do not require highly available resources. Each environment has the same set of networking components, including the following: 1 VPC 1 Application Load Balancer 4 subnets distributed across 2 Availability Zones 2 public subnets and 2 private subnets 2 NAT gateways 1 in each public subnet 1 internet gateway Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Do not change the production environment workload. For each non-production workload, remove one NAT gateway and update the route tables for private subnets to target the remaining NAT gateway for the destination 0.0.0.0/0.
options.B: Reduce the number of Availability Zones that all workloads in all environments use.
options.C: Replace every NAT gateway with a t4g.large NAT instance. Update the route tables for each private subnet to target the NAT instance that is in the same Availability Zone for the destination 0.0.0.0/0.
options.D: In each environment, create one transit gateway and remove one NAT gateway.

explanation.full_text: Production keeps 2 NAT gateways for HA. Non-production removes 1 NAT gateway to save costs, routes all private traffic through remaining gateway.
explanation.why_correct: Production = high availability required, keep 1 NAT per AZ (current design). Non-production = HA not required, consolidate to 1 NAT gateway. Savings: $0.045/hr * 24hr * 30d = $32.40/mo per removed gateway. Multiple non-prod environments = significant savings. Update route tables: both private subnets point to same NAT gateway.

why_wrong.B: Reducing AZs affects entire architecture: subnets, ALB targets, database replicas. Decreases fault tolerance even for production. More than just NAT cost—impacts design fundamentals. Too broad and risky.
why_wrong.C: NAT instance = operational overhead (patching, monitoring, scaling, HA setup). Cost similar when factoring EC2 + data transfer. t4g.large = $0.0672/hr ($48/mo) vs NAT Gateway $0.045/hr ($32/mo) + management effort.
why_wrong.D: Transit Gateway = for connecting multiple VPCs/on-premises ($0.05/hr + $0.02/GB). Unrelated to NAT gateway function. Doesn't provide internet egress. Wrong solution for different problem.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Production HA' vs 'non-production cost optimization' = common pattern. NAT Gateway HA = 1 per AZ. Single NAT = cross-AZ data transfer charges ($0.01/GB) but usually cheaper than second NAT hourly. Transit Gateway = VPC connectivity, not internet egress.
memorize: NAT Gateway cost: $0.045/hr + $0.045/GB processed
NAT Gateway HA: deploy 1 per AZ with route table per AZ
Cross-AZ data transfer: $0.01/GB (within region)
Transit Gateway: $0.05/hr per attachment + $0.02/GB
NAT instance: manage yourself, single point of failure without HA setup

question_en: A company is planning to migrate multiple workloads to Amazon EC2 instances and needs to determine an appropriate AWS account structure. The workloads must be isolated from one another and belong to separate business units. The company needs to be able to perform chargeback to the business units by using a consolidated monthly view. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?

options.A: Create a separate standalone AWS account for each business unit. Create a script to call AWS Cost Explorer APIs from each account to perform chargeback.
options.B: Create a single organization in AWS Organizations. Create a member account for each business unit. Use the bill from the organization management account to perform chargeback.
options.C: Create a single AWS account for all the business units. Assign tags to the EC2 instances that correspond with the business units. Activate the tags for cost allocation to perform chargeback by using AWS Cost Explorer.
options.D: Create a separate organization in AWS Organizations for each business unit. Use the bill in each organization management account to perform chargeback.

explanation.full_text: AWS Organizations with member account per business unit provides isolation and consolidated billing for chargeback.
explanation.why_correct: Organizations = single payer account (management), multiple member accounts (one per business unit). Consolidated billing = one bill with per-account breakdown. Chargeback = use Cost Explorer to group by account (linked account dimension). Isolation = complete account-level separation. Low overhead = AWS manages consolidation automatically.

why_wrong.A: Separate standalone accounts = no consolidated billing. Must call Cost Explorer API from each account separately, aggregate manually. High operational overhead. No centralized billing view.
why_wrong.C: Single account + tags = weaker isolation. Shared IAM, shared service limits, shared default VPC. Tags can be forgotten/misconfigured. Tag-based chargeback works but account-level isolation better for 'separate business units' requirement.
why_wrong.D: Separate organization per unit = no consolidation. Each org has own management account and bill. Defeats 'consolidated monthly view' requirement. Cannot aggregate across separate organizations easily.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Multiple business units' + 'isolation' + 'consolidated billing' = AWS Organizations. One org, multiple member accounts. Management account = consolidated bill. Tags = additional granularity within accounts. Separate orgs = when need separate legal entities or complete independence.
memorize: Organizations: 1 management account + member accounts
Consolidated billing: volume discounts, single payment method
Service Control Policies (SCPs): guardrails across accounts
Member account limit: soft limit 10, can increase to thousands
Cost Explorer: filter by linked account for chargeback

question_en: A company runs compute workloads across multiple private subnets across multiple VPCs. Sometimes the company opens shell access to Amazon EC2 instances in the private subnets to troubleshoot issues. The current design uses NAT gateways. The company wants to reduce costs. However, the company does not support the following: • Using public IP addresses • Installing agents on instances • Permitting inbound internet access Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint in each VPC. Grant IAM permissions for administrators to connect to instances by using SSH. Decommission all NAT gateways.
options.B: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to connect to instances.
options.C: Deploy auto scaling bastion hosts behind a Network Load Balancer in each VPC. Restrict inbound access by source IP.
options.D: Create an AWS Client VPN configuration. Create routes across each VPC. Decommission all NAT gateways except one. Target the remaining NAT gateway for outbound traffic from all VPCs.

explanation.full_text: EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint provides SSH access to private instances without public IPs, NAT gateways, or agents.
explanation.why_correct: Instance Connect Endpoint = AWS managed service, connects to private EC2 via SSH using IAM credentials. No public IP needed, no NAT gateway needed, no agent installation. Traffic stays within AWS network. Cost: free (no hourly charges). 'Decommission NAT gateways' = if only used for admin access, saves $32/mo per NAT gateway.

why_wrong.B: Systems Manager Session Manager = requires SSM Agent on instances. Violates 'not support installing agents' requirement. Otherwise valid solution for this use case.
why_wrong.C: Bastion hosts = EC2 instances requiring management, patching, scaling. Network Load Balancer = $0.0225/hr ($16/mo) + bastion instance costs. 'Restrict by source IP' = requires inbound internet access (violates requirements). More expensive than Instance Connect Endpoint (free).
why_wrong.D: Client VPN = $0.10/hr per connection ($72/mo) + $0.05/GB. Complex setup (certificates, CIDR routing). 'Keep one NAT gateway' = still paying $32/mo. More expensive and complex than Instance Connect Endpoint.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Private instance access' + 'no agent' + 'no public IP' = Instance Connect Endpoint. Session Manager = requires agent. Bastion = requires inbound access + instance management. Client VPN = for persistent connectivity. Instance Connect Endpoint = launched 2023, exam favorite for this scenario.
memorize: Instance Connect Endpoint: free, no hourly charge
Supports: EC2 instances in private subnets, any VPC
Protocol: SSH (port 22), uses IAM credentials
Requires: ec2-instance-connect:OpenTunnel IAM permission
Alternative: Session Manager (requires agent), bastion host

question_en: A company wants to migrate an application that processes logs to AWS. Currently, the application runs on an on-premises storage area network (SAN). The application reads and processes large log files sequentially. The application requires throughput of up to 500 MBps. A solutions architect needs to migrate the application with minimal change to the application architecture. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Use a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon EBS volume with 500 MBps provisioned throughput.
options.B: Use a Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) Amazon EBS volume with provisioned storage based on the throughput requirement.
options.C: Use a Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volume with provisioned storage based on the throughput requirement.
options.D: Use a Provisioned IOPS (io1) Amazon EBS volume with 500 MBps provisioned throughput.

explanation.full_text: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) provides 500 MBps throughput for sequential log file processing at lowest HDD cost.
explanation.why_correct: st1 = designed for sequential, throughput-intensive workloads. Max throughput: 500 MBps (matches requirement exactly). Cost: $0.045/GB (vs gp3 $0.08/GB = 44% cheaper). Ideal for: log processing, big data, data warehouses. 'Minimal change' = EBS preserves block storage model from SAN.

why_wrong.A: gp3 = general purpose SSD, good for mixed workloads. Cost: $0.08/GB + $0.006/provisioned IOPS. More expensive than st1 for sequential throughput workload. SSD premium unnecessary for log processing (doesn't need low latency).
why_wrong.C: sc1 (Cold HDD) = $0.015/GB cheapest but designed for infrequent access. Max throughput: 250 MBps (only half required 500 MBps). Would not meet performance requirement. For archival/cold storage.
why_wrong.D: io1 = Provisioned IOPS SSD, premium tier. Cost: $0.125/GB + $0.065/provisioned IOPS. Most expensive option. Designed for databases needing high IOPS (not throughput). Overkill for log processing.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Sequential' + 'throughput' = st1 or gp3. 'Large files' + 'log processing' = st1 optimized. SSD (gp3/io1/io2) = random I/O, low latency. HDD (st1/sc1) = sequential, high throughput. st1 = frequently accessed, sc1 = infrequently accessed.
memorize: st1: $0.045/GB, max 500 MBps, 500 IOPS, 125 MB/s per TiB baseline
sc1: $0.015/GB, max 250 MBps, 250 IOPS, cold storage
gp3: $0.08/GB, 3,000 IOPS baseline, 125 MBps baseline
io2: $0.125/GB, up to 64,000 IOPS, 1,000 MBps
st1 use cases: MapReduce, Kafka, log processing, data warehouse

question_en:
A company’s application is deployed on Amazon EC2 instances and uses AWS Lambda functions for an event-driven architecture. The company uses nonproduction development environments in a different AWS account to test new features before the company deploys the features to production. The production instances show constant usage because of customers in different time zones. The company uses nonproduction instances only during business hours on weekdays. The company does not use the



nonproduction instances on the weekends. The company wants to optimize the costs to run its application on AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Use On-Demand Instances for the production instances. Use Dedicated Hosts for the nonproduction instances on weekends only.
options.B: Use Reserved Instances for the production instances and the nonproduction instances. Shut down the nonproduction instances when not in use.
options.C: Use Compute Savings Plans for the production instances. Use On-Demand Instances for the nonproduction instances. Shut down the nonproduction instances when not in use.
options.D: Use Dedicated Hosts for the production instances. Use EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the nonproduction instances.

explanation.full_text: Compute Savings Plans for steady production workload. On-Demand for non-production, shut down outside business hours.
explanation.why_correct: Compute Savings Plans = flexible commitment (EC2, Lambda, Fargate), 1-3 year term, up to 66% discount. Production 24/7 usage = maximizes savings plan value. Non-production = 40 hours/week (8hrs * 5 days) = 24% utilization. On-Demand + shutdown = pay only active hours. 76% time savings by stopping instances.

why_wrong.A: Dedicated Hosts for non-production = $3+/hr per host ($2,160/mo minimum). Used for licensing (Oracle, Windows Server) or compliance. Massive overkill and expense for simple non-prod dev/test environments.
why_wrong.B: Reserved Instances for non-production = paying for 168 hours/week, using only 40 hours. Wastes 76% of reservation. RIs better than Savings Plans when: single instance family/region commitment acceptable.
why_wrong.D: Dedicated Hosts for production = most expensive option. Instance Savings Plans for non-prod = still wasting 76% of hours. Gets commitment type backwards (production should be Compute, not Dedicated).

explanation.exam_tips: 'Steady production' = Savings Plans or RIs. 'Part-time usage' = On-Demand + stop/start. Compute Savings Plans = most flexible (any instance, any region, any family). Instance Savings Plans = single family. Dedicated = licensing or isolation requirements only.
memorize: Compute Savings Plans: up to 66% discount, any instance/region/family
Instance Savings Plans: up to 72% discount, locked to instance family
EC2 Reserved: up to 72% discount, locked to instance type/region
Dedicated Hosts: from ~$3/hr ($2,160/mo), bring-your-own-license
Stop EC2: charged for EBS only, ~$0.80/mo per 20GB

question_en:
A company uses an Amazon RDS MySQL database to store data for several applications. The company wants to understand use patterns for the database so the company can identify oppor-tunities to optimize costs. A solutions architect needs to analyze the RDS DB instance to identify right-sizing opportuni-ties.



Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?

options.A: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events. Use Amazon Athena to query CloudTrail events. Right-size the RDS DB instance based on the number of transactions.
options.B: Enable Performance Insights for the RDS DB instance. Right-size the RDS DB instance based on the maximum CPU utilization.
options.C: Enable AWS X-Ray to understand the transactions that run on the RDS DB instance. Right-size the RDS DB instance based on the number of transactions.
options.D: Enable Amazon CloudWatch Logs for the applications. Aggregate the data from Cloud-Watch Logs for all the applications. Right-size the RDS DB instance based on the aggregated logs.

explanation.full_text: Performance Insights provides database performance metrics including CPU, waits, and queries for right-sizing analysis with minimal setup.
explanation.why_correct: Performance Insights = enable with 1 click, free for 7 days retention (paid for longer). Shows: DB load (average active sessions), top SQL queries, wait events, host metrics (CPU, memory, network). Right-sizing = analyze max CPU, memory, connections vs provisioned capacity. Identify over/under-provisioning. Built-in RDS feature, no infrastructure.

why_wrong.A: CloudTrail = API audit logs (who called what API when). Does NOT capture database performance, query execution, or transaction volume. Cannot determine CPU/memory utilization from CloudTrail. Wrong tool category.
why_wrong.B: Performance Insights DOES show CPU but answer says 'based on maximum CPU utilization' only—incomplete. Right-sizing needs: CPU, memory, IOPS, connections, query patterns. Single metric insufficient for optimization decisions.
why_wrong.C: X-Ray = application tracing (request flow through services). Doesn't capture database internal metrics (CPU, waits, buffer cache). Shows query latency from app perspective but not DB resource utilization.
why_wrong.D: Application CloudWatch Logs = application layer data. Doesn't include database metrics unless manually instrumented. 'Aggregate from all applications' = complex ETL pipeline. More effort than native Performance Insights.

explanation.exam_tips: 'RDS performance analysis' = Performance Insights first choice. CloudTrail = audit. X-Ray = distributed tracing. CloudWatch = metrics + logs. Performance Insights = free tier 7 days, paid $0.009/vCPU-hour for longer retention. Right-sizing = compare actual utilization vs capacity.
memorize: Performance Insights: 7-day free retention, $0.009/vCPU-hr beyond
Metrics: DB Load (AAS), top SQL, wait events, host metrics
Counter metrics: SelectQuery, Deadlocks, CommitLatency
Alternative: Enhanced Monitoring (OS metrics, RDS agent)
Right-sizing dimensions: CPU, memory, storage, IOPS, connections

question_en: A company needs to design a solution to process videos that users upload to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each video file is approximately 1 GB in size and takes approximately 20 minutes to process. During peak hours, the company expects to process approximately 100 simultaneous uploads. The video file processing is stateless and can run in parallel as soon as the video files arrive in the S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Use an AWS Lambda function to process each video. Split the video files into chunks, and use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate multiple processing steps.
options.B: Use an Amazon EKS cluster with AWS Fargate profiles to deploy one container for each uploaded video. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke the cluster when a user uploads a video.
options.C: Use Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group to process each file. Configure the Auto Scaling policy to increase the number of instances based on the number of files that the application needs to process.
options.D: Use an Amazon ECS cluster with the AWS Fargate launch type. Use Fargate Spot capacity to run one container task for each uploaded video. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke the cluster when a user uploads a video.

explanation.full_text: ECS on Fargate Spot runs event-driven container tasks at up to 70% discount. EventBridge triggers task per uploaded video.
explanation.why_correct: 20-minute processing = exceeds Lambda 15-min limit. Fargate = serverless containers, no instance management. Fargate Spot = up to 70% discount vs Fargate On-Demand. EventBridge = triggers ECS RunTask on S3 upload event. Pay only for 100 * 20 min = 33 hours/day during peak. Spot acceptable for stateless video processing (can retry if interrupted).

why_wrong.A: Lambda max execution = 15 minutes. Video processing = 20 minutes. Lambda would timeout and fail. 'Split into chunks + Step Functions' = major architectural change, adds complexity, still hits Lambda limits for large files.
why_wrong.B: EKS = Kubernetes, more operational overhead than ECS. Correct use of Fargate but EKS complexity unnecessary for simple parallel task pattern. ECS simpler for event-driven single-task workloads.
why_wrong.C: EC2 On-Demand Auto Scaling = managing instances. Always-on minimum capacity vs serverless pay-per-use. More expensive than Fargate Spot. Operational overhead (AMIs, patching, scaling policies).

explanation.exam_tips: '> 15 minutes' = exclude Lambda. 'Stateless parallel container' = Fargate. 'Cost-effective container' = Fargate Spot. ECS vs EKS: ECS = simpler, AWS-native; EKS = Kubernetes portability. EventBridge → ECS RunTask = standard event-driven pattern.
memorize: Lambda: 15-minute max execution time
Fargate Spot: up to 70% discount, 2-minute termination notice
Fargate pricing: per vCPU-second + per GB-second
ECS: simpler, integrated; EKS: Kubernetes, portable
EventBridge: 14M events/month free, then $1/million

question_en: A company runs an application that stores and shares photos. Users upload the photos to an Amazon S3 bucket. Every day, users upload approximately 150 photos. The company wants to design a solution that creates a thumbnail of each new photo and stores the thumbnail in a second S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to invoke a script every minute on a long-running Amazon EMR cluster. Configure the script to generate thumbnails for the photos that do not have thumbnails. Configure the script to upload the thumbnails to the second S3 bucket.
options.B: Configure an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to invoke a script every minute on a memoryoptimized Amazon EC2 instance that is always on. Configure the script to generate thumbnails for the photos that do not have thumbnails. Configure the script to upload the thumbnails to the second S3 bucket.
options.C: Configure an S3 event notification to invoke an AWS Lambda function each time a user uploads a new photo to the application. Configure the Lambda function to generate a thumbnail and to upload the thumbnail to the second S3 bucket.
options.D: Configure S3 Storage Lens to invoke an AWS Lambda function each time a user uploads a new photo to the application. Configure the Lambda function to generate a thumbnail and to upload the thumbnail to a second S3 bucket.

explanation.full_text: S3 event notification triggers Lambda on each photo upload. Lambda generates thumbnail and stores in second bucket.
explanation.why_correct: S3 event notification = free, automatic trigger on PUT object. Lambda = executes only when photo uploaded, 150 invocations/day. Cost: 150 * 5 seconds * 512MB = ~$0.01/month Lambda + negligible S3 events. Serverless, auto-scales, no idle costs. Perfect event-driven pattern.

why_wrong.A: EMR = Hadoop/Spark cluster for big data (petabyte scale). Minimum 3 nodes ~$0.50/hr = $360/month continuously. 36,000x more expensive than Lambda for 150 photos/day. Massive overkill.
why_wrong.B: Memory-optimized EC2 always-on = $48/month minimum (r6i.large). Idle 99.9% of time (150 photos in 1,440 minutes = 1 photo per 9.6 minutes). Polling script inefficient vs event-driven. 4,800x more expensive.
why_wrong.D: S3 Storage Lens = analytics dashboard for storage metrics (access patterns, cost optimization recommendations). NOT an event trigger mechanism. Cannot invoke Lambda. Wrong category of tool.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Photo upload' + 'generate thumbnail' = classic S3 event → Lambda pattern. EMR/EC2 = for sustained compute workloads. Storage Lens = storage analytics, not event processing. S3 events = free, unlimited notifications. Lambda = $0.20/1M requests + compute time.
memorize: S3 event notifications: support Lambda, SNS, SQS
Event types: ObjectCreated, ObjectRemoved, ObjectRestore, Replication
Lambda free tier: 1M requests/month, 400K GB-seconds/month
Thumbnail generation: typical 2-5 seconds, 256-512MB memory
Storage Lens: storage usage analytics, retention analysis

question_en: A company is designing a new application that uploads files to an Amazon S3 bucket. The uploaded files are processed to extract metadata. Processing must take less than 5 seconds. The volume and frequency of the uploads vary from a few files each hour to hundreds of concurrent uploads. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure AWS CloudTrail trails to log Amazon S3 API calls. Use AWS AppSync to process the files.
options.B: Configure a new object created S3 event notification within the bucket to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the files.
options.C: Configure Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to deliver the files to the S3 bucket. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the files.
options.D: Deploy an Amazon EC2 instance. Create a script that lists all files in the S3 bucket and processes new files. Use a cron job that runs every minute to run the script.

explanation.full_text: S3 event notification triggers Lambda on each upload. Lambda processes metadata extraction in under 5 seconds. Serverless, auto-scales, cost-effective.
explanation.why_correct: S3 event → Lambda = standard serverless pattern. Processing < 5 seconds fits within Lambda limits. Auto-scales from few files to hundreds concurrently. Cost: ~$0.20/1M requests + compute time. Zero idle costs. No infrastructure management.

why_wrong.A: CloudTrail = audit logging (who made what API call). NOT for file processing. AppSync = GraphQL API service for mobile/web apps. Wrong tool category—neither processes files.
why_wrong.B: Kinesis Data Streams = real-time streaming data ingestion (clickstreams, IoT). Overkill for simple S3 upload trigger. Additional cost: $0.015/hour per shard + $0.014/GB. More complex than direct S3 → Lambda.
why_wrong.D: EC2 cron polling = 1,440 checks/day (every minute) even with zero uploads. Always-on EC2 costs ~$7.50/mo minimum. Polling introduces latency up to 60 seconds. Manual scaling needed.

explanation.exam_tips: 'File upload' + 'variable volume' + 'quick processing' = S3 event → Lambda. CloudTrail = audit, not processing. Kinesis = high-throughput streaming. EC2 polling = anti-pattern for event-driven. S3 events = free, unlimited.
memorize: S3 event types: ObjectCreated (PUT/POST/COPY), ObjectRemoved, ObjectRestore
Lambda pricing: $0.20/1M requests + $0.0000166667/GB-second
S3 events: free, triggers Lambda/SNS/SQS
Kinesis shard: $0.015/hr + $0.014/GB PUT payload
Event-driven vs polling: push = immediate, poll = delay + waste

question_en: A media company stores customer-uploaded videos in an Amazon S3 bucket with the Standard storage class. The company wants to create an S3 Lifecycle configuration. The company will set the maximum retention time to 7 days. However, the configuration must delete any video that is more than 1 TB in size after 48 hours.

options.A: Create a single S3 Lifecycle configuration that has two rules. Configure the first rule to expire objects after 48 hours with a filter of ObjectSizeGreaterThan and a value of 1 TB. Configure the second rule to expire objects after 7 days.
options.B: Create two S3 Lifecycle configurations. Include a rule in the first configuration to expire objects after 48 hours by using a Prefix filter of LargeFiles. Include a rule in the second configuration to expire objects after 7 days.
options.C: Create a single S3 Lifecycle configuration that has two rules. Configure the first rule to expire objects after 48 hours. Configure the second rule to expire objects after 7 days.
options.D: Create two S3 Lifecycle configurations. Include a rule in the first configuration to expire objects after 48 hours. Include a rule in the second configuration to expire objects after 7 days by using a filter of ObjectSizeLessThan and a value of 1 TB.

explanation.full_text: Single Lifecycle configuration with two rules: Rule 1 expires objects >1TB after 48hrs using ObjectSizeGreaterThan filter. Rule 2 expires all objects after 7 days.
explanation.why_correct: S3 allows ONE lifecycle configuration per bucket with MULTIPLE rules. ObjectSizeGreaterThan filter = targets large files specifically. Rule 1 (size > 1TB, 48hr) + Rule 2 (no filter, 7 days) = both requirements met. S3 applies most specific matching rule first.

why_wrong.B: Cannot create two separate lifecycle configurations per bucket—S3 limitation. Prefix filter 'LargeFiles' = requires specific folder structure or naming convention not mentioned. Size-based filtering is native, prefix-based is workaround.
why_wrong.C: Single config with two generic expire rules = cannot distinguish by size. Both rules would apply to all objects—conflict. Would delete small files at 48hrs OR 7 days (whichever rule matches first). Doesn't meet requirement.
why_wrong.D: Two configurations = not supported by S3. ObjectSizeLessThan for 7-day rule = unnecessarily complex. Rule 2 should be catch-all without filter (applies to everything not caught by Rule 1).

explanation.exam_tips: S3 Lifecycle: 1 configuration per bucket, multiple rules allowed. Filters: Prefix, Tag, ObjectSizeGreaterThan, ObjectSizeLessThan. Multiple rules = most specific wins. Empty filter = applies to all objects not matched by other rules.
memorize: Lifecycle rules per bucket: 1 configuration, up to 1,000 rules
Size filters: ObjectSizeGreaterThan, ObjectSizeLessThan (bytes)
Expiration: DeleteObject or DeleteMarker actions
Transitions: Standard → IA (30d min) → Glacier (90d min from creation)
Rule priority: most specific filter wins (size > prefix > tag)

question_en: A company has migrated a two-tier application from its on-premises data center to the AWS Cloud. The data tier is a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for Oracle with 12 TiB of General Purpose SSD Amazon EBS storage. The application is designed to read and store documents in the database as binary large objects (BLOBs) with an average document size of 6 MB. The database size has grown over time, reducing performance and increasing the cost of storage. The company must improve the database performance and needs a solution that is highly available and resilient. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Reduce the RDS DB instance size. Increase the storage capacity to 24 TiB. Change the storage type to Magnetic.
options.B: Increase the RDS DB instance size. Increase the storage capacity to 24 TiB. Change the storage type to Provisioned IOPS.
options.C: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the application to store documents in the S3 bucket. Store the object metadata in the existing database.
options.D: Create an Amazon DynamoDB table. Update the application to use DynamoDB. Use AWS DMS to migrate data from the Oracle database to DynamoDB.

explanation.full_text: Store documents in S3, keep metadata and object keys in RDS. Separates large BLOB storage from relational data, reduces DB size and costs.
explanation.why_correct: S3 = designed for large objects (documents, images, videos). Cost: $0.023/GB vs RDS storage premium. RDS = optimized for transactional relational data, not BLOBs. Pattern: store S3 object key (s3://bucket/key) in DB column, retrieve via SDK. Improves DB performance (smaller size, less I/O), reduces costs, maintains HA (S3 11 9s durability).

why_wrong.A: Magnetic storage = legacy, deprecated EBS type. Terrible performance (~100 IOPS). Would degrade performance further, not improve. Reducing instance size with more storage = wrong direction.
why_wrong.B: Provisioned IOPS + 24TB = $0.125/GB storage + $0.065/IOPS = ~$5,000+/month for storage alone. Doesn't solve root problem (BLOBs don't belong in relational DB). Most expensive option.
why_wrong.D: DynamoDB = NoSQL key-value/document store. Migrating Oracle relational DB to DynamoDB = complete redesign (schema, queries, transactions). Massive effort, high risk. Doesn't address BLOB storage problem—DynamoDB 400KB item limit.

explanation.exam_tips: 'BLOBs in database' + 'growing size' = move to S3. RDS = structured relational data. S3 = unstructured objects. DynamoDB = NoSQL, not relational replacement. Pattern: S3 for content, RDS for metadata. Similar: videos, images, backups.
memorize: S3 Standard: $0.023/GB first 50TB
RDS storage: gp3 $0.115/GB, io1 $0.125/GB
DynamoDB item size: 400KB maximum
S3 object size: 5TB maximum single PUT, 5GB multipart required
Pattern: RDS stores S3 URL, application retrieves via SDK

question_en:
An ecommerce company hosts an application on AWS across multiple Availability Zones. The application experiences uniform load throughout most days.



The company hosts some components of the application in private subnets. The components need to access the internet to install and update patches. A solutions architect needs to design a cost-effective solution that provides secure outbound internet connectivity for private subnets across multiple Availability Zones. The solution must maintain high availability.

options.A: Deploy one NAT gateway in each Availability Zone. Configure the route table for each pri-vate subnet within an Availability Zone to route outbound traffic through the NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone.
options.B: Place one NAT gateway in a designated Availability Zone within the VPC. Configure the route tables of the private subnets in each Availability Zone to direct outbound traffic specifi-cally through the NAT gateway for internet access.
options.C: Deploy an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet. Configure the EC2 instance as a NAT instance. Set up the instance with security groups that allow inbound traffic from private sub-nets and outbound internet access. Configure route tables to direct traffic from the private sub-nets through the NAT instance.
options.D: Use one NAT Gateway in a Network Load Balancer (NLB) target group. Configure private subnets in each Availability Zone to route traffic to the NLB for outbound internet access.

explanation.full_text: Deploy 1 NAT Gateway per AZ. Route each private subnet through its local NAT Gateway. High availability with no single point of failure.
explanation.why_correct: NAT Gateway per AZ = zone-independent architecture. If AZ fails, other AZs unaffected. Same-AZ routing = no cross-AZ data charges ($0.01/GB saved). AWS best practice for production HA. Cost: $0.045/hr per NAT * 2 AZs = $65/month, but provides full redundancy.

why_wrong.B: Single NAT in one AZ = single point of failure. If that AZ fails, all other AZs lose internet access. Cross-AZ data transfer charges = $0.01/GB for traffic from other AZs. Violates high availability requirement.
why_wrong.C: NAT instance = legacy pattern. Manual management (patching, scaling, HA setup). Single EC2 = single point of failure. More operational overhead than managed NAT Gateway. Not recommended for production.
why_wrong.D: NLB cannot target NAT Gateway—unsupported configuration. NAT Gateway is not a valid NLB target type. NLB targets: EC2, IP, Lambda, ALB. Architectural impossibility.

explanation.exam_tips: 'High availability' + 'multiple AZs' = 1 NAT Gateway per AZ. Single NAT = cost savings for non-production but creates SPOF. Cross-AZ charges = $0.01/GB. NAT instance = legacy, avoid unless specific requirements. NAT Gateway = fully managed, HA within AZ.
memorize: NAT Gateway: $0.045/hr + $0.045/GB processed
NAT Gateway HA: 1 per AZ, route table per AZ to local NAT
Cross-AZ data transfer: $0.01/GB (same region)
NAT instance: you manage, single point of failure
NAT Gateway bandwidth: up to 45 Gbps (auto-scales)

question_en: A genomic research company analyzes approximately 50 TB of raw DNA sequence data for each project that the company stores in Amazon S3. The company accesses data files frequently during the first 30 days of each project. The company rarely accesses the data after the first 30 days. However, the company must retain the data for 7 years. The company needs a cost-effective storage solution for the data. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Store the data in Amazon EFS for the first 30 days. After 30 days, move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
options.B: Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard for the first 30 days. After 30 days, move the data to Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access S3 Standard-IA.
options.C: Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard for the first 30 days. After 30 days, move the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.D: Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard for the first 30 days. After 30 days, move the data to Amazon EBS volumes.

explanation.full_text: S3 Standard for first 30 days of frequent access, then Glacier Deep Archive for 7-year retention at lowest cost.
explanation.why_correct: S3 Standard = frequent access, low latency ($0.023/GB). Glacier Deep Archive = lowest storage cost ($0.00099/GB = 96% cheaper). 'Rarely accessed after 30 days' + '7-year retention' = perfect match for Deep Archive. Lifecycle policy automates transition. Retrieval = 12-48 hours acceptable for rare access.

why_wrong.A: EFS = file system for EC2 instances ($0.30/GB). Not designed for long-term archive. 15x more expensive than Deep Archive. Manual migration to Glacier = complex (need to copy to S3 first, then Glacier).
why_wrong.B: Standard-IA = $0.0125/GB (12x more than Deep Archive). Good for monthly access, wasteful for rare 7-year retention. 90-day minimum charge. Better choice if accessed quarterly, not annually.
why_wrong.D: EBS volumes = block storage attached to EC2 ($0.08-0.125/GB). Not designed for archival. Requires running EC2 instance to access. 80-125x more expensive than Deep Archive. Wrong storage type.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Frequent first 30 days' = Standard. 'Rarely after' + 'long retention' = Deep Archive. Standard-IA = monthly access. Flexible Retrieval = quarterly access. Deep Archive = annual or compliance. Lifecycle = automates transitions. EFS/EBS = not for archives.
memorize: S3 Standard: $0.023/GB, millisecond access
Standard-IA: $0.0125/GB, 30-day min, 90-day charge
Glacier Flexible: $0.004/GB, 90-day min, 3-5hr retrieval
Glacier Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB, 180-day min, 12-48hr retrieval
Lifecycle transitions: Standard → IA (30d) → Glacier (90d cumulative)

question_en: A company has Amazon EC2 instances that run nightly batch jobs to process data. The EC2 instances run in an Auto Scaling group that uses On-Demand billing. If a job fails on one instance, another instance will reprocess the job. The batch jobs run between 12:00 AM and 06:00 AM local time every day. Which solution will provide EC2 instances to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Purchase a 1-year Savings Plan for Amazon EC2 that covers the instance family of the Auto Scaling group that the batch job uses.
options.B: Purchase a 1-year Reserved Instance for the specific instance type and operating system of the instances in the Auto Scaling group that the batch job uses.
options.C: Create a new launch template for the Auto Scaling group. Set the instances to Spot Instances. Set a policy to scale out based on CPU usage.
options.D: Create a new launch template for the Auto Scaling group. Increase the instance size. Set a policy to scale out based on CPU usage.

explanation.full_text: Spot Instances with capacity-optimized allocation strategy for fault-tolerant nightly batch jobs. Up to 90% discount vs On-Demand.
explanation.why_correct: Fault-tolerant workload (jobs can reprocess) = perfect for Spot. 6-hour window daily = not 24/7, no benefit from Reserved/Savings. Spot discount = 60-90% vs On-Demand. Capacity-optimized = selects pools with lowest interruption risk. Auto Scaling + Spot = replaces interrupted instances automatically.

why_wrong.A: Savings Plan = 1-year commitment for 6hrs/day usage. Pays for 8,760 hours/year, uses only ~2,190 hours (25% utilization). Wastes 75% of commitment. Better for 24/7 workloads.
why_wrong.B: Reserved Instances = same problem as Savings Plan. 1-year term for part-time workload = poor utilization. Standard RIs locked to instance type = less flexible than needed.
why_wrong.D: Increasing instance size = vertical scaling, doesn't reduce cost. Larger instances often more expensive. CPU scaling = adds instances, doesn't change purchasing model. Doesn't address cost optimization.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Fault-tolerant' + 'batch' + 'part-time' = Spot Instances. 'Cannot tolerate interruption' = On-Demand or Reserved. Spot allocation strategies: capacity-optimized (minimize interruptions), price-capacity-optimized (balance), lowest-price (highest interruption risk). Reserved/Savings = for consistent usage.
memorize: Spot discount: 60-90% vs On-Demand (varies by instance/AZ)
Spot interruption: 2-minute warning via metadata
Capacity-optimized: chooses deepest capacity pools
Savings Plan utilization breakeven: ~50% uptime minimum
Spot use cases: batch, EMR, CI/CD, stateless web

question_en: A company is designing a new web application that will run on Amazon EC2 instances. The application will use Amazon DynamoDB for backend data storage. The application traffic will be unpredictable. The company expects that the application read and write throughput to the database will be moderate to high. The company needs to scale in response to application traffic. Which DynamoDB table configuration will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure DynamoDB with provisioned read and write by using the DynamoDB Standard table class. Set DynamoDB auto scaling to a maximum defined capacity.
options.B: Configure DynamoDB in on-demand mode by using the DynamoDB Standard table class.
options.C: Configure DynamoDB with provisioned read and write by using the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class. Set DynamoDB auto scaling to a maximum defined capacity.
options.D: Configure DynamoDB in on-demand mode by using the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class.

explanation.full_text: DynamoDB On-Demand mode with Standard table class. Auto-scales for unpredictable traffic, pay-per-request billing.
explanation.why_correct: On-Demand = no capacity planning, instant scaling to any request rate. 'Unpredictable traffic' = perfect fit. Pay per read/write request (WRU/RRU). Standard class = frequent access (moderate-high throughput stated). Cost: $1.25/million WRU, $0.25/million RRU.

why_wrong.A: Provisioned with auto scaling = need to predict baseline capacity. Auto scaling has cooldown periods (scale up fast, scale down slow). Can under-provision for sudden spikes. More management overhead than On-Demand.
why_wrong.C: Standard-IA class = storage costs 38% less but read/write costs 25% more than Standard. Good when storage > access costs (large items, infrequent access). 'Moderate-high throughput' = Standard better fit.
why_wrong.D: Standard-IA + On-Demand = correct capacity mode but wrong table class. High read/write activity = higher costs in IA class. IA saves on storage, costs more on operations.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Unpredictable traffic' = On-Demand. 'Predictable/steady' = Provisioned with auto scaling. Standard = frequent access. Standard-IA = infrequent access, large items. On-Demand = 2.5x cost per request vs provisioned but no minimum capacity.
memorize: On-Demand WRU: $1.25/million writes
On-Demand RRU: $0.25/million reads
Provisioned WCU: $0.65/month, RCU: $0.13/month
Standard-IA: storage 38% less, operations 25% more expensive
Break-even: On-Demand better if <50% capacity utilization

question_en: A company stores 5 PB of archived data on physical tapes in an on-premises data center. The company needs to retain the data for 10 years. The company does not want to change an existing backup workflow. The data center that stores the tapes has a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection to an AWS Region. The company wants to migrate the data to AWS as soon as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Use an on-premises backup application to read the data from the tapes. Use local storage to stage the data temporarily. Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage.
options.B: Use an on-premises backup application to read the data from the tapes. Use the backup application to write directly to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage.
options.C: Order multiple AWS Snowball Edge devices. Copy the physical tapes to virtual tapes on the Snowball Edge devices. Ship the Snowball Edge devices to AWS. Create an S3 Lifecycle policy to move the tapes to Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage.
options.D: Configure an on-premises AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway. Create virtual tapes on AWS. Use backup software to copy the physical tapes to the virtual tapes. Move the virtual tapes to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage.

explanation.full_text: Tape Gateway creates virtual tapes for backup software, stores in S3/Glacier Deep Archive. No workflow changes, lowest archive cost.
explanation.why_correct: Tape Gateway = VTL (Virtual Tape Library) compatible with backup software (Veeam, NetBackup, CommVault). No backup software changes needed. 10 Gbps Direct Connect = 5PB transfer in ~46 days. Virtual tapes → Glacier Deep Archive = $0.00099/GB (lowest cost). 10-year retention matches Deep Archive use case.

why_wrong.A: DataSync = file/object transfer tool, not tape workflow. Backup software expects tape interface. Flexible Retrieval = $0.004/GB (4x more than Deep Archive). DataSync doesn't preserve tape workflow requirement.
why_wrong.B: Backup software cannot write directly to Glacier—requires S3 API rewrite. Violates 'no workflow change' requirement. Glacier APIs different from tape protocols. Would need complete software redesign.
why_wrong.C: Snowball Edge = physical device for one-time migration. Cannot 'copy physical tapes to virtual tapes'—Snowball stores data, doesn't create VTL. Glacier Instant Retrieval = $0.01/GB (10x more than Deep Archive). Wrong device + wrong storage class.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Physical tapes' + 'no workflow change' = Tape Gateway. Tape Gateway = VTL emulation, works with existing backup software. Deep Archive = multi-year retention. Direct Connect = for large ongoing transfers. Snowball = one-time bulk migration, not continuous backup.
memorize: Tape Gateway: up to 1,500 virtual tapes, 1PB total
Virtual tape: 100GB - 5TB each
Supported software: Veeam, Veritas, CommVault, NetBackup, Arcserve
Archive tiers: Glacier Flexible or Deep Archive
Direct Connect: 1/10/100 Gbps, dedicated private connection

question_en: A solutions architect is investigating compute options for a critical analytics application. The application uses long-running processes to prepare and aggregate data. The processes cannot be interrupted. The application has a known baseline load. The application needs to handle occasional usage surges. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Set the Min capacity and Desired capacity parameters to the number of instances required to handle the baseline load. Purchase Reserved Instances for the Auto Scaling group.
options.B: Create an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Set the Min capacity, Max capacity, and Desired capacity parameters to the number of instances required to handle the baseline load. Use On-Demand Instances to address occasional usage surges.
options.C: Create an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Set the Min capacity and Desired capacity parameters to the number of instances required to handle the baseline load. Purchase Reserved Instances for the Auto Scaling group. Use the OnDemandPercentageAboveBaseCapacity parameter to configure the launch template to launch Spot Instances.
options.D: Re-architect the application to use AWS Lambda functions instead of Amazon EC2 instances. Purchase a one-year Compute Savings Plan to reduce the cost of Lambda usage.

explanation.full_text: Reserved Instances for known baseline load in Auto Scaling group. Auto Scaling handles surges with On-Demand beyond baseline.
explanation.why_correct: Known baseline = predictable usage, perfect for Reserved Instances (up to 72% discount). 'Cannot be interrupted' = excludes Spot. Auto Scaling Min/Desired = baseline (use RIs). Occasional surges = Auto Scaling scales above baseline with On-Demand automatically. RIs apply to baseline instances first, remainder billed On-Demand.

why_wrong.B: Setting Min = Max = Desired = no scaling headroom for surges. 'Handle occasional surges' requirement not met. Would need to manually increase Max later. On-Demand without commitment = highest cost for baseline.
why_wrong.C: OnDemandPercentageAboveBaseCapacity + Spot = correct for fault-tolerant workloads. Question states 'cannot be interrupted'—Spot violates requirement. Spot termination = 2-minute warning, job failure.
why_wrong.D: Re-architect to Lambda = major change for 'long-running processes'. Lambda max 15 minutes. Analytics aggregation likely > 15min. Lambda Compute Savings Plan possible but architecture change too disruptive.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Known baseline' + 'cannot interrupt' + 'occasional surges' = Reserved for baseline + Auto Scaling On-Demand. Spot = fault-tolerant only. Lambda = <15 min workloads. Reserved Instances = 1-3 year, 40-72% discount, capacity reservation.
memorize: Reserved Instance discount: 40-72% vs On-Demand
RI terms: 1-year or 3-year
RI payment: All/Partial/No upfront (upfront = higher discount)
Spot interruption: 2-min notice, 60-90% discount
Auto Scaling purchasing: mix RIs (baseline) + On-Demand (surges)

question_en: A company recently migrated its application to AWS. The application runs on Amazon EC2 Linux instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The application stores data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system that uses EFS Standard-Infrequent Access storage. The application indexes the company ' s files, and the index is stored in an Amazon RDS database. The company needs to optimize storage costs with some application and services changes. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create an Amazon S3 bucket that uses an Intelligent-Tiering lifecycle policy. Copy all files to the S3 bucket. Update the application to use Amazon S3 API to store and retrieve files.
options.B: Deploy Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file shares. Update the application to use CIFS protocol to store and retrieve files.
options.C: Deploy Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file system shares. Update the application to use the new mount point to store and retrieve files.
options.D: Create an Amazon S3 bucket that uses S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Copy all files to the S3 bucket. Update the application to use Amazon S3 API to store and retrieve files as standard retrievals.

explanation.full_text: Migrate from EFS to S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Update application to use S3 APIs. Automated cost optimization for varying access patterns.
explanation.why_correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering = automatic storage class transitions based on access. No retrieval fees. Tiers: Frequent ($0.023/GB), Infrequent ($0.0125/GB), Archive Instant ($0.004/GB), Deep Archive ($0.00099/GB). EFS Standard-IA = $0.025/GB vs S3 Intelligent best tier $0.00099/GB. Application change = S3 SDK calls instead of file I/O.

why_wrong.B: FSx for Windows = SMB file server, Active Directory integration. More expensive than S3: $0.013-0.20/GB/month. Unnecessary features (Windows, AD) for Linux application. Doesn't optimize costs—similar or higher than EFS.
why_wrong.C: FSx for OpenZFS = high-performance NFS, snapshots, compression. Cost: $0.15-0.54/GB/month. Good for low-latency workloads but more expensive than S3. Doesn't provide tiering like S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
why_wrong.D: Glacier Flexible Retrieval = manual storage class, not automatic. Retrieval = 3-5 hours, not suitable for application serving files. Would need application redesign to handle async retrieval. S3 API changes required anyway—Intelligent-Tiering better.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Optimize storage costs' + 'unpredictable access' = S3 Intelligent-Tiering. EFS = shared file system for EC2. FSx = managed file servers (Windows/Lustre/NetApp/OpenZFS). S3 = object storage, lowest cost at scale. File to object = application changes required.
memorize: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatic tiering, $0.0025/1K objects monitoring
EFS Standard: $0.30/GB, EFS IA: $0.025/GB
FSx Windows: $0.013-0.20/GB/month (Multi-AZ higher)
FSx OpenZFS: $0.15-0.54/GB/month
S3 API: PutObject, GetObject, ListObjects (REST/SDK)

question_en: A company processes large amounts of data by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The data processing jobs run for up to 48 hours each week. The data processing jobs can handle interruptions. However, the company wants to minimize the interruptions. The company wants to use the latest generation of Amazon EC2 instances each year. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances (RIs) on an All Upfront basis for a 3-year term for the instance types currently in use.
options.B: Purchase Standard Reserved Instances (RIs) on an All Upfront basis for a 1-year term for the instance types in use.
options.C: Purchase Spot Instances with a price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy. Override instance types in the Auto Scaling group.
options.D: Purchase Spot Instances with a capacity-optimized allocation strategy. Override instance types in the Auto Scaling group.

explanation.full_text: Spot Instances with capacity-optimized allocation strategy and instance type overrides. Minimizes interruptions while maximizing savings.
explanation.why_correct: Interruptible workload = Spot ideal (60-90% savings). 'Minimize interruptions' = capacity-optimized strategy (selects deepest capacity pools). Instance type overrides = diversify across generations/families for better availability. 48hrs/week = 29% utilization, Reserved/Savings wasteful. Latest generation yearly = overrides allow flexibility.

why_wrong.A: Convertible RIs = 1-3 year commitment, can exchange instance families. 3-year All Upfront = maximum discount but 48hrs/week = 29% utilization wastes 71% of reservation. Current instance types = doesn't meet 'latest generation yearly' goal.
why_wrong.B: Standard RIs = locked to specific instance family/type. 1-year better than 3-year but still poor utilization. 'Latest generation yearly' not possible—Standard RIs fixed to purchased type. Low flexibility.
why_wrong.C: Price-capacity-optimized = balances price + availability. Good option but 'minimize interruptions' prioritized over absolute lowest price. Capacity-optimized strictly focuses on lowest interruption risk, better matches requirement.

explanation.exam_tips: Spot allocation strategies: capacity-optimized (least interruptions), price-capacity-optimized (balanced), lowest-price (most interruptions). 'Latest generation' = need flexibility (overrides, Convertible RIs). Part-time workloads (<50% utilization) = avoid commitments. Instance overrides = specify multiple types.
memorize: Spot strategies: capacity-optimized, price-capacity-optimized, lowest-price
Capacity-optimized: ML training, big data, batch processing
Instance overrides: up to 40 instance types per Auto Scaling group
Convertible RI: exchange instance family, up to 54% discount
Standard RI: locked type, up to 72% discount

question_en: A company hosts a web application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group that scales in response to user demand. The company wants to optimize costs for the application but does not want to make any long-term commitments. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Purchase Dedicated Instances only.
options.B: Purchase Reserved Instances with a partial upfront payment.
options.C: Purchase a mix of On-Demand Instances and Spot Instances.
options.D: Purchase a mix of On-Demand Instances and Reserved Instances.

explanation.full_text: Mix of On-Demand and Spot Instances in Auto Scaling group. No commitments, cost-optimized, handles demand spikes.
explanation.why_correct: No commitments = excludes Reserved/Dedicated. On-Demand = baseline reliability, scales instantly. Spot = up to 90% discount for flexible capacity. Auto Scaling mixed instances = OnDemandBaseCapacity + OnDemandPercentageAboveBaseCapacity + Spot fills remainder. Web app = tolerate some Spot replacement, maintain On-Demand baseline for stability.

why_wrong.A: Dedicated Instances = $2/hr per region host fee + instance costs. Used for compliance (single-tenant hardware) or licensing. Most expensive option, no commitment advantage. Wrong use case.
why_wrong.B: Reserved partial upfront = 1-3 year commitment. Violates 'no long-term commitments' requirement. RIs good for predictable usage but question explicitly excludes commitments.
why_wrong.D: On-Demand + Reserved = violates 'no commitments' requirement. Otherwise valid cost optimization strategy if commitments acceptable.

explanation.exam_tips: 'No commitments' = On-Demand or Spot only. 'Cost optimize' = add Spot when tolerable. Reserved/Savings Plans = 1-3 year commitments. Dedicated = compliance/licensing, highest cost. Mixed instances = flexibility + savings.
memorize: On-Demand: no commitment, highest per-hour price
Spot: 60-90% discount, 2-min termination notice
Reserved: 1-3 year, 40-72% discount
Dedicated Instance: $2/hr region fee (1-time) + instance cost
Mixed ASG: OnDemandBaseCapacity + percentage + Spot

question_en: A company runs its application by using Amazon EC2 instances and AWS Lambda functions. The EC2 instances run in private subnets of a VPC. The Lambda functions need direct network access to the EC2 instances for the application to work. The application will run for 1 year. The number of Lambda functions that the application uses will increase during the 1-year period. The company must minimize costs on all application resources. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan. Connect the Lambda functions to the private sub-nets that contain the EC2 instances.
options.B: Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan. Connect the Lambda functions to new public sub-nets in the same VPC where the EC2 instances run.
options.C: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan. Connect the Lambda functions to the private subnets that contain the EC2 instances.
options.D: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan. Keep the Lambda functions in the Lambda service VPC.

explanation.full_text: Compute Savings Plan covers EC2 and Lambda. Connect Lambda to VPC private subnets for direct EC2 access.
explanation.why_correct: Compute Savings Plan = applies to EC2, Fargate, Lambda (up to 66% discount). EC2 + Lambda mixed architecture = perfect fit. Lambda VPC integration = creates ENIs in private subnets, direct network access to EC2. 1-year term matches timeline. 'Number of Lambda functions will increase' = flexibility needed (Compute vs EC2 Instance Savings).

why_wrong.A: EC2 Instance Savings Plan = only discounts EC2 in specific instance family. Lambda costs remain full price. Less flexible and incomplete coverage vs Compute Savings Plan.
why_wrong.B: Public subnets = Lambda could access EC2 if EC2 had public IPs. Violates typical security architecture (private EC2). Requires internet gateway, security group changes. EC2 Instance Savings Plan = doesn't cover Lambda.
why_wrong.D: Lambda in service VPC = cannot access EC2 in customer VPC privately. Would need public IPs or NAT Gateway traversal. Compute Savings Plan correct but networking wrong—Lambda needs VPC config.

explanation.exam_tips: 'EC2 + Lambda' + 'minimize costs' = Compute Savings Plan. 'Lambda access VPC resources' = Lambda VPC configuration with ENIs. EC2 Instance Savings = single instance family. Compute Savings = across services/families/regions. Lambda VPC = ~10-30 sec cold start delay.
memorize: Compute Savings Plan: EC2, Fargate, Lambda; up to 66% discount
EC2 Instance Savings: specific family; up to 72% discount
Lambda VPC: requires ENI in subnet, uses security groups
Lambda ENI: warm start reuses, cold start creates (~10-30 sec)
Savings Plan term: 1-year or 3-year commitment

question_en:
A company is designing an advertisement distribution application to run on AWS. The company wants to deploy the application as a container to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).



Advertisements must be displayed to users around the world with low latency. The company needs to optimize data transfer costs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy the application in a single AWS Region. Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution, and set the ALB as the origin.
options.B: Deploy the application in multiple AWS Regions. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each Region. Use Amazon Route 53 with a latency-based weighted routing policy to distribute traffic to the ALBs.
options.C: Deploy the application in multiple AWS Regions. Create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in each Region. Create a transit gateway in each Region. Route traffic between the ALBs and Amazon ECS through the transit gateways.
options.D: Deploy the application in a single AWS Region. Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic. Create an accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator. Associate the accelerator with the ALB.

explanation.full_text: CloudFront with ALB origin in single region. Cache at edge locations globally for low latency, optimized data transfer costs.
explanation.why_correct: CloudFront = CDN with 400+ edge locations globally. Caches content near users = low latency worldwide. ALB in single region = simpler infrastructure, lower operational cost. Data transfer: origin to CloudFront discounted, CloudFront to users = $0.085/GB (cheaper than direct S3/ALB). Cache reduces origin load and transfer costs.

why_wrong.B: Multi-region ALBs = complex deployment, higher costs (infrastructure in each region). Route 53 latency routing = works but more expensive than CloudFront caching. Inter-region data transfer = $0.02/GB. No caching benefits.
why_wrong.C: Transit Gateway = $0.05/hr per attachment + $0.02/GB. Wrong use case—Transit Gateway for VPC/on-prem connectivity, not user-facing content distribution. Multi-region = unnecessary complexity and cost.
why_wrong.D: Global Accelerator = $0.025/hr per accelerator + $0.015/GB. Anycast static IPs, routes to nearest healthy endpoint. No caching. More expensive than CloudFront for cacheable content. Better for non-HTTP/gaming/VoIP.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Global users' + 'low latency' + 'optimize costs' = CloudFront. Global Accelerator = non-cacheable/TCP/UDP. Multi-region = when need data residency or >50ms CloudFront latency. CloudFront caching = reduces origin costs significantly. Static/dynamic content = CloudFront handles both.
memorize: CloudFront edge locations: 400+ globally
CloudFront data transfer: $0.085/GB (varies by region)
Global Accelerator: $0.025/hr + $0.015/GB
CloudFront cache: TTL configurable, origin controls cache
CloudFront + ALB: common pattern for dynamic content

question_en: A company stores medical reports and images in Amazon S3 Standard storage. The company accesses each medical report only once each year. However, the company must be able to access the medical reports in real time when necessary. The company rarely accesses the medical images, but the company must retain each image for 7 years. The company can tolerate flexible retrieval times for the medical images. The company wants to optimize storage costs for the medical reports and images. Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Store the medical reports and images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.B: Store the medical reports in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Store the medical images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.C: Store the medical reports in S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Store the medical images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.D: Store the medical reports in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Store the medical images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanation.full_text: Medical reports in Glacier Instant Retrieval for real-time access. Medical images in Glacier Deep Archive for 7-year low-cost retention.
explanation.why_correct: Glacier Instant Retrieval = immediate access (milliseconds), $0.01/GB. 'Real-time when necessary' + 'once per year' = perfect match. Deep Archive = $0.00099/GB, lowest cost. 'Flexible retrieval' (12-48 hours) acceptable for rare image access. Different requirements = different storage classes.

why_wrong.A: Both in Deep Archive = reports cannot meet 'real-time access' requirement. Deep Archive retrieval = 12-48 hours standard. Would fail compliance or operational needs for immediate report access.
why_wrong.C: Intelligent-Tiering for reports = $0.023/GB frequent tier (initially). Monitoring fee $0.0025/1K objects. More expensive than Instant Retrieval ($0.01/GB). IT optimizes over time but reports already predictable (once/year) = Instant Retrieval better fit.
why_wrong.D: Flexible Retrieval for reports = 3-5 hour retrieval time. Violates 'real-time access' requirement. Less expensive than Instant ($0.004 vs $0.01/GB) but doesn't meet SLA.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Real-time' + 'archive' = Glacier Instant Retrieval (new in 2021). 'Flexible retrieval' = Glacier Flexible or Deep Archive. 'Once per year' = archive tier appropriate. Intelligent-Tiering = unpredictable access patterns. Match access requirements to storage class.
memorize: Glacier Instant Retrieval: $0.01/GB, millisecond access, 90-day min
Glacier Flexible: $0.004/GB, 3-5hr retrieval, 90-day min
Glacier Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB, 12-48hr retrieval, 180-day min
Intelligent-Tiering: auto-tiering, $0.0025/1K objects monitoring
Retrieval fees: Instant none, Flexible $0.01/GB, Deep Archive $0.02/GB

question_en: A company runs an application on an Amazon ECS cluster that uses AWS Fargate On-Demand capacity. The application cannot tolerate any sudden interruptions. The company wants to optimize costs for the application and ensure that the application remains operational. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation.
options.B: Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances.
options.C: Use Fargate Spot capacity instead of On-Demand capacity with a rolling update deployment type.
options.D: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan.

explanation.full_text: Compute Savings Plan applies to Fargate On-Demand with up to 66% discount. No interruptions, maintains reliability while optimizing costs.
explanation.why_correct: Fargate On-Demand = cannot be interrupted, reliable. Compute Savings Plan = discounts EC2, Fargate, Lambda (1-3 year commitment). 'Cannot tolerate interruptions' = must stay On-Demand. Savings Plan = up to 66% discount vs pay-as-you-go. Application remains operational, costs reduced significantly.

why_wrong.A: On-Demand Capacity Reservation = reserves EC2 capacity in specific AZ. Does NOT apply to Fargate. No cost savings—pays full On-Demand rate plus reservation fee. Wrong service type.
why_wrong.B: Convertible Reserved Instances = EC2 only, not Fargate. Fargate is serverless container service, doesn't use RIs. Wrong purchasing model for Fargate workloads.
why_wrong.C: Fargate Spot = up to 70% discount BUT 2-minute termination notice. 'Cannot tolerate interruptions' violated. Application could fail mid-task. Unacceptable for requirement.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Fargate' + 'cannot interrupt' + 'optimize cost' = Compute Savings Plan. Fargate Spot = interruptible only. RIs = EC2, not Fargate. Compute Savings = most flexible across services. Capacity Reservation = EC2 capacity guarantee, not Fargate.
memorize: Compute Savings Plan: EC2, Fargate, Lambda; up to 66% discount
Fargate Spot: up to 70% discount, 2-min termination notice
Fargate On-Demand: reliable, no interruptions, higher cost
Reserved Instances: EC2 only, not Fargate/Lambda
Capacity Reservation: EC2 capacity in specific AZ, full On-Demand cost

question_en: A solutions architect manages a web application for a company. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The Auto Scaling group configuration includes a minimum of 3 instances and a maximum of 300 instances. The maximum helps handle unpredictable, short-lived traffic surges. The application must scale to meet demand. However, to help manage costs, the number of running instances should not exceed 180 for longer than 1 continuous hour. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use a scheduled scaling policy. Set the maximum capacity of the Auto Scaling group to 180 during peak hours. Set the maximum capacity to 300 during non-peak hours.
options.B: Configure a target tracking scaling policy that scales based on average CPU utilization. Add an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to terminate instances after 1 hour when capacity exceeds 180.
options.C: Set the maximum instance lifetime of the Auto Scaling group to 1 hour to force replacement of instances when capacity exceeds 180.
options.D: Add a step scaling policy that uses an Amazon CloudWatch alarm. Trigger the alarm when the Auto Scaling group includes more than 180 instances for longer than 1 hour. Configure the alarm to reduce the group capacity to 180 when triggered.

explanation.full_text: Step scaling policy with CloudWatch alarm monitoring instance count >180 for 1 continuous hour. Reduces desired capacity when triggered.
explanation.why_correct: CloudWatch alarm = monitors GroupInServiceInstances metric. Configure alarm: threshold >180, evaluation periods = 60 (1-minute datapoints × 60 = 1 hour continuous). Step scaling action = reduces desired capacity to 180 when alarm triggers. Allows short spikes to 300, enforces 180 limit for sustained periods.

why_wrong.A: Scheduled scaling = for predictable patterns. 'Unpredictable short-lived surges' stated—schedule unknown. Cannot anticipate when surges occur. Peak/non-peak undefined in question.
why_wrong.B: Target tracking = maintains average CPU at target. Doesn't control instance count directly. CloudWatch alarm to terminate instances = bypasses Auto Scaling management, breaks health checks, unsafe.
why_wrong.C: Maximum instance lifetime = replaces instances periodically (hourly, daily). Doesn't control total capacity or reduce count after surges. Replaces individual instances, not group size management.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Unpredictable + time-based constraint' = step scaling + CloudWatch alarm. Scheduled = predictable patterns. Target tracking = metric-based (CPU, requests). Instance lifetime = periodic replacement, not capacity control. CloudWatch alarm evaluation periods = duration check.
memorize: Step scaling: CloudWatch alarm triggers, adjusts capacity by steps
Target tracking: maintains specific metric (CPU 50%, ALB requests)
Scheduled scaling: cron/rate expressions, time-based
Simple scaling: single adjustment, cooldown period
CloudWatch evaluation periods: consecutive periods threshold must be breached

question_en: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones in the same AWS Region. The EC2 instances share an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume that is mounted on all the instances. The EFS volume stores a variety of files such as installation media, third-party files, interface files, and other one-time files. The company accesses some EFS files frequently and needs to retrieve the files quickly. The company accesses other files rarely. The EFS volume is multiple terabytes in size. The company needs to optimize storage costs for Amazon EFS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?

options.A: Move the files to Amazon S3. Set up a lifecycle policy to move the files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
options.B: Apply a lifecycle policy to the EFS files to move the files to EFS Infrequent Access.
options.C: Move the files to Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Cold HDD Volumes (sc1).
options.D: Move the files to Amazon S3. Set up a lifecycle policy to move the rarely-used files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanation.full_text: EFS lifecycle policy automatically moves infrequently accessed files to EFS IA storage class. No application changes, minimal effort.
explanation.why_correct: EFS lifecycle management = built-in feature, configure transition age (1/7/14/30/60/90 days). Frequent files stay Standard ($0.30/GB), infrequent → IA ($0.025/GB) = 92% savings. Automatic transitions, no manual intervention. 'Least effort' = enable lifecycle policy, zero application changes, no data migration.

why_wrong.A: Move to S3 = requires application rewrite (file I/O → S3 API calls). Lifecycle to Glacier = hours retrieval delay. High effort, violates 'least effort' requirement. Application expects NFS, not object storage.
why_wrong.B: EBS sc1 (Cold HDD) = block storage attached to single EC2 instance. Cannot share across Auto Scaling group. Would break multi-instance access. Not NFS-compatible without additional NFS server software.
why_wrong.C: Lifecycle correct but S3 + Deep Archive = application changes required (NFS → S3 API). Deep Archive = 12-48hr retrieval. Frequent quick access not possible. High effort migration.

explanation.exam_tips: 'EFS + infrequent access' = EFS IA with lifecycle. 'Least effort' = use native features, avoid migrations. EFS lifecycle = automatic, no app changes. S3 = requires application rewrite. EBS = single-instance, not shared file system.
memorize: EFS Standard: $0.30/GB, millisecond latency
EFS IA: $0.025/GB, same performance, 92% cheaper
Lifecycle transition ages: 1/7/14/30/60/90 days since last access
EFS = NFS v4.1, shared across multiple AZs/instances
EBS = block storage, single EC2 instance attachment

question_en: A company wants to run its experimental workloads in the AWS Cloud. The company has a budget for cloud spending. The company ' s CFO is concerned about cloud spending accountabil-ity for each department. The CFO wants to receive notification when the spending threshold reaches 60% of the budget. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use cost allocation tags on AWS resources to label owners. Create usage budgets in AWS Budgets. Add an alert threshold to receive notification when spending exceeds 60% of the budget.
options.B: Use AWS Cost Explorer forecasts to determine resource owners. Use AWS Cost Anomaly Detection to create alert threshold notifications when spending exceeds 60% of the budget.
options.C: Use cost allocation tags on AWS resources to label owners. Use AWS Support API on AWS Trusted Advisor to create alert threshold notifications when spending exceeds 60% of the budget.
options.D: Use AWS Cost Explorer forecasts to determine resource owners. Create usage budgets in AWS Budgets. Add an alert threshold to receive notification when spending exceeds 60% of the budget.

explanation.full_text: Cost allocation tags identify resource owners. AWS Budgets with alert thresholds notify at 60% spending. Accountability and proactive monitoring.
explanation.why_correct: Cost allocation tags = user-defined tags (Department:Engineering, Project:X). Activate tags in Billing console → appear in cost reports. AWS Budgets = set budget amount, alert at 60% threshold. Notifications via email/SNS. Tracks actual or forecasted spend. Enables departmental chargeback and accountability.

why_wrong.B: Cost Explorer forecasts = visualization tool, NOT alerting mechanism. Cost Anomaly Detection = detects unusual spending patterns, not fixed thresholds. Cannot set '60% of budget' alert—different use case (anomalies vs budgets).
why_wrong.C: Trusted Advisor = best practice recommendations (security, cost, performance). Does NOT create budget alerts or track spending thresholds. Support API exists but not for budget notifications. Wrong tool category.
why_wrong.D: Cost Explorer forecasts identify trends, NOT resource owners. Without tags, cannot attribute costs to departments. Daily reports = manual review, not automated alerts. Missing ownership tracking requirement.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Accountability + spending alerts' = cost allocation tags + AWS Budgets. Cost Explorer = analysis/visualization. Budgets = alerts/notifications. Anomaly Detection = unusual patterns. Trusted Advisor = recommendations. Tags must be activated in Billing console (24hr delay).
memorize: Cost allocation tags: user-defined (custom) + AWS-generated (aws:)
