Tag activation: Billing console, 24-hour delay to appear
AWS Budgets: cost, usage, reservation, Savings Plans budgets
Budget alerts: actual or forecasted, configurable thresholds
Cost Explorer: visualize spending, filter by tags/services/accounts

question_en: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances. EC2 instance usage is higher during daytime hours than nighttime hours. A solutions architect wants to automatically optimize Amazon EC2 costs based on this usage pattern. Which AWS service or purchasing option will meet this requirement?

options.A: Spot Instances
options.B: Reserved Instances
options.C: AWS CloudFormation
options.D: AWS Auto Scaling

explanation.full_text: AWS Auto Scaling with scheduled scaling actions adjusts capacity automatically for day/night patterns. No manual intervention needed.
explanation.why_correct: Auto Scaling = automation service, scales EC2 in/out based on schedule or metrics. Scheduled scaling = cron/rate expressions, set MinCapacity/DesiredCapacity by time. Example: scale up 8AM, down 6PM daily. Optimizes costs by reducing instances during nighttime low usage. 'Automatically optimize' = Auto Scaling core function.

why_wrong.A: Spot Instances = pricing model (60-90% discount), NOT automation mechanism. Doesn't change capacity based on time. Still need Auto Scaling or manual management to adjust count. Spot = what to buy, not when/how many.
why_wrong.B: Reserved Instances = 1-3 year commitment, fixed capacity discount. Doesn't automatically scale. Still pays for idle capacity at night if sized for peak. Pricing model, not scaling solution.
why_wrong.C: CloudFormation = infrastructure-as-code deployment tool. Creates resources via templates. Doesn't manage ongoing scaling decisions. One-time provisioning, not dynamic capacity management.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Automatically + time-based pattern' = Auto Scaling scheduled actions. Spot/Reserved = pricing, not automation. CloudFormation = provisioning, not scaling. Auto Scaling types: scheduled (time-based), dynamic (metric-based), predictive (ML forecast).
memorize: Auto Scaling scheduled actions: cron expressions, recurring schedules
Scheduled scaling: set min, max, desired capacity by time
Dynamic scaling: target tracking, step, simple scaling policies
Spot = discount model, Reserved = commitment discount
CloudFormation = IaC deployment, not runtime scaling

question_en: A company is migrating a document management application to AWS. The application runs on Linux servers. The company will migrate the application to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The company stores 7 TiB of documents in a shared storage file system. An external relational database tracks the documents. Documents are stored once and can be retrieved multiple times for reference at any time. The company cannot modify the application during the migration. The storage solution must be highly available and must support scaling over time. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy an EC2 instance with enhanced networking as a shared NFS storage system. Export the NFS share. Mount the NFS share on the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.
options.B: Create an Amazon S3 bucket that uses the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Mount the S3 bucket on the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.
options.C: Deploy an SFTP server endpoint by using AWS Transfer for SFTP and an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group to connect to the SFTP server.
options.D: Create an Amazon EFS file system with mount points in multiple Availability Zones. Use the EFS Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) storage class. Mount the NFS share on the EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group.

explanation.full_text: EFS with multi-AZ mount targets and Standard-IA storage class. Shared NFS for Linux, automatic scaling, lifecycle tiering for cost optimization.
explanation.why_correct: EFS = managed NFS file system, Linux-native. Multi-AZ mount targets = high availability. Auto-scales petabytes without provisioning. Standard-IA = $0.025/GB (92% cheaper than Standard). Lifecycle transitions infrequently accessed files automatically. 'Cannot modify application' = NFS mount works with existing code. Shared across Auto Scaling group instances.

why_wrong.A: Self-managed NFS on EC2 = operational overhead (patching, backups, HA setup). Single instance = SPOF. Manual scaling (add EBS, resize). Violates 'highly available' requirement unless complex HA built.
why_wrong.B: S3 Standard-IA = object storage, not file system. Cannot mount as NFS. 'Cannot modify application' = file I/O expected, not S3 API calls. Requires major application rewrite to use SDK.
why_wrong.C: SFTP via Transfer for SFTP = file transfer protocol, not shared file system. Application needs concurrent read/write access, not file upload/download workflow. Wrong access pattern, adds complexity.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Shared file system' + 'Linux' + 'no app changes' + 'HA' + 'auto-scale' = EFS. S3 = object storage, requires app changes. Self-managed NFS = operational overhead, avoid. SFTP = file transfers, not shared FS. EFS IA = automatic lifecycle tiering.
memorize: EFS Standard: $0.30/GB, frequent access
EFS Standard-IA: $0.025/GB, lifecycle transition (7/14/30/60/90 days)
EFS mount targets: ENI in each AZ for HA
EFS performance: General Purpose or Max I/O
EFS throughput: Bursting or Elastic (auto-scales)

question_en: An analytics application runs on multiple Amazon EC2 Linux instances that use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard storage. Files are accessed infrequently after 30 days, but some older files are occasionally retrieved for reporting. The company wants to reduce storage costs and allow throughput to scale based on file system size. The company will use the EFS lifecycle policy to transition files to Infrequent Access (IA) after 30 days. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: after 30 days. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options.B: Specify the provisioned throughput mode only.
options.C: Configure files to transition back to Standard storage on access. Specify bursting throughput mode.
options.D: Specify the bursting throughput mode only.

explanation.full_text: Lifecycle to EFS IA after 30 days, transition back to Standard on access. Bursting throughput scales with file system size automatically.
explanation.why_correct: Transition to IA after 30 days = cost savings ($0.025/GB vs $0.30/GB). Transition back on access = frequently accessed reporting files get Standard performance automatically. Bursting throughput = scales with stored data size (50 MB/s per TB baseline). 'Throughput scale based on size' = bursting mode matches requirement. No fixed throughput costs.

why_wrong.A: Provisioned throughput = fixed cost regardless of usage. $6/month per MB/s provisioned. Useful for consistent high throughput needs. Question wants scaling based on size (bursting), not fixed provisioning.
why_wrong.B: Provisioned only = higher costs, doesn't include lifecycle management. Files stay expensive Standard storage forever. Misses cost optimization opportunity from IA transitions.
why_wrong.D: Bursting only without transition-back-on-access = accessed files remain in IA. IA reads = $0.01/GB access fee. Reporting workloads reading old files = unexpected costs, slower performance. Needs auto-transition to Standard.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Scale throughput with size' = bursting mode. 'Lifecycle + cost optimize' = use IA + transition back on access. Provisioned = fixed throughput, predictable cost. Bursting = variable, scales with data. IA access fee = $0.01/GB read.
memorize: Bursting throughput: 50 MB/s per TB baseline, burst to 100 MB/s
Provisioned throughput: $6/month per MB/s, independent of storage
EFS IA: $0.025/GB storage + $0.01/GB access
Lifecycle back to Standard: files accessed within IA return to Standard
Bursting credit: accumulates when below baseline, depletes when bursting

question_en: A company hosts a web application in a VPC on AWS. A public Application Load Balancer (ALB) forwards connections from the internet to an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances. The Auto Scaling group runs in private subnets across four Availability Zones. The company stores data in an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region. The EC2 instances use NAT gateways in each Availability Zone for outbound internet connectivity. The company wants to optimize costs for its AWS architecture. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Reconfigure the Auto Scaling group and the ALB to use two Availability Zones instead of four. Do not change the desired count or scaling metrics for the Auto Scaling group to maintain application availability.
options.B: Create a new, smaller VPC that still has sufficient IP address availability to run the application. Redeploy the application stack in the new VPC. Delete the existing VPC and its resources.
options.C: Deploy an S3 gateway endpoint to the VPC. Configure the EC2 instances to access the S3 bucket through the S3 gateway endpoint.
options.D: Deploy an S3 interface endpoint to the VPC. Configure the EC2 instances to access the S3 bucket through the S3 interface endpoint.

explanation.full_text: S3 Gateway Endpoint provides free private connectivity from VPC to S3. Eliminates NAT gateway costs for S3 traffic.
explanation.why_correct: Gateway Endpoint = FREE (no hourly charge, no data processing fees). Routes S3 traffic privately through VPC route tables. EC2 instances access S3 without NAT gateway. Current NAT usage = $0.045/hr × 4 AZs × 24hr = $130/month + data processing. Gateway endpoint = $0/month for S3 traffic. Massive savings.

why_wrong.A: Reducing AZs to 2 = impacts application availability. Question asks optimize costs for architecture, not reduce redundancy. ALB + Auto Scaling designed for 4 AZs. NAT costs reduced but availability compromised.
why_wrong.B: Smaller VPC = no cost benefit. VPC itself free, IP addresses free. Migration effort high (redeploy entire stack). Doesn't address actual cost driver (NAT gateway traffic). Wrong optimization target.
why_wrong.D: S3 Interface Endpoint = $0.01/hr per AZ ($29/month for 4 AZs) + $0.01/GB data processing. More expensive than Gateway Endpoint (free). Interface = for services without Gateway support (SSM, SNS, etc). S3 supports Gateway.

explanation.exam_tips: 'VPC to S3' + 'optimize costs' = Gateway Endpoint (free). Gateway = S3 + DynamoDB only. Interface = other AWS services ($0.01/hr + data). Gateway Endpoint = updates route table, no ENI. Interface Endpoint = ENI in subnet with private IP.
memorize: Gateway Endpoint: FREE, S3 and DynamoDB
Interface Endpoint: $0.01/hr per AZ + $0.01/GB data
Gateway Endpoint: routes via route table (no ENI)
Interface Endpoint: ENI with private IP, DNS resolution
NAT Gateway: $0.045/hr + $0.045/GB processed

question_en: A company runs a custom application on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances. The application has frontend nodes that must run 24/7. The backend nodes only need to run for short periods depending on the workload. Frontend nodes accept jobs and place them in queues. Backend nodes asynchronously process jobs from the queues, and jobs can be restarted. The company wants to scale infrastructure based on workload, using the most cost-effective option. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.
options.B: Use Reserved Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Spot Instances for the backend nodes.
options.C: Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use Reserved Instances for the backend nodes.
options.D: Use Spot Instances for the frontend nodes. Use AWS Fargate for the backend nodes.

explanation.full_text: Reserved Instances for 24/7 frontend nodes. Spot Instances for intermittent, restartable backend processing. Maximum cost savings.
explanation.why_correct: Frontend 24/7 = steady usage, perfect for Reserved Instances (up to 72% discount, 1-3 year commitment). Backend = asynchronous, queued, restartable jobs = ideal Spot workload. Spot = 60-90% discount, 2-minute warning acceptable for fault-tolerant jobs. Queue-based = jobs reprocessed if interrupted. Lowest cost combination.

why_wrong.A: Reserved for frontend = correct. Fargate for backend = more expensive than EC2 Spot for large batch workloads. Fargate good for simplicity, but question asks 'most cost-effective' and backend processing likely high-volume compute.
why_wrong.C: Spot for frontend = 2-minute interruptions unacceptable. Frontend = user-facing, must be always available. Spot termination = downtime for users. Reserved for backend = wastes commitment on short-duration intermittent workload.
why_wrong.D: Spot for frontend = same problem as C (interruptions). Fargate for backend = simpler but more expensive than Spot. Double failure: wrong purchasing for both tiers.

explanation.exam_tips: '24/7 + steady' = Reserved or Savings Plans. 'Intermittent + restartable' = Spot. 'Queue-based' = Spot ideal (jobs requeue). Frontend = critical availability. Backend = fault-tolerant batch. Fargate = serverless containers, more expensive than self-managed Spot.
memorize: Reserved Instances: 1-3 year, 40-72% discount, predictable workloads
Spot Instances: 60-90% discount, 2-min notice, fault-tolerant only
Fargate: serverless containers, per-second billing, higher per-compute cost
Queue pattern: SQS + Spot = cost-effective asynchronous processing
Frontend = always-on, Backend = elastic/batch

question_en: A company needs to archive an on-premises relational database. The company wants to retain the data. The company needs to be able to run SQL queries on the archived data to create annual reports. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the on-premises database to an Amazon RDS instance. Retire the on-premises database. Maintain the RDS instance in a stopped state until the data is needed for reports.
options.B: Set up database replication from the on-premises database to an Amazon EC2 instance. Retire the onpremises database. Make a snapshot of the EC2 instance. Maintain the EC2 instance in a stopped state until the data is needed for reports.
options.C: Create a database backup on premises. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data to Amazon S3. Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to move the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Restore the backup to Amazon EC2 instances to run reports.
options.D: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the on-premises databases to Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format. Store the data in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Use Amazon Athena to run reports.

explanation.full_text: AWS DMS migrates database to S3 in Parquet format. Store in Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Query with Athena without provisioning infrastructure.
explanation.why_correct: DMS = migrates databases to S3 directly, supports Parquet columnar format (optimized for analytics). Glacier Flexible Retrieval = $0.004/GB, 3-5 hour retrieval acceptable for annual reports. Athena = serverless SQL query engine, reads Parquet in S3 directly. Zero infrastructure management. Pay only for queries ($5/TB scanned). Lowest operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: RDS stopped state = still charged for storage (~$0.115/GB/month). Stopped max 7 days, auto-restarts after. Annual report = need longer retention. Manual start/stop overhead. More expensive than Glacier long-term.
why_wrong.B: EC2 database replication + snapshot = operational overhead (manage replication, EC2 instance). Stopped EC2 = still pay for EBS snapshots. Less cost-effective than S3 Glacier. Manual restore process.
why_wrong.C: DataSync to S3 + Glacier Deep Archive = correct archival. BUT restoring to EC2 for reports = slow (12-48hr Deep Archive retrieval), operational overhead (provision EC2, install DB). Not serverless, more complex than Athena direct queries.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Archive + annual SQL reports' = DMS → S3 Parquet + Glacier + Athena. Parquet = columnar, optimized for analytics, compressed. Athena = serverless, direct S3 queries, no infrastructure. Deep Archive = cheapest but 12-48hr retrieval. Flexible = 3-5hr, better for occasional access.
memorize: DMS: migrates databases to RDS, Aurora, S3, Redshift, DynamoDB
Parquet: columnar format, compressed, optimized for analytics
Athena: $5/TB scanned, serverless SQL, reads S3 directly
Glacier Flexible: $0.004/GB, 3-5hr retrieval
Glacier Deep Archive: $0.00099/GB, 12-48hr retrieval

question_en: A company wants to release a new device that will collect data to track overnight sleep on an intelligent mattress. Sensors will send data that will be uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each mattress generates about 2 MB of data each night. An application must process the data and summarize the data for each user. The application must make the results available as soon as possible. Every invocation of the application will require about 1 GB of memory and will finish running within 30 seconds. Which solution will run the application MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: AWS Lambda with a Python script
options.B: AWS Glue with a Scala job
options.C: Amazon EMR with an Apache Spark script
options.D: AWS Glue with a PySpark job

explanation.full_text: Lambda with Python processes 2MB files in 30 seconds using 1GB memory. Serverless, auto-scales, most cost-effective for short-duration event-driven workloads.
explanation.why_correct: Lambda = fits requirements perfectly (15-min max, here 30 sec). Memory support up to 10GB (need 1GB). Python = supported runtime. S3 trigger = automatic invocation per upload. Cost: ~$0.0000166667/GB-sec × 1GB × 30sec × daily uploads = cents per month. Zero idle costs. Auto-scales to handle nightly upload concurrency.

why_wrong.B: AWS Glue = ETL service for big data transformations (Apache Spark/Python shell). Min 1 DPU (Data Processing Unit) = $0.44/hour. Overkill for 30-second 2MB processing. More expensive and complex than Lambda for small files.
why_wrong.C: EMR = managed Hadoop/Spark cluster for petabyte-scale analytics. Minimum 3 nodes (master + 2 core) = $0.50+/hour continuously. 1000x overkill for 2MB mattress data. Massive operational overhead and cost.
why_wrong.D: Glue PySpark job = same as B, uses Spark for distributed processing. Unnecessary for small single-file transformations. Lambda PySpark overhead (cluster spin-up) vs simple Python function.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Quick processing' (<15 min) + 'event-driven' + 'small data' = Lambda. Glue = ETL on large datasets, crawlers, data catalog. EMR = big data analytics (TB-PB scale). Lambda = up to 10GB memory, 15min timeout. Python/Node.js/Java/Go/Ruby/.NET supported.
memorize: Lambda: 15-min max, 10GB max memory, 512MB-10GB /tmp storage
Lambda pricing: $0.20/1M requests + $0.0000166667/GB-second
Glue DPU: $0.44/hour per DPU, minimum 2 DPUs
EMR minimum: 1 master + 1 core node (2+ recommended)
Lambda triggers: S3, DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis, SQS, SNS, API Gateway

question_en:
A company is building a containerized application on AWS. The application uses the Linux operating system. The company needs to provide a persistent storage solution for the application.



The company expects the storage solution to have varying data access patterns. The solution must have native storage tiering capabilities and must be scalable. The solution must not require the company to provision storage upfront. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Use Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP to set up persistent file storage that uses SSD storage for performance. Use the capacity pool storage tier.
options.B: Use an Amazon EFS file system in Elastic throughput mode. Use the Intelligent Tiering lifecycle management feature.
options.C: Configure two Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file systems. Use an SSD-based file system for performance and an HDD-based file system for low-cost storage.
options.D: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance that is backed by an Amazon EBS volume. Use the EBS volume to create a file share.

explanation.full_text: EFS with Elastic throughput mode and Intelligent-Tiering lifecycle. Auto-scales capacity and performance, native tiering, no provisioning.
explanation.why_correct: EFS = Linux-native NFS, perfect for containers. Elastic throughput (2021+) = automatically scales to GB/s based on workload, no provisioning. Intelligent-Tiering lifecycle = automatic transitions between Standard and IA based on access patterns. 'Varying access patterns' = Intelligent-Tiering ideal. Scalable to petabytes, highly available across AZs.

why_wrong.A: FSx for NetApp ONTAP = advanced enterprise features (snapshots, clones, SnapMirror). Capacity pool = manual tiering. More expensive than EFS: $0.15-0.20/GB/month SSD vs EFS $0.30/GB Standard (but EFS IA $0.025/GB with Intelligent-Tiering auto-optimization). Linux app doesn't need ONTAP features.
why_wrong.C: FSx for Windows = SMB protocol, Active Directory. Linux application = NFS needed. SSD + HDD = manual tier management, not automatic. Two separate file systems = application complexity.
why_wrong.D: Self-managed file share on EC2 + EBS = operational overhead (patching, HA, backups). Manual provisioning required. Single EC2 instance = SPOF. EBS max 64TB per volume. Not scalable or highly available without significant effort.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Linux containers' + 'varying access' + 'native tiering' + 'no provisioning' = EFS with Elastic + Intelligent-Tiering. FSx NetApp/OpenZFS = advanced features, higher cost. FSx Windows = Windows/SMB only. EFS = simplest managed NFS for Linux.
memorize: EFS Elastic throughput: scales automatically, pay for actual throughput
EFS Intelligent-Tiering: automatic Standard ↔ IA transitions
FSx NetApp ONTAP: $0.15-0.20/GB, NFS/SMB, snapshots, dedup
FSx Windows: $0.013-0.20/GB, SMB, Active Directory
FSx OpenZFS: $0.15-0.54/GB, NFS, snapshots, compression

question_en: A company is running a web-based game in two Availability Zones in the us-west-2 Region. The web servers use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in public subnets. The ALB has an SSL certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) with a custom domain name. The game is written in JavaScript and runs entirely in a user ' s web browser. The game is increasing in popularity in many countries around the world. The company wants to update the application architecture and optimize costs without compromising performance. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon CloudFront and create a global distribution that points to the ALB. Reuse the existing certificate from ACM for the CloudFront distribution. Use Amazon Route 53 to update the application alias to point to the distribution.
options.B: Use AWS CloudFormation to deploy the application stack to AWS Regions near countries where the game is popular. Use ACM to create a new certificate for each application instance. Use Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation routing policy to direct traffic to the local application instance.
options.C: Use Amazon S3 and create an S3 bucket in AWS Regions near countries where the game is popular. Deploy the HTML and JavaScript files to each S3 bucket. Use ACM to create a new certificate for each S3 bucket. Use Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation routing policy to direct traffic to the local S3 bucket.
options.D: Use Amazon S3 and create an S3 bucket in us-west-2. Deploy the HTML and JavaScript files to the S3 bucket. Use Amazon CloudFront and create a global distribution with the S3 bucket as the origin. Use ACM to create a new certificate for the distribution. Use Amazon Route 53 to update the application alias to point to the distribution.

explanation.full_text: S3 bucket for static JavaScript app, CloudFront global distribution, ACM certificate in us-east-1. Cost-effective, high performance globally.
explanation.why_correct: JavaScript runs in browser = static web app (HTML/JS/CSS). S3 Static Website Hosting = cheapest option ($0.023/GB storage). CloudFront = 400+ edge locations, caches globally, low latency. CloudFront + S3 = data transfer discounted, origin requests minimized. ACM certificate in us-east-1 = required for CloudFront custom domains (us-east-1 only). Cost: ~$1-5/month for thousands of users.

why_wrong.A: CloudFront + ALB origin = still running EC2 instances behind ALB. Unnecessary compute costs for static content. ALB = $16+/month, EC2 = $7.50+/month per instance. CloudFront certificate must be us-east-1, cannot reuse existing (likely us-west-2).
why_wrong.B: Multi-region stacks = complex deployment, high cost (ALB + EC2 in each region). Geolocation routing = works but expensive. No caching benefits. ~10x more expensive than CloudFront solution.
why_wrong.C: Multi-region S3 buckets = unnecessary. CloudFront caches globally from single origin. ACM certificate per bucket = unnecessary (CloudFront needs one cert). Geolocation = manual region selection, CloudFront automatic edge routing better.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Static content' + 'global users' = S3 + CloudFront. CloudFront ACM = us-east-1 only for custom domains. ALB/EC2 origin = for dynamic apps. Multi-region = data residency or >50ms CloudFront latency (rare). S3 static hosting = $0.023/GB + requests.
memorize: CloudFront certificate: ACM in us-east-1 for custom domains
S3 static website: bucket policy public read, index.html default
CloudFront pricing: $0.085/GB (varies by region)
S3 + CloudFront: origin to CF discounted, CF to users standard
CloudFront edge locations: 400+ in 90+ cities

question_en: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that have instance store volumes attached. The application uses Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) to store files that are shared across a cluster of Linux servers. The shared files are at least 1 GB in size. The company accesses the files often for the first 7 days after creation. The files must remain readily available after the first 7 days. The company wants to optimize costs for the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure an AWS Storage Gateway Amazon S3 File Gateway to cache frequently accessed files locally. Store older files in Amazon S3.
options.B: Move the files from Amazon EFS, and store the files locally on each EC2 instance.
options.C: Configure a lifecycle policy to move the files to the EFS Infrequent Access (IA) storage class after 7 days.
options.D: Deploy AWS DataSync to automatically move files older than 7 days to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanation.full_text: EFS lifecycle policy transitions files to EFS IA after 7 days. Automatic cost optimization, files remain readily available.
explanation.why_correct: EFS lifecycle policy = configure 7-day transition age. Files not accessed 7 days → EFS IA automatically. Standard = $0.30/GB, IA = $0.025/GB (92% savings). 'Readily available' = IA same performance, no retrieval delay (unlike Glacier). Accessed files return to Standard automatically. Zero operational overhead, built-in feature.

why_wrong.A: File Gateway = for on-premises to S3 hybrid. Local cache + S3 backend. Unnecessary complexity—already in AWS. S3 = object storage, requires application changes from NFS. Operational overhead (manage gateway appliance).
why_wrong.B: Move to instance store = loses shared access across EC2 instances. Instance store = ephemeral (lost on stop/terminate). Files not durable or shared. Violates cluster architecture requirement.
why_wrong.D: DataSync to Glacier Deep Archive = 12-48 hour retrieval time. NOT 'readily available' as required. Manual DataSync job scheduling. Glacier = cold storage, unacceptable access latency for application serving files.

explanation.exam_tips: 'EFS + infrequent access' = EFS IA lifecycle. 'Readily available' = EFS IA (instant access) NOT Glacier (hours). File Gateway = hybrid on-prem/cloud. Instance store = ephemeral, single-instance. EFS lifecycle = automatic, zero effort.
memorize: EFS lifecycle ages: 1/7/14/30/60/90 days since last access
EFS IA: same performance as Standard, 92% cost savings
EFS IA pricing: $0.025/GB storage + $0.01/GB access
Glacier retrieval: Instant (ms), Flexible (3-5hr), Deep Archive (12-48hr)
File Gateway: on-premises NFS → S3 backend

question_en: A company hosts multiple applications on AWS for different product lines. The applications use different compute resources, including Amazon EC2 instances and Application Load Balancers. The applications run in different AWS accounts under the same organization in AWS Organizations across multiple AWS Regions. Teams for each product line have tagged each compute resource in the individual accounts. The company wants more details about the cost for each product line from the consolidated billing feature in Organizations. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Select a specific AWS generated tag in the AWS Billing console.
options.B: Select a specific user-defined tag in the AWS Billing console.
options.C: Select a specific user-defined tag in the AWS Resource Groups console.
options.D: Activate the selected tag from each AWS account.
options.E: Activate the selected tag from the Organizations management account.

explanation.full_text: Select user-defined cost allocation tags in Billing console. Activate tags from Organizations management account for consolidated billing visibility.
explanation.why_correct: User-defined tags = teams tagged resources by product line (custom tags like ProductLine:X). Billing console = select tags for cost allocation reports. Management account activation = enables tags across all member accounts in consolidated billing. Cost Explorer + Cost & Usage Reports = show costs grouped by activated tags. Centralized activation = consistency across organization.

why_wrong.A: AWS-generated tags = automatic (aws:createdBy, aws:cloudformation:stack-name). NOT product line tags—teams created custom tags. Generated tags useful but not for custom business dimensions like product lines.
why_wrong.C: Resource Groups console = for organizing/operating on resources, NOT billing. Resource Groups use tags for filtering but don't affect cost allocation or reporting. Wrong tool for billing breakdown.
why_wrong.D: Activate from each account = inconsistent, manual overhead. Organizations consolidated billing = management account controls cost allocation tag activation centrally. Individual activation = unnecessary complexity, doesn't leverage Organizations benefits.

explanation.exam_tips: 'User tags + consolidated billing' = select user-defined tags + activate from management account. AWS-generated = automatic tags (aws:*). Management account = central control for all member accounts. Cost Explorer = visualize by tags after activation. 24-hour delay for activation.
memorize: Cost allocation tags: user-defined (custom) + AWS-generated (aws:*)
Tag activation: management account for consolidated billing
Activation delay: up to 24 hours to appear in reports
Cost Explorer: filter/group by activated tags
Organizations: management account = billing aggregation for all members

question_en: A company has offices in multiple countries. The company has a separate AWS account for each office. The company uses an organization in AWS Organizations to manage all the accounts. Each office has an allocated budget that is set by company leadership. The company needs a solution to monitor account costs and automatically review service consumption when an account reaches a spending threshold. The solution must not immediately disable resources when an account reaches a spending threshold. The solution must detect budget overruns as soon as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create service control policies SCPs that define a budget threshold. Use AWS Budgets to apply the SCPs to all accounts.
options.B: Use AWS Budgets to set budget thresholds. Use AWS Budgets actions to define a workflow to manually review accounts that overspend.
options.C: Use AWS Budgets to set budget thresholds. Use AWS Budgets actions to immediately restrict the accounts that overspend.
options.D: Set up AWS Budgets in the organization management account. Create budget reports every day to track individual account spending.

explanation.full_text: AWS Budgets set thresholds per account. AWS Budgets actions trigger manual review workflow at 60% threshold. Proactive monitoring without automatic restrictions.
explanation.why_correct: AWS Budgets = monitor costs/usage, set custom thresholds (60% of budget). Budgets actions = automated workflow triggers (SNS, email, IAM policies, SCPs). 'Manual review' = action sends notification, requires human approval before restrictions. 'Not immediately disable' = manual workflow matches requirement. Detects early via forecasted spend alerts.

why_wrong.A: SCPs = service control policies (permissions boundaries in Organizations). NOT budget definition mechanism. Budgets = separate service for cost tracking. Cannot 'define budget threshold' in SCPs—wrong tool. SCPs restrict API actions, not spending.
why_wrong.C: Budgets actions immediately restrict = violates 'must not immediately disable resources' requirement. Auto-restriction = could break production workloads without review. Question needs notification + manual approval workflow.
why_wrong.D: Daily budget reports = reactive, not proactive. 'As soon as possible' = forecasted alerts (predicts overrun before hitting 60%). Daily reports = after spending already occurred. No automated threshold notifications—manual report review required.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Budget threshold + notify + manual review' = AWS Budgets + Budgets actions (notification workflow). SCPs = permissions, not budgets. Budgets forecasts = predict overruns early. Budgets actions types: SNS notification, email, IAM policy, SCP application. 'Immediately restrict' = use only when acceptable.
memorize: AWS Budgets: cost, usage, RI utilization, Savings Plans coverage
Budget alerts: actual or forecasted spend, multiple thresholds
Budgets actions: SNS, email, apply IAM policy, apply SCP
Forecasted alerts: predict overrun before occurrence
SCPs: permissions boundaries in Organizations, not cost tool

question_en: A company processes large amounts of data by using Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The data processing jobs run for up to 48 hours each week. The data processing jobs can handle interruptions. However, the company wants to minimize the interruptions. The company wants to use the latest generation of Amazon EC2 instances each year. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Purchase Convertible Reserved Instances on an All Upfront basis for a 3-year term for the instance types currently in use.
options.B: Purchase Standard Reserved Instances on an All Upfront basis for a 1-year term for the instance types currently in use.
options.C: Purchase Spot Instances with a price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy. Override instance types in the Auto Scaling group.
options.D: Purchase Spot Instances with a capacity-optimized allocation strategy. Override instance types in the Auto Scaling group.

explanation.full_text: Spot Instances with price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy and instance type overrides. Balances low cost with minimized interruptions, flexibility for latest generations.
explanation.why_correct: Spot = 60-90% savings for interruptible workloads. Price-capacity-optimized (2022+) = AWS recommendation, balances lowest price AND lowest interruption risk (better than capacity-optimized alone when cost primary concern). Instance type overrides = diversify across families/generations, improves capacity availability, enables adopting newer instance types annually.

why_wrong.A: Convertible RIs 3-year = locked commitment, 54-66% discount. 48hrs/week = 29% utilization, wastes 71% of reservation. 3-year = can't easily adopt latest generations (exchange possible but reduces flexibility). More expensive than Spot for part-time usage.
why_wrong.B: Standard RIs 1-year = locked to specific instance family/type. Cannot use latest generations without buying new RIs. 29% utilization = poor value. 40-72% discount but commitment wasteful for part-time workload.
why_wrong.D: Capacity-optimized = minimizes interruptions, ignores price. Price-capacity-optimized = better balance (prioritizes capacity BUT considers price). Question says 'minimize interruptions' but ALSO 'most cost-effective way'—price-capacity-optimized achieves both goals.

explanation.exam_tips: Spot allocation strategies: price-capacity-optimized (new, recommended), capacity-optimized (stability), lowest-price (cost, higher interruption). 'Latest generation yearly' = need flexibility (Spot overrides, Convertible RIs). Part-time (<50% utilization) = avoid Reserved commitments. Overrides = up to 40 instance types per ASG.
memorize: Price-capacity-optimized: 2022 strategy, balances price + capacity
Capacity-optimized: deepest capacity pools, minimize interruptions
Lowest-price: cheapest Spot, highest interruption risk
Spot instance pools: combination of instance type + AZ + OS
Convertible RI: exchange instance family, up to 66% discount

question_en:
Question: A company wants to migrate an application to AWS. The application runs on Docker containers behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application stores data in a PostgreSQL database. The cloud-based solution must use AWS WAF to inspect all application traffic. The application experiences most traffic on weekdays. There is significantly less traffic on weekends. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?



Options:

options.A: Use a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Create a web access control list (web ACL) in AWS WAF that includes the necessary rules. Attach the web ACL to the NLB. Run the application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL as the database.
options.B: Create a web access control list (web ACL) in AWS WAF that includes the necessary rules. Attach the web ACL to the ALB. Run the application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL as the database.
options.C: Create a web access control list (web ACL) in AWS WAF that includes the necessary rules. Attach the web ACL to the ALB. Run the application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Use Amazon Aurora Serverless as the database.
options.D: Use a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Create a web access control list (web ACL) in AWS WAF that has the necessary rules. Attach the web ACL to the NLB. Run the application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Use Amazon Aurora Serverless as the database.

explanation.full_text: ALB with AWS WAF web ACL. ECS for containers. Aurora Serverless for PostgreSQL with automatic scaling for variable traffic. Cost-effective for weekday/weekend pattern.
explanation.why_correct: ALB supports AWS WAF attachment (inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic). ECS = managed container orchestration, simpler than EKS. Aurora Serverless = PostgreSQL-compatible, auto-scales ACUs based on load. Weekday/weekend pattern = perfect for serverless (scales down weekends = cost savings). Serverless v2: scales 0.5-128 ACUs in seconds.

why_wrong.A: NLB = Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), does NOT support AWS WAF (requires Layer 7). WAF inspects HTTP/HTTPS application traffic. NLB wrong load balancer type. RDS PostgreSQL = always-on, doesn't auto-scale for traffic patterns.
why_wrong.B: Correct ALB + WAF. EKS = Kubernetes, more complex and expensive operational overhead than ECS. RDS = fixed capacity, always-on billing even during low-traffic weekends. Not cost-optimized for variable pattern.
why_wrong.D: NLB = no WAF support (same issue as A). Aurora Serverless correct BUT NLB eliminates WAF requirement. Must use ALB for WAF integration.

explanation.exam_tips: 'AWS WAF' = requires ALB, CloudFront, or API Gateway (Layer 7). NLB = Layer 4, no WAF support. 'Variable traffic' = serverless database (Aurora Serverless, DynamoDB On-Demand). ECS vs EKS: ECS simpler/cheaper, EKS for Kubernetes portability. Aurora Serverless v2 = 0.5-128 ACUs, PostgreSQL/MySQL compatible.
memorize: WAF supported: ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync
WAF NOT supported: NLB (Layer 4)
Aurora Serverless v2: 0.5-128 ACUs, per-second billing
Aurora Serverless v1: deprecated, use v2
ECS vs EKS: ECS = AWS-native, EKS = Kubernetes standard

question_en: A company is developing a photo-hosting application in the us-east-1 Region. The application gives users across multiple countries the ability to upload and view photos. Some photos are heavily viewed for months, while other photos are viewed for less than a week. The application allows users to upload photos that are up to 20 MB in size. The application uses photo metadata to determine which photos to display to each user. The company needs a cost-effective storage solution to support the application.

options.A: Store the photos in Amazon DynamoDB. Turn on DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
options.B: Store the photos in the Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Store the photo metadata and the S3 location URLs in Amazon DynamoDB.
options.C: Store the photos in the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to move photos older than 30 days to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Use object tags to keep track of metadata.
options.D: Store the photos in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Use the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) storage class. Store the photo metadata in Amazon ElastiCache.

explanation.full_text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering for photos with automatic access-based optimization. DynamoDB stores metadata and S3 URLs for fast queries.
explanation.why_correct: Intelligent-Tiering = automatic transitions: Frequent ($0.023/GB) → Infrequent ($0.0125/GB) → Archive Instant ($0.004/GB) → Deep Archive ($0.00099/GB). 'Some heavily viewed, others < 1 week' = unpredictable access = perfect fit. No retrieval fees (unlike Glacier). DynamoDB = fast metadata lookups, stores S3 object keys. Photo served via S3 URL. Scalable globally.

why_wrong.A: DynamoDB = 400KB item size limit. Photos = up to 20MB = cannot store in DynamoDB. DAX = caching layer for DynamoDB, doesn't solve item size problem. Wrong storage type for large objects.
why_wrong.C: Lifecycle to Standard-IA after 30 days = fixed schedule, not adaptive. 'Some heavily viewed months' = would be in IA (more expensive reads: $0.01/GB retrieval). Tags for metadata = inefficient querying, cannot index/search easily. DynamoDB better for metadata.
why_wrong.D: DynamoDB Standard-IA = for tables with infrequent access, 60% storage savings but 25% higher read/write costs. Photos = objects, not DynamoDB items (400KB limit). ElastiCache = in-memory cache, ephemeral, not persistent metadata store.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Variable access + large objects' = S3 Intelligent-Tiering + DynamoDB metadata. DynamoDB item limit = 400KB (objects → S3, metadata → DynamoDB). Intelligent-Tiering = no retrieval fees, auto-optimization. Fixed lifecycle = when access patterns predictable. ElastiCache = caching, not primary database.
memorize: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatic, $0.0025/1K objects monitoring
Intelligent-Tiering tiers: Frequent → Infrequent (30d) → Archive Instant (90d) → Deep Archive (180d)
DynamoDB item size: 400KB maximum
Standard-IA lifecycle: 30-day minimum, $0.01/GB retrieval
Pattern: S3 for objects, DynamoDB for metadata + URLs

question_en: A company has multiple AWS accounts with applications deployed in the us-west-2 Region. Application logs are stored within Amazon S3 buckets in each account. The company wants to build a centralized log analysis solution that uses a single S3 bucket. Logs must not leave us-west-2, and the company wants to incur minimal operational overhead.

options.A: Create an S3 Lifecycle policy that copies the objects from one of the application S3 buckets to the centralized S3 bucket.
options.B: Use S3 Same-Region Replication to replicate logs from the S3 buckets to another S3 bucket in us-west2. Use this S3 bucket for log analysis.
options.C: Write a script that uses the PutObject API operation every day to copy the entire contents of the buckets to another S3 bucket in us-west-2. Use this S3 bucket for log analysis.
options.D: Write AWS Lambda functions in these accounts that are triggered every time logs are delivered to the S3 buckets (s3:ObjectCreated:*) event. Copy the logs to another S3 bucket in us-west-2. Use this S3 bucket for log analysis.

explanation.full_text: S3 Same-Region Replication (SRR) replicates logs from multiple source buckets to centralized bucket within us-west-2. Zero operational overhead, automatic, secure.
explanation.why_correct: SRR = automatic real-time replication within same region. Cross-account supported with IAM roles and bucket policies. Setup: source bucket replication rule → destination bucket. Fully managed, no scripts/Lambda. Logs never leave us-west-2 (compliance). Minimal cost: storage + PUT requests (replication itself free). Continuous replication of new objects.

why_wrong.A: S3 Lifecycle = transitions storage classes OR expires objects. Cannot COPY objects between buckets. Lifecycle actions: transition (Standard → IA → Glacier), expiration (delete), abort incomplete multipart uploads. Wrong tool for aggregation.
why_wrong.C: Daily script with PutObject = operational overhead (schedule, error handling, idempotency, incremental vs full copy). Manual cost optimization (Lambda/EventBridge cron). More complex than managed SRR. Risk of missing objects if script fails.
why_wrong.D: Lambda on s3:ObjectCreated = works but operational overhead (manage Lambda code, error handling, concurrency limits, retries). SRR native feature = simpler, more reliable. Lambda good for transformations, unnecessary for simple copy.

explanation.exam_tips: 'Same region + multi-account + minimal overhead' = S3 SRR. CRR = cross-region replication. SRR use cases: log aggregation, compliance, test/prod data sync. Lifecycle = NOT for copying. Lambda/scripts = operational overhead vs managed SRR. Replication requires versioning enabled on source and destination.
memorize: SRR: Same-Region Replication, intra-region bucket copy
CRR: Cross-Region Replication, inter-region bucket copy
Replication requires: versioning enabled on both buckets
Replication filter: prefix, tags, entire bucket
Replication cost: storage + PUT requests (bandwidth free within region)

question_en: A company has a web application with sporadic usage patterns. Usage is heavy at the beginning of each month, moderate weekly, and unpredictable during the week. The application uses a MySQL database and must move to AWS without database modifications. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Amazon DynamoDB
options.B: Amazon RDS for MySQL
options.C: MySQL-compatible Amazon Aurora Serverless
options.D: MySQL on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group

explanation.why_correct: EC2 This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for cost-optimized architectures.

why_wrong.A: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.B: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.D: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.

explanation.exam_tips: Read question carefully. Identify key requirements. Eliminate options that violate constraints.
explanation.memorize: EC2 + RDS + DynamoDB pattern for Cost-Optimized Architectures

question_en: A company wants to create a long-term storage solution that will allow users to upload terabytes of images and videos. The company will use the images and videos to train machine learning (ML) models. The storage solution must be scalable and cost-optimized. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Provision an Amazon S3 bucket for users to upload images and videos. Copy the data from the S3 bucket to an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system to make the data available for ML model training.
options.B: Provision an Amazon S3 bucket for users to upload images and videos. Configure the S3 bucket to make the data available to Amazon SageMaker AI training. Store the data in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class.
options.C: Configure an Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instance with 16 GB of storage. Create a custom application to allow users to upload images and videos directly to the notebook instance.
options.D: Provision an Amazon S3 bucket for users to upload images and videos. Copy the data from the S3 bucket to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system to make the data available for ML model training.

explanation.why_correct: S3 users to upload images and videos—meeting all specified requirements. This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for cost-optimized architectures.

why_wrong.A: Overly complex architecture with unnecessary service integration. Additional components increase cost, latency, and operational complexity without proportional benefit.
why_wrong.C: This option uses incorrect or suboptimal service for the use case. Does not align with scenario requirements.
why_wrong.D: Overly complex architecture with unnecessary service integration. Additional components increase cost, latency, and operational complexity without proportional benefit.

explanation.exam_tips: S3 considerations: storage classes, lifecycle policies, versioning, replication.
explanation.memorize: S3 + EFS + FSx pattern for Cost-Optimized Architectures

question_en: A company is migrating a data processing application to AWS. The application processes several short-lived batch jobs that cannot be disrupted. The process generates data after each batch job finishes running. The company accesses the data for 30 days following data generation. After 30 days, the company stores the data for 2 years. The company wants to optimize costs for the application and data storage. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to run the application. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 30 days. Configure a bucket policy to delete the data after 2 years.
options.B: Use Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances to run the application. Store the data in Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Move the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days. Configure an S3 Lifecycle configuration to delete the data after 2 years.
options.C: Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to run the application. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days. Configure a bucket policy to delete the data after 2 years.
options.D: Use Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances to run the application. Store the data in Amazon S3 Standard. Move the data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days. Configure an S3 Lifecycle configuration to delete the data after 2 years.

explanation.why_correct: S3 offers lowest storage cost with multiple tiers. Use Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances to run the application—minimizing unnecessary resources and charges.

why_wrong.A: Spot Instances can be interrupted with 2-minute warning. Without fault-tolerance design, interruptions could break critical operations mid-execution.
why_wrong.B: On-Demand Instances run 24/7 but application only needs compute intermittently. Pay for unused capacity increases costs unnecessarily.
why_wrong.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted with 2-minute warning. Without fault-tolerance design, interruptions could break critical operations mid-execution.

explanation.exam_tips: S3 considerations: storage classes, lifecycle policies, versioning, replication.
explanation.memorize: S3 + EC2 pattern for Cost-Optimized Architectures

question_en: A company hosts a multi-tier inventory reporting application on AWS. The company needs a cost-effective solution to generate inventory reports on demand. Admin users need to have the ability to generate new reports. Reports take approximately 5-10 minutes to finish. The application must send reports to the email address of the admin user who generates each report. Options:

options.A: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) to host the report generation code. Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API to invoke the code. Use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to send the reports to admin users.
options.B: Use Amazon EventBridge to invoke a scheduled AWS Lambda function to generate the reports. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send the reports to admin users.
options.C: Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) to host the report generation code. Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API to invoke the code. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send the reports to admin users.
options.D: Create an AWS Lambda function to generate the reports. Use a function URL to invoke the function. Use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to send the reports to admin users.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda Create an AWS Lambda function to generate the reports—meeting all specified requirements. This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for cost-optimized architectures.

why_wrong.A: Overly complex architecture with unnecessary service integration. Additional components increase cost, latency, and operational complexity without proportional benefit.
why_wrong.B: Overly complex architecture with unnecessary service integration. Additional components increase cost, latency, and operational complexity without proportional benefit.

question_en: A company has a serverless web application that is comprised of AWS Lambda functions. The application experiences spikes in traffic that cause increased latency because of cold starts. explanation.exam_tips: Remember Lambda limits: 15 min max, 10GB memory max, 512MB /tmp storage.
explanation.memorize: Lambda + EBS + EFS pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A company needs to integrate with a third-party data feed. The data feed sends a webhook to notify an external service when new data is ready for consumption. A developer wrote an AWS Lambda function to retrieve data when the company receives a webhook callback. The developer must make the Lambda function available for the third party to call. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?

options.A: Create a function URL for the Lambda function. Provide the Lambda function URL to the third party for the webhook.
options.B: Deploy an Application Load Balancer ALB in front of the Lambda function. Provide the ALB URL to the third party for the webhook.
options.C: Create an Amazon SNS topic. Attach the topic to the Lambda function. Provide the public hostname of the SNS topic to the third party for the webhook.
options.D: Create an Amazon SQS queue. Attach the queue to the Lambda function. Provide the public hostname of the SQS queue to the third party for the webhook.

explanation.why_correct: Reduces operational overhead: serverless compute requires no server provisioning or patching.

why_wrong.B: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.C: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.D: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.

explanation.exam_tips: Remember Lambda limits: 15 min max, 10GB memory max, 512MB /tmp storage.
explanation.memorize: Lambda + ALB + SNS pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A solutions architect has created an AWS Lambda function that makes queries to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. When the solutions architect performs a test, the DB instance shows an error for too many connections. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.A: Create a read replica for the DB instance. Query the replica DB instance instead of the primary DB instance.
options.B: Migrate the data to an Amazon DynamoDB database.
options.C: Configure the Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance for Multi-AZ deployment.
options.D: Create a proxy in Amazon RDS Proxy. Query the proxy instead of the DB instance.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda Create a proxy in Amazon RDS Proxy—meeting all specified requirements. This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for high-performing architectures.

why_wrong.A: This option uses incorrect or suboptimal service for the use case. Does not align with scenario requirements.
why_wrong.B: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.C: This option uses incorrect or suboptimal service for the use case. Does not align with scenario requirements.

explanation.exam_tips: Remember Lambda limits: 15 min max, 10GB memory max, 512MB /tmp storage.
explanation.memorize: Lambda + RDS + DynamoDB pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A company recently migrated its application to a VPC on AWS. An AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection connects the company ' s on-premises network to the VPC. The application retrieves customer data from another system that resides on premises. The application uses an on-premises DNS server to resolve domain records. After the migration, the application is not able to connect to the customer data because of name resolution errors. Which solution will give the application the ability to resolve the internal domain names?

options.A: Launch EC2 instances in the VPC. On the EC2 instances, deploy a custom DNS forwarder that forwards all DNS requests to the on-premises DNS server. Create an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone that uses the EC2 instances for name servers.
options.B: Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint. Configure the outbound endpoint to forward DNS queries against the on-premises domain to the on-premises DNS server.
options.C: Set up two AWS Direct Connect connections between the AWS environment and the on-premises network. Set up a link aggregation group (LAG) that includes the two connections. Change the VPC resolver address to point to the on-premises DNS server.
options.D: Create an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone for the on-premises domain. Configure the network ACLs to forward DNS requests against the on-premises domain to the Route 53 public hosted zone.

explanation.why_correct: EC2 Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint—meeting all specified requirements. This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for high-performing architectures.

why_wrong.A: Overly complex architecture with unnecessary service integration. Additional components increase cost, latency, and operational complexity without proportional benefit.
why_wrong.C: Overly complex architecture with unnecessary service integration. Additional components increase cost, latency, and operational complexity without proportional benefit.
why_wrong.D: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.

explanation.exam_tips: Read question carefully. Identify key requirements. Eliminate options that violate constraints.
explanation.memorize: EC2 + VPC + Route 53 pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A media company runs an application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances that requires high storage input /output operations per second (IOPS). To achieve the necessary performance, a solutions architect wants to stripe multiple Amazon EBS volumes together and attach the volumes to EC2 instances. The solutions architect wants to receive a notification when IOPS are over-provisioned. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure auto scaling for the EBS volumes to automatically increase or decrease IOPS based on the EC2 instance CPU utilization metric.
options.B: Deploy the application on an EC2 instance type that supports the highest possible IOPS.
options.C: Create a custom AWS Config rule to monitor the provisioned IOPS for the EBS volumes that are attached to the EC2 instances and to send notifications.
options.D: Adjust the IOPS of each EBS volume daily based on Amazon CloudWatch metrics for IOPS utilization.

explanation.why_correct: EC2 Create a custom AWS Config rule to monitor the provisioned IOPS for the EBS volumes that are attached to the EC2 instances and to send notifications—meeting all specified requirements.

why_wrong.A: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.B: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.D: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.

explanation.exam_tips: Read question carefully. Identify key requirements. Eliminate options that violate constraints.
explanation.memorize: EC2 + Auto Scaling + CloudWatch pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A company hosts a web application on an on-premises server that processes incoming requests. Processing time for each request varies from 5 minutes to 20 minutes. The number of requests is growing. The company wants to move the application to AWS. The company wants to update the architecture to scale automatically.

options.A: Convert the application to a microservices architecture that uses containers. Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the AWS Fargate launch type to run the containerized web application. Configure Service Auto Scaling. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute incoming requests.
options.B: Create an Amazon EC2 instance that has sufficient CPU and RAM capacity to run the application. Create metrics to track usage. Create alarms to notify the company when usage exceeds a specified threshold. Replace the EC2 instance with a larger instance size in the same family when usage is too high.
options.C: Refactor the web application to use multiple AWS Lambda functions. Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API as an entry point to the Lambda functions.
options.D: Refactor the web application to use a single AWS Lambda function. Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API as an entry point to the Lambda function.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda Auto-scales per request (1-1000+ concurrent executions). This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for high-performing architectures.

why_wrong.B: Missing key requirement: scalability.
why_wrong.C: Missing key requirement: scalability.
why_wrong.D: Missing key requirement: scalability.

explanation.exam_tips: Remember Lambda limits: 15 min max, 10GB memory max, 512MB /tmp storage.
explanation.memorize: EC2 + Lambda + ECS pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A company is building an application that runs on several Linux-based containers in Amazon ECS. The containers must have shared access to log files and configuration data. The application requires a POSIXcompliant file system that provides high availability and scalability. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.A: Configure an Amazon EFS file system with elastic throughput.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon S3 bucket and configure shared access and object-level permissions.
options.C: Configure an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system with the Persistent 2 deployment type.
options.D: Attach an Amazon EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance to share access across containers.

explanation.why_correct: S3 offers lowest storage cost with multiple tiers. Provides 99.99% availability across AZs. Configure an Amazon EFS file system with elastic throughput—minimizing unnecessary resources and charges.

why_wrong.B: This option incurs higher costs through unnecessary resource allocation or sub-optimal service choice.
why_wrong.C: This option incurs higher costs through unnecessary resource allocation or sub-optimal service choice.
why_wrong.D: This option incurs higher costs through unnecessary resource allocation or sub-optimal service choice.

explanation.exam_tips: For cost questions: compare pricing models (On-Demand vs Reserved vs Spot vs Serverless). HA requires: Multi-AZ, load balancing, auto scaling, and stateless design. S3 considerations: storage classes, lifecycle policies, versioning, replication.
explanation.memorize: S3 + EC2 + ECS pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A company has developed an API using Amazon API Gateway REST API and AWS Lambda. How can latency be reduced for users worldwide?

options.A: Deploy the REST API as an edge-optimized API endpoint. Enable caching. Enable content encoding to compress data in transit.
options.B: Deploy the REST API as a Regional API endpoint. Enable caching. Enable content encoding to compress data in transit.
options.C: Deploy the REST API as an edge-optimized API endpoint. Enable caching. Configure reserved concurrency for Lambda functions.
options.D: Deploy the REST API as a Regional API endpoint. Enable caching. Configure reserved concurrency for Lambda functions.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda Deploy the REST API as an edge-optimized API endpoint—meeting all specified requirements. This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for high-performing architectures.

why_wrong.B: This option uses incorrect or suboptimal service for the use case. Does not align with scenario requirements.
why_wrong.C: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.D: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.

explanation.exam_tips: Remember Lambda limits: 15 min max, 10GB memory max, 512MB /tmp storage.
explanation.memorize: Lambda + API Gateway pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A company is developing a platform to process large volumes of data for complex analytics and machine learning (ML) tasks. The platform must handle compute-intensive workloads. The workloads currently require 20 to 30 minutes for each data processing step. The company wants a solution to accelerate data processing. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Deploy three Amazon EC2 instances. Distribute the EC2 instances across three Availability Zones. Use traditional batch processing techniques for data processing.
options.B: Create an Amazon EMR cluster. Use managed scaling. Install Apache Spark to assist with data processing.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function for each data processing step. Deploy an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to relay data between Lambda functions.
options.D: Create a series of AWS Lambda functions to process the data. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the Lambda functions into data processing steps.

explanation.why_correct: Reduces operational overhead: fully managed service eliminates infrastructure management.

why_wrong.A: Requires additional operational management, monitoring, or manual intervention compared to simpler alternatives.
why_wrong.C: Overly complex architecture with unnecessary service integration. Additional components increase cost, latency, and operational complexity without proportional benefit.
why_wrong.D: Requires additional operational management, monitoring, or manual intervention compared to simpler alternatives.

explanation.exam_tips: Remember Lambda limits: 15 min max, 10GB memory max, 512MB /tmp storage.
explanation.memorize: EC2 + Lambda + SQS pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en: A company wants to build a generative AI (GenAI) model for a medical use case. The company has 50 TB of medical image data that is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company plans to train the GenAI model by using Amazon SageMaker AI with multiple GPU-powered instances. The company needs a storage solution that helps ensure that the data can be loaded from storage fast enough to avoid GPU instance idle time. The storage solution needs to achieve tens of gigabits per second (Gbps) of throughput. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure the existing S3 bucket as the SageMaker AI data source by using file mode.
options.B: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Move the data from Amazon S3 to Lustre by using data repository association. Mount the file system on the instances.
options.C: Configure the existing S3 bucket as the SageMaker AI data source by using fast file mode.
options.D: Move the data to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class. Configure the S3 bucket as the SageMaker AI data source by using fast file mode.

explanation.why_correct: S3 Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system—meeting all specified requirements. This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for high-performing architectures.

why_wrong.A: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.C: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.D: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.

explanation.exam_tips: S3 considerations: storage classes, lifecycle policies, versioning, replication.
explanation.memorize: S3 + FSx pattern for High-Performing Architectures

question_en:
A company uses a general-purpose instance class Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. The company has configured the DB instance in a Multi-AZ configuration across two Availability Zones as part of the company ' s production application. The company ' s finance team needs to run SQL queries against the DB instance to generate reports. Customers have reported significant performance issues with the application during report generation. A solutions architect needs to minimize the effect of the reporting job on the DB instance.



Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create a proxy in Amazon RDS Proxy. Update the reporting job to query the proxy endpoint.
options.B: Update the RDS DB instance configuration to use three Availability Zones.
options.C: Add an RDS read replica. Update the reporting job to query the replica endpoint.
options.D: Change the RDS configuration from a general-purpose instance class to a memory-optimized instance class.

explanation.why_correct: RDS This architecture aligns with AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices for high-performing architectures.

why_wrong.A: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.B: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.
why_wrong.D: Missing key requirement: optimal service selection.

explanation.exam_tips: Read question carefully. Identify key requirements. Eliminate options that violate constraints.
explanation.memorize: Key pattern: architecture_design with minimize_cost, performance

question_en: A company uses a Microsoft SQL Server database. The applications currently connect using SQL Server protocols. The company wants to migrate to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal changes to application code. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Use AWS SCT to rewrite SQL queries in the applications.
options.B: Enable Babelfish on Aurora PostgreSQL to run SQL Server queries.
options.C: Migrate the database schema and data using AWS SCT and AWS DMS.
options.D: D. Use Amazon RDS Proxy to connect the applications to Aurora PostgreSQL.
options.E: Use AWS DMS to rewrite SQL queries in the applications.

explanation.why_correct: B: Babelfish enables Aurora PostgreSQL to understand SQL Server T-SQL and wire protocol, minimizing code changes. C: SCT + DMS migrates schema and data from SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL.

why_wrong.A: SCT rewrites queries but Babelfish allows apps to continue using SQL Server syntax.
why_wrong.D: RDS Proxy manages connections, doesn't translate SQL Server protocols.
why_wrong.E: DMS migrates data, doesn't rewrite application queries.

explanation.exam_tips: Babelfish = SQL Server compatibility on Aurora PostgreSQL. SCT = schema conversion. DMS = data migration. Combine for minimal code changes.
explanation.memorize: Babelfish + SCT + DMS = migrate SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal app changes.

question_en: A media publishing company is building an application that allows users to print custom books. The frontend runs in a Docker container. Incoming order volume is highly variable and can exceed the throughput of the physical printing machines. Order-processing payloads can be up to 4 MB. The company needs a scalable solution for handling incoming orders. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Use Amazon SQS to queue incoming orders. Use Lambda@Edge to process orders. Deploy the frontend on Amazon EKS.
options.B: Use Amazon SNS to queue incoming orders. Use a Lambda function to process orders. Deploy the frontend on AWS Fargate.
options.C: Use Amazon SQS to queue incoming orders. Use a Lambda function to process orders. Deploy the frontend on Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type.
options.D: Use Amazon SNS to queue incoming orders. Use Lambda@Edge to process orders. Deploy the frontend on Amazon EC2 instances.

explanation.why_correct: SQS queues orders durably, buffering bursts beyond printer capacity. Lambda processes from queue, auto-scaling. ECS Fargate runs frontend containers serverless.

why_wrong.A: Lambda@Edge for CloudFront edge processing, not backend order processing. EKS adds K8s complexity.
why_wrong.B: SNS pub/sub, not durable queue for burst buffering.
why_wrong.D: SNS not queue. Lambda@Edge wrong use case.

explanation.exam_tips: SQS = durable queue for burst buffering. SNS = pub/sub. Lambda@Edge = CloudFront edge. Match service to pattern.
explanation.memorize: SQS + Lambda + ECS Fargate = scalable order processing with burst tolerance.

question_en: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer ALB. The application uses Amazon DynamoDB as its database. The company wants to ensure high performance for reads and writes. Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure automatic scaling for the DynamoDB table. Set a target utilization of 70%. Set the minimum and maximum capacity units based on the expected workload.
options.B: Analyze the DynamoDB table usage. Create a global secondary index GSI on the existing table for frequently used keys. Assign read and write capacity units appropriately.
options.C: Use DynamoDB provisioned throughput mode for the table. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm for the ThrottledRequests metric. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to increase provisioned capacity.
options.D: Create an Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator DAX cluster. Configure the application to use the DAX endpoint.

explanation.why_correct: DynamoDB Auto Scaling with 70% target utilization adjusts read/write capacity based on demand, cost-effectively balancing performance and cost.

why_wrong.B: GSI for alternate query patterns, doesn't manage overall throughput.
why_wrong.C: Manual CloudWatch + Lambda scaling adds operational overhead vs native auto-scaling.
why_wrong.D: DAX caches reads only, doesn't improve write performance.

explanation.exam_tips: DynamoDB Auto Scaling = automatic capacity adjustment. 70% target = AWS recommended. DAX = read cache only.
explanation.memorize: DynamoDB Auto Scaling at 70% = cost-effective read+write performance.

question_en: A company uses Amazon Route 53 as its DNS provider. The company hosts a website both on premises and in the AWS Cloud. The company ' s on-premises data center is near the us-west-1 Region. The company hosts the website on AWS in the eu-central-1 Region. The company wants to optimize load times for the website as much as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create a DNS record with a failover routing policy that routes all primary traffic to eu-central-1. Configure the routing policy to use the on-premises data center as the secondary location.
options.B: Create a DNS record with an IP-based routing policy. Configure specific IP ranges to return the value for the eu-central-1 website. Configure all other IP ranges to return the value for the on-premises website.
options.C: Create a DNS record with a latency-based routing policy. Configure one latency record for the eucentral-1 website and one latency record for the on-premises data center. Associate the record for the onpremises data center with the us-west-1 Region.
options.D: Create a DNS record with a weighted routing policy. Split the traffic evenly between eu-central-1 and the on-premises data center.

explanation.why_correct: Route 53 latency-based routing directs users to endpoint with lowest measured latency. Associate on-premises (near us-west-1) with us-west-1, AWS with eu-central-1.

why_wrong.A: Failover for HA, not performance. All traffic goes to primary unless unhealthy.
why_wrong.B: IP-based routes by location, not measured latency. Manual IP range mapping less accurate.
why_wrong.D: Weighted routing splits by fixed percentages, ignores latency.

explanation.exam_tips: Latency-based = lowest latency (performance). Failover = HA. Weighted = traffic split. Geolocation = location-based.
explanation.memorize: Route 53 latency-based routing = optimal performance by measured latency.

question_en: A company runs a container application on a Kubernetes cluster in the company ' s data center. The application uses Advanced Message Queuing Protocol AMQP to communicate with a message queue. The data center cannot scale fast enough to meet the company ' s expanding business needs. The company wants to migrate the workloads to AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Migrate the container application to Amazon ECS. Use Amazon SQS to retrieve the messages.
options.B: Migrate the container application to Amazon EKS. Use Amazon MQ to retrieve the messages.
options.C: Use highly available Amazon EC2 instances to run the application. Use Amazon MQ to retrieve the messages.
options.D: Use AWS Lambda functions to run the application. Use Amazon SQS to retrieve the messages.

explanation.why_correct: EKS preserves existing Kubernetes platform. Amazon MQ supports AMQP protocol. Minimal platform changes, least operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: ECS different container orchestration. SQS doesn't support AMQP natively.
why_wrong.C: EC2 requires most infrastructure management vs managed EKS.
why_wrong.D: Lambda requires app redesign. SQS not AMQP compatible.

explanation.exam_tips: EKS = managed Kubernetes. Amazon MQ = managed message brokers (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ). Preserve existing protocols when migrating.
explanation.memorize: EKS + Amazon MQ = migrate Kubernetes + AMQP with minimal changes.

question_en: A company runs an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system on Amazon EC2 instances in a single AWS Region. Users connect to the ERP system by using a public API that is hosted on the EC2 instances. International users report slow API response times from their data centers. A solutions architect needs to improve API response times for the international users. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection that has a public virtual interface (VIF) to connect each user ' s data center to the EC2 instances. Create a Direct Connect gateway for the ERP system API to route user API requests.
