options.B: Deploy Amazon API Gateway endpoints in multiple Regions. Use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to route requests to the nearest endpoint. Configure a VPC peering connection between the Regions to connect to the ERP system.
options.C: Set up AWS Global Accelerator. Configure listeners for the necessary ports. Configure endpoint groups for the appropriate Regions to distribute traffic. Create an endpoint in each group for the API.
options.D: Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish dedicated VPN tunnels between multiple Regions and user networks. Route traffic to the API through the VPN connections.

explanation.why_correct: Global Accelerator routes traffic via AWS edge network using anycast IPs, reducing latency for international users accessing single-region API.

why_wrong.A: Direct Connect per user location extremely expensive and complex.
why_wrong.B: Multi-region API Gateway + VPC peering adds complexity and cost vs Global Accelerator.
why_wrong.D: Site-to-Site VPN adds encryption overhead, doesn't optimize latency like AWS backbone.

explanation.exam_tips: Global Accelerator = anycast IPs + AWS edge network for TCP/UDP. CloudFront = HTTP/HTTPS content caching. Choose based on protocol.
explanation.memorize: Global Accelerator = improve global latency for single-region applications.

question_en: An ecommerce company wants to collect user clickstream data from the company ' s website for real-time analysis. The website experiences fluctuating traffic patterns throughout the day. The company needs a scalable solution that can adapt to varying levels of traffic. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use a data stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams in on-demand mode to capture the clickstream data. Use AWS Lambda to process the data in real time.
options.B: Use Amazon Data Firehose to capture the clickstream data. Use AWS Glue to process the data in real time.
options.C: Use Amazon Kinesis Video Streams to capture the clickstream data. Use AWS Glue to process the data in real time.
options.D: Use Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink (previously known as Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics) to capture the clickstream data. Use AWS Lambda to process the data in real time.

explanation.why_correct: Kinesis Data Streams on-demand mode auto-scales with traffic. Lambda processes real-time from stream. Perfect for fluctuating clickstream data.

why_wrong.B: Firehose buffers/batches data, not real-time. Glue for ETL, not real-time processing.
why_wrong.C: Kinesis Video Streams for video data, not clickstream.
why_wrong.D: Flink for complex streaming analytics. Lambda simpler for basic real-time processing.

explanation.exam_tips: Kinesis Data Streams = real-time streaming. On-demand mode = auto-scale. Firehose = batch delivery to storage.
explanation.memorize: Kinesis Data Streams on-demand + Lambda = auto-scaling real-time processing.

question_en: A company tracks customer satisfaction by using surveys that the company hosts on its website. The surveys sometimes reach thousands of customers every hour. Survey results are currently sent in email messages to the company so company employees can manually review results and assess customer sentiment. The company wants to automate the customer survey process. Survey results must be available for the previous 12 months. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST scalable way?

options.A:
Send the survey results data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is connected to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Create an AWS Lambda function to poll the SQS queue,



call Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.
options.B: Send the survey results data to an API that is running on an Amazon EC2 instance. Configure the API to store the survey results as a new record in an Amazon DynamoDB table, call Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and save the results in a second DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.
options.C: Write the survey results data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function to read the data and call Amazon Rekognition for sentiment analysis. Store the sentiment analysis results in a second S3 bucket. Use S3 Lifecycle policies on each bucket to expire objects after 365 days.
options.D: Send the survey results data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that is connected to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the SQS queue to invoke an AWS Lambda function that calls Amazon Lex for sentiment analysis and saves the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Set the TTL for all records to 365 days in the future.

explanation.why_correct: API Gateway + SQS (durable buffer) + Lambda (polls SQS) + Comprehend (sentiment) + DynamoDB (TTL 365 days). Fully managed, scales automatically.

why_wrong.B: EC2 API requires managing instances, doesn't scale as easily.
why_wrong.C: Rekognition for images/video, not text sentiment analysis.
why_wrong.D: Lex for conversational interfaces, not sentiment analysis.

explanation.exam_tips: Comprehend = sentiment analysis. Rekognition = image/video. Lex = chatbots. Match service to content type.
explanation.memorize: API Gateway + SQS + Lambda + Comprehend + DynamoDB TTL = automated sentiment analysis.

question_en:
An ecommerce company is launching a new marketing campaign. The company anticipates the campaign to generate ten times the normal number of daily orders through the company ' s ecommerce application. The campaign will last 3 days.



The ecommerce application architecture is based on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group and an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. The application writes order transactions to an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system before the application writes orders to the database. During normal operations, the application write operations peak at 5,000 IOPS. A solutions architect needs to ensure that the application can handle the anticipated workload during the marketing campaign. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: For the duration of the campaign, increase the provisioned IOPS for the RDS for MySQL database. Set the Amazon EFS throughput mode to Bursting throughput.
options.B: For the duration of the campaign, increase the provisioned IOPS for the RDS for MySQL database. Set the Amazon EFS throughput mode to Elastic throughput.
options.C: Convert the database to a Multi-AZ deployment. Set the Amazon EFS throughput mode to Elastic throughput for the duration of the campaign.
options.D: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to convert the database to RDS for PostgreSQL. Set the Amazon EFS throughput mode to Bursting throughput.

explanation.why_correct: Increase RDS Provisioned IOPS for DB throughput. EFS Elastic throughput auto-scales with workload, handling 10x spike effectively.

why_wrong.A: EFS Bursting throughput limited by credits, may not sustain 10x for 3 days.
why_wrong.C: Multi-AZ for HA, doesn't improve throughput. Elastic throughput correct.
why_wrong.D: PostgreSQL migration unnecessary. Bursting throughput insufficient for sustained spike.

explanation.exam_tips: EFS Elastic throughput = auto-scales with usage. Bursting = credit-based. Choose Elastic for sustained high throughput.
explanation.memorize: RDS Provisioned IOPS + EFS Elastic throughput = handle sustained traffic spikes.

question_en: A company is building a serverless web application that will serve customers globally by using REST API endpoints. The application must minimize latency regardless of the application us-er ' s geographic location. The initial amount of traffic that the application will handle is un-known.

options.A: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API with edge-optimized API endpoints for all cus-tomers. Create AWS Lambda functions. Optimize Lambda performance by adjusting the memory settings and configuring provisioned concurrency.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API with Regional API endpoints for all customers. Create AWS Lambda functions. Optimize Lambda performance by adjusting the memory set-tings and configuring reserved concurrency.
options.C: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API with Regional API endpoints for all customers. Create AWS Lambda functions. Use an HTTP integration to optimize Lambda performance.
options.D: Deploy a Network Load Balancer in each AWS Region where customers are located. Create AWS Lambda functions. Optimize Lambda performance by adjusting the memory settings and configuring provisioned concurrency.

explanation.why_correct: Edge-optimized API Gateway routes via CloudFront edge locations globally. Lambda with provisioned concurrency ensures consistent low latency. Scales for unknown traffic.

why_wrong.B: Regional endpoints serve single region, no global edge acceleration. Reserved concurrency doesn't prevent cold starts.
why_wrong.C: HTTP integration doesn't optimize Lambda performance vs provisioned concurrency.
why_wrong.D: NLB per region not serverless, high operational overhead, no edge acceleration.

explanation.exam_tips: Edge-optimized API Gateway = CloudFront edge + global acceleration. Regional = single region. Provisioned concurrency = eliminate cold starts.
explanation.memorize: Edge-optimized API Gateway + Lambda provisioned concurrency = global low-latency serverless API.

question_en:
A company has multiple Amazon RDS DB instances that run in a development AWS account. All the instances have tags to identify them as development resources. The company needs the development DB instances to run on a schedule only during business hours.



Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to identify RDS instances that need to be stopped Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.
options.B: Create an AWS Trusted Advisor report to identify RDS instances to be started and stopped. Create an AWS Lambda function to start and stop the RDS instances.
options.C: Create AWS Systems Manager State Manager associations to start and stop the RDS instances.
options.D: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the RDS instances.

explanation.why_correct: EventBridge scheduled rule invokes Lambda to start/stop RDS instances on business hours schedule. Fully managed, least overhead.

why_wrong.A: CloudWatch alarms for monitoring thresholds, not scheduling.
why_wrong.B: Trusted Advisor for recommendations, not task scheduling.
why_wrong.C: Systems Manager State Manager can work but EventBridge + Lambda simpler for RDS start/stop.

explanation.exam_tips: EventBridge = event-driven automation and scheduling. CloudWatch alarms = metric thresholds. Choose EventBridge for scheduled tasks.
explanation.memorize: EventBridge scheduled rule + Lambda = automated RDS start/stop on schedule.

question_en: A company is migrating its databases to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The company is migrating its applications to Amazon EC2 instances. The company wants to optimize costs for long-running workloads. Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Use On-Demand Instances for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year Compute Savings Plan with the No Upfront option for the EC2 instances.
options.B: Purchase Reserved Instances for a 1 year term with the No Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the No Upfront option for the EC2 instances.
options.C: Purchase Reserved Instances for a 1 year term with the Partial Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 1 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the Partial Upfront option for the EC2 instances.
options.D: Purchase Reserved Instances for a 3 year term with the All Upfront option for the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL workloads. Purchase a 3 year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with the All Upfront option for the EC2 instances.

explanation.why_correct: 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instances (RDS) + 3-year All Upfront EC2 Instance Savings Plan = maximum savings for long-running workloads.

why_wrong.A: On-Demand RDS expensive for long-running. 1-year less savings than 3-year.
why_wrong.B: 1-year term less discount than 3-year for long-running workloads.
why_wrong.C: Partial Upfront less discount than All Upfront.

explanation.exam_tips: Longer term + All Upfront = maximum discount. No Upfront = no upfront cost but less discount. Match commitment to workload duration.
explanation.memorize: 3-year All Upfront Reserved/Savings Plans = most cost-effective for long-running workloads.

question_en: An ecommerce company hosts a three-tier web application in a VPC. The web tier runs on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. The company stores a product catalog and customer sales information in Amazon DynamoDB. The company ' s finance team uses a reporting application to generate reports of daily product sales. When the finance team runs the daily reports, a sudden performance decrease affects website customers. The company wants to improve the performance of the system. Which solution will meet these requirements with MINIMAL changes to the current architecture?

options.A: Migrate the application to larger EC2 instances. Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure a read replica of the database in a second Availability Zone.
options.B: Increase the compute capacity of the EC2 instances. Migrate the database to Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached).
options.C: Implement DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
options.D: Configure DynamoDB streams.

explanation.why_correct: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) provides microsecond in-memory cache for DynamoDB, offloading read-heavy report queries with minimal architecture changes.

why_wrong.A: RDS migration changes database platform. Read replica helps but doesn't address DynamoDB architecture.
why_wrong.B: ElastiCache requires app changes to use cache. Larger instances don't address DynamoDB.
why_wrong.D: DynamoDB Streams for change data capture, doesn't cache or accelerate reads.

explanation.exam_tips: DAX = in-memory cache for DynamoDB. ElastiCache = general caching (RDS, etc). Match cache to database type.
explanation.memorize: DAX = DynamoDB acceleration with minimal code changes.

question_en: Question: A genomics research company is designing a scalable architecture for a loosely coupled workload. Tasks in the workload are independent and can be processed in parallel. The architecture needs to minimize management overhead and provide automatic scaling based on demand. Options:

options.A: Use a cluster of Amazon EC2 instances. Use AWS Systems Manager to manage the workload.
options.B: Implement a serverless architecture that uses AWS Lambda functions.
options.C: Use AWS ParallelCluster to deploy a dedicated high-performance cluster.
options.D: Implement vertical scaling for each workload task.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda serverless, auto-scales per event. Independent parallel tasks ideal for Lambda. Zero infrastructure management.

why_wrong.A: EC2 cluster requires managing instances, scaling configuration.
why_wrong.C: ParallelCluster for tightly-coupled HPC, not loosely-coupled tasks.
why_wrong.D: Vertical scaling increases instance size, doesn't enable parallel processing.

explanation.exam_tips: Lambda = serverless, event-driven, auto-scale. ParallelCluster = HPC. Match compute to coupling (loose vs tight).
explanation.memorize: Lambda = loosely-coupled parallel tasks with minimal management.

question_en: Question: A machine learning (ML) team is building an application that uses data that is in an Amazon S3 bucket. The ML team needs a storage solution for its model training workflow on AWS. The ML team requires highperformance storage that supports frequent access to training datasets. The storage solution must integrate natively with Amazon S3. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? Options:

options.A: Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes to provide high-performance storage. Use AWS DataSync to migrate data from the S3 bucket to EBS volumes.
options.B: Use Amazon EC2 ML instances to provide high-performance storage. Store training data on Amazon EBS volumes. Use the S3 Copy API to copy data from the S3 bucket to EBS volumes.
options.C: Use Amazon FSx for Lustre to provide high-performance storage. Store training datasets in Amazon S3 Standard storage.
options.D: Use Amazon EMR to provide high-performance storage. Store training datasets in Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage.

explanation.why_correct: FSx for Lustre provides high-performance file system, integrates natively with S3. Ideal for ML training with frequent dataset access.

why_wrong.A: EBS single-instance. DataSync for migration, adds operational overhead.
why_wrong.B: EC2 + EBS requires managing instances and storage.
why_wrong.D: EMR for big data processing. Glacier Instant Retrieval too slow for frequent training access.

explanation.exam_tips: FSx Lustre = HPC/ML file system + S3 integration. EBS = single-instance block storage. Match storage to access pattern.
explanation.memorize: FSx for Lustre + S3 = high-performance ML training storage with native integration.

question_en: A company runs a Windows-based ecommerce application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application has a very high transaction rate. The company requires a durable storage solution that can deliver 200,000 IOPS for each EC2 instance. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Host the application on EC2 instances that have Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Block Express Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes attached.
options.B: Install the application on an Amazon EMR cluster. Use Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) with General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes.
options.C: Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as shared storage across the EC2 instances that run the application.
options.D: Host the application on EC2 instances that have SSD instance store volumes and General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes attached.

explanation.why_correct: io2 Block Express delivers up to 256K IOPS per volume with sub-ms latency and high durability. Meets 200K IOPS requirement per instance.

why_wrong.B: EMR + HDFS for big data, not transactional ecommerce. gp3 max 16K IOPS insufficient.
why_wrong.C: FSx Lustre for HPC, not Windows ecommerce application.
why_wrong.D: Instance store ephemeral. gp3 insufficient IOPS.

explanation.exam_tips: io2 Block Express = up to 256K IOPS. io2 = up to 64K IOPS. gp3 = up to 16K IOPS. Match IOPS requirement to volume type.
explanation.memorize: io2 Block Express = ultra-high IOPS (256K) for demanding workloads.

question_en: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application is deployed in private subnets in three Availability Zones of the us-east-1 Region. The instances must be able to connect to the internet to download files. The company wants a design that is highly available across the Region. Which solution should be implemented to ensure that there are no disruptions to internet connectivity?

options.A: Deploy a NAT instance in a private subnet of each Availability Zone.
options.B: Deploy a NAT gateway in a public subnet of each Availability Zone.
options.C: Deploy a transit gateway in a private subnet of each Availability Zone.
options.D: Deploy an internet gateway in a public subnet of each Availability Zone.

explanation.why_correct: NAT gateway in public subnet per AZ enables private subnet internet access with HA. Fully managed, no disruptions.

why_wrong.A: NAT instance requires managing EC2, less reliable than NAT gateway.
why_wrong.C: Transit Gateway for VPC interconnection, not internet access.
why_wrong.D: Internet Gateway per VPC, not per AZ. Doesn't help private subnets.

explanation.exam_tips: NAT gateway = managed HA internet access for private subnets. One per AZ for HA. Internet gateway = VPC-level.
explanation.memorize: NAT gateway per AZ in public subnet = HA internet access for private subnets.

question_en: A company runs HPC workloads requiring high IOPS. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO)

options.A: Use Amazon EFS as a high-performance file system.
options.B: Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as a high-performance file system.
options.C: Create an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances. Use Reserved Instances. Configure a spread placement group. Use AWS Batch for analytics.
options.D: Use Mountpoint for Amazon S3 as a high-performance file system.
options.E: Create an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances. Use mixed instance types and a cluster placement group. Use Amazon EMR for analytics.

explanation.why_correct: B: FSx for Lustre delivers high IOPS for HPC. E: Cluster placement group provides low-latency networking. EMR for analytics. Mixed instances optimize cost.

why_wrong.A: EFS not optimized for HPC high IOPS.
why_wrong.C: Spread placement for HA, not low latency. Reserved Instances for cost, Batch not for HPC analytics.
why_wrong.D: Mountpoint for S3 doesn't meet high IOPS needs.

explanation.exam_tips: FSx Lustre = HPC file system. Cluster placement = low latency. Spread placement = HA. Match to workload requirement.
explanation.memorize: FSx Lustre + cluster placement + EMR = HPC analytics with high IOPS.

question_en: A solutions architect needs to implement a solution that can handle up to 5,000 messages per second. The solution must publish messages as events to multiple consumers. The messages are up to 500 KB in size. The message consumers need to have the ability to use multiple programming languages to consume the messages with minimal latency. The solution must retain published messages for more than 3 months. The solution must enforce strict ordering of the messages.

options.A: Publish messages to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams data stream. Enable enhanced fan-out. Ensure that consumers ingest the data stream by using dedicated throughput.
options.B: Publish messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Ensure that consumers use an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue to subscribe to the topic.
options.C: Publish messages to Amazon EventBridge. Allow each consumer to create rules to deliver messages to the consumer ' s own target.
options.D: Publish messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Ensure that consumers use Amazon Data Firehose to subscribe to the topic.

explanation.why_correct: Kinesis Data Streams supports 5K msgs/sec, 500KB messages, strict ordering per shard, 365-day retention. Enhanced fan-out for multiple consumers with dedicated throughput.

why_wrong.B: SNS doesn't enforce ordering. SQS FIFO 256KB limit, lower throughput.
why_wrong.C: EventBridge no ordering guarantees, 24-hour retention only.
why_wrong.D: SNS + Firehose batch-oriented, no strict ordering.

explanation.exam_tips: Kinesis = high throughput + ordering + long retention + multi-consumer. SQS FIFO = ordering but lower scale. Choose based on requirements.
explanation.memorize: Kinesis Data Streams = 5K msgs/sec + ordering + 365-day retention + enhanced fan-out.

question_en: A company is developing a serverless, bidirectional chat application that can broadcast messages to connected clients. The application is based on AWS Lambda functions. The Lambda functions receive incoming messages in JSON format. The company needs to provide a frontend component for the application. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API to direct incoming JSON messages to backend destinations.
options.B: Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API that is configured with a Lambda proxy integration.
options.C: Use an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API to direct incoming JSON messages to backend destinations.
options.D: Use an Amazon CloudFront distribution that is configured with a Lambda function URL as a custom origin.

explanation.why_correct: WebSocket API enables bidirectional, real-time communication for chat. Long-lived connections between clients and Lambda backend.

why_wrong.A: HTTP API request-response only, not bidirectional persistent connections.
why_wrong.B: REST API request-response model, not real-time bidirectional.
why_wrong.D: CloudFront + Lambda URL can't maintain stateful WebSocket connections.

explanation.exam_tips: WebSocket API = bidirectional real-time. HTTP/REST API = request-response. Match API type to communication pattern.
explanation.memorize: API Gateway WebSocket API = bidirectional real-time chat applications.

question_en: A company runs an HPC workload that uses a 200-TB file system on premises. The company needs to migrate this data to Amazon FSx for Lustre. Internet capacity is 10 Mbps, and all data must be migrated within 30 days. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Use AWS DMS to transfer data into S3 and link FSx for Lustre to the bucket.
options.B: Deploy AWS DataSync on premises and transfer directly into FSx for Lustre.
options.C: Use AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway to move data into FSx for Lustre.
options.D: Use an AWS Snowball Edge storage-optimized device to transfer data into S3 and link FSx for Lustre to the bucket.

explanation.why_correct: 200TB / 10Mbps = impossible in 30 days online. Snowball Edge offline transfer to S3, then link FSx for Lustre to S3 bucket. Only viable solution.

why_wrong.A: DMS for database migration, not file system. Still limited by 10Mbps.
why_wrong.B: DataSync limited by 10Mbps internet, can't transfer 200TB in 30 days.
why_wrong.C: Storage Gateway limited by 10Mbps bandwidth.

explanation.exam_tips: Snowball Edge for petabyte/multi-hundred-TB offline transfers. DataSync for online transfers. Calculate bandwidth × time to determine feasibility.
explanation.memorize: Snowball Edge = offline bulk data transfer when bandwidth insufficient.

question_en: A company is deploying an application that processes streaming data in near-real time. The company plans to use Amazon EC2 instances for the workload. The network architecture must be configurable to provide the lowest possible latency between nodes. Which networking solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Place the EC2 instances in multiple VPCs, and configure VPC peering.
options.B: Attach an Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) to each EC2 instance.
options.C: Run the EC2 instances in a spread placement group.
options.D: Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) optimized instance types.

explanation.why_correct: Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) provides ultra-low latency, high throughput networking for tightly-coupled workloads. Bypasses traditional TCP/IP.

why_wrong.A: VPC peering adds network hops, increases latency.
why_wrong.C: Spread placement separates instances for HA, increases latency vs cluster.
why_wrong.D: EBS optimized for storage performance, not network latency.

explanation.exam_tips: EFA = ultra-low network latency for HPC/ML. Enhanced networking = improved network performance. Cluster placement = physical proximity.
explanation.memorize: EFA = lowest possible inter-instance network latency for streaming/HPC.

question_en: A company hosts its multi-tier, public web application in the AWS Cloud. The web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances, and its database runs on Amazon RDS. The company is anticipating a large increase in sales during an upcoming holiday weekend. A solutions architect needs to build asolution to analyze the performance of the web application with a granularity of no more than 2 minutes. What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

options.A: Send Amazon CloudWatch logs to Amazon Redshift. Use Amazon QuickSight to perform further analysis.
options.B: Enable detailed monitoring on all EC2 instances. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to perform further analysis.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function to fetch EC2 logs from Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to perform further analysis.
options.D: Send EC2 logs to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Redshift to fetch togs from the S3 bucket to process raw data tor further analysis with Amazon QuickSight.

explanation.why_correct: Detailed monitoring on EC2 provides 1-minute granularity CloudWatch metrics. Default is 5-minute. Meets 2-minute requirement.

why_wrong.A: Logs to Redshift overcomplicated. CloudWatch metrics simpler for performance monitoring.
why_wrong.C: Lambda to fetch logs unnecessary. CloudWatch metrics already provide needed data.
why_wrong.D: S3 + Redshift overly complex for simple performance analysis.

explanation.exam_tips: Detailed monitoring = 1-min metrics. Default = 5-min. Enable detailed monitoring for finer granularity performance analysis.
explanation.memorize: EC2 detailed monitoring = 1-minute CloudWatch metrics for performance analysis.

question_en: How can trade data from DynamoDB be ingested into an S3 data lake for near real-time analysis?

options.A: Use DynamoDB Streams to invoke a Lambda function that writes to S3.
options.B: Use DynamoDB Streams to invoke a Lambda function that writes to Data Firehose, which writes to S3.
options.C: Enable Kinesis Data Streams on DynamoDB. Configure it to invoke a Lambda function that writes to S3.
options.D: Enable Kinesis Data Streams on DynamoDB. Use Data Firehose to write to S3.

explanation.why_correct: DynamoDB Streams capture changes. Lambda triggered by stream writes directly to S3. Simple, real-time, serverless ingestion.

why_wrong.B: Adding Firehose unnecessary complexity for simple S3 write.
why_wrong.C: Kinesis Data Streams adds complexity vs DynamoDB Streams direct integration.
why_wrong.D: Kinesis + Firehose overcomplicated for DynamoDB to S3 ingestion.

explanation.exam_tips: DynamoDB Streams = CDC for DynamoDB. Lambda = serverless processing. Direct integration simpler than adding Kinesis/Firehose.
explanation.memorize: DynamoDB Streams → Lambda → S3 = simple real-time data lake ingestion.

question_en: A company uses Amazon S3 to host its static website. The company wants to add a contact form to the webpage. The contact form will have dynamic server-side components for users to input their name, email address, phone number, and user message. The company expects fewer than 100 site visits each month. The contact form must notify the company by email when a customer fills out the form. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Host the dynamic contact form in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Set up Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to connect to a third-party email provider.
options.B: Create an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that returns the contact form from an AWS Lambda function. Configure another Lambda function on the API Gateway to publish a message to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic.
options.C: Host the website by using AWS Amplify Hosting for static content and dynamic content. Use serverside scripting to build the contact form. Configure Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to deliver the message to the company.
options.D: Migrate the website from Amazon S3 to Amazon EC2 instances that run Windows Server. Use Internet Information Services (IIS) for Windows Server to host the webpage. Use client-side scripting to build the contact form. Integrate the form with Amazon WorkMail.

explanation.why_correct: API Gateway + Lambda (serverless form processing) + SNS (email notifications). Scales automatically, no servers, cost-effective for <100 visits/month.

why_wrong.A: ECS requires container management, overkill for simple form.
why_wrong.C: Amplify + SQS more complex than API Gateway + SNS for email notifications.
why_wrong.D: EC2 + IIS highest cost and management overhead, not cost-effective.

explanation.exam_tips: API Gateway + Lambda + SNS = serverless form processing with email. Pay per use, ideal for low traffic.
explanation.memorize: API Gateway + Lambda + SNS = cost-effective serverless contact form.

question_en: A company wants to run a hybrid workload for data processing. The data needs to be accessed by on-premises applications for local data processing using an NFS protocol, and must also be accessible from the AWS Cloud for further analytics and batch processing. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway to provide file storage to AWS, then perform analytics on this data in the AWS Cloud.
options.B: Use an AWS Storage Gateway tape gateway to copy the backup of the local data to AWS, then perform analytics on this data in the AWS Cloud.
options.C: Use an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway in a stored volume configuration to regularly take snapshots of the local data, then copy the data to AWS.
options.D: Use an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway in a cached volume configuration to back up all the local storage in the AWS Cloud, then perform analytics on this data in the cloud.

explanation.why_correct: Storage Gateway file gateway presents NFS interface backed by S3. On-premises apps use NFS, cloud apps use S3 data. Hybrid workload solution.

why_wrong.B: Tape gateway for backup/archive, not active file sharing.
why_wrong.C: Volume gateway stored volumes for iSCSI block storage, not NFS file access.
why_wrong.D: Volume gateway cached volumes for iSCSI, not NFS.

explanation.exam_tips: File gateway = NFS/SMB to S3. Volume gateway = iSCSI block. Tape gateway = backup/archive. Match protocol to requirement.
explanation.memorize: Storage Gateway file gateway = NFS local access + S3 cloud access for hybrid workloads.

question_en: A company has an online gaming application that has TCP and UDP multiplayer gaming capabilities. The company uses Amazon Route 53 to point the application traffic to multiple Network Load Balancers (NLBs) in different AWS Regions. The company needs to improve application performance and decrease latency for the online game in preparation for user growth. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the NLBs. Increase the Cache-Control: max-age parameter.
options.B: Replace the NLBs with Application Load Balancers (ALBs). Configure Route 53 to use latency-based routing.
options.C: Add AWS Global Accelerator in front of the NLBs. Configure a Global Accelerator endpoint to use the correct listener ports.
options.D: Add an Amazon API Gateway endpoint behind the NLBs. Enable API caching. Override method caching for the different stages.

explanation.why_correct: Global Accelerator routes TCP/UDP traffic via AWS edge network to optimal endpoint (NLB), reducing latency and jitter for global gaming traffic.

why_wrong.A: CloudFront for HTTP/HTTPS caching, doesn't support TCP/UDP gaming traffic.
why_wrong.B: ALB doesn't support UDP. Route 53 alone doesn't optimize network path.
why_wrong.D: API Gateway for HTTP APIs, not TCP/UDP game traffic.

explanation.exam_tips: Global Accelerator = TCP/UDP optimization via AWS edge. CloudFront = HTTP/HTTPS content caching. Choose based on protocol.
explanation.memorize: Global Accelerator + NLB = optimize TCP/UDP gaming latency globally.

question_en: A startup company is hosting a website for its customers on an Amazon EC2 instance. The website consists of a stateless Python application and a MySQL database. The website serves only a small amount of traffic. The company is concerned about the reliability of the instance and needs to migrate to a highly available architecture. The company cannot modify the application code. Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to achieve high availability for the website? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Provision an internet gateway in each Availability Zone in use.
options.B: Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance.
options.C: Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB. and enable DynamoDB auto scaling.
options.D: Use AWS DataSync to synchronize the database data across multiple EC2 instances.
options.E: Create an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic to an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances that are distributed across two Availability Zones.

explanation.why_correct: B: RDS Multi-AZ provides automatic failover for DB HA. E: ALB + Auto Scaling across 2 AZs provides application tier HA.

why_wrong.A: Internet Gateway per AZ unnecessary; region-wide resource.
why_wrong.C: DynamoDB requires app code changes; violates requirement.
why_wrong.D: DataSync for data transfer, not HA.

explanation.exam_tips: Multi-AZ = DB HA with automatic failover. ALB + Auto Scaling = app tier HA. Combine for full stack HA.
explanation.memorize: RDS Multi-AZ + ALB + Auto Scaling (multi-AZ) = highly available application.

question_en: A company has an API that receives real-time data from a fleet of monitoring devices. The API stores this data in an Amazon RDS DB instance for later analysis. The amount of data that the monitoring devices send to the API fluctuates. During periods of heavy traffic, the API often returns timeout errors. After an inspection of the logs, the company determines that the database is not capable of processing the volume of write traffic that comes from the API. A solutions architect must minimize the number of connections to the database and must ensure that data is not lost during periods of heavy traffic.

options.A: Increase the size of the DB instance to an instance type that has more available memory.
options.B: Modify the DB instance to be a Multi-AZ DB instance. Configure the application to write to all active RDS DB instances.
options.C: Modify the API to write incoming data to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Use an AWS Lambda function that Amazon SQS invokes to write data from the queue to the database.
options.D: Modify the API to write incoming data to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Use an AWS Lambda function that Amazon SNS invokes to write data from the topic to the database.

explanation.why_correct: SQS buffers bursts, preventing data loss. Lambda polls SQS at sustainable rate, writing to RDS. Decouples API from DB, reduces connection pressure.

why_wrong.A: Vertical scaling doesn't address connection spikes or burst buffering.
why_wrong.B: Multi-AZ for availability, not write throughput.
why_wrong.D: SNS fan-out, not queue buffering for burst absorption.

explanation.exam_tips: SQS = durable message buffer for burst traffic. Lambda = process at sustainable rate. Decoupling prevents overwhelming backend.
explanation.memorize: API → SQS → Lambda → RDS = decouple and buffer bursts, prevent data loss.

question_en: A company wants to create a payment processing application. The application must run when a payment record arrives in an existing Amazon S3 bucket. The application must process each payment record exactly once. The company wants to use an AWS Lambda function to process the payments. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure the existing S3 bucket to send object creation events to Amazon EventBridge. Configure EventBridge to route events to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue. Configure the Lambda function to run when a new event arrives in the SQS queue.
options.B: Configure the existing S3 bucket to send object creation events to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Configure the Lambda function to run when a new event arrives in the SNS topic.
options.C: Configure the existing S3 bucket to send object creation events to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure the Lambda function to run when a new event arrives in the SQS queue.
options.D: Configure the existing S3 bucket to send object creation events directly to the Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to handle object creation events and to process the payments.

explanation.why_correct: S3 Events → EventBridge → SQS FIFO → Lambda ensures exactly-once processing with FIFO ordering and deduplication.

why_wrong.B: SNS doesn't guarantee exactly-once delivery.
why_wrong.C: Standard SQS doesn't guarantee exactly-once; at-least-once semantics.
why_wrong.D: Direct S3 to Lambda can have retries and duplicates.

explanation.exam_tips: SQS FIFO = exactly-once processing + ordering. Standard SQS = at-least-once. Choose FIFO for exactly-once requirement.
explanation.memorize: S3 Events → EventBridge → SQS FIFO → Lambda = exactly-once payment processing.

question_en: A company is planning to deploy its application on an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 cluster. The application will receive large amounts of traffic. The company wants to optimize the storage performance of the cluster as the load on the application increases Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure the cluster to use the Aurora Standard storage configuration.
options.B: Configure the cluster storage type as Provisioned IOPS.
options.C: Configure the cluster storage type as General Purpose.
options.D: Configure the cluster to use the Aurora l/O-Optimized storage configuration.

explanation.why_correct: Aurora I/O-Optimized auto-scales IOPS with workload, provides consistent high performance. Pay for storage and I/O used, cost-effective for variable high loads.

why_wrong.A: Aurora Standard charges per I/O request, expensive at high volume.
why_wrong.B: Provisioned IOPS requires capacity planning, higher cost if overprovisioned.
why_wrong.C: General Purpose burst-based, not consistent high performance.

explanation.exam_tips: Aurora I/O-Optimized = auto-scale IOPS + cost-effective for high I/O. Standard = pay per I/O. Choose I/O-Optimized for high sustained I/O.
explanation.memorize: Aurora I/O-Optimized = auto-scaling consistent performance for high traffic.

question_en: An ecommerce company runs an application that uses an Amazon DynamoDB table in a single AWS Region. The company wants to deploy the application to a second Region. The company needs to support multi-active replication with low latency reads and writes to the existing DynamoDB table in both Regions. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.A: Create a DynamoDB global secondary index (GSI) for the existing table. Create a new table in the second Region. Convert the existing DynamoDB table to a global table. Specify the new table as the secondary table.
options.B: Enable Amazon DynamoDB Streams for the existing table. Create a new table in the second Region. Create a new application that uses the DynamoDB Streams Kinesis Adapter and the Amazon Kinesis Client Library (KCL). Configure the new application to read data from the DynamoDB table in the first Region and to write the data to the new table in the second Region.
options.C: Convert the existing DynamoDB table to a global table. Choose the appropriate second Region to achieve active-active write capabilities in both Regions.
options.D: Enable Amazon DynamoDB Streams for the existing table. Create a new table in the second Region. Create an AWS Lambda function in the first Region that reads data from the table in the first Region and writes the data to the new table in the second Region. Set a DynamoDB stream as the input trigger for the Lambda function.

explanation.why_correct: DynamoDB global table provides multi-active replication with low-latency reads/writes in both regions. Automatic cross-region replication, fully managed.

why_wrong.A: GSI doesn't provide multi-region replication.
why_wrong.B: DynamoDB Streams + custom app adds operational complexity vs native global tables.
why_wrong.D: Streams + Lambda custom replication less efficient than native global tables.

explanation.exam_tips: DynamoDB global table = multi-active multi-region replication. Fully managed, automatic conflict resolution. Least operational overhead.
explanation.memorize: DynamoDB global table = multi-active replication across regions with low latency.

question_en: A company wants to re-architect an application to use Amazon SQS queues. The company must ensure that the application can handle sudden increases in traffic. Which Amazon SQS feature will help meet this requirement?

options.A: FIFO queues
options.B: Visibility timeout
options.C: Message batching
options.D: Long polling

explanation.why_correct: Message batching sends/receives up to 10 messages per API call, increasing throughput and reducing costs. Handles traffic spikes efficiently.

why_wrong.A: FIFO for ordering and deduplication, not throughput.
why_wrong.B: Visibility timeout controls message hiding after receive, not throughput.
why_wrong.D: Long polling reduces empty responses and cost, but batching better for throughput.

explanation.exam_tips: Batching = higher throughput (10 msgs/request). Long polling = reduce empty receives. FIFO = ordering. Match feature to requirement.
explanation.memorize: SQS message batching = handle traffic spikes with higher throughput.

question_en: A company is building an application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application needs to handle a large number of transactions. The application requires an Amazon EBS data volume that has configurable and consistent input/output operations per second (IOPS). Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Provision EC2 instances with a Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) EBS root volume and a Cold HDD (sc1) EBS data volume.
options.B: Provision EC2 instances with a Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) EBS volume that will serve as both a root volume and a data volume.
options.C: Provision EC2 instances with a General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS root volume and a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS data volume.
options.D: Provision EC2 instances with a General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS root volume. Configure the application to store data in an Amazon S3 bucket.

explanation.why_correct: gp3 root volume for OS. io2 data volume provides configurable, consistent IOPS for transaction-heavy application workload.

why_wrong.A: st1 and sc1 HDD for large sequential, not high-transaction workloads.
why_wrong.B: st1 doesn't provide configurable consistent IOPS.
why_wrong.D: S3 object storage, not block storage EBS volume.

explanation.exam_tips: io2 = configurable IOPS for transactional workloads. gp3 = balanced general purpose. st1/sc1 = HDD sequential. Match volume to workload.
explanation.memorize: gp3 root + io2 data = separate OS and high-IOPS transaction storage.

question_en: A company is building a stock trading application in the AWS Cloud. The company requires a highly available solution that provides low-latency access to block storage across multiple Availability Zones.

options.A: Use an Amazon S3 bucket and an S3 File Gateway as shared storage for the application.
options.B: Create an Amazon EC2 instance in each Availability Zone. Attach a General Purpose SSD (gp3) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume to each EC2 instance. Create a Bash script to sync data between volumes.
options.C: Use an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ file system to access data by using the iSCSI protocol.
options.D: Create an Amazon EC2 instance in each Availability Zone. Attach a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume to each EC2 instance. Create a Python script to sync data between volumes.

explanation.why_correct: FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ provides HA with automatic failover. iSCSI LUNs deliver block storage across AZs with low latency for trading application.

why_wrong.A: S3 object storage, not block. File Gateway for files, not block.
why_wrong.B: EBS single-AZ, can't share across instances/AZs. Scripts add latency and complexity.
why_wrong.D: EBS can't be shared. Manual sync doesn't provide true HA.

explanation.exam_tips: FSx ONTAP = Multi-AZ HA + iSCSI block storage. EBS = single-instance, single-AZ. Choose FSx ONTAP for shared block across AZs.
explanation.memorize: FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ + iSCSI = HA block storage across AZs with low latency.

question_en: A company asks a solutions architect to review the architecture for its messaging application. The application uses TCP and UDP traffic. The company is planning to deploy a new VoIP feature, but its 10 test users in other countries are reporting poor call quality. The VoIP application runs on an Amazon EC2 instance with more than enough resources. The HTTP portion of the company ' s application behind an Application Load Balancer has no issues. What should the solutions architect recommend for the company to do to address the VoIP performance issues?

options.A: Use AWS Global Accelerator.
options.B: Implement Amazon CloudFront into the architecture.
options.C: Use an Amazon Route 53 geoproximity routing policy.
options.D: Migrate from Application Load Balancers to Network Load Balancers.

explanation.why_correct: Global Accelerator optimizes TCP/UDP traffic over AWS edge network, reducing latency and jitter for VoIP calls from international users.

why_wrong.B: CloudFront for HTTP/HTTPS content, not TCP/UDP VoIP.
why_wrong.C: Route 53 geoproximity DNS routing doesn't optimize network path.
why_wrong.D: NLB supports TCP/UDP but doesn't provide global acceleration.

explanation.exam_tips: Global Accelerator = TCP/UDP performance via AWS edge. CloudFront = HTTP/HTTPS. Match service to protocol and performance need.
explanation.memorize: Global Accelerator = improve global VoIP (TCP/UDP) call quality via AWS backbone.

question_en: The customers of a finance company request appointments with financial advisors by sending text messages. A web application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances accepts the appointment requests. The text messages are published to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue through the web application. Another application that runs on EC2 instances then sends meeting invitations and meeting confirmation email messages to the customers. After successful scheduling, this application stores the meeting information in an Amazon DynamoDB database. As the company expands, customers report that their meeting invitations are taking longer to arrive. What should a solutions architect recommend to resolve this issue?

options.A: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the DynamoDB database.
options.B: Add an Amazon API Gateway API in front of the web application that accepts the appointment requests.
options.C: Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Set the origin as the web application that accepts the appointment requests.
options.D: Add an Auto Scaling group for the application that sends meeting invitations. Configure the Auto Scaling group to scale based on the depth of the SQS queue.

explanation.why_correct: Auto Scaling group scaled by SQS queue depth automatically adds workers when backlog grows, reducing email invitation latency. SQS-driven scaling = elastic capacity.

why_wrong.A: DAX accelerates DynamoDB reads, doesn't help email processing throughput.
why_wrong.B: API Gateway doesn't address async email processing bottleneck.
why_wrong.C: CloudFront for content delivery, not backend async processing.

explanation.exam_tips: Scale SQS consumers with Auto Scaling based on queue metrics (depth, age). Automatically adjusts worker capacity to queue backlog.
explanation.memorize: Auto Scaling + SQS queue depth metric = elastic async worker scaling.

question_en: An application is experiencing performance issues based on increased demand. This increased demand is on read-only historical records that are pulled from an Amazon RDS-hosted database with custom views and queries. A solutions architect must improve performance without changing the database structure. Which approach will improve performance and MINIMIZE management overhead?

options.A: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB, move all the data, and point to DynamoDB.
options.B: Deploy Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) and cache the data for the application.
options.C: Deploy Memcached on Amazon EC2 and cache the data for the application.
options.D: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) on Amazon RDS to improve cache performance.

explanation.why_correct: ElastiCache Redis in-memory cache for RDS query results. Offloads read-heavy historical queries, no database structure changes. Fully managed.

why_wrong.A: DynamoDB requires data migration and app changes.
why_wrong.C: Memcached on EC2 requires managing instances, more overhead than ElastiCache.
why_wrong.D: DAX only for DynamoDB, not RDS.

explanation.exam_tips: ElastiCache = cache layer for RDS. Fully managed. DAX = DynamoDB only. Match cache to database type.
explanation.memorize: ElastiCache Redis + RDS = cache read-heavy queries without DB schema changes.

question_en: A company is deploying a critical application by using Amazon RDS for MySQL. The application must be highly available and must recover automatically. The company needs to support interactive users (transactional queries) and batch reporting (analytical queries) with no more than a 4-hour lag. The analytical queries must not affect the performance of the transactional queries.

options.A: Configure Amazon RDS for MySQL in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with one standby instance. Point the transactional queries to the primary DB instance. Point the analytical queries to a secondary DB instance that runs in a different Availability Zone.
options.B: Configure Amazon RDS for MySQL in a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment with two standby instances. Point the transactional queries to the primary DB instance. Point the analytical queries to the reader endpoint.
options.C: Configure Amazon RDS for MySQL to use multiple read replicas across multiple Availability Zones. Point the transactional queries to the primary DB instance. Point the analytical queries to one of the replicas in a different Availability Zone.
options.D: Configure Amazon RDS for MySQL as the primary database for the transactional queries with automated backups enabled. Configure automated backups. Each night, create a read-only database from the most recent snapshot to support the analytical queries. Terminate the previously created database.

explanation.why_correct: Multi-AZ read replicas across AZs provide HA and automatic recovery. Transactional queries to primary, analytical to replica isolates workloads. Up to 4-hour replication lag acceptable.

why_wrong.A: Multi-AZ standby doesn't serve reads, can't isolate analytical queries.
why_wrong.B: Multi-AZ cluster with reader endpoint valid but mentioned as Aurora feature, question specifies RDS MySQL.
why_wrong.D: Nightly snapshots don't support 4-hour lag requirement, high operational overhead.

explanation.exam_tips: Read replicas = offload reads with async replication lag. Multi-AZ = HA with sync standby (no read). Choose based on HA vs read scaling need.
explanation.memorize: RDS read replicas = separate transactional and analytical queries with acceptable lag.

question_en: An ecommerce company has an application that uses Amazon DynamoDB tables that are configured with provisioned capacity. Order data is stored in a table named Orders. The Orders table has a primary key of order-ID and a sort key of product-ID. The company configured an AWS Lambda function to receive DynamoDB streams from the Orders table and to update a table named Inventory. The company has noticed that during peak sales periods, updates to the Inventory table take longer than the company can tolerate. Which solutions will resolve the slow table updates? Select TWO.

options.A: Add a global secondary index to the Orders table. Include the product-ID attribute.
options.B: Set the batch size attribute of the DynamoDB streams to be based on the size of items in the Orders table.
options.C: Increase the DynamoDB table provisioned capacity by 1,000 write capacity units WCUs.
options.D: Increase the DynamoDB table provisioned capacity by 1,000 read capacity units RCUs.
options.E: Increase the timeout of the Lambda function to 15 minutes.

explanation.why_correct: B: Tune Lambda batch size for efficient stream processing. C: Increase DynamoDB write capacity to handle peak update traffic to Inventory table.

why_wrong.A: GSI on Orders doesn't improve Inventory table write performance.
why_wrong.D: Increasing read capacity doesn't help write performance bottleneck.
why_wrong.E: Lambda timeout doesn't solve throughput issue, only prevents timeouts.

explanation.exam_tips: DynamoDB Streams batch size = processing efficiency. Write capacity = throughput. Read capacity = query performance. Match capacity type to bottleneck.
explanation.memorize: Stream batch size + write capacity = optimize DynamoDB stream-driven updates.

question_en: A finance company uses an on-premises search application to collect streaming data from various producers. The application provides real-time updates to search and visualization features. The company is planning to migrate to AWS and wants to use an AWS native solution. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon EC2 instances to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon S3 buckets for storage. Use Amazon Athena to search the data. Use Amazon Managed Grafana to create visualizations.
options.B: Use Amazon EMR to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon Redshift for storage. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to search the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to create visualizations.
options.C: Use Amazon EKS to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon DynamoDB for storage. Use Amazon CloudWatch to create graphical dashboards to search and visualize the data.
options.D: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest and process the data streams to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use OpenSearch Service to search the data. Use Amazon QuickSight to create visualizations.

explanation.why_correct: Kinesis Data Streams ingests real-time streaming. OpenSearch Service provides search and analytics. QuickSight creates visualizations. AWS-native real-time solution.

why_wrong.A: EC2 + Athena batch-oriented, not real-time search.
why_wrong.B: EMR + Redshift batch processing, not real-time.
why_wrong.C: EKS + DynamoDB doesn't provide search/visualization.

explanation.exam_tips: Kinesis = real-time streaming. OpenSearch = real-time search/analytics. QuickSight = dashboards. Combine for end-to-end real-time pipeline.
explanation.memorize: Kinesis → OpenSearch → QuickSight = real-time streaming search and visualization.

question_en: A company stores data in an on-premises Oracle relational database. The company needs to make the data available in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL for analysis The company uses an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to connect its on-premises network to AWS. The company must capture the changes that occur to the source database during the migration to Aurora PostgreSQL. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to convert the Oracle schema to Aurora PostgreSQL schema. Use the AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) full-load migration task to migrate the data.
options.B: Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Import the S3 data to Aurora PostgreSQL by using the Aurora PostgreSQL aws_s3 extension.
options.C: Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to convert the Oracle schema to Aurora PostgreSQL schema. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the existing data and replicate the ongoing changes.
options.D: Use an AWS Snowball device to migrate the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Import the S3 data to Aurora PostgreSQL by using the Aurora PostgreSQL aws_s3 extension.

explanation.why_correct: SCT converts schema. DMS performs full-load + CDC (change data capture) for ongoing replication. Captures changes during migration.

why_wrong.A: Full-load only doesn't capture ongoing changes during migration.
why_wrong.B: DataSync for file transfers, not database CDC.
why_wrong.D: Snowball offline transfer doesn't capture ongoing changes.

explanation.exam_tips: SCT = schema conversion. DMS full-load = initial migration. DMS CDC = ongoing replication. Combine for live database migration.
explanation.memorize: SCT + DMS (full-load + CDC) = migrate Oracle to Aurora with ongoing changes.

question_en: A company ' s application uses Network Load Balancers, Auto Scaling groups, Amazon EC2 instances, and databases that are deployed in an Amazon VPC. The company wants to capture information about traffic to and from the network interfaces in near real time in its Amazon VPC. The company wants to send the information to Amazon OpenSearch Service for analysis. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create a log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the log group. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the logs from the log group to OpenSearch Service.
options.B: Create a log group in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the log group. Use Amazon Data Firehose to stream the logs from the log group to OpenSearch Service.
options.C: Create a trail in AWS CloudTrail. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the trail. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to stream the logs from the trail to OpenSearch Service.
options.D: Create a trail in AWS CloudTrail. Configure VPC Flow Logs to send the log data to the trail. Use Amazon Data Firehose to stream the logs from the trail to OpenSearch Service.

explanation.why_correct: VPC Flow Logs capture network traffic. CloudWatch Logs collects logs. Firehose streams to OpenSearch with managed delivery. Minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: Kinesis Data Streams requires custom consumer vs Firehose managed delivery.
why_wrong.C: CloudTrail for API calls, not network flow logs.
why_wrong.D: CloudTrail doesn't receive VPC Flow Logs.

explanation.exam_tips: VPC Flow Logs = network traffic metadata. CloudWatch Logs = log aggregation. Firehose = managed delivery to destinations.
explanation.memorize: VPC Flow Logs → CloudWatch Logs → Firehose → OpenSearch = managed network analytics.

question_en:
A company is developing a latency-sensitive application. Part of the application includes several AWS Lambda functions that need to initialize as quickly as possible. The Lambda functions are written in Java and contain initialization code outside the handlers to load libraries, initialize classes, and generate unique IDs.



Which solution will meet the startup performance requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Move all the initialization code to the handlers for each Lambda function. Activate Lambda SnapStart for each Lambda function. Configure SnapStart to reference the $LATEST version of each Lambda function.
options.B: Publish a version of each Lambda function. Create an alias for each Lambda function. Configure each alias to point to its corresponding version. Set up provisioned concurrency configuration for each Lambda function to point to the corresponding alias.
options.C: Publish a version of each Lambda function. Set up a provisioned concurrency configuration for each Lambda function to point to the corresponding version. Activate Lambda SnapStart for the published versions of the Lambda functions.
options.D: Update the Lambda functions to add a pre-snapshot hook. Move the code that generates unique IDs into the handlers. Publish a version of each Lambda function. Activate Lambda SnapStart for the published versions of the Lambda functions.

explanation.why_correct: SnapStart for Java reduces cold starts. Pre-snapshot hook for non-deterministic code. Move unique ID generation to handler. Publish version required for SnapStart.

why_wrong.A: SnapStart not supported on $LATEST, only published versions.
why_wrong.B: Provisioned concurrency more expensive than SnapStart for cold start reduction.
why_wrong.C: Provisioned concurrency unnecessary with SnapStart; adds cost.

explanation.exam_tips: SnapStart = cost-effective cold start reduction for Java. Pre-snapshot hook for non-deterministic code. Provisioned concurrency = pre-warmed instances (expensive).
explanation.memorize: SnapStart + pre-snapshot hook + published version = cost-effective Java Lambda startup.

question_en: A company hosts a public product catalog. The product catalog is accessible through an Amazon API Gateway REST API with AWS Lambda function integrations in a single AWS Region. Most traffic consists of read-only GET requests to the /products resource from global users. The catalog changes approximately once every hour. The company needs to lower latency for global users and reduce the load on the Lambda functions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Enable API Gateway response caching for the GET /products resource. Set a 1-hour TTL.
options.B: Place an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of API Gateway. Cache GET responses with a 1-hour TTL.
options.C: Increase the Lambda function memory for the functions that handle the GET /products resource.
options.D: Move the API to an Application Load Balancer that uses Amazon EC2 instances to cache the catalog.

explanation.why_correct: CloudFront caches GET responses at edge locations globally. 1-hour TTL matches catalog update frequency. Reduces latency and Lambda invocations.

why_wrong.A: API Gateway caching regional, not global edge caching.
why_wrong.C: Increasing Lambda memory doesn't eliminate repeated identical requests.
why_wrong.D: ALB + EC2 cache adds infrastructure management overhead.

explanation.exam_tips: CloudFront = global edge caching. API Gateway cache = regional stage cache. CloudFront better for global users.
explanation.memorize: CloudFront in front of API Gateway = global caching reduces latency and backend load.

question_en: A company that analyzes the stock market has two offices: one in the us-east-1 Region and another in the euwest-2 Region. The company wants to implement an AWS database solution that can provide fast and accurate updates. The office in eu-west-2 has dashboards with complex analytical queries to display the data. The company will use these dashboards to make buying decisions, so the dashboards must have access to the application data in less than 1 second. Which solution meets these requirements and provides the MOST up-todate dashboard?

options.A: Deploy an Amazon RDS DB instance in us-east-1 with a read replica instance in eu-west-2. Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster in eu-west-2 to cache data from the read replica to generate the dashboards.
options.B: Use an Amazon DynamoDB global table in us-east-1 with replication into eu-west-2. Use multi-active replication to ensure that updates are quickly propagated to eu-west-2.
options.C: Use an Amazon Aurora global database. Deploy the primary DB cluster in us-east-1. Deploy the secondary DB cluster in eu-west-2. Configure the dashboard application to read from the secondary cluster.
options.D: Deploy an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in us-east-1 with a read replica instance in eu-west-2. Configure the dashboard application to read from the read replica.

explanation.why_correct: Aurora Global Database replicates cross-region with typically <1 second lag. Secondary cluster in eu-west-2 serves low-latency reads. Up-to-date dashboards.

why_wrong.A: RDS read replica + ElastiCache adds complexity. Read replica lag higher than Aurora Global.
why_wrong.B: DynamoDB global for NoSQL. Question needs relational for complex analytical queries.
why_wrong.D: Standard RDS read replicas have higher lag than Aurora Global Database.

explanation.exam_tips: Aurora Global Database = <1s cross-region replication. RDS read replicas = higher lag. Choose Aurora Global for lowest cross-region lag.
explanation.memorize: Aurora Global Database = sub-second cross-region replication for up-to-date dashboards.

question_en: A company hosts an industrial control application that receives sensor input through Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The application needs to support new sensors for real-time anomaly detection in monitored equipment. The company wants to integrate new sensors in a loosely-coupled, fully managed, and serverless way. The company cannot modify the application code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Forward the existing stream in Kinesis Data Streams to Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink for anomaly detection. Use a second stream in Kinesis Data Streams to send the Flink output to the application.
options.B: Use Amazon Data Firehose to stream data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to perform anomaly detection on the S3 data. Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke an AWS Lambda function that sends analyzed data to the application through a second stream in Kinesis Data Streams.
options.C: Configure Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to consume data from the data stream and to perform anomaly detection. Create a second stream in Kinesis Data Streams to send data from the EC2 instances to the application.
options.D: Configure an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task that uses Amazon EC2 instances to consume data from the data stream and to perform anomaly detection. Create a second stream in Kinesis Data Streams to send data from the containers to the application.

explanation.why_correct: Managed Service for Apache Flink (Kinesis Data Analytics) processes Kinesis streams in real-time for anomaly detection. Second stream delivers to application. Serverless, fully managed.

why_wrong.B: Firehose + S3 + Redshift Spectrum not real-time.
why_wrong.C: EC2 Auto Scaling not fully managed or serverless.
why_wrong.D: ECS on EC2 not serverless, requires managing infrastructure.

explanation.exam_tips: Managed Flink (KDA) = real-time streaming analytics. Serverless, integrates with Kinesis. Choose for real-time anomaly detection.
explanation.memorize: Kinesis → Managed Flink → Kinesis = serverless real-time anomaly detection pipeline.

question_en: A company is developing a highly available natural language processing NLP application. The application handles large volumes of concurrent requests. The application performs NLP tasks such as entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and key phrase extraction on text data. The company needs to store data that the application processes in a highly available and scalable database. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API endpoint to handle incoming requests. Configure the REST API to invoke an AWS Lambda function for each request. Configure the Lambda function to call Amazon Comprehend to perform NLP tasks on the text data. Store the processed data in Amazon DynamoDB.
options.B: Create an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API endpoint to handle incoming requests. Configure the HTTP API to invoke an AWS Lambda function for each request. Configure the Lambda function to call Amazon Translate to perform NLP tasks on the text data. Store the processed data in Amazon ElastiCache.
options.C: Create an Amazon SQS queue to buffer incoming requests. Deploy the NLP application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Use Amazon Comprehend to perform NLP tasks. Store the processed data in an Amazon RDS database.
options.D: Create an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API endpoint to handle incoming requests. Configure the WebSocket API to invoke an AWS Lambda function for each request. Configure the Lambda function to call Amazon Textract to perform NLP tasks on the text data. Store the processed data in Amazon ElastiCache.

explanation.why_correct: API Gateway + Lambda serverless. Comprehend for NLP (entities, sentiment, key phrases). DynamoDB scales for high throughput concurrent requests.

why_wrong.B: Translate for translation, not NLP. ElastiCache not durable database.
why_wrong.C: SQS + EC2 not serverless. RDS doesn't scale as easily as DynamoDB for high concurrent writes.
why_wrong.D: Textract for document text extraction, not NLP. ElastiCache not durable.

explanation.exam_tips: Comprehend = NLP (entities, sentiment, phrases). Translate = language translation. Textract = extract text from documents. Match service to task.
explanation.memorize: API Gateway + Lambda + Comprehend + DynamoDB = serverless scalable NLP processing.

question_en: A company runs an ecommerce website on AWS. The website architecture uses a single Amazon EC2 instance to run a custom application that handles the website ' s functions. The website functions include product catalog management and customer checkout. The company ' s website traffic and transaction volume are increasing rapidly. The company wants to rearchitect the application from its current monolithic architecture to a loosely coupled architecture to enable independent scaling. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure an Auto Scaling group that includes multiple EC2 instances that each run a copy of the application. Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic across the EC2 instances.
options.B: Refactor the application into microservices that run on Amazon ECS containers. Deploy each service to its own container. Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic.
options.C: Refactor the web application and split the logic into frontend and backend tiers. Run the frontend tier on the existing EC2 instance. Add a second EC2 instance to run the backend tier.
options.D: Migrate the entire application to a Kubernetes cluster that has a single container by using Amazon EKS. Implement Amazon Route 53 to geographically distribute traffic.

explanation.why_correct: ECS microservices with separate containers enable independent scaling per service. ALB routes traffic. Moves from monolith to loosely coupled architecture.

why_wrong.A: Auto Scaling multiple EC2 copies of monolith doesn't enable independent scaling.
why_wrong.C: Two-tier split basic but not fully loosely coupled microservices.
why_wrong.D: Single container in EKS doesn't enable independent component scaling; adds K8s complexity.

explanation.exam_tips: Microservices = independent deployment and scaling. Monolith = single codebase. ECS simpler than EKS for basic microservices.
explanation.memorize: ECS microservices + ALB = loosely coupled architecture with independent scaling.

question_en: A solutions architect is designing the architecture for a company website that is composed of static content. The company ' s target customers are located in the United States and Europe. Which architecture should the solutions architect recommend to MINIMIZE cost?

options.A: Store the website files on Amazon S3 in the us-east-2 Region. Use an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the price class configured to limit the edge locations in use.
options.B: Store the website files on Amazon S3 in the us-east-2 Region. Use an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the price class configured to maximize the use of edge locations.
options.C: Store the website files on Amazon S3 in the us-east-2 Region and the eu-west-1 Region. Use an Amazon CloudFront geolocation routing policy to route requests to the closest Region to the user.
options.D: Store the website files on Amazon S3 in the us-east-2 Region and the eu-west-1 Region. Use an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to route requests to the closest Region to the user.

explanation.why_correct: Single S3 bucket in us-east-2. CloudFront with limited price class (US + Europe only) minimizes cost while serving target customers.

why_wrong.B: Maximize edge locations increases costs unnecessarily for regions outside target markets.
why_wrong.C: Multi-region S3 storage doubles storage costs unnecessarily.
why_wrong.D: Multi-region S3 + CloudFront + Route 53 most expensive and complex.

explanation.exam_tips: CloudFront price classes: All, 200 (all except expensive), 100 (US/Europe/Asia). Limit to target regions for cost optimization.
explanation.memorize: Single S3 region + CloudFront limited price class = minimize CDN cost for specific markets.

question_en: A media streaming company is redesigning its infrastructure to accommodate increasing demand for video content that users consume daily. The company needs to process terabyte-sized videos to block some content in the videos. Video processing can take up to 20 minutes. The company needs a solution that is cost-effective, highly available, and scalable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use AWS Lambda functions to process the videos. Store video metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Store video content in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
options.B: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the AWS Fargate launch type to implement microservices to process videos. Store video metadata in Amazon Aurora. Store video content in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
options.C: Use Amazon EMR to process the videos with Apache Spark. Store video content in Amazon FSx for Lustre. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest videos in real time.
options.D: Deploy a containerized video processing application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with the Amazon EC2 launch type. Store video metadata in Amazon RDS in a single Availability Zone. Store video content in Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanation.why_correct: ECS Fargate serverless containers, no infrastructure management. Aurora scalable managed database. S3 Intelligent-Tiering cost-optimizes variable-access video storage. Supports 20-min processing.

why_wrong.A: Lambda 15-min max, can't handle 20-min processing.
why_wrong.C: EMR for big data analytics. FSx Lustre for HPC. Kinesis for streaming. Not best fit for video processing.
why_wrong.D: EKS on EC2 high management overhead. Single-AZ RDS not HA. Glacier Deep Archive for infrequent access.

explanation.exam_tips: Lambda max 15 min. ECS/EKS for long-running containers. Fargate = serverless. EC2 launch = manage instances.
explanation.memorize: ECS Fargate + Aurora + S3 Intelligent-Tiering = scalable HA video processing with least overhead.

question_en: A company needs a solution to ingest streaming sensor data from 100,000 devices, transform the data in near real time, and load the data into Amazon S3 for analysis. The solution must be fully managed, scalable, and maintain sub-second ingestion latency.

options.A: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest the data. Use Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink to process the data in near real time. Use an Amazon Data Firehose stream to send processed data to Amazon S3.
options.B: Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queues to collect the sensor data. Invoke AWS Lambda functions to transform and process SQS messages in batches. Configure the Lambda functions to use an AWS SDK to write transformed data to Amazon S3.
options.C: Deploy a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances that run Apache Kafka to ingest the data. Run Apache Spark on Amazon EMR clusters to process the data. Configure Spark to write processed data directly to Amazon S3.
options.D: Implement Amazon EventBridge to capture all sensor data. Use AWS Batch to run containerized transformation jobs on a schedule. Configure AWS Batch jobs to process data in chunks. Save results to Amazon S3.

explanation.why_correct: Kinesis Data Streams ingests 100K devices with sub-second latency. Managed Flink processes real-time. Firehose delivers to S3. Fully managed, scalable.
