why_wrong.B: SQS not optimized for real-time high-volume streaming.
why_wrong.C: EC2 Kafka + EMR high operational overhead, not fully managed.
why_wrong.D: EventBridge event-driven, not for high-throughput streaming. Batch for scheduled processing, not real-time.

explanation.exam_tips: Kinesis = real-time streaming ingestion at scale. Managed Flink = stream processing. Firehose = managed delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch.
explanation.memorize: Kinesis → Managed Flink → Firehose → S3 = fully managed real-time streaming pipeline.

question_en: A company has an industrial application that controls a process in real time. The company plans to rearchitect the application to distribute jobs across several Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC. The solution needs to maximize the network throughput and minimize the network latency between the instances.

options.A: Place the instances in a host-level partition placement group. Choose instance types that support enhanced networking.
options.B: Place the instances in several dedicated hosts in the same partition of a partition placement group. Choose dedicated hosts that support enhanced networking.
options.C: Place the instances in several dedicated hosts in the same rack of a rack-level placement group. Choose dedicated hosts that support enhanced networking.
options.D: Place the instances in a cluster placement group. Choose instance types that support enhanced networking.

explanation.why_correct: Cluster placement group places instances physically close in same AZ for lowest latency. Enhanced networking for high throughput and low latency.

why_wrong.A: Host-level partition placement not a valid placement group type.
why_wrong.B: Partition placement for distributed workloads across hardware, not lowest latency.
why_wrong.C: Rack-level placement not a valid placement group type.

explanation.exam_tips: Cluster placement = lowest latency, same AZ. Spread placement = HA across hardware. Partition placement = large distributed apps.
explanation.memorize: Cluster placement group + enhanced networking = maximum throughput, minimum latency.

question_en: A company runs container applications by using Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler. The workload is not consistent throughout the day. A solutions architect notices that the number of nodes does not automatically scale out when the existing nodes have reached maximum capacity in the cluster, which causes performance issues. Which solution will resolve this issue with the LEAST administrative overhead?

options.A: Scale out the nodes by tracking the memory usage.
options.B: Use the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler to manage the number of nodes in the cluster.
options.C: Use an AWS Lambda function to resize the EKS cluster automatically.
options.D: Use an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to distribute the workload.

explanation.why_correct: Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler watches pending pods and scales nodes automatically when capacity insufficient. Integrates with EKS Auto Scaling groups natively.

why_wrong.A: Tracking memory doesn't automatically scale nodes or integrate with K8s.
why_wrong.C: Lambda custom resize adds complexity vs native Cluster Autoscaler.
why_wrong.D: Auto Scaling group alone doesn't respond to pod scheduling pressure.

explanation.exam_tips: HPA scales pods. Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes. Combine for full EKS auto-scaling. Cluster Autoscaler least overhead for node scaling.
explanation.memorize: Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler = automatic node scaling based on pod demand.

question_en: A company hosts a training website on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances that run web server software. The company anticipates that a new training product will be extremely popular and will receive high user traffic. The training product consists of dozens of training videos that are hosted on the website. A solutions architect must minimize the load on the company ' s web servers. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Store the videos in Amazon ElastiCache Redis OSS. Update the web servers to serve the videos by using the ElastiCache API.
options.B: Store the videos in an Amazon EFS volume. Create a user data script to mount the EFS volume to the web servers.
options.C: Store the videos in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution, and set the S3 bucket as the origin. Create an origin access control OAC to secure access to the S3 bucket.
options.D: Store the videos in an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an AWS Storage Gateway Amazon S3 File Gateway to access the S3 bucket. Create a user data script to mount the S3 File Gateway to the web servers.

explanation.why_correct: S3 stores videos. CloudFront caches at edge globally, serving videos without hitting web servers. OAC secures S3 origin access. Minimizes server load.

why_wrong.A: ElastiCache not for video origin storage.
why_wrong.B: EFS keeps web servers in delivery path, doesn't reduce load.
why_wrong.D: File Gateway for hybrid file access, not internet content distribution.

explanation.exam_tips: S3 + CloudFront = offload static content from web servers. OAC = secure origin access (replaces OAI). Videos = static content.
explanation.memorize: S3 + CloudFront + OAC = minimize server load for high-traffic video delivery.

question_en: A solutions architect needs to design a solution for a high performance computing (HPC) workload. The solution must include multiple Amazon EC2 instances. Each EC2 instance requires 10 Gbps of bandwidth individually for single-flow traffic. The EC2 instances require an aggregate throughput of 100 Gbps of bandwidth across all EC2 instances. Communication between the EC2 instances must have low latency. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Place the EC2 instances in a single subnet of a VPC. Configure a cluster placement group. Ensure that the latest Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) drivers are installed on the EC2 instances with a supported operating system.
options.B: Place the EC2 instances in multiple subnets in a single VPC. Configure a spread placement group. Ensure that the EC2 instances support Elastic Network Adapters (ENAs) and that the drivers are updated on each instance operating system.
options.C: Place the EC2 instances in multiple VPCs. Use AWS Transit Gateway to route traffic between the VPCs. Ensure that the latest Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) drivers are installed on the EC2 instances with a supported operating system.
options.D: Place the EC2 instances in multiple subnets across multiple Availability Zones. Configure a cluster placement group. Ensure that the EC2 instances support Elastic Network Adapters (ENAs) and that the drivers are updated on each instance operating system.

explanation.why_correct: Cluster placement group + EFA (Elastic Fabric Adapter) provides ultra-low latency, high throughput (10 Gbps/instance) for tightly-coupled HPC workloads. Single AZ, physical proximity.

why_wrong.B: Spread placement separates instances for HA, increases latency. ENA good but EFA better for HPC.
why_wrong.C: Multi-VPC + Transit Gateway adds network hops, increases latency.
why_wrong.D: Multi-AZ cluster placement invalid; cluster is single-AZ. ENA sufficient but EFA optimal for HPC.

explanation.exam_tips: EFA = OS-bypass networking for HPC. ENA = enhanced networking. Cluster placement = physical proximity. Choose EFA + cluster for HPC.
explanation.memorize: Cluster placement + EFA = 10 Gbps per instance, 100 Gbps aggregate for HPC.

question_en: A company hosts a website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The instances run Amazon Linux in an Auto Scaling group. Each instance stores product manuals on Amazon EBS volumes. New instances often start with outdated data and may take up to 30 minutes to download updates. The company needs a solution ensuring all instances always have up-to-date product manuals, can scale rapidly, and does not require application code changes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Store the product manuals on instance store volumes attached to each EC2 instance.
options.B: Store the product manuals in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure EC2 instances to download updates from the bucket.
options.C: Store the product manuals in an Amazon EFS file system. Mount the EFS volume on the EC2 instances.
options.D: Store the product manuals in an S3 bucket using S3 Standard-IA. Configure EC2 instances to download updates from S3.

explanation.why_correct: EFS shared file system mounted by all instances. Updates immediately visible to all. Auto-scales storage. No app changes needed.

why_wrong.A: Instance store ephemeral, not shared, data lost on termination.
why_wrong.B: S3 download delay causes stale data on new instances.
why_wrong.D: S3 Standard-IA for infrequent access; download still causes delay.

explanation.exam_tips: EFS = shared file system across instances. EBS = single-instance. Instance store = ephemeral. Choose EFS for shared persistent data.
explanation.memorize: EFS = shared file system, instant updates across all instances, no app changes.

question_en: A company has an ordering application that stores customer information in Amazon RDS for MySQL. During regular business hours, employees run one-time queries for reporting purposes. Timeouts are occurring during order processing because the reporting queries are taking a long time to run. The company needs to eliminate the timeouts without preventing employees from performing queries.

options.A: Create a read replica. Move reporting queries to the read replica.
options.B: Create a read replica. Distribute the ordering application to the primary DB instance and the read replica.
options.C: Migrate the ordering application to Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity.
options.D: Schedule the reporting queries for non-peak hours.

explanation.why_correct: Read replica offloads reporting queries from primary, eliminating timeouts during order processing. Async replication provides up-to-date data for reports.

why_wrong.B: Distributing ordering app to replica causes writes to replica (not supported; replica read-only).
why_wrong.C: DynamoDB migration requires app redesign, major effort.
why_wrong.D: Scheduling doesn't prevent employees from running queries as stated.

explanation.exam_tips: Read replica = offload read traffic. Primary handles writes. Async replication = slight lag acceptable for reporting.
explanation.memorize: RDS read replica = isolate reporting queries from transactional workload.

question_en: A company has an application on AWS. The company hosts the backend database in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company uses Amazon ECS containers to host the application. Read operations are primarily keybased lookups. The application is read-heavy and often encounters a DynamoDB throughput exceeded exception. A solutions architect needs to design a cost-effective solution that will resolve the DynamoDB throughput exceeded exceptions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the current architecture?

options.A: Use Amazon ElastiCache Memcached to create a cache. Point key-based read operations to the cache.
options.B: Increase the read capacity of the DynamoDB table manually every time there is a spike in read requests.
options.C: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator DAX cluster. Point key-based read operations to the DAX cluster.
options.D: Use Amazon RDS to create a copy of the DynamoDB table. Point read operations to the Amazon RDS instance.

explanation.why_correct: DAX in-memory cache for DynamoDB, optimized for key-based lookups. Fully managed, minimal architecture changes. Reduces read load on DynamoDB table.

why_wrong.A: ElastiCache Memcached requires more cache management vs DAX DynamoDB-specific integration.
why_wrong.B: Manual capacity increase reactive, not automatic, less cost-effective.
why_wrong.D: RDS copy major architecture change, adds complexity.

explanation.exam_tips: DAX = DynamoDB-specific cache. ElastiCache = general caching. DAX simpler for DynamoDB key-based reads.
explanation.memorize: DAX = fewest changes to resolve DynamoDB read throughput exceptions.

question_en: A solutions architect is designing the cloud architecture for a new stateless application that will be deployed on AWS. The solutions architect created an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) and launch template for the application. Based on the number of jobs that need to be processed, the processing must run in parallel while adding and removing application Amazon EC2 instances as needed. The application must be loosely coupled. The job items must be durably stored. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on CPU usage.
options.B: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on network usage.
options.C: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to hold the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on the number of items in the SQS queue.
options.D: Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to send the jobs that need to be processed. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template with the scaling policy set to add and remove EC2 instances based on the number of messages published to the SNS topic.

explanation.why_correct: SQS durably stores jobs. Auto Scaling based on SQS queue depth automatically adjusts workers to match job volume. Parallel processing, loosely coupled.

why_wrong.A: SNS pub/sub, not durable job queue. CPU usage doesn't reflect job queue depth.
why_wrong.B: Network usage poor metric for job processing. SQS correct but wrong scaling metric.
why_wrong.D: SNS not durable queue. Can't scale based on SNS messages.

explanation.exam_tips: SQS = durable job queue. Scale workers by queue depth (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible). SNS = pub/sub notifications.
explanation.memorize: SQS queue + Auto Scaling (queue depth metric) = elastic parallel job processing.

question_en: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances. The instances are in an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a single AWS Region. In the application, multiple users share the same long-running session. These shared sessions result in uneven loads across the EC2 instances. The company plans to launch the application in additional AWS Regions. The company will deploy an ALB and an Auto Scaling group in each additional Region. The company requires a solution that keeps users who share a session connected to the same EC2 instance. The solution must minimize network latency and distribute loads more evenly across the EC2 instances. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Use an Amazon Route 53 geoproximity routing policy to route traffic to an EC2 instance behind the ALB in the Region closest to each user.
options.B: Use AWS Global Accelerator to create a custom routing accelerator. Configure the accelerator to route traffic to an EC2 instance behind the ALB in the Region closest to each user.
options.C: Configure the ALB to use the weighted random routing algorithm.
options.D: Use AWS Global Accelerator to create a standard accelerator. Configure the accelerator to route traffic to the ALB in the Region closest to each user.
options.E: Configure the ALB to use the least outstanding requests routing algorithm.

explanation.why_correct: D: Global Accelerator routes globally to closest region. E: Least outstanding requests algorithm distributes load more evenly across instances for variable-duration sessions.

why_wrong.A: Route 53 geoproximity DNS-based, not continuous connection routing.
why_wrong.B: Custom routing accelerator for direct EC2 port routing, not automatic health-based routing.
why_wrong.C: Weighted random doesn't account for active request load.

explanation.exam_tips: Global Accelerator = global routing to optimal region. Least outstanding requests = even load for variable sessions. Weighted random = equal probability distribution.
explanation.memorize: Global Accelerator (global) + Least outstanding requests (local) = low latency + even load distribution.

question_en: A company is building a gaming application that needs to send unique events to multiple leaderboards, player matchmaking systems, and authentication services concurrently. The company requires an AWS-based eventdriven system that delivers events in order and supports a publish-subscribe model. The gaming application must be the publisher, and the leaderboards, matchmaking systems, and authentication services must be the subscribers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Amazon EventBridge event buses
options.B: Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) FIFO topics
options.C: Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) standard topics
options.D: Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues

explanation.why_correct: SNS FIFO topics provide pub/sub with strict ordering and exactly-once delivery to multiple subscribers. Ideal for ordered events to multiple systems.

why_wrong.A: EventBridge no ordering guarantees across subscribers.
why_wrong.C: SNS standard topics no ordering guarantees.
why_wrong.D: SQS FIFO queues point-to-point, not pub/sub.

explanation.exam_tips: SNS FIFO = ordered pub/sub. SQS FIFO = ordered queue. SNS standard = unordered pub/sub. EventBridge = event routing.
explanation.memorize: SNS FIFO topics = ordered publish-subscribe to multiple subscribers.

question_en: An application uses an Amazon SQS queue and two AWS Lambda functions. One of the Lambda functions pushes messages to the queue, and the other function polls the queue and receives queued messages. A solutions architect needs to ensure that only the two Lambda functions can write to or read from the queue. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Attach an IAM policy to the SQS queue that grants the Lambda function principals read and write access. Attach an IAM policy to the execution role of each Lambda function that denies all access to the SQS queue except for the principal of each function.
options.B: Attach a resource-based policy to the SQS queue to deny read and write access to the queue for any entity except the principal of each Lambda function. Attach an IAM policy to the execution role of each Lambda function that allows read and write access to the queue.
options.C: Attach a resource-based policy to the SQS queue that grants the Lambda function principals read and write access to the queue. Attach an IAM policy to the execution role of each Lambda function that allows read and write access to the queue.
options.D: Attach a resource-based policy to the SQS queue to deny all access to the queue. Attach an IAM policy to the execution role of each Lambda function that grants read and write access to the queue.

explanation.why_correct: Resource-based policy on SQS grants Lambda function principals access. IAM policies on Lambda execution roles allow SQS operations. Dual-layer security.

why_wrong.A: IAM policy denying all except function principals contradictory; resource-based policy simpler.
why_wrong.B: Deny-all resource policy prevents Lambda access unless overridden.
why_wrong.D: Deny-all blocks Lambda functions; contradictory with execution role permissions.

explanation.exam_tips: Resource-based policy = queue level. IAM role policy = function level. Combine for least privilege access control.
explanation.memorize: SQS resource policy (allow functions) + Lambda IAM policy (allow SQS) = secure exclusive access.

question_en: A gaming company is building an application with Voice over IP capabilities. The application will serve traffic to users across the world. The application needs to be highly available with automated failover across AWS Regions. The company wants to minimize the latency of users without relying on IP address caching on user devices. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.A: Use AWS Global Accelerator with health checks.
options.B: Use Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation routing policy.
options.C: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that includes multiple origins.
options.D: Create an Application Load Balancer that uses path-based routing.

explanation.why_correct: Global Accelerator uses static anycast IPs, routes via AWS edge network. Health checks enable automated cross-region failover. No DNS caching issues. Optimal for VoIP latency.

why_wrong.B: Route 53 geolocation DNS-based; affected by client caching, slower failover than Global Accelerator.
why_wrong.C: CloudFront for HTTP/HTTPS content, not VoIP UDP traffic.
why_wrong.D: ALB single-region, doesn't provide global routing or multi-region failover.

explanation.exam_tips: Global Accelerator = anycast IPs + AWS backbone for TCP/UDP. CloudFront = HTTP/HTTPS. Route 53 = DNS routing.
explanation.memorize: Global Accelerator + health checks = low-latency VoIP with automated cross-region failover.

question_en: A company is using microservices to build an ecommerce application on AWS. The company wants to preserve customer transaction information after customers submit orders. The company wants to store transaction data in an Amazon Aurora database. The company expects sales volumes to vary throughout each year.

options.A: Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API to invoke an AWS Lambda function to send transaction data to the Aurora database. Send transaction data to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue that has a dead-letter queue. Use a second Lambda function to read from the SQS queue and to update the Aurora database.
options.B: Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API to send transaction data to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Use the ALB to send the transaction data to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on Amazon EC2. Use ECS tasks to store the data in Aurora database.
options.C: Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to route transaction data to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use Amazon EKS to send the data to the Aurora database.
options.D: Use Amazon Data Firehose to send transaction data to Amazon S3. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the data from Amazon S3 to the Aurora database.

explanation.why_correct: API Gateway + Lambda (serverless scalability). SQS buffers transactions for variable volumes. DLQ captures failures. Second Lambda processes from queue to Aurora.

why_wrong.B: ALB + ECS on EC2 requires managing instances, higher overhead.
why_wrong.C: EKS Kubernetes management overhead unnecessary for microservices pattern.
why_wrong.D: Firehose + DMS not for real-time transactional workflows.

explanation.exam_tips: API Gateway + Lambda + SQS = serverless scalable async processing. DLQ = capture failures for retry. ECS/EKS for containerized apps.
explanation.memorize: API Gateway + Lambda + SQS + Aurora = serverless scalable transaction processing.

question_en: A media company hosts a mobile app backend in the AWS Cloud. The company is releasing a new feature to allow users to upload short videos and apply special effects by using the mobile app. The company uses AWS Amplify to store the videos that customers upload in an Amazon S3 bucket. The videos must be processed immediately. Users must receive a notification when processing is finished. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to schedule an AWS Lambda function to process the videos. Save the processed videos to the S3 bucket. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send push notifications to customers when processing is finished.
options.B: Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to schedule AWS Fargate to process the videos. Save the processed videos to the S3 bucket. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send push notifications to customers when processing is finished.
options.C: Use an S3 trigger to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the videos. Save the processed videos to the S3 bucket. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send push notifications to customers when processing is finished.
options.D: Use an S3 trigger to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the videos. Save the processed videos to the S3 bucket. Use AWS Amplify to send push notifications to customers when processing is finished.

explanation.why_correct: S3 Event Notifications trigger Lambda immediately on upload. Lambda processes video, saves to S3. SNS sends push notifications to users. Event-driven, real-time.

why_wrong.A: EventBridge Scheduler for scheduled tasks, not immediate event-driven processing.
why_wrong.B: Fargate scheduled not immediate event-driven.
why_wrong.D: Amplify doesn't natively send push notifications for backend workflows; SNS designed for it.

explanation.exam_tips: S3 Events = immediate object creation trigger. EventBridge Scheduler = scheduled tasks. SNS = notifications. Match trigger to timing requirement.
explanation.memorize: S3 trigger + Lambda + SNS = immediate event-driven video processing with notification.

question_en: A company stores sensitive customer data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The company frequently updates the data. The company wants to use the data to personalize offers for customers. The company ' s analytics team has its own AWS account. The analytics team runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that needs to process data from the DynamoDB tables. The company needs to follow security best practices to create a process to regularly share data from DynamoDB to the analytics team. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Export the required data from the DynamoDB table to an Amazon S3 bucket as multiple JSON files. Provide the analytics team with the necessary IAM permissions to access the S3 bucket.
options.B: Allow public access to the DynamoDB table. Create an IAM user that has permission to access DynamoDB. Share the IAM user with the analytics team.
options.C: Allow public access to the DynamoDB table. Create an IAM user that has read-only permission for DynamoDB. Share the IAM user with the analytics team.
options.D: Create a cross-account IAM role. Create an IAM policy that allows the AWS account ID of the analytics team to access the DynamoDB table. Attach the IAM policy to the IAM role. Establish a trust relationship between accounts.

explanation.why_correct: Cross-account IAM role with trust relationship enables analytics team to assume role and access DynamoDB securely. No credentials sharing, follows security best practices.

why_wrong.A: Export to S3 adds duplication, operational overhead, potential data lag.
why_wrong.B: Public access violates security for sensitive data; credential sharing discouraged.
why_wrong.C: Public access insecure; credential sharing bad practice.

explanation.exam_tips: Cross-account access: use IAM roles with trust relationships. Never share credentials or make resources public for sensitive data.
explanation.memorize: Cross-account IAM role + trust relationship = secure data sharing between AWS accounts.

question_en: Question: An ecommerce company hosts an API that handles sales requests. The company hosts the API frontend on Amazon EC2 instances that run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company hosts the API backend on EC2 instances that perform the transactions. The backend tiers are loosely coupled by an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The company anticipates a significant increase in request volume during a new product launch event. The company wants to ensure that the API can handle increased loads successfully. Options:

options.A: Double the number of frontend and backend EC2 instances to handle the increased traffic during the product launch event. Create a dead-letter queue to retain unprocessed sales requests when the demand exceeds the system capacity.
options.B: Place the frontend EC2 instances into an Auto Scaling group. Create an Auto Scaling policy to launch new instances to handle the incoming network traffic.
options.C: Place the frontend EC2 instances into an Auto Scaling group. Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster in front of the ALB to reduce the amount of traffic the API needs to handle.
options.D: Place the frontend and backend EC2 instances into separate Auto Scaling groups. Create a policy for the frontend Auto Scaling group to launch instances based on incoming network traffic. Create a policy for the backend Auto Scaling group to launch instances based on the SQS queue backlog.

explanation.why_correct: Frontend Auto Scaling based on network traffic handles user requests. Backend Auto Scaling based on SQS backlog processes transactions. Independent tier scaling.

why_wrong.A: Doubling capacity static, doesn't scale dynamically with load.
why_wrong.B: Only scales frontend; backend may still bottleneck on SQS processing.
why_wrong.C: ElastiCache doesn't reduce API request volume; caches aren't relevant for transaction processing.

explanation.exam_tips: Scale frontend by incoming traffic. Scale backend by queue depth. Independent Auto Scaling per tier for optimal resource utilization.
explanation.memorize: Separate Auto Scaling groups per tier = independent scaling based on tier-specific metrics.

question_en: A company has deployed an application that uses Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling. The Auto Scaling group is associated with a Network Load Balancer and has a minimum desired capacity of 1 and a maximum desired capacity of 6. The CPU utilization of the single running EC2 instance occasionally reaches 90%, which causes the application to become unstable. Which solution will resolve the stability issue with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Adjust the Auto Scaling group to a minimum desired capacity of 2 whenever the application becomes unstable.
options.B: Create a target tracking scaling policy. Set the ASGAverageCPUUtilization target value to 75%.
options.C: Create a target tracking scaling policy. Set the ASGAverageCPUUtilization target value to 90%.
options.D: Create a scheduled scaling policy. Create a daily scheduled scaling action that sets the minimum capacity to 2 instances at 9:00 a.m. Create a second action that sets the minimum capacity to 1 instance at 5:00 p.m.

explanation.why_correct: Target tracking at 75% CPU causes Auto Scaling to add capacity before reaching 90% instability threshold. Automatic, continuous adjustment without manual intervention.

why_wrong.A: Manual adjustment reactive, high operational overhead.
why_wrong.C: 90% target allows reaching known failure point before scaling.
why_wrong.D: Scheduled scaling for predictable patterns; utilization is occasional, not predictable daily.

explanation.exam_tips: Target tracking = reactive auto-scaling to metric target. Set target below failure threshold to scale before issues occur.
explanation.memorize: Target tracking at 75% CPU = auto-scale before 90% instability point.

question_en: A company has developed an API using an Amazon API Gateway REST API and AWS Lambda functions. The API serves static and dynamic content to users worldwide. The company wants to decrease the latency of transferring content for API requests. Options:

options.A: Deploy the REST API as an edge-optimized API endpoint. Enable caching. Enable content encoding in the API definition to compress the application data in transit.
options.B: Deploy the REST API as a Regional API endpoint. Enable caching. Enable content encoding in the API definition to compress the application data in transit.
options.C: Deploy the REST API as an edge-optimized API endpoint. Enable caching. Configure reserved concurrency for the Lambda functions.
options.D: Deploy the REST API as a Regional API endpoint. Enable caching. Configure reserved concurrency for the Lambda functions.

explanation.why_correct: Edge-optimized API Gateway uses CloudFront edge locations globally. Caching reduces latency. Content encoding compresses data, reducing transfer time.

why_wrong.B: Regional API Gateway serves single region, no global edge optimization.
why_wrong.C: Reserved concurrency ensures capacity, doesn't reduce content transfer latency.
why_wrong.D: Regional API + reserved concurrency doesn't optimize global latency.

explanation.exam_tips: Edge-optimized = CloudFront edge locations. Regional = single region. Caching + compression = reduce latency.
explanation.memorize: Edge-optimized API + caching + compression = minimize global latency.

question_en: A company runs a latency-sensitive gaming service in the AWS Cloud. The gaming service runs on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). An Amazon DynamoDB table stores the gaming data. All the infrastructure is in a single AWS Region. The main user base is in that same Region. A solutions architect needs to update the architecture to support a global expansion of the gaming service. The gaming service must operate with the least possible latency. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the ALB.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway regional API endpoint. Integrate the API endpoint with the ALB.
options.C: Create an accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator. Add a listener. Configure the endpoint to point to the ALB.
options.D: Deploy the ALB and the fleet of EC2 instances to another Region. Use Amazon Route 53 with geolocation routing.

explanation.why_correct: Global Accelerator routes traffic via AWS backbone to nearest healthy endpoint (ALB). Reduces latency and jitter for global gaming traffic. Anycast IPs.

why_wrong.A: CloudFront caches HTTP/HTTPS, not for real-time stateful gaming traffic.
why_wrong.B: API Gateway adds abstraction; doesn't optimize network path like Global Accelerator.
why_wrong.D: Multi-region deployment + Route 53 more complex and slower to react than Global Accelerator.

explanation.exam_tips: Global Accelerator = TCP/UDP low-latency global routing. CloudFront = HTTP/HTTPS content caching. Choose based on traffic type.
explanation.memorize: Global Accelerator + ALB = minimize latency for global real-time gaming.

question_en:
A company is running a two-tier web-based application in an on-premises data center. The application layer consists of a single server running a stateful application. The application connects to a PostgreSQL database running on a separate server. The user base is expected to grow significantly, so the company is migrating the application and database to AWS. The solution will use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, and Elastic Load Balancing.



Which solution will provide a consistent user experience that will allow the application and database tiers to scale?

options.A: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas. Use a Network Load Balancer with the least outstanding requests routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.
options.B: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora writers. Use an Application Load Balancer with the round robin routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.
options.C: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas. Use an Application Load Balancer with the round robin routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.
options.D: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora writers. Use a Network Load Balancer with the least outstanding requests routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.

explanation.why_correct: Aurora Auto Scaling for Replicas scales read capacity. ALB with sticky sessions maintains user state to same instance. Round robin with sticky balances new sessions.

why_wrong.A: NLB Layer 4, doesn't provide Layer 7 sticky sessions as effectively as ALB for web apps.
why_wrong.B: Aurora writers don't scale horizontally; one writer endpoint.
why_wrong.D: NLB + Aurora writers incorrect scaling mechanism.

explanation.exam_tips: Aurora Replicas = scale reads. Sticky sessions = stateful apps. ALB = Layer 7 HTTP sticky sessions. NLB = Layer 4 TCP sticky.
explanation.memorize: Aurora Replica Auto Scaling + ALB sticky sessions = scale stateful web app + database.

question_en:
A company is developing a new application that uses a relational database to store user data and application configurations. The company expects the application to have steady user growth. The company expects the database usage to be variable and read-heavy, with occasional writes. The company wants to cost-optimize the database solution. The company wants to use an AWS managed database solution that will provide the necessary performance.



Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Deploy the database on Amazon RDS. Use Provisioned IOPS SSD storage to ensure consistent performance for read and write operations.
options.B: Deploy the database on Amazon Aurora Serveriess to automatically scale the database capacity based on actual usage to accommodate the workload.
options.C: Deploy the database on Amazon DynamoDB. Use on-demand capacity mode to automatically scale throughput to accommodate the workload.
options.D: Deploy the database on Amazon RDS Use magnetic storage and use read replicas to accommodate the workload

explanation.why_correct: Aurora Serverless auto-scales capacity based on demand. Pay only for capacity used. Ideal for variable read-heavy workloads with occasional writes. Cost-effective for steady growth.

why_wrong.A: Provisioned IOPS always-on costs, less cost-effective for variable usage.
why_wrong.C: DynamoDB NoSQL; question requires relational database.
why_wrong.D: Magnetic storage outdated, slow. Read replicas don't provide auto-scaling compute.

explanation.exam_tips: Aurora Serverless = auto-scale compute capacity based on demand. Provisioned = fixed capacity. Choose Serverless for variable workloads.
explanation.memorize: Aurora Serverless = cost-effective auto-scaling for variable relational workloads.

question_en: A company is designing the network for an online multi-player game. The game uses the UDP networking protocol and will be deployed in eight AWS Regions. The network architecture needs to minimize latency and packet loss to give end users a high-quality gaming experience. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Set up a transit gateway in each Region. Create inter-Region peering attachments between each transit gateway.
options.B: Set up AWS Global Accelerator with UDP listeners and endpoint groups in each Region.
options.C: Set up Amazon CloudFront with UDP turned on. Configure an origin in each Region.
options.D: Set up a VPC peering mesh between each Region. Turn on UDP for each VPC.

explanation.why_correct: Global Accelerator with UDP listeners routes traffic via AWS edge network to optimal region. Reduces latency and packet loss for global multiplayer gaming.

why_wrong.A: Transit Gateway for VPC interconnection, not end-user traffic optimization.
why_wrong.C: CloudFront doesn't support generic UDP traffic acceleration.
why_wrong.D: VPC peering for private network connectivity, not end-user traffic routing.

explanation.exam_tips: Global Accelerator = TCP/UDP traffic optimization via AWS edge. Supports UDP listeners for gaming. CloudFront = HTTP/HTTPS only.
explanation.memorize: Global Accelerator + UDP listeners = minimize latency/packet loss for global gaming.

question_en: Question: A company wants to migrate an application that uses a microservice architecture to AWS. The services currently run on Docker containers on-premises. The application has an event-driven architecture that uses Apache Kafka. The company configured Kafka to use multiple queues to send and receive messages. Some messages must be processed by multiple services. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST management overhead? Options:

options.A: Migrate the services to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the Amazon EC2 launch type. Deploy a Kafka cluster on EC2 instances to handle service-to-service communication.
options.B: Migrate the services to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the AWS Fargate launch type. Create multiple Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queues to handle service-toservice communication.
options.C: Migrate the services to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the AWS Fargate launch type. Deploy an Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) cluster to handle service-to-service communication.
options.D: Migrate the services to Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the Amazon EC2 launch type. Use Amazon EventBridge to handle service-to-service communication.

explanation.why_correct: ECS Fargate serverless containers, no infrastructure management. Amazon MSK managed Kafka preserves existing Kafka queues/architecture. Minimal migration changes.

why_wrong.A: ECS EC2 launch requires managing instances. Self-managed Kafka on EC2 high operational overhead.
why_wrong.B: SQS doesn't support multiple consumers per message like Kafka topics (fan-out pattern different).
why_wrong.D: EventBridge different messaging model than Kafka; requires application redesign.

explanation.exam_tips: MSK = managed Kafka preserving existing architecture. Fargate = serverless containers. EC2 launch = manage instances.
explanation.memorize: ECS Fargate + Amazon MSK = serverless microservices with managed Kafka, least overhead.

question_en: A company is developing a latency-sensitive application. Part of the application includes several AWS Lambda functions that need to initialize as quickly as possible. The Lambda functions are written in Java and contain initialization code outside the handlers to load libraries, initialize classes, and generate unique IDs. Which solution will meet the startup performance requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Move all the initialization code to the handlers for each Lambda function. Activate Lambda SnapStart for each Lambda function. Configure SnapStart to reference the $LATEST version of each Lambda function.
options.B: Publish a version of each Lambda function. Create an alias for each Lambda function. Configure each alias to point to its corresponding version. Set up a provisioned concurrency configuration for each Lambda function to point to the corresponding alias.
options.C: Publish a version of each Lambda function. Set up a provisioned concurrency configuration for each Lambda function to point to the corresponding version. Activate Lambda SnapStart for the published versions of the Lambda functions.
options.D: Update the Lambda functions to add a pre-snapshot hook. Move the code that generates unique IDs into the handlers. Publish a version of each Lambda function. Activate Lambda SnapStart for the published versions of the Lambda functions.

explanation.why_correct: SnapStart reduces cold starts for Java. Pre-snapshot hook for setup. Move unique IDs to handler for per-invocation execution. Publish version required. Most cost-effective.

why_wrong.A: SnapStart not supported on $LATEST version.
why_wrong.B: Provisioned concurrency prevents cold starts but more expensive than SnapStart.
why_wrong.C: Provisioned concurrency + SnapStart redundant and expensive; SnapStart alone sufficient.

explanation.exam_tips: SnapStart = cost-effective Java cold start reduction. Pre-snapshot hook for non-deterministic code. Provisioned concurrency = expensive alternative.
explanation.memorize: SnapStart + pre-snapshot hook + published version = cost-effective Java Lambda cold start solution.

question_en: A company allows users to upload and store photos through its website. The website has users from all around the world. All images that users upload are stored in a centralized Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to increase the speed in which its entire user base can upload photos through the website. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Amazon S3 Standard storage class to store files.
options.B: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Configure the distribution settings and origin.
options.C: Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration on the S3 bucket. Use the standard S3 endpoint to upload files.
options.D: Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration on the S3 bucket. Use the S3 Accelerate endpoint to upload files.

explanation.why_correct: S3 Transfer Acceleration + S3 Accelerate endpoint routes uploads via CloudFront edge locations and AWS backbone. Speeds up global uploads dramatically.

why_wrong.A: CloudFront optimized for downloads/content delivery, not uploads.
why_wrong.B: CloudFront distribution doesn't require origin configuration for accelerating uploads.
why_wrong.C: Transfer Acceleration enabled but using standard endpoint doesn't provide acceleration benefit.

explanation.exam_tips: S3 Transfer Acceleration = speed up uploads from global users. Must use S3 Accelerate endpoint, not standard. CloudFront = download acceleration.
explanation.memorize: S3 Transfer Acceleration + Accelerate endpoint = fast global uploads.

question_en: A financial services company plans to launch a new application on AWS to handle sensitive financial transactions. The company will deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances. The company will use Amazon RDS for MySQL as the database. The company ' s security policies mandate that data must be encrypted at rest and in transit. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.
options.B: Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys. Configure IPsec tunnels for encryption in transit
options.C: Implement third-party application-level data encryption before storing data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) SSL/TLS certificates for encryption in transit.
options.D: Configure encryption at rest for Amazon RDS for MySQL by using AWS KMS managed keys Configure a VPN connection to enable private connectivity to encrypt data in transit.

explanation.why_correct: RDS encryption at rest via KMS keys. SSL/TLS via ACM certificates for in-transit encryption. Both fully managed, least operational overhead.

why_wrong.B: IPsec tunnels complex to manage, higher overhead than SSL/TLS.
why_wrong.C: Application-level encryption adds code complexity and overhead.
why_wrong.D: VPN for in-transit encryption unnecessary complexity vs SSL/TLS.

explanation.exam_tips: Encryption at rest = KMS keys on RDS. Encryption in transit = SSL/TLS certificates. ACM = managed certificate lifecycle.
explanation.memorize: RDS + KMS (at rest) + ACM SSL/TLS (in transit) = least overhead encryption solution.

question_en: A company stores a large dataset for an online advertising business in an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. The company wants to run business reporting queries on the data without affecting write operations to the DB instance. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy RDS read replicas to process the business reporting queries.
options.B: Scale out the DB instance horizontally by placing the instance behind an Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) load balancer.
options.C: Scale up the DB instance to a larger instance type to handle write operations and reporting queries.
options.D: D. Configure Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the DB instance. Deploy standby DB instances when a latency metric threshold is exceeded.

explanation.why_correct: RDS read replicas offload read-heavy reporting queries from primary instance. Primary handles writes unaffected. Async replication provides near-current data.

why_wrong.B: ELB doesn't scale databases; load balances app servers. RDS single-writer endpoint.
why_wrong.C: Vertical scaling doesn't separate read and write workloads; both still hit same instance.
why_wrong.D: CloudWatch monitoring + standby instances reactive, not proactive query separation.

explanation.exam_tips: Read replica = offload reads. Vertical scaling = larger instance. Horizontal scaling = multiple instances/shards. Choose replica for read workload separation.
explanation.memorize: RDS read replicas = run reporting queries without affecting write operations.

question_en: A media company needs to migrate its Windows-based video editing environment to AWS. The company ' s current environment processes 4K video files that require sustained throughput of 2 GB per second across multiple concurrent users. The company ' s storage needs increase by 1 TB each week. The company needs a shared file system that supports SMB protocol and can scale automatically based on storage demands. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system with SSD storage.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system in Max I/O mode. Provision mount targets in multiple Availability Zones.
options.C: Deploy an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system with a Persistent 2 deployment type. Provision the file system with 2 TB of storage.
options.D: Deploy Amazon S3 File Gateway by using multiple cached gateway instances. Configure S3 Transfer Acceleration.

explanation.why_correct: FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB protocol, high throughput (2 GB/s), auto-scaling storage. Multi-AZ SSD for HA and performance. Windows-native.

why_wrong.B: EFS provides NFS, not SMB. Optimized for Linux, not Windows.
why_wrong.C: FSx Lustre POSIX file system for Linux HPC, not Windows SMB.
why_wrong.D: S3 File Gateway not designed for sustained multi-GB/s shared editing performance.

explanation.exam_tips: FSx Windows = SMB for Windows. FSx Lustre = POSIX for Linux HPC. EFS = NFS for Linux. Match protocol and OS.
explanation.memorize: FSx for Windows Multi-AZ SSD = SMB, auto-scale, high throughput for Windows video editing.

question_en: A company has a serverless web application that is comprised of AWS Lambda functions. The application experiences spikes in traffic that cause increased latency because of cold starts. The company wants to improve the application’s ability to handle traffic spikes and to minimize latency. The solution must optimize costs during periods when traffic is low.

options.A: Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda functions. Use AWS Application Auto Scaling to adjust the provisioned concurrency.
options.B: Launch Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Add a scheduled scaling policy to launch additional EC2 instances during peak traffic periods.
options.C: Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda functions. Set a fixed concurrency level to handle the maximum expected traffic.
options.D: Create a recurring schedule in Amazon EventBridge Scheduler. Use the schedule to invoke the Lambda functions periodically to warm the functions.

explanation.why_correct: Provisioned concurrency pre-warms Lambda environments, eliminating cold starts. Application Auto Scaling adjusts concurrency dynamically based on demand, optimizing costs during low traffic while maintaining performance during spikes.

why_wrong.B: EC2 with Auto Scaling contradicts serverless architecture philosophy, adds operational overhead, and doesn't address Lambda cold starts.
why_wrong.C: Fixed concurrency level maintains unnecessary instances during low traffic, failing to optimize costs as required.
why_wrong.D: EventBridge periodic invocations don't scale dynamically with traffic patterns and cause unnecessary invocations during idle periods.

explanation.exam_tips: For Lambda cold start mitigation with cost optimization, use provisioned concurrency with Application Auto Scaling. Fixed provisioned concurrency wastes money; periodic warming doesn't handle traffic spikes.
explanation.memorize: Provisioned concurrency + Application Auto Scaling = cold start mitigation + cost optimization for Lambda traffic spikes

question_en:
A company runs a web application that uses Amazon RDS for MySQL to store relational data. Data in the database does not change frequently. A solutions architect notices that during peak usage times, the database has performance issues when it serves the data. The company wants to improve the performance of the database.



Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Integrate AWS WAF with the application.
options.B: Create a read replica for the database. Redirect read traffic to the read replica.
options.C: Create an Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached) cluster. Configure the application and the database to integrate with the cluster.
options.D: Use the Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) storage class to store the data that changes infrequently.
options.E: Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB. Configure the application to use the DynamoDB database.

explanation.why_correct: Read replicas offload read traffic from primary RDS instance. ElastiCache (Memcached) caches frequent queries in memory, reducing database load for infrequently changing data. Both improve read performance under peak load.

why_wrong.A: AWS WAF provides web application security, not database performance improvements.
why_wrong.D: S3 One Zone-IA is storage optimization, doesn't address database query latency or performance.
why_wrong.E: Migrating from MySQL to DynamoDB requires complete re-architecture, unnecessary complexity for read performance issue.

explanation.exam_tips: For RDS read performance: use read replicas for read scalability + ElastiCache for frequently accessed data. Don't confuse storage optimization (S3) with database performance solutions.
explanation.memorize: RDS read performance = Read Replicas (offload reads) + ElastiCache (cache queries)

question_en: A company needs a solution to integrate transaction data from several Amazon DynamoDB tables into an existing Amazon Redshift data warehouse. The solution must maintain the provisioned throughput of DynamoDB. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure DynamoDB to export to the bucket on a regular schedule. Use an Amazon Redshift COPY command to read from the S3 bucket.
options.B: Use an Amazon Redshift COPY command to read directly from each DynamoDB table.
options.C: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an AWS Lambda function to read from the DynamoDB tables and write to the S3 bucket on a regular schedule. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to access the data in the S3 bucket.
options.D: Use Amazon Athena Federated Query with a DynamoDB connector and an Amazon Redshift connector to read directly from the DynamoDB tables.

explanation.why_correct: DynamoDB export to S3 doesn't consume read capacity units (RCU), preserving provisioned throughput. Redshift COPY from S3 provides parallel, high-throughput bulk loading with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.B: Direct COPY from DynamoDB performs table scan consuming provisioned throughput, risking throttling.
why_wrong.C: Lambda-based pipeline adds custom code complexity, scheduling overhead, and operational management burden.
why_wrong.D: Athena federated queries are for ad-hoc analytics, not optimized for recurring bulk warehouse loads.

explanation.exam_tips: For DynamoDB-to-Redshift ETL: export to S3 (no RCU consumption) + Redshift COPY. Direct reads from DynamoDB consume throughput. Stage data in S3 for warehouse loads.
explanation.memorize: DynamoDB export to S3 = zero RCU impact + Redshift COPY = optimal bulk load

question_en: A solutions architect is migrating an on-premises application to AWS. The application currently runs on containers. The components of the application are loosely coupled. The application consumes messages from a message queue. The solutions architect needs to design a new architecture for the application on AWS. The solutions architect wants to use fully managed AWS services for the new architecture. The new architecture must provide unlimited scalability for the message queue’s throughput. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon SQS to create a new message queue. Subscribe the SQS queue to an Amazon SNS topic. Use Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances that run Kubernetes containers to consume messages from the message queue.
options.B: Use Amazon MQ to create a new message queue. Subscribe the Amazon MQ queue to an Amazon SNS topic. Use Amazon EKS containers on AWS Fargate to consume messages from the message queue.
options.C: Use Amazon MQ to create a new message queue. Subscribe the Amazon MQ queue to an Amazon SNS topic. Use AWS Lambda functions to poll messages from the Amazon MQ queue by using Lambda event source mappings.
options.D: Use Amazon SQS to create a new message queue. Subscribe the SQS queue to an Amazon SNS topic. Use Amazon ECS containers on AWS Fargate to consume messages from the message queue.

explanation.why_correct: SQS provides unlimited throughput scaling for message queues without infrastructure management. ECS on Fargate runs containers without managing EC2 instances or Kubernetes clusters. SNS enables pub/sub fan-out when needed.

why_wrong.A: EC2 Reserved Instances require instance management, violating fully managed requirement.
why_wrong.B: Amazon MQ doesn't provide unlimited scaling like SQS. EKS requires Kubernetes management overhead.
why_wrong.C: Amazon MQ has scaling limitations compared to SQS. Lambda polling from MQ adds complexity vs. native SQS integration.

explanation.exam_tips: For unlimited message queue scaling with containers: SQS (not Amazon MQ) + ECS on Fargate (not EC2 or EKS). Amazon MQ is for traditional broker compatibility, not unlimited scale.
explanation.memorize: Unlimited queue throughput + fully managed containers = SQS + ECS Fargate

question_en: A company has an on-premises application that uses SFTP to collect financial data from multiple vendors. The company is migrating to the AWS Cloud. The company has created an application that uses Amazon S3 APIs to upload files from vendors. Some vendors run their systems on legacy applications that do not support S3 APIs. The vendors want to continue to use SFTP-based applications to upload data. The company wants to use managed services for the needs of the vendors that use legacy applications. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) instance to replicate data from the storage of the vendors that use legacy applications to Amazon S3. Provide the vendors with the credentials to access the AWS DMS instance.
options.B: B. Create an AWS Transfer Family endpoint for vendors that use legacy applications.
options.C: Configure an Amazon EC2 instance to run an SFTP server. Instruct the vendors that use legacy applications to use the SFTP server to upload data.
options.D: Configure an Amazon S3 File Gateway for vendors that use legacy applications to upload files to an SMB file share.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Transfer Family provides fully managed SFTP, FTPS, and FTP endpoints directly to S3. Vendors use familiar SFTP protocol while files land directly in S3 with zero infrastructure management.

why_wrong.A: AWS DMS is for database replication, not SFTP file transfers.
why_wrong.C: EC2-based SFTP server requires instance management, patching, scaling—violating managed service requirement.
why_wrong.D: S3 File Gateway provides SMB/NFS, not SFTP protocol required by vendors.

explanation.exam_tips: For legacy SFTP support to S3: use AWS Transfer Family (fully managed). Don't build custom SFTP servers on EC2 when Transfer Family exists.
explanation.memorize: SFTP to S3 = AWS Transfer Family (fully managed, zero infrastructure)

question_en: A company currently runs a Linux-based application in a self-managed Docker container that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The application runs a lightweight data processing tool that always completes its job within 3 minutes. The company wants an alternative deployment solution for the application to reduce infrastructure management overhead. The company is willing to make any required changes to the image. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Deploy the application as an AWS Lambda function that uses the container image.
options.B: Deploy the application on Amazon EKS with the AWS Fargate launch type.
options.C: Deploy the application on Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type.
options.D: Deploy the application as a custom Amazon Machine Image (AMI) by using AWS Batch.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda supports container images up to 10GB. 3-minute execution fits Lambda's 15-minute limit. Lambda is fully managed (no servers, clusters, or capacity planning), eliminating infrastructure overhead for short-lived processing.

why_wrong.B: EKS with Fargate requires Kubernetes management, introducing unnecessary operational complexity.
why_wrong.C: ECS with Fargate still requires task definitions, services, and networking management—more overhead than Lambda.
why_wrong.D: Custom AMI with AWS Batch adds compute management unnecessary for short, lightweight workload.

explanation.exam_tips: For short-lived containerized workloads (<15 min): use Lambda container images. Lambda eliminates infrastructure management vs. ECS/EKS. Serverless-first for minimal overhead.
explanation.memorize: Short container jobs (<15 min) = Lambda container image (least overhead)

question_en: A company is using an AWS Lambda function in a VPC. The Lambda function needs to access dependencies that exceed the size of the Lambda layer quota. The data that the Lambda function retrieves must be encrypted in transit. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Store the dependencies in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Mount the file system to the Lambda function. Retrieve the dependencies from the file system.
options.B: Store the dependencies on an Amazon EC2 instance that has an instance store volume and web server software. Use HTTPS API calls to retrieve the dependencies each time the Lambda function runs.
options.C: Store the dependencies on an Amazon EC2 instance that hosts an NFS file server. Read the files from the EC2 instance each time the Lambda function runs.
options.D: Store the dependencies in two separate Lambda layers. Redesign the application to have two Lambda functions that use different Lambda layers.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda supports mounting Amazon EFS file systems for dependencies exceeding 250MB layer quota. EFS automatically encrypts data in transit using TLS, meeting encryption requirement with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.B: EC2 with instance store and web server requires managing instances, web server software, and HTTPS configuration—significant operational overhead.
why_wrong.C: EC2-based NFS server requires managing EC2 instances and NFS configuration, adding operational burden.
why_wrong.D: Lambda layers have 250MB quota. Splitting into two layers and two functions is architectural workaround, not addressing >250MB requirement efficiently.

explanation.exam_tips: For Lambda dependencies >250MB: mount EFS file system (not multiple layers). EFS provides automatic encryption in transit via TLS.
explanation.memorize: Lambda large dependencies = EFS mount (automatic TLS encryption)

question_en: A company runs production workloads in its AWS account. Multiple teams create and maintain the workloads. The company needs to be able to detect changes in resource configurations. The company needs to capture changes as configuration items without changing or modifying the existing resources. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use AWS Config. Start the configuration recorder for AWS resources to detect changes in resource configurations.
options.B: Use AWS CloudFormation. Initiate drift detection to capture changes in resource configurations.
options.C: Use Amazon Detective to detect, analyze, and investigate changes in resource configurations.
options.D: Use AWS Audit Manager to capture management events and global service events for resource configurations.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Config continuously monitors and records resource configuration changes as configuration items. Configuration recorder captures changes without modifying resources, providing full configuration history and compliance tracking.

why_wrong.B: CloudFormation drift detection only works for CloudFormation-managed resources, not all AWS resources.
why_wrong.C: Amazon Detective analyzes security findings, not resource configuration tracking.
why_wrong.D: AWS Audit Manager collects audit evidence, not specifically for resource configuration tracking.

explanation.exam_tips: For resource configuration change tracking: use AWS Config with configuration recorder. Config provides historical configuration data across all resource types.
explanation.memorize: Configuration change tracking = AWS Config configuration recorder

question_en: A company has a web application that stores user transactions in an Amazon DynamoDB table. To comply with regulations, the company must retain a copy of user transaction data for 7 years. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use DynamoDB point-in-time recovery to back up the table continuously.
options.B: Use AWS Backup to create backup schedules and retention policies for the table.
options.C: Create an on-demand backup of the table by using DynamoDB. Store the backup in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set an S3 Lifecycle configuration for the S3 bucket.
options.D: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to back up the table and to store the backup in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set an S3 Lifecycle configuration for the S3 bucket.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Backup provides centralized backup scheduling, retention policies (7 years), and compliance monitoring for DynamoDB with minimal operational overhead. Fully managed solution eliminates custom automation.

why_wrong.A: Point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores within 35 days only, insufficient for 7-year retention requirement.
why_wrong.C: Manual on-demand backups require custom scheduling and lifecycle management, increasing operational complexity.
why_wrong.D: Lambda-based backup automation requires custom code development and maintenance, adding operational overhead.

explanation.exam_tips: For long-term backup retention (>35 days): use AWS Backup, not PITR. AWS Backup handles scheduling, retention, and compliance automatically.
explanation.memorize: DynamoDB long-term retention = AWS Backup (centralized, automated policies)

question_en: A company uses an Amazon EC2 instance to run a script to poll for and process messages in an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The company wants to reduce operational overhead while maintaining its ability to process an increasing number of messages that are added to the queue. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Increase the size of the EC2 instance to process messages in the SQS queue faster.
options.B: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to turn off the EC2 instance when the SQS queue is empty.
options.C: Migrate the script on the EC2 instance to an AWS Lambda function with an event source of the SQS queue.
options.D: Configure an AWS Systems Manager Run Command to run the script on demand.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda with SQS event source eliminates EC2 instance management. Lambda automatically polls queue, scales based on message volume, and processes messages without infrastructure provisioning or capacity planning.

why_wrong.A: Increasing EC2 instance size doesn't address operational overhead or automatic scaling requirements.
why_wrong.B: EventBridge to turn off EC2 reduces costs when idle but doesn't address scaling with message volume.
why_wrong.D: Systems Manager Run Command requires manual triggering, not continuous automatic processing.

explanation.exam_tips: For SQS message processing at scale: migrate to Lambda with SQS event source. Lambda eliminates EC2 management and auto-scales with queue depth.
explanation.memorize: SQS processing + reduce overhead = Lambda event source (auto-scale, no infra)

question_en: A company runs a multi-tier application on premises by using virtual machines (VMs). The application tiers communicate asynchronously through third-party middleware that guarantees exactly-once delivery. The company is planning to migrate the application to AWS and needs to replace the middleware solution. The solution must provide exactly-once delivery for messages from the application. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements with the LEAST infrastructure management? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Use AWS Lambda functions to provide compute layers in the architecture.
options.B: Use Amazon EC2 instances to provide compute layers in the architecture.
options.C: Use Amazon SNS as a messaging component between the compute layers.
options.D: Use Amazon SQS FIFO queues as a messaging component between the compute layers.
options.E: Run containers on Amazon EKS to provide compute layers in the architecture.

explanation.why_correct: SQS FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once delivery with ordered processing. Lambda provides fully managed compute without infrastructure management (no VMs, OS, or clusters). Perfect for asynchronous multi-tier communication.

why_wrong.B: EC2 instances require managing provisioning, patching, scaling, and availability—violating least management requirement.
why_wrong.C: Amazon SNS provides pub/sub but lacks exactly-once delivery guarantees required for this migration.
why_wrong.E: Amazon EKS introduces Kubernetes management overhead, not the lowest-management option.

explanation.exam_tips: For exactly-once message delivery: use SQS FIFO (not SNS). For least infrastructure management: Lambda (not EC2 or EKS). FIFO guarantees order + exactly-once.
explanation.memorize: Exactly-once + least management = SQS FIFO + Lambda

question_en: A company requires centralized auditing for all AWS accounts and compliance monitoring against AWS Foundational Security Best Practices (FSBP) with minimal operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy AWS Control Tower in the management account. Enable AWS Security Hub and Account Factory.
options.B: Deploy AWS Control Tower in a member account.
options.C: Use AWS Managed Services (AMS) with GuardDuty.
options.D: Use AWS Managed Services (AMS) with Security Hub.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Control Tower deployed in management account provides centralized governance, CloudTrail aggregation, and Account Factory. Security Hub integration evaluates compliance against FSBP standards automatically with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.B: Control Tower must be deployed in management account, not member account.
why_wrong.C: GuardDuty provides threat detection, not centralized compliance monitoring against FSBP.
why_wrong.D: AWS Managed Services adds managed operations but doesn't provide automated FSBP compliance as efficiently as Control Tower + Security Hub.

explanation.exam_tips: For multi-account governance + FSBP compliance: deploy Control Tower in management account with Security Hub enabled. Control Tower provides automated account governance.
explanation.memorize: Multi-account governance + FSBP = Control Tower (management account) + Security Hub

question_en: An insurance company runs an application on premises to process contracts. The application processes jobs that are comprised of many tasks. The individual tasks run for up to 5 minutes. Some jobs can take up to 24 hours in total to finish. If a task fails, the task must be reprocessed. The company wants to migrate the application to AWS. The company will use Amazon S3 as part of the solution. The company wants to configure jobs to start automatically when a contract is uploaded to an S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use AWS Lambda functions to process individual tasks. Create a primary Lambda function to handle the overall job processing by calling individual Lambda functions in sequence. Configure the S3 bucket to send an event notification to invoke the primary Lambda function to begin processing.
options.B: Use a state machine in AWS Step Functions to handle the overall contract processing job. Configure the S3 bucket to send an event notification to Amazon EventBridge. Create a rule in Amazon EventBridge to target the state machine.
options.C: Use an AWS Batch job to handle the overall contract processing job. Configure the S3 bucket to send an event notification to initiate the Batch job.
options.D: Use an S3 event notification to notify an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue when a contract is uploaded. Configure an AWS Lambda function to read messages from the queue and to run the contract processing job.

explanation.why_correct: Step Functions manages long-running workflows (up to 1 year) with task coordination and retry logic. EventBridge rule triggers state machine from S3 upload event automatically. Ideal for multi-task jobs requiring orchestration.

why_wrong.A: Lambda has 15-minute execution limit, insufficient for 24-hour jobs. Chaining Lambda functions adds complexity for long workflows.
why_wrong.C: AWS Batch is for batch computing jobs, not workflow orchestration with multiple dependent tasks requiring retry logic.
why_wrong.D: SQS + Lambda doesn't provide workflow orchestration or built-in retry logic for complex multi-task jobs.

explanation.exam_tips: For long-running multi-task workflows (>15 min): use Step Functions (not Lambda chains). EventBridge triggers workflows from S3 events. Step Functions handles retries automatically.
explanation.memorize: Long workflow orchestration = Step Functions + EventBridge S3 trigger

question_en: A social media company wants to store its database of user profiles, relationships, and interactions in the AWS Cloud. The company needs an application to monitor any changes in the database. The application needs to analyze the relationships between the data entities and to provide recommendations to users. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use Amazon Neptune to store the information. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to process changes in the database.
options.B: Use Amazon Neptune to store the information. Use Neptune Streams to process changes in the database.
options.C: Use Amazon Quantum Ledger Database (Amazon QLDB) to store the information. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to process changes in the database.
options.D: Use Amazon Quantum Ledger Database (Amazon QLDB) to store the information. Use Neptune Streams to process changes in the database.

explanation.why_correct: Neptune is purpose-built graph database for storing relationships between entities (profiles, interactions). Neptune Streams captures graph changes in real-time with tight integration, minimizing operational overhead for change monitoring.

why_wrong.A: Kinesis Data Streams requires additional infrastructure and integration vs. native Neptune Streams.
why_wrong.C: Amazon QLDB is immutable ledger database, not optimized for graph relationships and recommendations.
why_wrong.D: QLDB doesn't support Neptune Streams (different database services)—architecturally incompatible.

explanation.exam_tips: For graph data with relationships: use Neptune (not QLDB). For Neptune change monitoring: use Neptune Streams (native integration, not Kinesis).
explanation.memorize: Graph relationships + change monitoring = Neptune + Neptune Streams

question_en: A security audit reveals that Amazon EC2 instances are not being patched regularly. A solutions architect needs to provide a solution that will run regular security scans across a large fleet of EC2 instances. The solution should also patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule and provide a report of each instance ' s patch status. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Set up Amazon Macie to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up a cron job on each EC2 instance to patch the instance on a regular schedule.
options.B: Turn on Amazon GuardDuty in the account. Configure GuardDuty to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.
options.C: Set up Amazon Detective to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.
options.D: Turn on Amazon Inspector in the account. Configure Amazon Inspector to scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities. Set up AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch the EC2 instances on a regular schedule.

explanation.why_correct: Amazon Inspector provides automated vulnerability scanning for EC2 fleet, detecting missing patches and vulnerabilities. Systems Manager Patch Manager orchestrates scheduled patching across fleet with centralized compliance reporting and patch status tracking.

why_wrong.A: Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in S3, not EC2 vulnerability scanning. Cron jobs on each instance lack centralized reporting and add operational overhead.
why_wrong.B: GuardDuty detects threats from logs/events, not software vulnerabilities or patch management.
why_wrong.C: Amazon Detective investigates security events, not vulnerability scanning or patch deployment.

explanation.exam_tips: For EC2 vulnerability scanning: use Inspector (not GuardDuty/Detective/Macie). For automated patching with reporting: use Systems Manager Patch Manager (not cron jobs).
explanation.memorize: EC2 vulnerability + patching = Inspector (scan) + Patch Manager (patch + report)

question_en: A company is designing a solution to capture customer activity on the company ' s web applications. The company wants to analyze the activity data to make predictions. Customer activity on the web applications is unpredictable and can increase suddenly. The company requires a solution that integrates with other web applications. The solution must include an authorization step. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in front of an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) container instance. Store the data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Configure the applications to pass an authorization header to the GWLB.
options.B: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway endpoint in front of an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use an AWS Lambda function to handle authorization.
