options.C: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway endpoint in front of an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream. Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use an API Gateway Lambda authorizer to handle authorization.
options.D: Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in front of an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) container instance. Store the data in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Use an AWS Lambda function to handle authorization.

explanation.why_correct: API Gateway provides scalable web API integration with Lambda authorizer for flexible authorization. Kinesis Data Firehose is fully managed streaming service that handles unpredictable traffic spikes, ingesting data directly to S3 for analytics without infrastructure management.

why_wrong.A: Gateway Load Balancer is for network traffic inspection, not web API data capture. ECS + EFS adds infrastructure management overhead.
why_wrong.B: Kinesis Data Streams requires more management than Firehose and lacks direct API Gateway integration for streaming ingestion.
why_wrong.D: Gateway Load Balancer + ECS + EFS architecture is unnecessarily complex for web activity capture with authorization.

explanation.exam_tips: For streaming web data capture with authorization: API Gateway + Lambda authorizer + Firehose. Don't use Gateway Load Balancer for application data capture.
explanation.memorize: Web streaming + auth = API Gateway (Lambda authorizer) + Kinesis Firehose

question_en: A company has resources across multiple AWS Regions and accounts. A new solutions architect needs to build a map of the workloads and their relationships but has no documentation from the previous employee. Which solution will provide these details with the least operational effort?

options.A: Use AWS Systems Manager Inventory to generate a map from the detailed report.
options.B: Use AWS Step Functions to collect workload details and build diagrams manually.
options.C: Use Workload Discovery on AWS to generate architecture diagrams.
options.D: Use AWS X-Ray to view workload details and manually draw diagrams.

explanation.why_correct: Workload Discovery on AWS automatically scans AWS accounts and Regions, identifies resources, and generates relationship-aware architecture diagrams. Provides complete workload map with minimal operational effort without existing documentation.

why_wrong.A: Systems Manager Inventory collects instance metadata but doesn't build multi-account/region architecture diagrams.
why_wrong.B: Step Functions collects data but requires manual diagram creation, not automated visualization.
why_wrong.D: X-Ray traces application requests but requires manual diagramming of workload relationships.

explanation.exam_tips: For automated workload discovery and diagramming: use Workload Discovery on AWS (not manual tools). Automatically generates architecture maps across accounts/regions.
explanation.memorize: Multi-account workload mapping = Workload Discovery on AWS (auto-generates diagrams)

question_en: A company uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL databases for its data tier. The company must implement password rotation for the databases. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager. Enable automatic rotation on the secret.
options.B: Store the password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Enable automatic rotation on the parameter.
options.C: Store the password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Write an AWS Lambda function that rotates the password.
options.D: Store the password in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Enable automatic rotation on the AWS KMS key.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Secrets Manager natively integrates with RDS for PostgreSQL, providing built-in automatic password rotation functionality with versioning and auditing. Minimal setup required, fully managed rotation process.

why_wrong.B: Systems Manager Parameter Store doesn't natively support automatic credential rotation.
why_wrong.C: Parameter Store with Lambda rotation function requires custom code development and management—increased operational overhead.
why_wrong.D: AWS KMS manages encryption keys, not application secrets or credentials—wrong service for password management.

explanation.exam_tips: For RDS password rotation: use Secrets Manager (native RDS integration, automatic rotation). Parameter Store doesn't auto-rotate credentials. KMS is for keys, not secrets.
explanation.memorize: RDS password rotation = Secrets Manager (automatic, native RDS integration)

question_en: A company needs a solution to give customers the ability to upload encrypted files to a directory in an Amazon S3 bucket by using SFTP. After customers upload files, the solution must automatically decrypt the files and move them to a second directory within the same S3 bucket for downstream processing. The solution must not require authentication services. The solution must fully automate all post-upload operations and require minimal ongoing operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)

options.A: Use AWS Transfer Family with the SFTP protocol. Configure the S3 bucket as the home directory for uploaded files.
options.B: Use an S3 event notification to invoke an AWS Lambda function that moves uploaded files between folders.
options.C: Use an AWS Transfer Family workflow and a DECRYPT action to decrypt uploaded files.
options.D: Tag incoming S3 objects. Periodically query objects by using an external script that runs in a container.
options.E: Use an AWS Transfer Family workflow and a COPY action to move files to a new directory within the S3 bucket after decryption.
options.F: Use an AWS Batch job to poll the S3 bucket and run a decryption script on new files.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP endpoint to S3 without authentication services. Transfer Family workflows with DECRYPT action automatically decrypt uploaded files. COPY action moves decrypted files to second directory—fully automated post-upload operations.

why_wrong.B: S3 event + Lambda adds custom orchestration when native Transfer Family workflow handles requirements more simply.
why_wrong.D: External polling script in container introduces infrastructure and operational overhead unnecessarily.
why_wrong.F: AWS Batch polling adds complexity beyond managed Transfer Family workflow capabilities.

explanation.exam_tips: For SFTP to S3 with post-processing: use Transfer Family + workflows (DECRYPT + COPY actions). Workflows eliminate custom Lambda/Batch code. Fully automated, minimal overhead.
explanation.memorize: SFTP + decrypt + move = Transfer Family + workflow (DECRYPT + COPY)

question_en: A solutions architect needs to save a particular automated database snapshot from an Amazon RDS for Microsoft SQL Server DB instance for longer than the maximum number of days. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.A: Create a manual copy of the snapshot.
options.B: Export the contents of the snapshot to an Amazon S3 bucket.
options.C: Change the retention period of the snapshot to 45 days.
options.D: Create a native SQL Server backup. Save the backup to an Amazon S3 bucket.

explanation.why_correct: Creating manual copy of automated snapshot converts it to manual snapshot retained indefinitely until explicitly deleted. Most operationally efficient—single action preserves specific snapshot beyond automated retention window without additional processes.

why_wrong.B: Exporting snapshot to S3 adds workflow complexity, format considerations, and ongoing S3 management—less efficient for snapshot retention goal.
why_wrong.C: Cannot extend automated snapshot retention beyond service maximum. Fixed retention period doesn't guarantee indefinite retention.
why_wrong.D: Native SQL Server backups require managing backup jobs, storage, restores, and permissions—higher operational overhead than RDS snapshot copy.

explanation.exam_tips: For long-term RDS snapshot retention: copy automated snapshot to manual snapshot (indefinite retention). Manual snapshots persist until deleted. Don't use native backups when RDS snapshots suffice.
explanation.memorize: Extend RDS snapshot retention = copy automated to manual snapshot

question_en: A company wants to migrate an on-premises video processing application to AWS. Processing times range from 5–30 minutes. The application must run multiple jobs in parallel. The application processes videos that users upload to an Amazon S3 bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Configure the S3 bucket to send S3 event notifications to an Amazon SQS standard queue. Deploy the application on an Amazon ECS cluster. Configure automatic scaling for AWS Fargate tasks based on the SQS queue size.
options.B: Configure the S3 bucket to send S3 event notifications to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue. Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Create an Auto Scaling group to scale based on the SQS queue size.
options.C: Configure the S3 bucket to send S3 event notifications to an Amazon SQS standard queue. Deploy the application as an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to poll the SQS queue.
options.D: Configure the S3 bucket to send S3 event notifications to an Amazon SNS topic. Deploy the application as an AWS Lambda function. Configure the SNS topic to invoke the Lambda function.

explanation.why_correct: ECS with Fargate eliminates EC2 instance management while supporting long-running video processing (5-30 minutes). SQS standard queue decouples uploads from processing, buffers traffic spikes, and enables parallel processing. Auto-scaling based on queue depth ensures cost-effective capacity management.

why_wrong.B: FIFO queue enforces ordering unnecessary for independent video processing. EC2 instances add operational overhead vs. Fargate.
why_wrong.C: Lambda 15-minute timeout limit insufficient for videos requiring 30 minutes processing time.
why_wrong.D: SNS + Lambda doesn't provide durable queuing or handle long processing times. Lambda timeout constraint remains.

explanation.exam_tips: For processing >15 min: use ECS Fargate (not Lambda). For traffic spikes + parallel jobs: SQS standard queue (not FIFO unless ordering required). Auto-scale on queue depth for cost efficiency.
explanation.memorize: Long processing (>15 min) + spikes = SQS + ECS Fargate (queue-based scaling)

question_en: A company wants to re-architect a large-scale web application to a serverless microservices architecture. The application uses Amazon EC2 instances and is written in Python. The company selected one component of the web application to test as a microservice. The component supports hundreds of requests per second. The company wants to create and test the microservice on an AWS solution that supports Python. The solution must also scale automatically and require minimal infrastructure and minimal operational support. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use a Spot Fleet with Auto Scaling of EC2 instances that run the most recent Amazon Linux operating system.
options.B: Use an AWS Elastic Beanstalk web server environment that has high availability configured.
options.C: Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Launch Auto Scaling groups of self-managed EC2 instances.
options.D: Use an AWS Lambda function that runs custom-developed code.

explanation.why_correct: Lambda is serverless compute requiring zero infrastructure management. Supports Python runtime natively. Automatically scales to hundreds of requests per second without capacity planning. Perfect fit for testing serverless microservices migration with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: Spot Fleet with EC2 requires managing instances, AMIs, patching, and scaling policies—significant operational overhead.
why_wrong.B: Elastic Beanstalk reduces some management but still manages underlying instances, not fully serverless.
why_wrong.C: EKS with self-managed EC2 nodes requires highest operational burden: cluster management, node scaling, patching, Kubernetes operations.

explanation.exam_tips: For minimal infrastructure + serverless: choose Lambda over EC2/EKS/Beanstalk. Lambda scales automatically without capacity planning. Python supported natively.
explanation.memorize: Serverless microservices + minimal infra = Lambda (not EC2, EKS, Beanstalk)

question_en: A company has resources across multiple AWS Regions and accounts. A newly hired solutions architect discovers that a previous employee did not provide details about the resources inventory. The solutions architect needs to build and map the relationship details of the various workloads across all accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.A: Use AWS Systems Manager Inventory to generate a map view from the detailed view report.
options.B: Use AWS Step Functions to collect workload details. Build architecture diagrams of the workloads manually.
options.C: Use Workload Discovery on AWS to generate architecture diagrams of the workloads.
options.D: Use AWS X-Ray to view the workload details. Build architecture diagrams with relationships.

explanation.why_correct: Workload Discovery on AWS automatically scans accounts/Regions, identifies resources, and generates relationship-aware architecture diagrams. Purpose-built for discovering and mapping workloads with minimal manual effort—exactly what's needed for undocumented infrastructure.

why_wrong.A: Systems Manager Inventory collects instance metadata but doesn't generate multi-account architecture diagrams or relationship maps.
why_wrong.B: Step Functions collects data programmatically but requires manual diagram creation—high operational effort.
why_wrong.D: X-Ray traces application requests but doesn't provide infrastructure discovery or automated diagramming.

explanation.exam_tips: For automated workload discovery + diagrams across accounts/regions: use Workload Discovery on AWS. Don't confuse with Systems Manager Inventory (instance data only) or X-Ray (request tracing).
explanation.memorize: Multi-account workload mapping = Workload Discovery on AWS (auto-diagrams)

question_en:
A company runs a critical data analysis job each week before the first day of the work week. The job requires at least 1 hour to complete the analysis. The job is stateful and cannot tolerate interruptions. The company needs a solution to run the job on AWS.



Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create a container for the job. Schedule the job to run as an AWS Fargate task on an Amazon ECS cluster by using Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.
options.B: Configure the job to run in an AWS Lambda function. Create a scheduled rule in Amazon EventBridge to invoke the Lambda function.
options.C: Configure an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances that run Amazon Linux. Configure a crontab entry on the instances to run the analysis.
options.D: Configure an AWS DataSync task to run the job. Configure a cron expression to run the task on a schedule.

explanation.why_correct: ECS Fargate task provides stateful container execution without managing EC2 instances. EventBridge Scheduler triggers weekly execution reliably. Fargate supports >1 hour execution. No instance interruptions (unlike Spot). Operationally efficient serverless container solution.

why_wrong.B: Lambda 15-minute maximum timeout insufficient for 1+ hour analysis job.
why_wrong.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted, violating stateful non-interruption requirement. Manual crontab management adds operational overhead.
why_wrong.D: AWS DataSync is for data transfer/sync between storage systems, not for running custom analysis jobs.

explanation.exam_tips: For long-running stateful jobs (>15 min): use ECS Fargate (not Lambda). For scheduled execution: EventBridge Scheduler. Avoid Spot for non-interruptible workloads.
explanation.memorize: Weekly stateful job (>1 hr) = EventBridge Scheduler + ECS Fargate

question_en: A company is using a loosely coupled serverless architecture on AWS. The architecture consists of multiple web applications and APIs distributed across multiple teams. The company uses AWS Control Tower to provision AWS accounts. The company ' s development teams use AWS CloudFormation. The company wants to improve trace monitoring and gain insight into how individual services in application stacks are performing. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Enable AWS CloudTrail across all accounts by using AWS Control Tower.
options.B: Enable AWS X-Ray across all accounts by using AWS Control Tower.
options.C: Enable Amazon CloudWatch in the CloudFormation templates.
options.D: Enable AWS X-Ray in the CloudFormation templates.

explanation.why_correct: X-Ray provides distributed tracing across serverless/microservices. Enabling X-Ray in CloudFormation templates instruments each stack automatically during deployment. Provides service maps, latency analysis, and performance insights per service—exactly what's required with minimal operational effort.

why_wrong.A: CloudTrail logs API calls for auditing, not application performance tracing or service relationships.
why_wrong.B: Control Tower provisions accounts and guardrails but cannot instrument applications for distributed tracing.
why_wrong.C: CloudWatch provides metrics/logs but lacks request-level distributed tracing across multiple microservices.

explanation.exam_tips: For distributed tracing + microservices performance: use X-Ray (not CloudTrail/CloudWatch). Enable in CloudFormation templates for automatic instrumentation across stacks.
explanation.memorize: Microservices tracing + performance = X-Ray in CloudFormation templates

question_en: Question: A company runs a mobile game app that stores session data (up to 256 KB) for up to 48 hours. The data updates frequently and must be deleted automatically after expiration. Restorability is also required. Options:

options.A: Use an Amazon DynamoDB table to store the session data. Enable point-in-time recovery (PITR) and TTL.
options.B: Use Amazon MemoryDB and enable PITR and TTL.
options.C: Store session data in S3 Standard. Enable Versioning and a Lifecycle rule to expire objects after 48 hours.
options.D: Store data in S3 Intelligent-Tiering with Versioning and a Lifecycle rule to expire after 48 hours.

explanation.why_correct: DynamoDB supports TTL for automatic item deletion after 48 hours without manual cleanup. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) enables restoring table to any second within 35 days. Handles frequent updates efficiently. Scales automatically for variable workload. Supports items up to 400KB (sufficient for 256KB sessions).

why_wrong.B: MemoryDB is Redis-compatible in-memory database, more expensive than DynamoDB for session storage. Not optimized for automatic expiration patterns.
why_wrong.C: S3 is object storage, not optimized for frequent updates (session data changes constantly). Versioning adds complexity and cost for session data.
why_wrong.D: S3 Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage costs but doesn't address frequent update performance issues. Versioning overhead remains.

explanation.exam_tips: For session data with TTL + frequent updates: DynamoDB with TTL (not S3 for frequent writes). PITR for restore capability. S3 is for objects, not frequently updated session state.
explanation.memorize: Session data + TTL + restore = DynamoDB (TTL + PITR)

question_en: A transaction processing company has weekly scripted batch jobs that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in an Auto Scaling group. The number of transactions can vary, but the baseline CPU utilization that is noted on each run is at least 60%. The company needs to provision the capacity 30 minutes before the jobs run. Currently, engineers complete this task by manually modifying the Auto Scaling group parameters. The company does not have the resources to analyze the required capacity trends for the Auto Scaling group counts. The company needs an automated way to modify the Auto Scaling group ' s desired capacity. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Configure the policy to scale based on the CPU utilization metric. Set the target value for the metric to 60%.
options.B: Create a scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Set the appropriate desired capacity, minimum capacity, and maximum capacity. Set the recurrence to weekly. Set the start time to 30 minutes before the batch jobs run.
options.C: Create a predictive scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group. Configure the policy to scale based on forecast. Set the scaling metric to CPU utilization. Set the target value for the metric to 60%. In the policy, set the instances to pre-launch 30 minutes before the jobs run.
options.D: Create an Amazon EventBridge event to invoke an AWS Lambda function when the CPU utilization metric value for the Auto Scaling group reaches 60%. Configure the Lambda function to increase the Auto Scaling group ' s desired capacity and maximum capacity by 20%.

explanation.why_correct: Predictive scaling uses ML to forecast capacity needs based on historical patterns. Pre-launches instances 30 minutes before predicted demand. Perfect for recurring weekly workloads without manual capacity analysis. Automates entire scaling process with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: Dynamic scaling reacts after CPU reaches 60%, not 30 minutes before jobs run. Doesn't meet pre-provisioning requirement.
why_wrong.B: Scheduled scaling requires manual capacity calculation and ongoing adjustment. More operational overhead than predictive scaling.
why_wrong.D: EventBridge + Lambda custom logic adds complexity. Reacts after CPU hits 60%, doesn't pre-launch 30 minutes early.

explanation.exam_tips: For recurring weekly workloads with pre-launch requirement: use predictive scaling (not scheduled or dynamic). Predictive scaling learns patterns automatically, eliminating manual analysis.
explanation.memorize: Recurring workload + pre-launch + no analysis = Predictive Scaling

question_en: A company is moving a legacy data processing application to the AWS Cloud. The application needs to run on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application must handle incoming traffic spikes and continue to work in the event of an application fault in one Availability Zone. The company requires that a Web Application Firewall (WAF) must be attached to the ALB. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy the application to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that is in a single Availability Zone. Use an ALB to distribute traffic. Use AWS WAF.
options.B: Deploy the application to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an ALB to distribute traffic. Use AWS WAF.
options.C: Deploy the application to EC2 instances in Auto Scaling groups across multiple AWS Regions. Use Route 53 latency routing. Attach AWS WAF to Route 53.
options.D: Deploy the application to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Use AWS WAF.

explanation.why_correct: Multi-AZ deployment with ALB distributes traffic across multiple Availability Zones, ensuring resilience to AZ failures. Auto Scaling handles traffic spikes automatically. AWS WAF attaches directly to ALB for application-layer protection. Complete high-availability solution.

why_wrong.A: Single AZ deployment eliminates fault tolerance—vulnerable to AZ-level failures.
why_wrong.C: Multi-Region adds unnecessary complexity and cost. AWS WAF doesn't attach to Route 53.
why_wrong.D: Network Load Balancer (NLB) doesn't support AWS WAF attachment. WAF requires ALB or CloudFront.

explanation.exam_tips: For multi-AZ HA + WAF: use ALB (not NLB). WAF attaches to ALB/CloudFront only. Multi-AZ protects against AZ failures. Don't confuse ALB (Layer 7 + WAF) with NLB (Layer 4, no WAF).
explanation.memorize: Multi-AZ HA + WAF = ALB + Auto Scaling + Multi-AZ

question_en: A company needs to set up a centralized solution to audit API calls to AWS for workloads that run on AWS services and non AWS services. The company must store logs of the audits for 7 years. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Set up a data lake in Amazon S3. Incorporate AWS CloudTrail logs and logs from non AWS services into the data lake. Use CloudTrail to store the logs for 7 years.
options.B: Configure custom integrations for AWS CloudTrail Lake to collect and store CloudTrail events from AWS services and non AWS services. Use CloudTrail to store the logs for 7 years.
options.C: Enable AWS CloudTrail for AWS services. Ingest non AWS services into CloudTrail to store the logs for 7 years
options.D: Create new Amazon CloudWatch Logs groups. Send the audit data from non AWS services to the CloudWatch Logs groups. Enable AWS CloudTrail for workloads that run on AWS. Use CloudTrail to store the logs for 7 years.

explanation.why_correct: CloudTrail Lake provides managed centralized audit solution for AWS and non-AWS API calls. Supports custom integrations to collect non-AWS service logs. Stores and queries events up to 7 years natively. Purpose-built for audit compliance with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: Data lake in S3 requires custom ETL pipeline, query infrastructure, and retention management—high operational overhead.
why_wrong.C: CloudTrail ingests AWS service events only, cannot directly ingest non-AWS service logs without custom integration.
why_wrong.D: CloudWatch Logs requires separate log groups and custom ingestion. CloudTrail stores AWS events, not unified audit solution for mixed environments.

explanation.exam_tips: For centralized audit (AWS + non-AWS) with long retention: use CloudTrail Lake. Supports custom integrations for non-AWS services. Don't build custom data lakes when CloudTrail Lake exists.
explanation.memorize: Centralized audit (AWS + non-AWS) + 7-year retention = CloudTrail Lake

question_en: A company generates SSL certificates from a third-party provider. The company imports the certificates into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to use with public web applications. A solutions architect must implement a solution to notify the company ' s security team 30 days before an imported certificate expires. The company already has an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The company also has an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that has the security team ' s email address as a subscriber. Which solution will provide the security team with the required notification about certificates?

options.A: Create an AWS Lambda function to scan for expiring certificates. Program the Lambda function to list the certificates in a JSON message and to deliver the message to the SQS queue.
options.B: Create an AWS Lambda function to scan for expiring certificates. Program the Lambda function to list the certificates in a JSON message and to deliver the message to the SNS topic.
options.C: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that specifies the ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration event type. Set the SQS queue as the rule ' s target.
options.D: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that specifies the ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration event type. Set the SNS topic as the rule ' s target.

explanation.why_correct: EventBridge natively receives ACM certificate expiration events (Certificate Approaching Expiration). SNS topic delivers notifications to email subscribers directly. No custom scanning or scheduling required. Fully managed, event-driven notification with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: SQS queue requires consumer to process messages and send notifications—adds unnecessary complexity vs. direct SNS email.
why_wrong.B: Custom Lambda scanning adds operational burden: scheduling, error handling, pagination. EventBridge ACM events eliminate custom polling.
why_wrong.C: EventBridge to SQS requires additional component to read queue and notify—unnecessary intermediate step.

explanation.exam_tips: For ACM certificate expiration notifications: use EventBridge rule (Certificate Approaching Expiration event) + SNS topic. Don't build custom Lambda scanners when native events exist.
explanation.memorize: ACM expiration alerts = EventBridge (ACM event) + SNS topic

question_en: A security team needs to enforce rotation of all IAM users ' access keys every 90 days. Keys older than 90 days must be automatically deactivated and removed. A solutions architect must create a remediation solution with minimal operational effort. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Create an AWS Config rule to check key age. Configure the rule to run an AWS Batch job to remove the key.
options.B: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to check key age. Configure it to run an AWS Batch job to remove the key.
options.C: Create an AWS Config rule to check key age. Define an EventBridge rule that schedules an AWS Lambda function to remove the key.
options.D: Create an EventBridge rule to check key age. Define a second EventBridge rule to run an AWS Batch job to remove the key.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Config managed rule (access-keys-rotated) automatically detects IAM keys older than 90 days. EventBridge triggers Lambda function when non-compliance detected. Lambda provides serverless remediation without managing servers. Minimal operational overhead for compliance enforcement.

why_wrong.A: AWS Batch adds unnecessary infrastructure complexity for simple key rotation task. Config rule is correct, but Batch overkill.
why_wrong.B: EventBridge cannot evaluate IAM key age—requires AWS Config for compliance checks.
why_wrong.D: EventBridge cannot check key age. Batch adds operational overhead. Two EventBridge rules add unnecessary complexity.

explanation.exam_tips: For compliance checks: use AWS Config rules (not EventBridge alone). For remediation: Lambda (not Batch for simple tasks). Config detects non-compliance, EventBridge triggers remediation.
explanation.memorize: IAM key rotation enforcement = AWS Config + EventBridge + Lambda

question_en: A company runs its applications on both Amazon EKS clusters and on-premises Kubernetes clusters. The company wants to view all clusters and workloads from a central location. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to collect and group the cluster information.
options.B: Use Amazon EKS Connector to register and connect all Kubernetes clusters.
options.C: Use AWS Systems Manager to collect and view the cluster information.
options.D: Use Amazon EKS Anywhere as the primary cluster to view the other clusters with native Kubernetes commands.

explanation.why_correct: EKS Connector registers external Kubernetes clusters (on-prem or other clouds) to AWS, enabling centralized visibility in EKS console. Displays clusters and workloads from multiple locations with minimal operational overhead. Purpose-built for hybrid Kubernetes management.

why_wrong.A: CloudWatch Container Insights provides metrics/logs but doesn't centrally register and display cluster inventory across environments.
why_wrong.C: Systems Manager doesn't provide Kubernetes cluster centralized management or workload visibility.
why_wrong.D: EKS Anywhere runs Kubernetes on-prem but isn't designed for centralized viewing of existing clusters—requires migration.

explanation.exam_tips: For hybrid Kubernetes visibility (EKS + on-prem): use EKS Connector. Don't confuse with Container Insights (monitoring only) or EKS Anywhere (run K8s on-prem).
explanation.memorize: Centralized K8s view (EKS + on-prem) = EKS Connector

question_en: A company is running a web application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The web application is deployed across multiple Amazon EC2 instances that are behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company plans to release a new version of the application. The company wants to test the new version of the application by using a subset of production traffic before a full rollout. The company needs to design a solution that helps ensure minimal disruption during testing. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Launch the new version of the application as a separate environment in Elastic Beanstalk. Update the ALB listener rules to forward partial traffic to the new environment.
options.B: Launch the new version of the application as a separate environment in Elastic Beanstalk. Configure the Elastic Beanstalk traffic-splitting feature to route a percentage of live traffic to the new environment.
options.C: Replace the existing EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group with new instances that run the new version of the application. Monitor the production traffic.
options.D: Deploy the new version of the application as a new AWS Lambda function alias. Use weighted alias routing to gradually shift traffic from the old version to the new version.

explanation.why_correct: Elastic Beanstalk traffic splitting provides managed canary deployment, routing percentage of production traffic to new version while monitoring health. Enables testing in production with automatic rollback if issues detected. Minimal operational overhead—built-in feature, no manual ALB configuration.

why_wrong.A: Manual ALB listener rule changes add operational overhead and error risk. Requires careful traffic weight management.
why_wrong.C: Replacing all instances risks full production impact. No gradual testing or rollback capability.
why_wrong.D: Lambda weighted aliases apply to serverless functions, not Elastic Beanstalk EC2-based applications.

explanation.exam_tips: For Beanstalk canary testing: use traffic splitting (managed feature). Don't manually configure ALB rules. Lambda aliases are for Lambda only, not Beanstalk.
explanation.memorize: Beanstalk canary deployment = Traffic Splitting feature (managed)

question_en: A company runs an application that uses Docker containers in an on-premises data center. The application runs on a container host that stores persistent data files in a local volume. Container instances use the stored persistent data. The company wants to migrate the application to fully managed AWS services. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with self-managed nodes. Attach an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume to an Amazon EC2 instance. Mount the EBS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.
options.B: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Mount the EFS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.
options.C: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the AWS Fargate launch type. Create an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure the application to use the DynamoDB table for persistent storage.
options.D: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with the Amazon EC2 launch type. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) volume. Mount the EFS volume on the containers to provide persistent storage.

explanation.why_correct: ECS with Fargate eliminates EC2/Kubernetes management—fully managed container orchestration. EFS provides shared, persistent file system accessible across Fargate tasks. Replaces on-prem local volumes with managed cloud storage. Complete serverless container solution.

why_wrong.A: EKS with self-managed nodes requires managing EC2 instances and Kubernetes—not fully managed.
why_wrong.C: DynamoDB is NoSQL database, not file storage replacement for container volumes.
why_wrong.D: ECS with EC2 launch type requires managing EC2 instances—not fully managed.

explanation.exam_tips: For fully managed containers + persistent storage: ECS Fargate + EFS. Don't use EC2 launch type (requires instance management) or EKS with self-managed nodes (high overhead).
explanation.memorize: Fully managed containers + persistent files = ECS Fargate + EFS

question_en: A company runs a container application on a Kubernetes cluster in the company ' s data center. The application uses Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP) to communicate with a message queue. The data center cannot scale fast enough to meet the company ' s expanding business needs. The company wants to migrate the workloads to AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST overhead?

options.A: Migrate the container application to Amazon ECS. Use Amazon SQS to retrieve the messages.
options.B: Migrate the container application to Amazon EKS. Use Amazon MQ to retrieve the messages.
options.C: Use highly available Amazon EC2 instances to run the application. Use Amazon MQ to retrieve the messages.
options.D: Use AWS Lambda functions to run the application. Use Amazon SQS to retrieve the messages.

explanation.why_correct: EKS preserves existing Kubernetes deployment model, minimizing migration changes. Amazon MQ supports AMQP protocol natively, ensuring application compatibility without code changes. Managed services reduce operational overhead while maintaining architectural compatibility.

why_wrong.A: ECS changes container orchestration platform from Kubernetes. SQS doesn't support AMQP, requiring application changes.
why_wrong.C: EC2 instances add infrastructure management overhead vs. managed EKS control plane.
why_wrong.D: Lambda requires re-architecting containerized Kubernetes application. SQS doesn't support AMQP.

explanation.exam_tips: For Kubernetes migration with AMQP: EKS (preserve K8s) + Amazon MQ (AMQP support). SQS doesn't support AMQP. Don't change orchestration (EKS) and protocol (MQ) together.
explanation.memorize: Kubernetes + AMQP migration = EKS + Amazon MQ (protocol compatibility)

question_en: An ecommerce company has an application that collects order-related information from customers. The company uses one Amazon DynamoDB table to store customer home addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses. Customers can check out without creating an account. The application copies the customer information to a second DynamoDB table if a customer does create an account. The company requires a solution to delete personally identifiable information (PII) for customers who did not create an account within 28 days. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create an AWS Lambda function to delete items from the first DynamoDB table that have a delivery date more than 28 days in the past. Use a scheduled Amazon EventBridge rule to run the Lambda function every day.
options.B: Update the application to store PII in an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to expire the objects after 28 days. Move the data to DynamoDB when a user creates an account.
options.C: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Configure a daily cron job to run on the instance. Configure the cron job to use AWS CLI commands to delete items from DynamoDB.
options.D: Use a createdAt timestamp to set TTL for data in the first DynamoDB table to 28 days.

explanation.why_correct: DynamoDB TTL automatically deletes items after specified time period (28 days). Requires only timestamp attribute configuration. No custom Lambda, cron jobs, or external processes. Zero operational overhead—native DynamoDB feature handles expiration automatically.

why_wrong.A: Lambda + EventBridge adds custom code, scheduling, and error handling—unnecessary operational complexity.
why_wrong.B: S3 Lifecycle rules + moving data to DynamoDB adds multiple steps and storage layers—complex workflow.
why_wrong.C: EC2 + cron jobs requires managing instances, scripts, and scheduling—high operational overhead.

explanation.exam_tips: For automatic data expiration in DynamoDB: use TTL (native feature). Don't build custom Lambda/cron solutions. TTL requires only timestamp attribute, no code.
explanation.memorize: DynamoDB auto-delete after N days = TTL attribute (zero overhead)

question_en: A company hosts dozens of multi-tier applications on AWS. The presentation layer and logic layer are Amazon EC2 Linux instances that use Amazon EBS volumes. The company needs a solution to ensure that operating system vulnerabilities are not introduced to the EC2 instances when the company deploys new features. The company uses custom AMIs to deploy EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The solution must scale to handle all applications that the company hosts. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon Inspector to patch operating system vulnerabilities. Invoke Amazon Inspector when a new AMI is deployed.
options.B: Use AWS Backup to back up the EBS volume of each updated instance. Use the EBS backup volumes to create new AMIs. Use the existing Auto Scaling group to deploy the new AMIs.
options.C: Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch operating system vulnerabilities in the custom AMIs.
options.D: Use EC2 Image Builder to create new AMIs when the company deploys new features. Include the update-linux component in the build components of the new AMIs. Use the existing Auto Scaling group to deploy the new AMIs.

explanation.why_correct: EC2 Image Builder automates AMI creation with patching, testing, and hardening. Update-linux component applies OS security patches during image build. Creates golden AMIs preventing vulnerabilities at deployment time. Scales across applications via reusable pipelines with minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: Inspector identifies vulnerabilities but doesn't patch AMIs. Cannot be invoked to patch images during creation.
why_wrong.B: AWS Backup backs up data, doesn't patch or create AMIs. Wrong tool for vulnerability management.
why_wrong.C: Patch Manager patches running instances, not base AMIs. Doesn't prevent vulnerabilities in new deployments.

explanation.exam_tips: For patched AMI creation at scale: EC2 Image Builder with update-linux component. Inspector scans (doesn't patch), Patch Manager patches live instances (not AMIs).
explanation.memorize: Patched golden AMIs at scale = EC2 Image Builder + update-linux component

question_en: A company uses an Amazon CloudFront distribution to serve content pages for its website. The company needs to ensure that clients use a TLS certificate when accessing the company ' s website. The company wants to automate the creation and renewal of the TLS certificates. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?

options.A: Use a CloudFront security policy to create a certificate.
options.B: Use a CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to create a certificate.
options.C: Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a certificate. Use DNS validation for the domain.
options.D: Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create a certificate. Use email validation for the domain.

explanation.why_correct: ACM provides free TLS certificates with automatic renewal. DNS validation creates CNAME records for domain ownership proof, enabling fully automated renewals without manual intervention. CloudFront uses ACM certificates (must be in us-east-1). Most operationally efficient solution.

why_wrong.A: CloudFront security policies configure cipher suites, not certificate issuance or management.
why_wrong.B: Origin Access Control (OAC) secures S3 origins, unrelated to TLS certificate management.
why_wrong.D: Email validation requires manual mailbox approval at issuance and renewal—operational overhead vs. DNS validation.

explanation.exam_tips: For CloudFront TLS certificates: ACM with DNS validation (automatic renewal). Email validation requires manual steps. ACM certificates for CloudFront must be in us-east-1 region.
explanation.memorize: CloudFront automated TLS = ACM + DNS validation (us-east-1)

question_en: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application also uses an Amazon DynamoDB table. The application generates sporadic HTTP 500 errors. The DynamoDB table is operating in on-demand mode, and other applications use the table without any issues. A solutions architect wants to resolve the HTTP 500 errors without disrupting the web application. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure DynamoDB to support larger write requests for increased throughput.
options.B: Enable DynamoDB Streams to monitor changes in the table.
options.C: Configure the application to use exponential backoff and retries to query the table.
options.D: Configure the application to use strongly consistent reads.

explanation.why_correct: Sporadic HTTP 500 errors with DynamoDB on-demand mode suggest transient failures (throttling, timeouts, network issues). Exponential backoff with retries gracefully handles temporary failures, reducing user-visible errors. Non-disruptive—configuration/code change only, no architecture migration.

why_wrong.A: No standard DynamoDB configuration for 'larger write requests'. On-demand mode handles throughput automatically.
why_wrong.B: DynamoDB Streams provides change data capture, doesn't prevent or fix HTTP 500 errors.
why_wrong.D: Strongly consistent reads increase cost and RCU consumption, don't address transient failures causing 500 errors.

explanation.exam_tips: For sporadic DynamoDB errors: implement exponential backoff + retries (AWS SDK best practice). Don't change consistency model or add Streams for error handling.
explanation.memorize: Sporadic DynamoDB errors = Exponential backoff + retries

question_en: A company wants to run transient workloads in an Amazon EMR cluster that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The company wants to use On-Demand Instances for core nodes and Spot Instances for task nodes. The company wants to use memory optimized EC2 instances to launch EMR clusters in the AWS Region where the company operates. The company has configured multiple subnets in multiple Availability Zones. The company must ensure that the EMR clusters are launched only in Availability Zones where specified instance types and purchasing options are available. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?

options.A: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance group configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into multiple subnets that are associated with multiple Availability Zones.
options.B: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance group configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into a single subnet. Configure Amazon EMR to determine whether an Availability Zone has the necessary capacity when an EMR cluster is launched.
options.C: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance fleet configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into multiple subnets that are associated with multiple Availability Zones.
options.D: Deploy Amazon EMR with an instance fleet configuration. Launch the EMR clusters into a single subnet. Configure Amazon EMR to determine whether an Availability Zone has the necessary capacity when an EMR cluster is launched.

explanation.why_correct: Instance fleets provide flexibility to launch EMR across multiple instance types, AZs, and purchasing options (On-Demand + Spot). Automatically selects AZs with available capacity for requested instance types. Multiple subnets enable multi-AZ deployment. Most operationally efficient for capacity optimization.

why_wrong.A: Instance groups are rigid, tied to fixed instance configuration. Less flexible than fleets for capacity availability.
why_wrong.B: Single subnet limits to one AZ. Cannot leverage capacity across multiple AZs as required.
why_wrong.D: Single subnet eliminates multi-AZ benefit. Configuration cannot determine capacity availability at launch.

explanation.exam_tips: For EMR capacity flexibility across AZs + instance types: use instance fleets (not groups). Multiple subnets enable multi-AZ deployment. Fleets auto-select AZs with capacity.
explanation.memorize: EMR capacity flexibility + multi-AZ = Instance fleets + multiple subnets

question_en:
A company has a non-production application that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. The EC2 instance has an instance profile and an associated IAM role.



The company wants to automate patching for the EC2 instance. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Create a new IAM role. Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the new IAM role. Attach the new IAM role to the EC2 instance profile. Use AWS Systems Manager to patch the instance.
options.B: Create an IAM user. Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the IAM user. Configure AWS Systems Manager to use the IAM user to patch the instance.
options.C: Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the existing IAM role. Use AWS Systems Manager to patch the EC2 instance.
options.D: Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to an existing IAM user. Use EC2 Image Builder to patch the EC2 instance.

explanation.why_correct: EC2 instance already has IAM role via instance profile. Adding AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to existing role enables Systems Manager management without creating new roles. Minimal change, least operational overhead. Enables automated patching via Patch Manager.

why_wrong.A: Creating new IAM role adds unnecessary step when existing role can be modified. More operational overhead.
why_wrong.B: Systems Manager uses instance IAM role (not IAM user). Using IAM user for instance operations violates best practices.
why_wrong.D: EC2 Image Builder creates AMIs, doesn't patch running instances. IAM user approach wrong for EC2 management.

explanation.exam_tips: For EC2 + Systems Manager: attach AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore to existing IAM role (modify, don't create new). Never use IAM users for EC2 instance permissions.
explanation.memorize: EC2 automated patching = Add policy to existing role + Systems Manager

question_en:
A company wants to run big data workloads on Amazon EMR. The workloads need to process terabytes of data in memory.



A solutions architect needs to identify the appropriate EMR cluster instance configuration for the workloads. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use a storage optimized instance for the primary node. Use compute optimized instances for core nodes and task nodes.
options.B: Use a memory optimized instance for the primary node. Use storage optimized instances for core nodes and task nodes.
options.C: Use a general purpose instance for the primary node. Use memory optimized instances for core nodes and task nodes.
options.D: Use general purpose instances for the primary, core, and task nodes.

explanation.why_correct: Primary node manages coordination/monitoring, doesn't process data—general purpose instance sufficient. Core and task nodes perform in-memory data processing requiring high memory-to-CPU ratios. Memory-optimized instances (R5, R6i, X1) ideal for terabytes of in-memory processing.

why_wrong.A: Storage-optimized for high disk I/O, not in-memory processing. Compute-optimized for CPU-intensive, not memory-intensive workloads.
why_wrong.B: Memory-optimized primary node unnecessary—primary doesn't process data directly.
why_wrong.D: General purpose instances lack sufficient memory for terabytes of in-memory data processing.

explanation.exam_tips: For EMR in-memory big data: general purpose primary + memory-optimized core/task nodes. Primary coordinates (low memory need), workers process data (high memory need).
explanation.memorize: EMR in-memory processing = General purpose primary + Memory-optimized workers

question_en: A media streaming company needs to deploy its video processing application across multiple Availability Zones for high availability. The application consists of containerized microservices that process video files. The microservices must automatically recover from failures. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Deploy the containers to Amazon ECS with the EC2 launch type.
options.B: Deploy the containers to Amazon EKS with self-managed nodes.
options.C: Deploy the containers to Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type.
options.D: Deploy the containers directly to Amazon EC2 instances.

explanation.why_correct: ECS Fargate provides serverless container orchestration across multiple AZs. AWS manages underlying infrastructure (no EC2 to manage). ECS service scheduling automatically replaces failed containers. Multi-AZ deployment via subnet configuration. Least operational overhead for HA containerized microservices.

why_wrong.A: ECS with EC2 launch type requires managing EC2 capacity, patching, and instance lifecycle—operational overhead.
why_wrong.B: EKS with self-managed nodes requires managing Kubernetes control plane, node groups, and infrastructure—highest overhead.
why_wrong.D: Direct EC2 deployment lacks managed orchestration and automatic failover—requires custom health checks and recovery.

explanation.exam_tips: For HA containers + least overhead: ECS Fargate (not EC2 launch type or EKS). Fargate eliminates infrastructure management. ECS auto-replaces failed tasks.
explanation.memorize: HA containers + minimal ops = ECS Fargate (multi-AZ, auto-recovery)

question_en: A company wants to send data from its on-premises systems to Amazon S3 buckets. The company created the S3 buckets in three different accounts. The company must send the data privately without traveling across the internet. The company has no existing dedicated connectivity to AWS. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Establish a networking account in the AWS Cloud. Create a private VPC in the networking account. Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection with a private VIF between the on-premises environment and the private VPC.
options.B: Establish a networking account in the AWS Cloud. Create a private VPC in the networking account. Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection with a public VIF between the on-premises environment and the private VPC.
options.C: Create an Amazon S3 interface endpoint in the networking account.
options.D: Create an Amazon S3 gateway endpoint in the networking account.
options.E: Establish a networking account in the AWS Cloud. Create a private VPC in the networking account. Peer VPCs from the accounts that host the S3 buckets with the VPC in the network account.

explanation.why_correct: Direct Connect with private VIF provides private connectivity from on-prem to VPC without internet traversal. VPC peering connects VPCs across accounts, enabling access to S3 buckets in different accounts via VPC endpoints. Complete private connectivity solution.

why_wrong.B: Public VIF sends traffic over public AWS services, not fully private connectivity.
why_wrong.C: S3 interface endpoint doesn't solve cross-account VPC routing. Needs VPC connectivity mechanism.
why_wrong.D: Gateway endpoint doesn't provide cross-account routing capabilities.

explanation.exam_tips: For private on-prem to multi-account S3: Direct Connect private VIF + VPC peering. Public VIF not fully private. Interface/gateway endpoints need VPC connectivity first.
explanation.memorize: Private on-prem to multi-account S3 = Direct Connect private VIF + VPC peering

question_en: A transaction-processing company has weekly batch jobs that run on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Transaction volume varies, but CPU utilization is always at least 60% during the batch runs. Capacity must be provisioned 30 minutes before the jobs begin. Engineers currently scale the Auto Scaling group manually. The company needs an automated solution but cannot allocate time to analyze scaling trends. Which solution will meet these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.A: Create a dynamic scaling policy based on CPU utilization at 60%.
options.B: Create a scheduled scaling policy. Set desired, minimum, and maximum capacity. Set recurrence weekly. Set the start time to 30 minutes before the jobs run.
options.C: Create a predictive scaling policy that forecasts CPU usage and pre-launches instances 30 minutes before the jobs run.
options.D: Create an EventBridge rule that invokes a Lambda function when CPU reaches 60%. The Lambda function increases the Auto Scaling group size by 20%.

explanation.why_correct: Predictive scaling analyzes historical CPU patterns from weekly batch jobs, forecasts future capacity needs, and pre-launches instances 30 minutes before demand. Eliminates manual trend analysis. Purpose-built for recurring, cyclical workloads with pre-launch requirements.

why_wrong.A: Dynamic scaling reacts after CPU reaches 60%, doesn't pre-launch capacity before jobs start.
why_wrong.B: Scheduled scaling requires manual capacity calculation and ongoing updates as patterns change.
why_wrong.D: EventBridge + Lambda custom solution reacts after CPU hits 60%, doesn't pre-launch. Adds operational complexity.

explanation.exam_tips: For recurring workload + pre-launch + no manual analysis: predictive scaling. Don't confuse with scheduled (manual config) or dynamic (reactive, not proactive).
explanation.memorize: Weekly recurring + pre-launch 30 min = Predictive Scaling (ML-based)

question_en: A company’s platform has reported multiple instances of duplicate orders in its order-processing system. The company uses Amazon SQS FIFO queues to ensure that orders are processed in the order in which they were received. The company needs to identify the root cause of the duplicate orders to prevent future occurrences. The company also needs to determine whether the duplicate orders originate from the company’s message producers. Which Amazon CloudWatch metric for Amazon SQS should the company analyze?

options.A: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
options.B: NumberOfDeduplicatedSentMessages
options.C: ApproximateNumberOfGroupsWithInflightMessages
options.D: NumberOfMessagesSent

explanation.why_correct: NumberOfDeduplicatedSentMessages counts messages SQS accepted but didn't add to FIFO queue due to duplicate deduplication ID or content. High values indicate producers repeatedly sending duplicates. Directly identifies whether duplicates originate from message producers.

why_wrong.A: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible shows queue backlog, doesn't identify duplicate send attempts from producers.
why_wrong.C: ApproximateNumberOfGroupsWithInflightMessages measures active message groups, not duplicate submissions.
why_wrong.D: NumberOfMessagesSent reports total messages added to queue, doesn't distinguish duplicates blocked by deduplication.

explanation.exam_tips: For diagnosing duplicate sends to FIFO queue: use NumberOfDeduplicatedSentMessages metric. Shows messages blocked by deduplication (indicates producer-side duplicates).
explanation.memorize: FIFO duplicate diagnosis = NumberOfDeduplicatedSentMessages (blocked duplicates)

question_en: A company runs a monolithic application in its on-premises data center. The company used Java/Tomcat to build the application. The application uses Microsoft SQL Server as a database. The company wants to migrate the application to AWS. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use AWS App2Container to containerize the application. Deploy the application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Deploy the database to Amazon RDS for SQL Server. Configure a Multi-AZ deployment.
options.B: Containerize the application and deploy the application on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster on an Amazon EC2 instance. Deploy the database on a separate EC2 instance. Set up Microsoft SQL Server Always On availability groups.
options.C: Deploy the frontend of the web application as a website on Amazon S3. Use Amazon DynamoDB for the database tier.
options.D: Use AWS App2Container to containerize the application. Deploy the application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use Amazon DynamoDB for the database tier.

explanation.why_correct: App2Container containerizes existing Java/Tomcat applications with minimal changes. EKS provides managed Kubernetes for container orchestration. RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ provides managed database with automatic failover. Least operational overhead for lift-and-shift migration.

why_wrong.B: Self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 requires cluster management, node patching, high availability configuration—significant overhead.
why_wrong.C: S3 + DynamoDB requires complete application re-architecture from monolithic to serverless. High migration effort.
why_wrong.D: DynamoDB requires changing from relational SQL Server to NoSQL—major application changes incompatible with lift-and-shift.

explanation.exam_tips: For Java/Tomcat migration: App2Container + EKS. For SQL Server: RDS Multi-AZ (managed HA). Don't change database type (DynamoDB) for lift-and-shift migrations.
explanation.memorize: Java app + SQL Server migration = App2Container + EKS + RDS SQL Multi-AZ

question_en: A company runs an internet-facing web application on AWS and uses Amazon Route 53 with a public hosted zone. The company wants to log DNS response codes to support future root cause analysis. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Route 53 to configure query logging.
options.B: Use AWS CloudTrail to record all Route 53 queries.
options.C: Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics for Route 53.
options.D: Use AWS Trusted Advisor for root cause analysis.

explanation.why_correct: Route 53 query logging captures detailed DNS query information including domain queried, record type, source IP, and DNS response code. Logs delivered to CloudWatch Logs for analysis and retention. Purpose-built for DNS troubleshooting and root cause analysis.

why_wrong.B: CloudTrail records API calls to AWS services, not DNS query traffic or response codes.
why_wrong.C: CloudWatch metrics provide aggregated query counts, not per-query response codes needed for root cause analysis.
why_wrong.D: Trusted Advisor provides best-practice recommendations, doesn't collect or analyze DNS query data.

explanation.exam_tips: For DNS query + response code logging: Route 53 query logging. CloudTrail logs API calls (not queries). CloudWatch metrics are aggregated (not per-query details).
explanation.memorize: DNS response code logging = Route 53 Query Logging (to CloudWatch Logs)

question_en: An automobile company collects several terabytes of sensor data from vehicles every day and stores the data in Amazon S3. The company wants to use Amazon SageMaker AI and the sensor data to run an inference model. The company needs to pre-process the data to remove noise or bias that interferes with inference. The company wants to run the inference model once each week. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use AWS Batch to pre-process the data. Use a SageMaker AI processing job to run the inference workloads.
options.B: Use Amazon EMR to pre-process the data. Use a SageMaker AI processing job to run the inference workloads.
options.C: Use a SageMaker AI batch transform job to pre-process the data and to run the inference workloads.
options.D: Use AWS Glue to pre-process the data. Use a SageMaker AI processing job to run the inference workloads.

explanation.why_correct: SageMaker batch transform designed for offline batch inference on large datasets in S3. Runs weekly without maintaining persistent endpoints. Handles preprocessing and inference in single managed workflow. Least operational overhead—no separate preprocessing service or endpoint management.

why_wrong.A: AWS Batch + SageMaker processing separates preprocessing and inference, adding orchestration complexity.
why_wrong.B: EMR for preprocessing adds cluster management overhead. Separate processing job less efficient than integrated batch transform.
why_wrong.D: AWS Glue for ETL + processing job separates concerns. Batch transform handles both preprocessing and inference together.

explanation.exam_tips: For weekly batch ML inference on S3 data: SageMaker batch transform (handles preprocessing + inference). Don't separate into multiple services when batch transform does both.
explanation.memorize: Weekly batch inference + preprocessing = SageMaker Batch Transform (all-in-one)

question_en: A company runs an application that consists of multiple microservices. The company mandates that the microservices use messages to communicate with each other. The application must archive the microservices ' messages for 30 days. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of development effort?

options.A: Use an Amazon EventBridge event bus to route messages between the microservices. Use message filtering to ensure that each microservice receives only messages that are relevant to each microservice. Create an archive in Amazon EventBridge to store the messages for 30 days.
options.B: Use a single Amazon SNS topic to distribute the messages. Subscribe each microservice to the topic. Use message filtering to ensure that each microservice receives only messages that are relevant to each microservice. Use an Amazon SQS queue to store the messages for 30 days.
options.C: Use a single Amazon SNS topic to distribute the messages. Subscribe each microservice to the topic. Use message filtering to ensure that each microservice receives only messages that are relevant to each microservice. Store messages in an Amazon S3 bucket for 30 days.
options.D: Create a private Amazon API Gateway HTTP API for the microservices to send messages. Use an AWS Lambda function to forward the messages to the appropriate microservices based on query parameters. Archive messages in Amazon S3 for 30 days.

explanation.why_correct: EventBridge provides event bus for routing messages between microservices. Built-in message filtering ensures targeted delivery. Event archive feature stores events for 30 days natively. Complete messaging solution with archival in single managed service—least development effort.

why_wrong.B: SNS + SQS distributes messages but lacks native 30-day archive capability. Requires custom S3 archival pipeline.
why_wrong.C: SNS + SQS + S3 requires custom archival logic, adding development and operational complexity.
why_wrong.D: API Gateway + Lambda adds custom routing logic. No native message archival—requires custom S3 solution.

explanation.exam_tips: For microservices messaging + 30-day archive: EventBridge with archive feature. Don't build custom S3 archival when EventBridge archives natively.
explanation.memorize: Microservices messaging + archive = EventBridge (filtering + native archive)

question_en: A company is designing a new Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) deployment to host multitenant applications that use a single cluster. The company wants to ensure that each pod has its own hosted environment. The environments must not share CPU, memory, storage, or elastic network interfaces. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon EC2 instances to host self-managed Kubernetes clusters. Use taints and tolerations to enforce isolation boundaries.
options.B: Use Amazon EKS with AWS Fargate. Use Fargate to manage resources and to enforce isolation boundaries.
options.C: Use Amazon EKS and self-managed node groups. Use taints and tolerations to enforce isolation boundaries.
options.D: Use Amazon EKS and managed node groups. Use taints and tolerations to enforce isolation boundaries.

explanation.why_correct: EKS with Fargate provides per-pod isolation—each pod runs on dedicated compute with isolated CPU, memory, storage, and ENI. No shared infrastructure between pods. Perfect for multi-tenant security requirements without managing node infrastructure.

why_wrong.A: Self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 requires cluster management. Taints/tolerations provide soft isolation, not guaranteed hardware separation.
why_wrong.C: Self-managed node groups require EC2 management. Taints/tolerations don't guarantee physical isolation.
why_wrong.D: Managed node groups reduce some overhead but still share nodes. Taints/tolerations insufficient for strict isolation requirement.

explanation.exam_tips: For per-pod isolation (no shared resources): EKS with Fargate. Taints/tolerations provide scheduling preferences, not physical isolation. Fargate guarantees isolated compute per pod.
explanation.memorize: Pod-level isolation (no sharing) = EKS + Fargate (dedicated resources)

question_en: A company has a single AWS account. The company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in multiple VPCs in one AWS Region. The company also runs workloads in an on-premises data center that connects to the company ' s AWS account by using AWS Direct Connect. The company needs all EC2 instances in the VPCs to resolve DNS queries for the internal.example.com domain to the authoritative DNS server that is located in the on-premises data center. The solution must use private communication between the VPCs and the on-premises network. All route tables, network ACLs, and security groups are configured correctly between AWS and the on-premises data center. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)

options.A: Create an Amazon Route 53 inbound endpoint in all the workload VPCs.
options.B: Create an Amazon Route 53 outbound endpoint in one of the workload VPCs.
options.C: Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the Forward type configured to forward queries for internal.example.com to the on-premises DNS server.
options.D: Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the System type configured to forward queries for internal.example.com to the on-premises DNS server.
options.E: Associate the Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with all the workload VPCs.
options.F: Associate the Amazon Route 53 Resolver rule with the workload VPC with the new Route 53 endpoint.

explanation.why_correct: Outbound endpoint in one VPC forwards DNS queries from VPCs to on-premises. Forward-type Resolver rule forwards internal.example.com queries to on-prem DNS. Associating rule with all VPCs enables consistent resolution across workload VPCs. Complete hybrid DNS solution.

why_wrong.A: Inbound endpoints receive queries from on-prem to AWS, wrong direction for this requirement.
why_wrong.D: System-type rules use Route 53 Resolver, don't forward to external DNS servers.
why_wrong.F: Rule must be associated with all VPCs, not just the VPC with endpoint.

explanation.exam_tips: For VPC-to-on-prem DNS: outbound endpoint + Forward rule. Inbound is for on-prem-to-AWS direction. Associate rule with all VPCs needing resolution. System rules don't forward externally.
explanation.memorize: VPC to on-prem DNS = Outbound endpoint + Forward rule + Associate all VPCs

question_en: A solutions architect runs a web application on multiple Amazon EC2 instances that are in individual target groups behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Users can reach the application through a public website. The solutions architect wants to allow engineers to use a development version of the website to access one specific development EC2 instance to test new features for the application. The solutions architect wants to use an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone to give the engineers access to the development instance. The solution must automatically route to the development instance even if the development instance is replaced. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an A record for the development website that has the value set to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB that forwards requests for the development website to the target group that contains the development instance.
options.B: Recreate the development instance with a public IP address. Create an A record for the development website that has the value set to the public IP address of the development instance.
options.C: Create an A record for the development website that has the value set to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB to redirect requests for the development website to the public IP address of the development instance.
options.D: Place all the instances in the same target group. Create an A record for the development website. Set the value to the ALB. Create a listener rule on the ALB that forwards requests for the development website to the target group.

explanation.why_correct: Route 53 A record points development hostname to ALB (stable endpoint). ALB listener rule matches development hostname and forwards to dedicated target group containing development instance. When instance replaced, target group simply registers new instance. DNS unchanged, automatic routing continuity.

why_wrong.B: Public IP changes when instance replaced, breaking DNS resolution. Requires manual DNS update.
why_wrong.C: ALB can't redirect to instance public IP directly. Architectural mismatch.
why_wrong.D: All instances in same target group means all receive development traffic, not just development instance.

explanation.exam_tips: For stable DNS to specific instance: Route 53 to ALB + listener rule + dedicated target group. Target group handles instance replacement automatically. Don't use public IPs (change on replacement).
explanation.memorize: Stable dev access + instance replacement = A record + ALB + listener rule + target group

question_en: A company has set up hybrid connectivity between an on-premises data center and AWS by using AWS Siteto-Site VPN. The company is migrating a workload to AWS. The company sets up a VPC that has two public subnets and two private subnets. The company wants to monitor the total packet loss and round-trip-time (RTT) between the data center and AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitor to set up Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) probe monitoring from each subnet to the on-premises destination.
options.B: Create an Amazon EC2 instance in each subnet. Create a scheduled job to send Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) packets to the on-premises destination.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function in each subnet. Write a script to perform Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) connectivity checks.
options.D: Create an AWS Batch job in each subnet. Write a script to perform Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) connectivity checks.

explanation.why_correct: CloudWatch Network Monitor uses managed ICMP probes to monitor packet loss and RTT between on-prem and AWS. Fully managed service eliminates infrastructure management. Integrates with CloudWatch dashboards and alarms. Least operational overhead for network performance monitoring.

why_wrong.B: EC2 instances require management (patching, scheduling, scripting). Scheduled jobs add operational complexity.
why_wrong.C: Lambda in each subnet requires custom scripts, scheduling, and error handling. More operational overhead than managed solution.
why_wrong.D: AWS Batch adds job management complexity. Custom scripts require maintenance.

explanation.exam_tips: For Site-to-Site VPN packet loss + RTT monitoring: CloudWatch Network Monitor (managed probes). Don't build custom EC2/Lambda/Batch solutions when managed service exists.
explanation.memorize: VPN packet loss/RTT monitoring = CloudWatch Network Monitor (managed probes)

question_en: A company receives data transfers from a small number of external clients that use SFTP software on an Amazon EC2 instance. The clients use an SFTP client to upload data. The clients use SSH keys for authentication. Every hour, an automated script transfers new uploads to an Amazon S3 bucket for processing. The company wants to move the transfer process to an AWS managed service and to reduce the time required to start data processing. The company wants to retain the existing user management and SSH key generation process. The solution must not require clients to make significant changes to their existing processes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Reconfigure the script that runs on the EC2 instance to run every 15 minutes. Create an S3 Event Notifications rule for all new object creation events. Set an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic as the destination.
options.B: Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server that uses the existing S3 bucket as a target. Use servicemanaged users to enable authentication.
options.C: Require clients to add the AWS DataSync agent into their local environments. Create an IAM user for each client that has permission to upload data to the target S3 bucket.
options.D: Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP connector that has permission to access the target S3 bucket for each client. Store credentials in AWS Systems Manager. Create an IAM role to allow the SFTP connector to securely use the credentials.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP endpoint directly to S3. Service-managed users enable authentication without external systems. Files uploaded directly to S3, eliminating hourly transfer delay. Reduces time to processing start. Minimal operational overhead—fully managed service.

why_wrong.A: Keeping EC2 script doesn't eliminate infrastructure management or improve transfer time significantly.
why_wrong.C: DataSync agent in client environments requires client-side installation and management. IAM users for upload violate managed service principle.
why_wrong.D: SFTP connector typically for connecting to external SFTP servers, not receiving uploads. Systems Manager credentials add complexity.

explanation.exam_tips: For SFTP to S3 with existing SSH keys: Transfer Family with service-managed users. Eliminates EC2 management and transfer delays. Don't use DataSync for inbound uploads.
explanation.memorize: SFTP uploads to S3 = Transfer Family + service-managed users (instant S3 delivery)

question_en: A company runs a critical public application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) clusters. The application has a microservices architecture. The company needs to implement a solution that collects, aggregates, and summarizes metrics and logs from the application in a centralized location. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.A: Run the Amazon CloudWatch agent in the existing EKS cluster. Use a CloudWatch dashboard to view the metrics and logs.
options.B: Configure a data stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to read events and to deliver the events to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to view the events.
options.C: Configure AWS CloudTrail to capture data events. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to query CloudTrail.
options.D: Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights in the existing EKS cluster. Use a CloudWatch dashboard to view the metrics and logs.

explanation.why_correct: CloudWatch Container Insights designed specifically for EKS monitoring. Collects and aggregates metrics and logs from containerized applications. Provides centralized CloudWatch dashboard for visualization. Purpose-built for EKS with minimal operational overhead—native integration.

why_wrong.A: CloudWatch agent provides basic metrics but lacks EKS-specific container insights and centralized aggregation.
why_wrong.B: Kinesis Data Streams + Firehose + S3 + Athena adds multiple services and complexity. Not operationally efficient for monitoring.
