why_wrong.C: CloudTrail captures API audit logs, not application metrics and logs for EKS workloads.

explanation.exam_tips: For EKS metrics + logs + central view: Container Insights (not basic CloudWatch agent). Don't build custom Kinesis pipelines when Container Insights provides native EKS integration.
explanation.memorize: EKS centralized monitoring = CloudWatch Container Insights

question_en: A company wants to receive an email notification when IAM users are added to or deleted from an AWS account. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Enable Amazon Inspector. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to Amazon Inspector findings. Set the target as an Amazon SNS topic. Set the company ' s email address as a subscriber to the SNS topic.
options.B: Enable Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to GuardDuty findings. Configure an event pattern of Impact:IAMUser/AnomalousBehavior. Set the target as an Amazon SNS topic. Set the company’s email address as a subscriber to the SNS topic.
options.C: Enable Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to Macie findings. Set the target as an Amazon SNS topic. Set the company’s email address as a subscriber to the SNS topic.
options.D: Enable management events in AWS CloudTrail. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to AWS API calls through CloudTrail. Configure an event pattern for CreateUser and DeleteUser actions. Set the target as an Amazon SNS topic. Set the company’s email address as a subscriber to the SNS topic.

explanation.why_correct: CloudTrail management events capture IAM CreateUser and DeleteUser API calls. EventBridge rule matches these specific API calls via event pattern. SNS topic delivers email notifications. Complete event-driven notification pipeline for IAM lifecycle events.

why_wrong.A: Inspector performs vulnerability scanning, doesn't monitor IAM user lifecycle events.
why_wrong.B: GuardDuty detects suspicious behavior, not deterministic notification for every IAM user creation/deletion.
why_wrong.C: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3, unrelated to IAM user management notifications.

explanation.exam_tips: For IAM user creation/deletion notifications: CloudTrail + EventBridge (CreateUser/DeleteUser events) + SNS. Inspector/GuardDuty/Macie don't monitor IAM lifecycle.
explanation.memorize: IAM user change alerts = CloudTrail + EventBridge (API events) + SNS

question_en: A company runs a containerized application on a Kubernetes cluster in an on-premises data center. The company is using a MongoDB database for data storage. The company wants to migrate some of these environments to AWS, but no code changes or deployment method changes are possible at this time. The company needs a solution that minimizes operational overhead.

options.A: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 worker nodes for compute and MongoDB on EC2 for data storage.
options.B: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate for compute and Amazon DynamoDB for data storage.
options.C: Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with Amazon EC2 worker nodes for compute and Amazon DynamoDB for data storage.
options.D: Use Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with AWS Fargate for compute and Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) for data storage.

explanation.why_correct: EKS preserves Kubernetes deployment method (no changes required). Fargate eliminates server management for minimal operational overhead. DocumentDB provides MongoDB-compatible API (no code changes), with automatic scaling, Multi-AZ HA, and managed operations.

why_wrong.A: ECS changes orchestration from Kubernetes. MongoDB on EC2 requires database management.
why_wrong.C: EKS preserved but DynamoDB changes database API, requiring code changes.
why_wrong.D: EC2 worker nodes require instance management, contradicting minimal operational overhead.

explanation.exam_tips: For Kubernetes + MongoDB migration: EKS (preserve K8s) + Fargate (no servers) + DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible). Don't change orchestrator (ECS) or database API (DynamoDB) when compatibility required.
explanation.memorize: Kubernetes + MongoDB + minimal ops = EKS Fargate + DocumentDB

question_en:
A company is redesigning its data intake process. In the existing process, the company receives data transfers and uploads the data to an Amazon S3 bucket every night. The company uses AWS Glue crawlers and jobs to prepare the data for a machine learning (ML) workflow.



The company needs a low-code solution to run multiple AWS Glue jobs in sequence and provide a visual workflow. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use an Amazon EC2 instance to run a cron job and a script to check for the S3 files and call the AWS Glue jobs. Create an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard to visualize the workflow.
options.B: Use Amazon EventBridge to call an AWS Step Functions workflow for the AWS Glue jobs. Use Step Functions to create a visual workflow.
options.C: Use S3 Event Notifications to invoke a series of AWS Lambda functions and AWS Glue jobs in sequence. Use Amazon QuickSight to create a visual workflow.
options.D: Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task that contains a Python script that manages the AWS Glue jobs and creates a visual workflow. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to start the ECS task.

explanation.why_correct: EventBridge triggers Step Functions workflow on S3 upload or schedule. Step Functions provides visual workflow designer and orchestrates multiple Glue jobs in sequence. Low-code solution with native Glue integration. No custom scripts or servers required.

why_wrong.A: EC2 + cron + script requires managing instances and custom code. CloudWatch dashboards don't provide workflow orchestration visualization.
why_wrong.C: S3 events + Lambda + Glue chain requires custom orchestration code. QuickSight is BI tool, not workflow visualizer.
why_wrong.D: ECS task + Python script requires container management and custom orchestration code. EventBridge Scheduler timing only, not workflow visualization.

explanation.exam_tips: For visual Glue job workflow: Step Functions (low-code orchestrator). EventBridge triggers workflow. Don't build custom EC2/Lambda/ECS orchestration when Step Functions provides visual designer.
explanation.memorize: Visual Glue workflow = EventBridge + Step Functions (native Glue integration)

question_en:
A company runs several custom applications on Amazon EC2 instances. Each team within the company manages its own set of applications and backups. To comply with regulations, the company must be able to report on the status of backups and ensure that backups are encrypted.



Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?

options.A: Create an AWS Lambda function that processes AWS Config events. Configure the Lambda function to query AWS Config for backup-related data and to generate daily reports.
options.B: Check the backup status of the EC2 instances daily by reviewing the backup configurations in AWS Backup and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) snapshots.
options.C: Use an AWS Lambda function to query Amazon EBS snapshots, Amazon RDS snapshots, and AWS Backup jobs. Configure the Lambda function to process and report on the data. Schedule the function to run daily.
options.D: Use AWS Config and AWS Backup Audit Manager to ensure compliance. Review generated reports daily.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Backup Audit Manager automates backup compliance auditing across resources. Predefined frameworks monitor backup activity and encryption status. Generates ready-to-use compliance reports automatically. AWS Config provides configuration change visibility. Least operational effort—managed compliance solution.

why_wrong.A: Lambda + AWS Config custom processing requires code development and maintenance—operational overhead.
why_wrong.B: Manual daily review of backup configurations across multiple services is error-prone and time-consuming.
why_wrong.C: Lambda querying snapshots and jobs requires custom code, scheduling, and report generation—high maintenance.

explanation.exam_tips: For automated backup compliance reporting: Backup Audit Manager + AWS Config. Don't build custom Lambda solutions when managed audit service exists. Backup Audit Manager provides encryption verification.
explanation.memorize: Backup compliance + encryption reports = Backup Audit Manager + AWS Config

question_en: A company is moving its data management application to AWS. The company wants to transition to an eventdriven architecture. The architecture needs to be more distributed and to use serverless concepts while performing the different aspects of the workflow. The company also wants to minimize operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Build out the workflow in AWS Glue. Use AWS Glue to invoke AWS Lambda functions to process the workflow steps.
options.B: Build out the workflow in AWS Step Functions. Deploy the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Use Step Functions to invoke the workflow steps on the EC2 instances.
options.C: Build out the workflow in Amazon EventBridge. Use EventBridge to invoke AWS Lambda functions on a schedule to process the workflow steps.
options.D: Build out the workflow in AWS Step Functions. Use Step Functions to create a state machine. Use the state machine to invoke AWS Lambda functions to process the workflow steps.

explanation.why_correct: Step Functions provides managed state machine for distributed workflow orchestration. Lambda provides serverless compute for each workflow step. Together enable event-driven, loosely coupled architecture. Step Functions handles coordination, retries, error handling without custom code. Minimal operational overhead.

why_wrong.A: AWS Glue primarily for ETL/data integration. Invoking Lambda from Glue less direct than Step Functions for general workflow orchestration.
why_wrong.B: EC2 instances contradict serverless requirement. Adds infrastructure management overhead.
why_wrong.C: EventBridge scheduled invocation doesn't provide multi-step workflow orchestration with state tracking and error handling.

explanation.exam_tips: For serverless distributed workflow: Step Functions + Lambda. Glue is for ETL (not general orchestration). Don't use EC2 when serverless required. EventBridge routes events, Step Functions orchestrates workflows.
explanation.memorize: Event-driven serverless workflow = Step Functions + Lambda (state machine orchestration)

question_en: A company needs to migrate its customer transactions database from on-premises to AWS. The database resides on an Oracle DB instance that runs on a Linux server. According to a new security requirement, the company must rotate the database password each year. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Convert the database to Amazon DynamoDB by using AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT). Store the password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke an AWS Lambda function for yearly password rotation.
options.B: Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager. Turn on automatic rotation. Configure a yearly rotation schedule.
options.C: Migrate the database to an Amazon EC2 instance. Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to keep and rotate the connection string by using an AWS Lambda function on a yearly schedule.
options.D: Migrate the database to Amazon Neptune by using AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT). Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke an AWS Lambda function for yearly password rotation.

explanation.why_correct: RDS for Oracle provides managed database service reducing operational overhead. Secrets Manager natively integrates with RDS for automatic password rotation. Yearly rotation schedule configurable without custom code. Least operational overhead—fully managed secret rotation.

why_wrong.A: DynamoDB requires re-architecting from relational Oracle to NoSQL. CloudWatch alarm + Lambda adds custom rotation logic.
why_wrong.C: EC2-hosted Oracle requires database management (patching, backups, HA). Parameter Store with Lambda needs custom rotation code.
why_wrong.D: Neptune is graph database. Schema Conversion Tool doesn't convert Oracle to Neptune. Architectural mismatch.

explanation.exam_tips: For Oracle migration + yearly password rotation: RDS Oracle + Secrets Manager (automatic rotation). Don't change database type (DynamoDB/Neptune) for simple migration. Secrets Manager handles rotation without Lambda.
explanation.memorize: Oracle migration + auto password rotation = RDS Oracle + Secrets Manager

question_en: An e-commerce company stores inventory, order, and user information in multiple Amazon Redshift clusters. The Redshift clusters must comply with the company ' s security policies. The company must receive notifications about any security configuration violations. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that uses the Redshift clusters as the source. Create an AWS Lambda function to evaluate the Redshift cluster security configuration. Configure theLambda function to notify the company of any violations of the security policies. Add the Lambda function as a target of the EventBridge rule.
options.B: Create an AWS Lambda function to check the validity of the Redshift cluster security configurations. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes the Lambda function when Redshift clusters are created. Notify the company of any violations of security policies.
options.C: Set up Amazon Redshift Advisor in the company ' s AWS account to monitor cluster configurations. Configure Redshift Advisor to generate notifications for security items that the company must address.
options.D: Create an AWS Lambda function to check the Redshift clusters for any violation of the security configurations. Create an AWS Config custom rule to invoke the Lambda function when Redshift cluster security configurations are modified. Provide the compliance state of each Redshift cluster to AWS Config. Configure AWS Config to notify the company of any violations of the security policies.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Config tracks Redshift cluster configuration changes continuously. Custom Config rule with Lambda evaluates security compliance on modifications. Provides compliance state per cluster. Config notifications alert on violations. Purpose-built for continuous compliance monitoring.

why_wrong.A: EventBridge Redshift events don't continuously monitor security configuration state. Lambda checks only on specific events, not ongoing compliance.
why_wrong.B: EventBridge only at cluster creation misses configuration changes after creation. No continuous monitoring.
why_wrong.C: Redshift Advisor provides performance recommendations, not security compliance monitoring or notifications.

explanation.exam_tips: For continuous security compliance monitoring: AWS Config custom rules (not EventBridge events). Config tracks changes and compliance state. Advisor is for performance tuning, not security compliance.
explanation.memorize: Redshift security compliance monitoring = AWS Config custom rule + Lambda

question_en: A company hosts an application on AWS that uses an Amazon S3 bucket and an Amazon Aurora database. The company wants to implement a multi-Region disaster recovery DR strategy that minimizes potential data loss. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an Aurora read replica in a second Availability Zone within the same AWS Region. Enable S3 Versioning for the bucket.
options.B: Create an Aurora read replica in a second AWS Region. Configure AWS Backup to create continuous backups of the S3 bucket to a second bucket in a second Availability Zone.
options.C: Enable Aurora native database backups across multiple AWS Regions. Use S3 cross-account backups within the company ' s local Region.
options.D: Migrate the database to an Aurora global database. Create a second S3 bucket in a second Region. Configure Cross-Region Replication.

explanation.why_correct: Aurora global database provides continuous cross-Region replication with sub-second lag, minimizing data loss for multi-Region DR. S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) automatically replicates objects to destination bucket in second Region. Both provide active replication, not backup-based recovery.

why_wrong.A: Read replica in second AZ within same Region doesn't meet multi-Region DR requirement. S3 Versioning protects against accidental deletion, not Region-level disasters.
why_wrong.B: Read replica in second Region correct for database, but AWS Backup continuous backups to second AZ (not Region) doesn't provide multi-Region S3 protection.
why_wrong.C: Aurora backups and S3 cross-account (not cross-Region) don't meet multi-Region requirement. Backups have longer recovery time vs. continuous replication.

explanation.exam_tips: For multi-Region DR: Aurora global database (not read replicas) + S3 CRR. Don't confuse Multi-AZ (HA within Region) with multi-Region (DR across Regions). Continuous replication minimizes data loss vs. backups.
explanation.memorize: Multi-Region DR minimal data loss = Aurora global database + S3 CRR

question_en:
A software company needs to upgrade a critical web application. The application currently runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance that the company hosts in a public subnet. The EC2 instance runs a MySQL database. The application ' s DNS records are published in an Amazon Route 53 zone.



A solutions architect must reconfigure the application to be scalable and highly available. The solutions architect must also reduce MySQL read latency. Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? Select TWO.

options.A: Launch a second EC2 instance in a second AWS Region. Use a Route 53 failover routing policy to redirect the traffic to the second EC2 instance.
options.B: Create and configure an Auto Scaling group to launch private EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones. Add the instances to a target group behind a new Application Load Balancer.
options.C: Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster. Create the primary DB instance and reader DB instance in separate Availability Zones.
options.D: Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance without a read replica.
options.E: Place the current EC2 instance behind a Network Load Balancer and move the database to Amazon EBS gp2 volumes.

explanation.why_correct: Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs behind ALB provides horizontal scaling and multi-AZ high availability. Aurora MySQL cluster with primary and reader instances in separate AZs reduces read latency via reader endpoints while maintaining HA.

why_wrong.A: Second EC2 in second Region with Route 53 failover doesn't provide scalability within Region or reduce read latency. Cross-Region adds complexity.
why_wrong.D: RDS Multi-AZ provides HA but doesn't reduce read latency—Multi-AZ is for failover, not read scaling.
why_wrong.E: Network Load Balancer for single EC2 doesn't add scalability. EBS gp2 volumes don't improve database read performance.

explanation.exam_tips: For scalability + HA: Auto Scaling + ALB (multi-AZ). For MySQL read latency: Aurora with reader instances (not Multi-AZ alone). Multi-AZ = failover, Read replicas = read scaling.
explanation.memorize: Web scalability + DB read performance = ASG + ALB + Aurora (primary + readers)

question_en: A company runs a video processing application. Users upload videos directly to an Amazon S3 bucket. The S3 bucket generates S3 Event Notifications to invoke AWS Lambda functions that process the videos. The Lambda functions take 5–10 minutes to process each video. During peak hours, when multiple videos are uploaded simultaneously, some Lambda functions experience timeout errors and fail to complete processing. The company needs a scalable solution to solve the timeout issues. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API that has an extended timeout limit of 10 minutes. Modify the application to call the REST API. Integrate the REST API with the Lambda functions.
options.B: Configure Amazon S3 to directly invoke AWS Batch with AWS Fargate to bypass event notifications and process the videos synchronously.
options.C: Configure S3 Event Notifications to send messages to an Amazon SQS queue. Configure the Lambda functions to use reserved concurrency. Subscribe the Lambda functions to the SQS queue.
options.D: Use an Amazon ECS Fargate task to continuously monitor Amazon S3 and process the videos sequentially.

explanation.why_correct: SQS queue buffers video upload events, decoupling uploads from processing. Lambda polls queue and processes videos asynchronously. Reserved concurrency prevents over-scaling. Lambda 15-minute timeout sufficient for 5-10 minute processing. Queue-based pattern handles bursts gracefully.

why_wrong.A: API Gateway 10-minute timeout doesn't solve Lambda 15-minute limit issue. Synchronous integration doesn't decouple workload.
why_wrong.B: S3 can't directly invoke AWS Batch. Removes event notification architecture. Synchronous processing doesn't handle bursts.
why_wrong.D: Single Fargate task monitoring S3 creates bottleneck. Sequential processing can't handle thousands of concurrent uploads.

explanation.exam_tips: For Lambda timeout issues with burst traffic: add SQS queue for decoupling + buffering. Lambda max timeout 15 min (900s) sufficient for 5-10 min jobs. Don't remove event architecture for synchronous processing.
explanation.memorize: Lambda burst + timeout = SQS queue (decouple + buffer) + reserved concurrency

question_en: An ecommerce company is redesigning a web application to run on the AWS Cloud. The application needs to store static website content and must use a Microsoft SQL Server database to store customer data. The company needs to deploy the application in a resilient way across multiple Availability Zones. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store static content. Deploy an Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server DB instance for the database.
options.B: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store static content. Create an Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ deployment for the database.
options.C: Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach volume to store static content. Deploy an Amazon RDS for SQL Server DB instance for the database.
options.D: Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach volume to store static content. Deploy SQL Server on two Amazon EC2 instances in separate Availability Zones.

explanation.why_correct: S3 provides durable, highly available static content storage with 99.999999999% durability. RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ maintains standby replica in different AZ with automatic failover. Both services natively support multi-AZ resilience with minimal manual intervention.

why_wrong.A: RDS Custom requires OS-level management, increasing operational overhead vs. standard RDS Multi-AZ for simple HA requirement.
why_wrong.C: EBS Multi-Attach not designed for static website content—limited functionality, wrong tool. Lacks object storage semantics.
why_wrong.D: EBS Multi-Attach wrong for static content. Self-managed SQL Server on EC2 requires manual clustering, patching, backup configuration—high operational overhead.

explanation.exam_tips: For static website content: S3 (not EBS). For SQL Server Multi-AZ HA: RDS Multi-AZ (not RDS Custom or EC2). RDS Custom is for deep OS/DB customization, not basic HA.
explanation.memorize: Multi-AZ web app = S3 (static) + RDS Multi-AZ (database resilience)

question_en: A company is migrating its order processing system to the AWS Cloud. The order processing system must use exact message ordering, a highly available architecture, and loosely coupled components. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Ingest the orders in an Amazon SQS standard queue. Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the orders.
options.B: Push the orders to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe an AWS Lambda function to the SNS topic to process the orders.
options.C: Push the orders to a stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the orders.
options.D: Ingest the orders in an Amazon SQS FIFO queue. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the orders.

explanation.why_correct: SQS FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing and preserve message order (FIFO = First-In-First-Out). Lambda polls queue and processes orders without server management. SQS provides durable buffering, decoupling producers from consumers. Perfect for order processing requiring strict ordering.

why_wrong.A: SQS standard queue provides at-least-once delivery but doesn't guarantee message ordering—unacceptable for order processing.
why_wrong.B: SNS is pub/sub fanout, doesn't provide ordered queue processing or exactly-once delivery semantics.
why_wrong.C: Kinesis preserves ordering within shards but EC2 Spot Instances can be interrupted—violates high availability requirement. More operational overhead.

explanation.exam_tips: For exact ordering + exactly-once processing: SQS FIFO (not standard SQS or SNS). Standard SQS = at-least-once, out-of-order. FIFO = exactly-once, ordered. Don't use Spot for critical workloads.
explanation.memorize: Order processing (exact order + exactly-once) = SQS FIFO + Lambda

question_en: An ecommerce company wants a disaster recovery solution for its Amazon RDS DB instances that run Microsoft SQL Server Enterprise Edition. The company ' s current recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO) are 24 hours. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create a cross-Region read replica and promote the read replica to the primary instance
options.B: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to create RDS cross-Region replication.
options.C: Use cross-Region replication every 24 hours to copy native backups to an Amazon S3 bucket
options.D: Copy automatic snapshots to another Region every 24 hours.

explanation.why_correct: RDS automatic snapshots occur daily. Copying snapshots to another Region every 24 hours meets 24-hour RPO/RTO requirement. Most cost-effective—no ongoing cross-Region replication costs. Restore from snapshot in target Region for DR.

why_wrong.A: Cross-Region read replica provides faster recovery but incurs ongoing replication and instance costs in second Region—more expensive for 24-hour RPO/RTO.
why_wrong.B: DMS continuous cross-Region replication adds complexity and cost unnecessary for 24-hour RPO/RTO window.
why_wrong.C: Native backup copy involves more manual steps vs. automated snapshot copying. Less straightforward than automated RDS snapshot copy feature.

explanation.exam_tips: For 24-hour RPO/RTO: automated snapshot copy to another Region (cost-effective). For sub-minute RTO: read replicas (higher cost). Match DR solution cost to business requirements.
explanation.memorize: 24-hour RPO/RTO DR = Copy automated snapshots cross-Region daily

question_en: A company runs its critical storage application in the AWS Cloud. The application uses Amazon S3 in two AWS Regions. The company wants the application to send remote user data to the nearest S3 bucket with no public network congestion. The company also wants the application to fail over with the least amount of management of Amazon S3. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Implement an active-active design between the two Regions. Configure the application to use the regional S3 endpoints closest to the user.
options.B: Use an active-passive configuration with S3 Multi-Region Access Points. Create a global endpoint for each of the Regions.
options.C: Send user data to the regional S3 endpoints closest to the user. Configure an S3 cross-account replication rule to keep the S3 buckets synchronized.
options.D: Set up Amazon S3 to use Multi-Region Access Points in an active-active configuration with a single global endpoint. Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication.

explanation.why_correct: S3 Multi-Region Access Points provide single global endpoint routing requests to nearest Region automatically. Active-active configuration ensures high availability. S3 Cross-Region Replication keeps buckets synchronized across Regions. Minimal S3 management—fully managed service.

why_wrong.A: Active-active with regional endpoints requires application to determine closest Region—more management vs. global endpoint.
why_wrong.B: Incorrectly describes Multi-Region Access Points. One global endpoint serves both Regions, not separate endpoints per Region. Active-passive doesn't meet requirements.
why_wrong.C: Regional endpoints + cross-account replication adds complexity. No global endpoint for automatic routing. Cross-account unnecessary if same organization.

explanation.exam_tips: For multi-Region S3 with single endpoint: Multi-Region Access Points + CRR. Don't confuse cross-account (different AWS accounts) with cross-Region (geographic). Global endpoint routes to nearest Region automatically.
explanation.memorize: Multi-Region S3 + single endpoint = Multi-Region Access Points + CRR

question_en: A company is using Amazon DocumentDB global clusters to support an ecommerce application. The application serves customers across multiple AWS Regions. To ensure business continuity, the company needs a solution to minimize downtime during maintenance windows or other disruptions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Regularly create manual snapshots of the DocumentDB instance in the primary Region.
options.B: Perform a managed failover to a secondary Region when needed.
options.C: Perform a failover to a replica DocumentDB instance within the primary Region.
options.D: Configure increased replication lag to manage cross-Region replication.

explanation.why_correct: DocumentDB global clusters support managed cross-Region failover. Promotes secondary Region to primary with minimal downtime during maintenance or regional disruptions. AWS-managed process ensures business continuity without manual intervention.

why_wrong.A: Manual snapshots provide backup but don't minimize downtime during disruptions. Recovery from snapshot slower than managed failover.
why_wrong.C: Failover to replica within primary Region doesn't protect against Region-level disruptions. Same-Region HA, not multi-Region DR.
why_wrong.D: Increasing replication lag worsens RPO (data loss potential), doesn't improve availability or minimize downtime.

explanation.exam_tips: For DocumentDB multi-Region HA: use managed cross-Region failover (not snapshots). Within-Region failover doesn't protect against regional disruptions. Don't confuse replication lag (data synchronization delay) with failover capability.
explanation.memorize: DocumentDB multi-Region DR = Managed cross-Region failover

question_en: A company hosts a database that runs on an Amazon RDS instance deployed to multiple Availability Zones. A periodic script negatively affects a critical application by querying the database. How can application performance be improved with minimal costs?

options.A: Add functionality to the script to identify the instance with the fewest active connections and query that instance.
options.B: Create a read replica of the database. Configure the script to query only the read replica.
options.C: Instruct the development team to manually export new entries at the end of the day.
options.D: Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache the common queries the script runs.

explanation.why_correct: RDS read replica offloads read traffic from primary instance to separate instance. Periodic script queries read replica only, eliminating impact on critical application using primary. Cost-effective—single additional instance vs. caching infrastructure.

why_wrong.A: Connection routing logic adds complexity. Doesn't solve fundamental issue—both instances still share primary database load.
why_wrong.C: Manual export is inefficient, not automated, and doesn't address real-time application performance.
why_wrong.D: ElastiCache adds caching layer complexity and cost. Overkill if queries not truly cacheable or script accesses different data each time.

explanation.exam_tips: For periodic read queries impacting primary RDS: create read replica (offload reads). Read replicas separate read traffic from write traffic. ElastiCache best for frequently accessed data, not one-time analytical queries.
explanation.memorize: RDS read load separation = Read replica (offload periodic queries)

question_en: A company is designing a website that displays stock market prices to users. The company wants to use Amazon ElastiCache Redis OSS for the data caching layer. The company needs to ensure that the website’s data caching layer can automatically fail over to another node if necessary. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Enable read replicas in ElastiCache Redis OSS. Promote the read replica when necessary.
options.B: Enable Multi-AZ in ElastiCache Redis OSS. Fail over to a second node when necessary.
options.C: Export a backup of the ElastiCache Redis OSS cache to an Amazon S3 bucket. Restore the cache to a second cluster when necessary.
options.D: Export a backup of the ElastiCache Redis OSS cache by using AWS Backup. Restore the cache to a second cluster when necessary.

explanation.why_correct: ElastiCache Redis Multi-AZ with automatic failover maintains read replica in different AZ. When primary node fails, ElastiCache automatically promotes replica to primary without manual intervention. Minimizes downtime, restores write capability automatically.

why_wrong.A: Enabling read replicas alone doesn't provide automatic failover—requires manual promotion step.
why_wrong.C: Backup to S3 provides disaster recovery but not operational failover. Restore process takes time, doesn't minimize downtime.
why_wrong.D: AWS Backup export and restore adds unnecessary complexity vs. native Multi-AZ automatic failover. Longer recovery time.

explanation.exam_tips: For automatic ElastiCache failover: enable Multi-AZ (not just read replicas). Multi-AZ includes automatic promotion. Backups are for DR, not operational HA. Question keyword 'automatically' indicates Multi-AZ.
explanation.memorize: ElastiCache automatic failover = Multi-AZ (auto-promotes replica)

question_en: A company is developing an ecommerce application that will consist of a load-balanced front end, a containerbased application, and a relational database. A solutions architect needs to create a highly available solution that operates with as little manual intervention as possible. Which solutions meet these requirements? Select TWO.

options.A: Create an Amazon RDS DB instance in Multi-AZ mode.
options.B: Create an Amazon RDS DB instance and one or more replicas in another Availability Zone.
options.C: Create an Amazon EC2 instance-based Docker cluster to handle the dynamic application load.
options.D: Create an Amazon ECS cluster with a Fargate launch type to handle the dynamic application load.
options.E: Create an Amazon ECS cluster with an Amazon EC2 launch type to handle the dynamic application load.

explanation.why_correct: RDS Multi-AZ provides managed standby instance with automatic failover—high availability without manual intervention. ECS with Fargate removes container infrastructure management—AWS handles underlying compute. Both fully managed, minimal manual intervention.

why_wrong.B: Read replicas in another AZ help scale reads but don't provide automatic primary failover like Multi-AZ. Requires manual promotion.
why_wrong.C: EC2-based Docker cluster requires managing instances—patching, scaling, availability configuration. More manual intervention.
why_wrong.E: ECS with EC2 launch type requires managing EC2 instance capacity, lifecycle, patching. More overhead than Fargate.

explanation.exam_tips: For minimal manual intervention: RDS Multi-AZ (not read replicas) + ECS Fargate (not EC2). Multi-AZ = automatic failover. Read replicas = read scaling. Fargate = no server management.
explanation.memorize: HA minimal intervention = RDS Multi-AZ + ECS Fargate (fully managed)

question_en: A company ' s data platform uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. The database has multiple read replicas and multiple DB instances across different Availability Zones. Users have recently reported errors from the database that indicate that there are too many connections. The company wants to reduce the failover time by 20% when a read replica is promoted to primary writer. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Switch from Aurora to Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ cluster deployment.
options.B: Use Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora database.
options.C: Switch to Amazon DynamoDB with DynamoDB Accelerator DAX for read connections.
options.D: Switch to Amazon Redshift with relocation capability.

explanation.why_correct: RDS Proxy pools database connections, reducing connection overhead. During Aurora failover, proxy automatically redirects to new writer instance. Applications reconnect to proxy (stable endpoint), not individual database instances. Improves failover time and handles connection surges.

why_wrong.A: Switching to RDS Multi-AZ cluster from Aurora unnecessary and disruptive. Doesn't address connection management issue.
why_wrong.C: DynamoDB with DAX requires complete re-architecture from relational to NoSQL. Incompatible solution for Aurora MySQL workload.
why_wrong.D: Redshift is data warehouse, not operational database replacement for Aurora. Wrong use case entirely.

explanation.exam_tips: For Aurora connection issues + failover improvement: RDS Proxy (connection pooling). Don't switch database engines to solve connection management. Proxy abstracts connection handling from application.
explanation.memorize: Aurora connection management + failover = RDS Proxy (connection pooling)

question_en: A company has primary and secondary data centers that are 500 miles (804.7 km) apart and interconnected with high-speed fiber-optic cable. The company needs a highly available and secure network connection between its data centers and a VPC on AWS for a mission-critical workload. A solutions architect must choose a connection solution that provides maximum resiliency. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Two AWS Direct Connect connections from the primary data center terminating at two Direct Connect locations on two separate devices
options.B: A single AWS Direct Connect connection from each of the primary and secondary data centers terminating at one Direct Connect location on the same device
options.C: Two AWS Direct Connect connections from each of the primary and secondary data centers terminating at two Direct Connect locations on two separate devices
options.D: A single AWS Direct Connect connection from each of the primary and secondary data centers terminating at one Direct Connect location on two separate devices

explanation.why_correct: Two Direct Connect connections from each data center (4 total) to two Direct Connect locations on separate devices provides maximum resiliency. Protects against: single data center failure, single Direct Connect location failure, single device failure. AWS maximum resiliency model.

why_wrong.A: Both connections from primary data center only—vulnerable to primary data center failure. Doesn't leverage secondary data center.
why_wrong.B: Single connection per data center to same device—single points of failure (device, location). Doesn't meet maximum resiliency.
why_wrong.D: Single connection per data center to same location—vulnerable to location-level outage despite separate devices.

explanation.exam_tips: For maximum Direct Connect resiliency: multiple connections from multiple locations to multiple DX locations on separate devices. Keywords: 'maximum resiliency', 'mission-critical' indicate highest redundancy option.
explanation.memorize: Maximum DX resiliency = 2 connections × 2 data centers → 2 DX locations × separate devices

question_en: A company runs a database on Amazon Aurora in the us-east-1 Region. The company has a disaster recovery requirement that the database be available in another Region. Which solution meets this requirement with minimal disruption to the database operations?

options.A: Perform an Aurora Multi-AZ deployment.
options.B: Deploy Aurora cross-Region read replicas.
options.C: Create Amazon EBS volume snapshots for Aurora and copy them to another Region.
options.D: Deploy Aurora Replicas.

explanation.why_correct: Aurora cross-Region read replicas create replica cluster in second Region using engine-native replication. Provides low-disruption disaster recovery—continuous asynchronous replication. Can be promoted to standalone cluster for DR. Minimal operational impact on primary.

why_wrong.A: Multi-AZ deployment provides high availability within single Region, not across Regions. Doesn't meet cross-Region DR requirement.
why_wrong.C: EBS snapshots not how Aurora backup/DR works—Aurora uses automated backups and replicas, not EBS-level snapshots.
why_wrong.D: Aurora Replicas (without 'cross-Region' qualifier) are within same Region. Don't provide Region-level disaster recovery.

explanation.exam_tips: For Aurora cross-Region DR: cross-Region read replicas (not Multi-AZ or same-Region replicas). Multi-AZ = within-Region HA. Cross-Region replicas = DR across Regions. Aurora doesn't use EBS snapshots.
explanation.memorize: Aurora cross-Region DR = Cross-Region read replicas (engine-native)

question_en: An online gaming company hosts its platform on Amazon EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers (NLBs) across multiple AWS Regions. The NLBs can route requests to targets overthe internet. The company wants to improve the customer playing experience by reducing end-to-end load time for its global customer base. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create Application Load Balancers (ALBs) in each Region to replace the existing NLBs. Register the existing EC2 instances as targets for the ALBs in each Region.
options.B: Configure Amazon Route 53 to route equally weighted traffic to the NLBs in each Region.
options.C: Create additional NLBs and EC2 instances in other Regions where the company has large customer bases.
options.D: Create a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator. Configure the existing NLBs as target endpoints.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Global Accelerator routes traffic through AWS global network via anycast IPs at edge locations. Provides optimized network paths to nearest Region, reducing latency and packet loss. NLBs become target endpoints—no infrastructure changes needed. Improves global user experience significantly.

why_wrong.A: ALB vs NLB doesn't address global latency issue. Load balancer type doesn't optimize network paths across internet.
why_wrong.B: Route 53 weighted routing balances traffic but doesn't optimize network performance—still uses public internet paths.
why_wrong.C: Adding more Regions/instances helps regional coverage but doesn't optimize network transit between user and AWS.

explanation.exam_tips: For global latency reduction with existing infrastructure: Global Accelerator (edge-based routing). Don't confuse load balancer types (ALB/NLB) with global network optimization. Global Accelerator uses AWS backbone, not public internet.
explanation.memorize: Reduce global latency = Global Accelerator (AWS edge network routing)

question_en: A company is building a new furniture inventory application. The company has deployed the application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances run behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in their VPC. A solutions architect has observed that incoming traffic seems to favor one EC2 instance, resulting in latency for some requests. What should the solutions architect do to resolve this issue?

options.A: Disable session affinity (sticky sessions) on the ALB.
options.B: Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer.
options.C: Increase the number of EC2 instances in each Availability Zone.
options.D: Adjust the frequency of the health checks on the ALB ' s target group.

explanation.why_correct: Session affinity (sticky sessions) routes requests from same client to same instance. Causes traffic imbalance when enabled—one instance receives disproportionate traffic. Disabling ensures ALB distributes traffic evenly using round-robin or least-outstanding-requests algorithm.

why_wrong.B: NLB operates at Layer 4 (TCP), ALB at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). Problem is load balancing logic, not protocol layer. ALB appropriate for web traffic.
why_wrong.C: Adding instances doesn't fix root cause—uneven distribution due to sticky sessions. More instances still receive unbalanced traffic.
why_wrong.D: Health check frequency affects failure detection, not traffic distribution balance. Doesn't address sticky session issue.

explanation.exam_tips: Traffic favoring one instance = session affinity/sticky sessions enabled. Disable for even distribution. Don't change load balancer type or add capacity when distribution logic is the issue.
explanation.memorize: Uneven ALB traffic distribution = Disable sticky sessions (session affinity)

question_en: A company wants to build a serverless application in which multiple microservices need to exchange messages. The company needs to ensure that messages that the microservices send to one another are processed exactly once in the exact order the messages are sent. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.A: Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue. Configure the microservices to use the SQS queue to exchange messages.
options.B: Use Amazon SNS topics to connect the microservices to one another. Subscribe the microservices to the SNS topics. Use the Amazon SNS API to send and receive notifications between microservices.
options.C: Create an Amazon SQS standard queue. Connect the microservices to one another by using Amazon EventBridge events that the microservices exchange through the SQS queue.
options.D: Use Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka Amazon MSK on Amazon EC2 instances to deploy the application.

explanation.why_correct: SQS FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing via deduplication and preserve first-in-first-out message order. Purpose-built for workflows requiring both ordered delivery and exactly-once semantics. Fully managed, minimal operational overhead. Perfect for serverless microservices.

why_wrong.B: SNS pub/sub doesn't provide exactly-once delivery or ordered queue processing guarantees. Designed for fanout, not ordered workflows.
why_wrong.C: SQS standard queue provides at-least-once delivery (possible duplicates) and doesn't guarantee message order. Fails both requirements.
why_wrong.D: Amazon MSK on EC2 introduces significant operational overhead—managing Kafka clusters, instances, configurations. Contradicts serverless and operational efficiency goals.

explanation.exam_tips: For exactly-once + ordered processing: SQS FIFO (not standard SQS, SNS, or MSK). FIFO = exactly-once + ordering. Standard SQS = at-least-once + best-effort ordering. MSK requires management.
explanation.memorize: Exactly-once + exact order serverless = SQS FIFO queue

question_en: A company runs a website that allows users to connect with lawyers. Users and lawyers upload documents to the website frequently. The company hosts the website on a single Amazon EC2 instance. The website stores documents directly on the instance. The company scales the website by adding two more EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer ALB. Afterwards, users report 404 Resource Not Found errors when the users try to access their documents. The company must restore access to the documents. Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Set up an Amazon EFS file system. Mount the file system on all the instances. Copy all files from each instance to the file system. Update the application to use the file system.
options.B: Copy all documents to an Amazon S3 bucket that uses the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Update the application to use the S3 bucket.
options.C: Set up an Amazon EFS file system. Mount the file system on all the instances. Write a cron job that copies the documents from each instance to the file system every hour. Update the application to use the file system.
options.D: Write a cron job that copies the documents from each instance to an Amazon S3 bucket every hour.

explanation.why_correct: Amazon EFS provides shared file system accessible from all EC2 instances simultaneously across multiple AZs. Mounting EFS on all instances gives every server access to same documents. Immediate consistency—no replication delay. Least disruptive—minimal application changes.

why_wrong.B: S3 requires application code changes from file system access to object storage API calls. More disruptive than EFS mount.
why_wrong.C: Cron-based hourly copy introduces up to 1-hour delay for document availability. Creates inconsistency window—users may still see 404 errors.
why_wrong.D: Hourly cron copy to S3 has same delay issue. Documents unavailable during copy interval. Still requires application changes for S3 access.

explanation.exam_tips: For multi-instance file sharing: EFS (shared file system). S3 requires application changes (object storage API). Don't use cron/scheduled copies—introduces delays and inconsistency. EFS provides immediate shared access.
explanation.memorize: Multi-instance file access = EFS (shared, immediate, file system)

question_en: A company runs a critical Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in a single Availability Zone. The company must improve the availability of the DB instance. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Configure the DB instance to use a multi-Region DB instance deployment.
options.B: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue in the AWS Region where the company hosts the DB instance to manage writes to the DB instance.
options.C: Configure the DB instance to use a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.
options.D: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue in a different AWS Region than the Region where the company hosts the DB instance to manage writes to the DB instance.

explanation.why_correct: RDS Multi-AZ deployment automatically maintains synchronous standby replica in different Availability Zone. If primary AZ fails, RDS performs automatic failover to standby—minimal downtime, no manual intervention. AWS-managed high availability feature.

why_wrong.A: Multi-Region deployment is for disaster recovery across Regions, not high availability within Region. More complex and costly than needed.
why_wrong.B: SQS queue manages write buffering, doesn't make database highly available. Queues decouple components, don't provide database failover.
why_wrong.D: Cross-Region SQS queue doesn't address database availability. Wrong tool—SQS is for messaging, not database HA.

explanation.exam_tips: For RDS high availability within Region: Multi-AZ (not multi-Region). Multi-AZ = automatic failover to standby. Don't confuse HA (Multi-AZ) with DR (cross-Region). SQS doesn't provide database availability.
explanation.memorize: RDS high availability = Multi-AZ deployment (automatic failover)

question_en: A company runs a critical three-tier web application that consists of multiple virtual machines (VMs) and virtual databases in an on-premises environment. The company wants to set up a disaster recovery (DR) environment in AWS. The company requires a 15-minute recovery time objective (RTO). The company must be able to test the failover solution to validate the recovery. The solution must provide an automated failover mechanism. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use AWS Backup to create backups of the on-premises VMs and to restore the backups in AWS. Configure recovery to Amazon EC2 instances to meet the RTO requirement.
options.B: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to replicate the on-premises databases to Amazon RDS. Set up AWS Storage Gateway for baseline and incremental data replication to AWS to meet the RTO requirement.
options.C: Use AWS DataSync and AWS Storage Gateway to migrate the baseline and incremental data to AWS. Use Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, and an Application Load Balancer to set up the DR environment.
options.D: Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the VMs incrementally to AWS. Configure Elastic Disaster Recovery to automate the DR process.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) provides continuous block-level replication of on-prem VMs to AWS. Supports 15-minute RTO with automated failover testing. Purpose-built for VM disaster recovery with automated orchestration. Minimal management—AWS-managed replication and recovery.

why_wrong.A: AWS Backup creates periodic backups, not continuous replication. Longer RTO for full restoration vs. continuous DR. Can't meet aggressive 15-minute RTO.
why_wrong.B: DMS replicates databases only, not complete VMs. Storage Gateway doesn't provide complete DR solution for full applications.
why_wrong.C: DataSync + Storage Gateway + manual EC2/S3/ALB setup requires significant manual DR orchestration. No automated failover mechanism.

explanation.exam_tips: For VM disaster recovery with 15-min RTO: Elastic Disaster Recovery (continuous replication + automation). Don't use periodic backups for aggressive RTO. DMS = databases only, not full VMs.
explanation.memorize: On-prem VM DR (15-min RTO) = Elastic Disaster Recovery (continuous + automated)

question_en: A company has a web application that uses Amazon API Gateway to route HTTPS requests to AWS Lambda functions. The application uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL database for its data storage. The application has experienced unpredictable surges in traffic that overwhelm the database with too many connection requests. The company wants to implement a scalable solution that is more resilient to database failures. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create an Amazon RDS proxy for the database. Replace the database endpoint with the proxy endpoint in the Lambda functions.
options.B: Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB tables by using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS).
options.C: Review the existing connections. Call MySQL queries to end any connections in the sleep state.
options.D: Increase the instance class of the database with more memory. Set a larger value for the max_connections parameter.

explanation.why_correct: RDS Proxy pools and manages database connections from Lambda functions. Reduces connection storm impact during traffic surges. Handles failover transparently—applications connect to proxy, not database directly. Improves scalability and resilience without application changes. Most cost-effective managed solution.

why_wrong.B: DynamoDB migration requires complete re-architecture from relational to NoSQL. High initial cost and development effort. Unnecessary for connection management issue.
why_wrong.C: Manual connection cleanup insufficient for unpredictable surges. Reactive approach, doesn't prevent overwhelming database. High operational burden.
why_wrong.D: Scaling instance vertically increases cost continuously. Doesn't solve connection management inefficiency. Larger max_connections without pooling still vulnerable to storms.

explanation.exam_tips: For Lambda + Aurora connection surges: RDS Proxy (connection pooling). Don't migrate databases to solve connection issues. Proxy manages connections efficiently, improves failover resilience. Scaling up costly without addressing root cause.
explanation.memorize: Lambda + Aurora connection storms = RDS Proxy (connection pooling)

question_en: A company hosts an application on AWS that stores files that users need to access. The application uses two Amazon EC2 instances. One instance is in Availability Zone A, and the second instance is in Availability Zone B. Both instances use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. Users must be able to access the files at any time without delay. Users report that the two instances occasionally contain different versions of the same file. Users occasionally receive HTTP 404 errors when they try to download files. The company must address the customer issues. The company cannot make changes to the application code. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

options.A: Run the robocopy command on one of the EC2 instances on a schedule to copy files from the Availability Zone A instance to the Availability Zone B instance.
options.B: Configure the application to store the files on both EBS volumes each time a user writes or updates a file.
options.C: Mount an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system to the EC2 instances. Copy the files from the EBS volumes to the EFS file system. Configure the application to store files in the EFS file system.
options.D: Create an EC2 instance profile that allows the instance in Availability Zone A to access the S3 bucket. Re-associate the instance profile to the instance in Availability Zone B when needed.

explanation.why_correct: Amazon EFS provides shared file system mountable by multiple EC2 instances across AZs simultaneously. Single source of truth—all instances read/write same files. Eliminates version inconsistencies and 404 errors. No application code changes required—transparent file system mount.

why_wrong.A: Robocopy scheduled copy creates replication lag. Files inconsistent between copies. Operational overhead managing schedules.
why_wrong.B: Dual-write to both EBS volumes requires application code changes (violates requirement). Race conditions, complexity managing synchronization.
why_wrong.D: Instance profile switching doesn't solve multi-instance file consistency. S3 requires application API changes. Complex manual reassociation.

explanation.exam_tips: For multi-instance file consistency: EFS (shared file system). EBS is single-instance (can't share). Don't build custom replication when EFS provides native sharing. No code changes with EFS mount.
explanation.memorize: Multi-AZ file consistency + no code changes = EFS (shared mount)

question_en: A company has deployed a multi-tier web application to support a website. The architecture includes an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in public subnets, two Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) tasks in the public subnets, and a PostgreSQL cluster that runs on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. The EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database run shell scripts that need to access an external API to retrieve product information. A solutions architect must design a solution to allow the EC2 instances to securely communicate with the external API without increasing operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Assign public IP addresses to the EC2 instances in the private subnets. Configure security groups to allow outbound internet access.
options.B: Configure a NAT gateway in the public subnets. Update the route table for the private subnets to route traffic to the NAT gateway.
options.C: Configure a VPC peering connection between the private subnets and a public subnet that has access to the external API.
options.D: Deploy an interface VPC endpoint to securely connect to the external API.

explanation.why_correct: NAT Gateway in public subnet enables private subnet instances to initiate outbound internet connections. Route table update directs private subnet traffic destined for internet (0.0.0.0/0) through NAT Gateway. Most operationally efficient—fully managed by AWS. Secure—inbound traffic blocked, outbound allowed.

why_wrong.A: Private subnets by definition don't support public IPs. Architecturally incorrect—defeats purpose of private subnets.
why_wrong.C: VPC peering connects VPCs privately, doesn't provide internet access. Peering doesn't route to public internet.
why_wrong.D: VPC endpoints connect to AWS services privately, not external APIs on public internet. Wrong use case for VPC endpoints.

explanation.exam_tips: For private subnet internet access: NAT Gateway in public subnet + route table update. Private subnets can't have public IPs. VPC endpoints = AWS services only (not external internet). VPC peering = VPC-to-VPC (not internet).
explanation.memorize: Private subnet → internet = NAT Gateway (in public subnet)

question_en: A company is building a serverless application to process ecommerce orders. The application must handle bursts of traffic and process orders asynchronously in the order received. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon SNS with AWS Lambda.
options.B: Use Amazon SQS FIFO with AWS Lambda.
options.C: Use Amazon SQS standard with AWS Batch.
options.D: Use Amazon SNS with AWS Batch.

explanation.why_correct: SQS FIFO queue guarantees exactly-once processing and preserves message order (FIFO). Lambda provides serverless compute with automatic scaling. Lambda polls FIFO queue, maintaining order guarantees. Handles traffic bursts automatically—queue buffers, Lambda scales. Perfect for order processing workflows.

why_wrong.A: SNS pub/sub doesn't guarantee message ordering or exactly-once delivery. Wrong pattern for ordered order processing.
why_wrong.C: SQS standard queue provides at-least-once delivery (possible duplicates) and doesn't guarantee order. Fails ordering requirement.
why_wrong.D: SNS + AWS Batch adds unnecessary batch infrastructure. Doesn't provide ordering or exactly-once guarantees. Higher latency vs. Lambda.

explanation.exam_tips: For asynchronous ordered processing: SQS FIFO + Lambda. Standard SQS = no ordering guarantee. SNS = no ordering. FIFO = order + exactly-once. Lambda auto-scales for bursts.
explanation.memorize: Async + ordered + burst handling = SQS FIFO + Lambda

question_en: A company is migrating a distributed application to AWS. The application serves variable workloads. The legacy platform consists of a primary server that coordinates jobs across multiple compute nodes. The company wants to modernize the application with a solution that maximizes resiliency and scalability. How should a solutions architect design the architecture to meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a destination for the jobs. Implement the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling to use scheduled scaling.
options.B: Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as a destination for the jobs. Implement the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the size of the queue.
options.C: Implement the primary server and the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure AWS CloudTrail as a destination for the jobs. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the load on the primary server.
options.D: Implement the primary server and the compute nodes with Amazon EC2 instances that are managed in an Auto Scaling group. Configure Amazon EventBridge as a destination for the jobs. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling based on the load on the compute nodes.

explanation.why_correct: SQS queue decouples job submission from processing—eliminates single coordinator point of failure. EC2 Auto Scaling based on queue depth (ApproximateNumberOfMessages) scales workers dynamically with workload. Queue provides durability and automatic scaling for variable workloads. Maximum resiliency and scalability.

why_wrong.A: Scheduled scaling doesn't respond to variable workloads—fixed schedule can't adapt to unpredictable demand.
why_wrong.C: CloudTrail logs API calls for auditing, not job coordination. Scaling based on primary server load preserves single point of failure.
why_wrong.D: EventBridge routes events but isn't job queue. Preserves coordinator architecture. Scaling on compute nodes doesn't address workload distribution.

explanation.exam_tips: For distributed job processing: SQS queue (decouple + buffer) + Auto Scaling on queue depth. Don't preserve coordinator (single point of failure). CloudTrail/EventBridge aren't job queues. Queue-based scaling most responsive.
explanation.memorize: Variable distributed workload = SQS queue + ASG (scale on queue depth)

question_en: A company wants to use a cloud storage service to store text and media files that are associated with active global marketing campaigns. The storage solution must be highly available. The company must protect the solution with a backup system that reduces the possibility of data loss as much as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Store the text and media files on an Amazon EC2 instance with an instance store volume. Configure the instance as an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint. Use AWS Backup to take daily backups of the instance.
options.B: Store the text and media files in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set the S3 bucket as the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use AWS Backup to take continuous backups of the S3 bucket.
options.C: Store the text and media files on an Amazon EC2 instance with an Amazon EBS volume. Set the EBS volume as the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use AWS Backup to take continuous backups of the EBS volume.
options.D: Store the text and media files in an AWS Lambda function with ephemeral storage. Set the function as the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use AWS Backup to take continuous backups of the Lambda function.

explanation.why_correct: S3 provides 11 nines durability (99.999999999%), highly available across AZs. CloudFront globally distributes content with low latency. AWS Backup continuous backups for S3 enable point-in-time recovery, minimizing data loss better than daily backups. Fully managed solution.

why_wrong.A: Instance store ephemeral—data lost if instance fails. Global Accelerator optimizes network, doesn't distribute content. Daily backups insufficient vs. continuous.
why_wrong.C: EBS single-AZ storage less durable than S3. CloudFront with EBS origin adds complexity. EBS not designed for global content distribution.
why_wrong.D: Lambda ephemeral storage temporary, not durable. Lambda not content storage solution. Architecturally incorrect for file storage.

explanation.exam_tips: For global content storage + minimal data loss: S3 + CloudFront + AWS Backup continuous backups. Don't use instance store (ephemeral) or Lambda (temporary) for durable storage. S3 = 11 nines durability.
explanation.memorize: Global content + backup = S3 + CloudFront + AWS Backup (continuous)

question_en: A company is developing a photo sharing web application on AWS. The application allows users to upload, durably store, and share photos. The application processes uploaded photos into a variety of sizes. The company needs to ensure that the application can handle thousands of uploads each hour. The company wants to decouple upload operations from processing operations. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.A: Use Amazon EC2 instances to directly upload and process the images. Store the processed images in an Amazon S3 bucket and enable S3 Transfer Acceleration.
options.B: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store uploaded images. Use an S3 event notification to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process each image. Store the processed images in a second S3 bucket.
options.C: Use an Amazon S3 bucket to store uploaded images. Use an Amazon EC2 instance to poll the S3 bucket for new images and to process them. Store each processed image in the original S3 bucket.
options.D: Use an Amazon EFS file system to store uploaded images. Use an Amazon EC2 instance to process uploaded images. Store the processed images in the original EFS file system.

explanation.why_correct: S3 for durable upload storage. S3 event notifications invoke Lambda automatically when object created. Lambda processes image resizing, stores results in second bucket. Event-driven, serverless, auto-scaling. Completely decouples upload from processing. Least operational effort—no servers to manage.

why_wrong.A: EC2 instances require management (patching, scaling, availability). S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads, doesn't decouple operations. Tightly coupled architecture.
why_wrong.C: EC2 polling S3 adds operational overhead. Custom polling logic, instance management. Not event-driven—inefficient.
why_wrong.D: EFS + EC2 processing requires managing both file system and instances. Operational overhead vs. serverless S3 + Lambda.

explanation.exam_tips: For upload/process decoupling at scale: S3 event notifications + Lambda. Don't use EC2 polling (operational overhead). Event-driven serverless patterns scale automatically. Store originals and processed separately.
explanation.memorize: Upload + process decoupling = S3 events + Lambda (auto-scale, event-driven)

question_en: An events company runs a web application on Amazon EKS that uses an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table has 1,000 RCUs and 500 WCUs provisioned. The application uses eventually consistent reads. Traffic is usually low but occasionally spikes. During spikes, DynamoDB throttles requests, causing userfacing errors. What should a solutions architect do to reduce these errors?

options.A: Change the DynamoDB table to on-demand capacity mode.
options.B: Create a DynamoDB read replica.
options.C: Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity.
options.D: Use strongly consistent reads.

explanation.why_correct: DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode automatically scales read/write capacity to handle unpredictable traffic spikes without provisioning. Eliminates throttling—no more RCU/WCU limits to exceed. No capacity planning required. Perfect for variable workloads with occasional spikes. Pay per request.

why_wrong.B: DynamoDB doesn't support read replicas like relational databases. Not a feature of DynamoDB architecture.
why_wrong.C: Reserved capacity reduces cost for predictable workloads but doesn't prevent throttling if limits exceeded. Pre-purchases capacity, doesn't auto-scale.
why_wrong.D: Strongly consistent reads consume more RCUs, don't address capacity constraints. Changes read consistency, not scaling behavior.

explanation.exam_tips: For DynamoDB throttling with spikes: switch to on-demand mode (auto-scales). Provisioned = fixed capacity (can throttle). On-demand = auto-scales (no throttling). Reserved capacity = cost optimization, not scaling solution.
explanation.memorize: DynamoDB unpredictable spikes + throttling = On-demand capacity mode

question_en: A company hosts a website analytics application on a single Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance. The analytics application is highly resilient and is designed to run in stateless mode. The company notices that the application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.
options.B: Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization is more than 75%.
options.D: Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group that includes the launch template. Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.

explanation.why_correct: Auto Scaling group automatically adds/removes instances based on demand. Spot Fleet reduces costs (up to 90% vs. On-Demand). ALB distributes traffic across instances. Launch template defines instance configuration. Stateless application perfect for Spot Instances. Seamless scaling with cost optimization.

why_wrong.A: Manual two-instance deployment doesn't scale automatically. Fixed capacity can't handle variable load. No automatic scaling mechanism.
why_wrong.B: Route 53 weighted routing manual traffic distribution. Doesn't automatically scale based on load. Requires manual weight adjustments.
why_wrong.C: Lambda changing instance type (vertical scaling) doesn't scale horizontally. Single instance remains bottleneck. Doesn't handle thousands of concurrent requests.

explanation.exam_tips: For seamless scaling cost-effectively: Auto Scaling + Spot Fleet + ALB. Don't use fixed instances (no auto-scale) or Route 53 manual routing. Stateless + resilient = Spot compatible. Horizontal > vertical scaling.
explanation.memorize: Seamless scale + cost-effective = Auto Scaling + Spot Fleet + ALB

question_en: A company has an application that uses a MySQL database that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. The instance currently runs in a single Availability Zone. The company requires a fault-tolerant database solution that provides a recovery time objective (RTO) and a recovery point objective (RPO) of 2 minutes or less. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS. Create a read replica in a second Availability Zone. Create a script that detects availability interruptions and promotes the read replica when needed.
options.B: Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure the new RDS for MySQL database to use a Multi-AZ deployment.
options.C: Create a second MySQL database in a second Availability Zone. Use native MySQL commands to sync the two databases every 2 minutes. Create a script that detects availability interruptions and promotes the second MySQL database when needed.
options.D: Create a copy of the EC2 instance that runs the MySQL database. Deploy the copy in a second Availability Zone. Create a Network Load Balancer. Add both instances as targets.

explanation.why_correct: RDS Multi-AZ maintains synchronous standby replica in separate AZ. Automatic failover typically completes within 1-2 minutes (meets <2 min RTO). Synchronous replication means minimal data loss (RPO <2 min). AWS-managed, fault-tolerant, no manual intervention required.

why_wrong.A: Read replica with manual promotion script introduces delay—requires failure detection, script execution, promotion. Can't guarantee <2 min RTO. Manual process prone to errors.
why_wrong.C: Native MySQL sync every 2 minutes creates up to 2-minute replication lag (RPO boundary). Manual script for promotion adds RTO. Complex to manage, operational risk.
why_wrong.D: EC2-based MySQL clusters with NLB require manual failover configuration. No automatic synchronous replication. High operational overhead, can't guarantee <2 min RTO/RPO.

explanation.exam_tips: For aggressive RTO/RPO (<2 min): RDS Multi-AZ (automatic failover, synchronous). Read replicas require manual promotion (slower). Don't build custom EC2 solutions when RDS Multi-AZ provides managed HA.
explanation.memorize: RTO/RPO <2 min = RDS Multi-AZ (synchronous replication, auto-failover)

question_en: A company wants to use AWS to scale up the number of its long-running critical simulations. The company wants to perform large-scale parallel simulations that run for days. The simulations cannot be stopped. The company must store the output for later review by using durable and fault-tolerant storage. The output includes structured and unstructured data. The structured data includes simulation results. The unstructured data includes images up to 1 MB in size. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use AWS Lambda functions to perform simulations. Store structured data in Amazon RDS. Store unstructured data in Amazon S3.
options.B: Use AWS Batch to perform simulations. Store structured data in Amazon RDS. Store unstructured data in Amazon S3.
options.C: Use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to perform simulations. Store structured data in Amazon RDS. Store unstructured data in Amazon DynamoDB.
options.D: Use AWS Batch to perform simulations. Store all data in an Amazon EBS volume.

explanation.why_correct: AWS Batch designed for long-running parallel simulations—manages job scheduling, compute environments, queues. RDS provides durable, fault-tolerant relational storage for structured simulation results. S3 offers highly durable (11 nines) object storage for unstructured images. Reliable capacity for non-interruptible jobs.

why_wrong.A: Lambda 15-minute maximum execution time insufficient for simulations running days. Can't use Lambda for long-running workloads.
why_wrong.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted—violates 'cannot be stopped' requirement. DynamoDB 400KB item limit potentially inadequate for simulation data.
why_wrong.D: Single EBS volume not durable shared storage across parallel workers. EBS single-AZ—lacks fault tolerance for critical data.

explanation.exam_tips: For long-running parallel compute: AWS Batch (not Lambda <15 min). For non-interruptible: avoid Spot (can interrupt). Structured data → RDS, unstructured → S3. Lambda max 15 min, Batch for days.
explanation.memorize: Long parallel simulations = AWS Batch + RDS (structured) + S3 (unstructured)

question_en: A company runs multiple applications in multiple AWS accounts within the same organization in AWS Organizations. A content management system (CMS) runs on Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC. The CMS needs to access shared files from an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system that is deployed in a separate AWS account. The EFS account is in a separate VPC. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.A: Mount the EFS file system on the EC2 instances by using the EFS Elastic IP address.
options.B: Enable VPC sharing between the two accounts. Use the EFS mount helper to mount the file system on the EC2 instances. Redeploy the EFS file system in a shared subnet.
options.C: Configure AWS Systems Manager Run Command to mount the EFS file system on the EC2 instances.
options.D: Install the amazon-efs-utils package on the EC2 instances. Add the mount target in the efs-config file. Mount the EFS file system by using the EFS access point.

explanation.why_correct: Amazon-efs-utils package enables EFS mounting with IAM authentication and encryption. Cross-account EFS access requires VPC peering/Transit Gateway plus proper security group configuration. EFS access point provides application-specific entry point with enforced POSIX identity. Simplifies cross-account access management.

why_wrong.A: EFS doesn't have Elastic IPs—uses mount targets in VPCs. Incorrect mounting approach.
why_wrong.B: VPC sharing requires resource redeployment into shared subnets—complex for existing EFS. Not most direct solution.
